15 June

Questions-Oral
THURSDAY, 15 JUNE 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
QUESTIONS ORAL
Housing Corporation Loans
1. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St Kilda) to the Minister of Housing: Is he aware that in a
statement dated 4 February 1976 his predecessor as Minister of Housing, the member for
North Shore, promised there would be "no sudden withdrawal of State funds for the home
construction industry... the transition will be gradual", and can he give the total amounts in
Housing Corporation loans advanced for the erection of dwellings in the financial years
ended March 1976, 1977, and 1978 respectively, in each case indicating the percentage
increase or decrease in the amounts authorised?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I accept the statement attributed to my
predecessor. The total loans advanced to build new houses in the financial years ended 31
March 1976, 1977, and 1978, and the percentage increase or decrease were as follows: for the
year ended 31 March 1976, erect loans authorised, $177.9 million; year ended 31 March
1977, $133.5 million, a decrease of 24.95 percent; and year ended 31 March 1978, $124.6
million, a decrease of 6.66 percent. The honourable member will not overlook the fact that
the policies of the previous Administration created a demand on the resources of the
Housing Corporation in 1976 that could not be sustained.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: In view of the true housing needs of the people, how does the
Minister square off the clear, unqualified assurance given by his predecessor with the
massive reduction shown in the March 1977 year when compared with 1976?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I do not attempt to square off anything, but I remind the
honourable member that in the year ended 31 March 1977 the Government undertook the
erection of 28 000 new houses, and that total was achieved. I also remind him that for this
year we have made provision for 8100 erect loans, each averaging $20,000. It is estimated
that these will require $169 million, an increase of 36 percent on last year.
Mr Wellington: Did the figures given by the Minister in his answer to the original
question include advances through the Housing Corporation for home improvement loans,
that sector comprising about 20 percent of building activity?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: No, the figures I gave related solely to direct loans for the
erection of new houses.
Housing Corporation Subdivision-Te Atatu North
2. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Housing: Will the sections at Te
Atatu north in the new Housing Corporation subdivision be made available for sale to the
public free of any qualifications?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing). As far as can be foreseen at the
moment, sections in the Housing Corporation's subdivision at Te Atatu north will be
available in the same manner as other past offerings, subject to such things as ballots, if
necessary, and preference to first home seekers.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: How many sections are involved in the subdivision, and how many
will be available for State housing?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: Stage I of the subdivision, which is at present under
development, is expected to produce about 111 sections. No firm arrangements have been
made, but it is expected that about 11 might be used for State rental houses.
Hon. W. A. Fraser: Will all the sections to be made available to the public for home
ownership be offered at current market value, or does the Minister intend to make a
1-Vol 418


## p. 900 (#10) #############################################

900

percentage of them available at remitted value for low-income applicants?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: It is difficult to forecast the market conditions under which
these sections will be sold. It is probable that the initial sections, 13 of which are expected to
be available by the end of this year, will be offered for tender in the normal manner. The
manner in which future sections are offered will depend entirely on the reaction to the offer
of those sections.
Tokoroa Hospital
3. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: What steps is he taking to assist the
Waikato Hospital Board to provide the staff and other facilities for the two wards at the
Tokoroa Hospital that are lying idle, and is he aware that patients and families are forced to
travel to Hamilton or to use the Matamata private hospital?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): It is the responsibility of the Waikato Hospital
Board to recruit staff for its institutions. The only way in which I can assist is to ask my
department to channel any inquiries from local or overseas doctors, who might be interested
in applying for vacant posts at Tokoroa Hospital, to the board. This has been done. My
information is that only one ward at Tokoroa Hospital is not in use. It is a new medical ward,
yet to be commissioned and awaiting the appointment of a specialist physician. The Waikato
Hospital Board has advertised extensively, but so far unsuccessfully, for a suitable specialist
to fill this vacancy. In the meantime, additional medical staff at a more junior level have
been recruited for the hospital, and the surgical wards are now fully staffed.
Mr Hunt: Since one specialist ward is still lying idle and not being used, can the Minister
say whether patients and the families of patients forced to travel from Tokoroa to Hamilton
qualify for any form of assistance such as a travel concession?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No, if a hospital board patient is required to travel from that board's
area to another board's area, the hospital board pays, but within a board's area those people
are at no disadvantage when compared with other people living at a distance from the
hospital.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Since the Tokoroa Hospital represents a very large capital
investment provided out of public funds, and since the Minister is responsible for financing
that board's activities, will he take immediate steps to see that staff is available so that the
benefit of that capital investment is available for all the people?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I would take immediate steps to ensure the availability of staff if the
member would tell me how. Does he want me to go out with a lasso and catch a doctor, or to
introduce legislation such as a Labour Government would have introduced to give me
powers to direct people as to when, where, and how they will work?
Domestic Purposes Beneficiaries
4. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Social Welfare: Since the
introduction of the recommendations of the Domestic Purposes Benefit Committee in
September 1977, how many of the total number of new applicants have had a reduced
benefit for the first 6 months, and how many have received an additional supplementary
benefit because their circumstances have been adjudged to be more serious?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): Statistics relating to the total
number of grants of emergency maintenance allowances approved at the restricted rate in
the period September 1977 to March 1978 are not available. Statistical procedures to obtain
this kind of information are being developed. I can tell the honourable member that, based
on the situation in March 1978, it is estimated that a total of approximately 5300 grants of
emergency maintenance allowances at the restricted rate were approved in the period
September to 31 March 1978. Of these, approximately 1900 have been supplemented by
additional benefit payments.
Mr Hunt: Is the figure of 5300 people receiving the limited rate of emergency
maintenance allowance, and the further figure recently given by the Minister of 8706 people
receiving the emergency maintenance allowance at the same rate as the statutory domestic


## p. 901 (#11) #############################################

15 June
901
Questions-Oral
purposes benefit, included in the 31 465 domestic purposes benefits in force at 31 March
1978?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The figure I gave in my original reply was for the period 26
September to 31 March. The other figure relates to the full year to 31 March 1978.
Mr Hunt: Perhaps I did not make myself quite clear. Is the number of people receiving
the limited rate of emergency maintenance allowance, and the further figure of people
receiving the emergency maintenance allowance at the same rate as the statutory domestic
purposes benefit, included in the total number of people receiving a domestic purposes
benefit as at 31 March 1978?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes.
Electoral Enrolment, Maoris
5. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori) to the Minister of
Justice: Did the Electoral Office take note of the choice of those of Maori descent to enrol
for a Maori electoral district on the electoral enrolment forms distributed with the last
census, and, if so, why have some who expressed a wish to enrol as Maori now received a
form saying that their names have been entered on the Parliamentary Electoral Roll for a
general district?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The answer to the first part of the
honourable member's question is yes. Every effort has been made to assign to their correct
rolls those who marked their wish to enrol for a Maori electoral district. Anyone who
believes he expressed the wish to be enrolled on a Maori roll but is advised that his name is
entered on a general roll should advise the electorate officer or the Chief Electoral Officer.
If his recorded wish has not been given effect to, the mistake will be corrected. I should add
that some who believed they indicated their wish to be enrolled on a Maori roll did not in fact
do so.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: In view of the fact that the Southern Maori
electorate stretches from Gisborne County to Stewart Island, to what office should electors
direct their attempts to have this error corrected?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: That information is contained in the electoral information
sheet I distributed to members about a month ago. Any person affected should contact the
post office in his district, which will transmit the information through to the Southern Maori
chief electorate officer, who is the chief postmaster at Blenheim.
Mr Fenton: Does the Minister know whether the claim made in the original question is
correct?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I have not been approached by the member for Southern
Maori except through this question.

Mr Birch: Can the Minister confirm that a trade deficit of more than $200 million for the
last quarter of the Labour Government's term of office has been converted into a surplus of
more than $200 million for the most recent quarter?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: That is correct. Strangely enough, the figures are the same,
but in a reverse aspect. The figure for the December 1975 quarter under the Labour
Government was minus 202, and for the March 1978 quarter was plus 202.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: May we now assume that the balance of payments problem has
been solved?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I could put it another way and say that the balance of
payments problem is well on the way to being solved, because the National Government has
converted a 1975-year deficit of $600 million into a 1977-year surplus of $200 million. On an
overseas exchange transactions basis it is expected that the $1,000 million deficit of the last
year of the Labour Government will be a $500 million deficit in this June year, reducing to
$400 million for the next June year. When Maui gas comes onstream there will be a further
reduction of $150 million, which would bring the deficit down to $250 million. That is a
manageable deficit, and is about the same as we had during the 1960s when we considered
we were in no difficulty whatsoever.
Youth Unemployment—OECD Recommendations
7. Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori) to the Minister of Labour: What steps has he taken to
implement the recommendations of the OECD high-level conference on youth
unemployment, which he attended in June 1977?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I assume the member for Eastern Maori is
referring to the conference I attended in December, not June, 1977. The Government has
established an ad hoc Cabinet committee on the training and employment of youth, which is
implementing the recommendations of the OECD high-level conference on youth
unemployment. On 7 March 1978 I announced the addition of three new measures to the
Government's programme of selective job creation. Two of these measures, the first job
programme and the skill promotion programme, were specifically designed to promote the
employment of youth. The first job programme assists employers in the provision of jobs for
school leavers, while the skill promotion programme promotes the availability of
apprenticeships, farm cadetships, technician traineeships, and other jobs that provide
systematic training. In addition to these direct job creation measures, the Government has
continued to implement the special training programmes for unemployed youth announced
last October.
Mr Reweti: Could the Minister indicate how much progress has been made in
implementing programmes for the employment of youth, who represent 50 percent of the
people registered as unemployed, and how does the progress made compare with progress in
Canada, France, the United States, and the United Kingdom?
Mr SPEAKER: The Minister may answer the first part of the question, but not the
second.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Programmes for the promotion of jobs for youth were specifically
spelt out in the communique from Paris. I have a copy of that communique and would be
happy to make it available to the member for Eastern Maori. He would then see that the
measures adopted in New Zealand are in line with the measures adopted by other OECD
countries.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: The Minister said that two of the recommendations are being
implemented at the moment. Is he able to say when we may expect to see a significant drop
in youth unemployment?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The key to a reduction in the number of young people
unemployed is an improvement in the terms of trade and the number of job opportunities
available.

Questions-Oral
Fertiliser Purchases
8. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Agriculture: What figures are
available for the amount of fertiliser purchased this season, and how do these compare with
the figures for a similar period last year?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The latest figures show that in the 10
months up to 30 April this year, fertiliser sales amounted to 1 949 067 tonnes. This is an
increase of 7.6 percent on the same period last year, when sales amounted to 1 811 785
tonnes.
Mr W. R. Austin: In view of the fact that there has been a 7.6 percent increase in
production, is the Minister satisfied that the industry has the capacity to continue that rate of
increase next year?
Mr SPEAKER: The Minister might be, but he is not going to answer that question now,
because it is not related to the original question.
Freight Rate Subsidies, Otago
9. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) to the Minister of Regional Development: In
view of the fact that freight rates have doubled since December 1975, how many companies
in Otago still receiving subsidies for freight have had their subsidies compensatingly
increased?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): The Minister of Regional
Development replies: "Freight subsidies are granted to individual recipients on the basis of
specified percentages of qualifying freight costs rather than for absolute amounts. Similar
percentages of freight cost increases would thus be payable as additional subsidies to each of
the 11 companies in Otago still receiving freight subsidies."
Mr MacDonell: Can I ask the Minister the same supplementary question I asked him
yesterday? How many companies are still receiving the full 25 percent that applied under the
Labour Government, and how many companies are receiving assistance on a diminishing
basis, which will be phased out after 3 years?
Mr SPEAKER: Did the honourable member ask the question yesterday?
Mr MacDonell: I did, but I did not receive an answer from the Minister.
Mr SPEAKER: Did the Minister have the material?
Mr MacDonell: He did not have it yesterday, but I thought he might have it today.
Mr SPEAKER: Normally we do not ask the same question twice.
Mr MacDonell: It is not exactly the same question, but it is a similar question.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I have the information for the member. Two companies are
still receiving the full 25 percent increase. The other 9 of the 11 companies are receiving the
20 percent increase, which will be reduced to 15 percent and 10 percent and be phased out in
1980.
Mr Cooper: Can the Minister tell the House how many companies failed to apply for the
freight subsidy on the due date?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I thought I mentioned that yesterday. Three companies
failed to apply. All companies are eligible for the unit freight increase, of which I am sure the
member for Dunedin Central is aware.
Unemployment Benefits
10. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Social Welfare: If, as advised in his
answer to a question from the member for Avon on 7 June, there is no discrimination
between unemployed male and female breadwinners on unemployment benefit, would he
consider extending the same provisions applying to females in that situation to cover all
males as well?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): At this stage the Government does
not intend to amend the law relating to the benefit entitlement of unemployed male and
female breadwinners.
Marilyn Waring: If, as members were advised yesterday in a supplementary answer by
the Acting Minister of Social Welfare, the Government is to remove the discriminatory
provisions relating to sickness benefits, will the Government review the same discriminatory


## p. 904 (#14) #############################################

904
15 June
Questions-Oral
provision for the unemployed?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Not at this stage. The matter was considered by the Royal
Commission on Social Security between 1969 and 1972. The commission considered that
such action would lead to abuse of the benefit. It would, for example, allow payment of an
unemployment benefit to a dependent husband when a married man had become voluntarily
unemployed, knowing that his wife's chance of obtaining suitable employment was less than
his own.
Mr Prebble: Following on from the Minister's answer that no action will be taken to
remove the discrimination against women, what change of circumstance would be necessary
before the Government removed the anti-women provisions?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I think I am correct in saying that the anti-women provisions in
the Act were introduced by a Labour Government and have been continued by successive
National Governments. At present, if a woman who is a breadwinner is unemployed and has
dependent children, she will receive an unemployment benefit plus an allowance for her
children. If a male is unemployed and has a dependent wife and children, he will receive a
benefit for himself, his wife, and his dependent children. The circumstance does not arise
whereby a female breadwinner is not able to apply for a benefit or would need to apply for a
benefit, because, if she has a husband, other forms of income would always be available to
the husband through the unemployment benefit, plus benefits for his dependent wife and
children, or through a sickness benefit, plus a benefit for his dependent wife and children.
Community Development Officers-Government Subsidy

Import Volumes
18. Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: Have the
Government's fiscal policies been successful in reducing imports, and can he give a
comparison of the volume of imports since 1972 and predict future trends?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): Yes, the
Government has succeeded in reducing the volume of imports through its fiscal and
monetary policies. The Government Statistician's index of the volume of imports shows that
the following changes have occurred since 1972: in 1973-74, an increase of 31.8 percent; in
1974-75, an increase of 2.6 percent; in 1975-76, a decrease of 18.7 percent; in 1976-77,
virtually no change in the volume of imports compared with that of 1975-76; and in the first 6
months of 1977-78, on provisional figures, a decrease of around 9 percent. On the basis of a
survey of forward orders, the Government Statistician has projected a steady fall in private
import payments each month through to October of this year, which is an indication that the
declining trend in the volume of imports will continue for the rest of 1978.
Mr Talbot: What are the Government Statistician's projections for the coming months?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The Government Statistician has published the
following: "The actual figure for April 1978 was $2,898 million, and the projection from then
on to October is down to $2,608 million.”

Regional Local Government, Wellington
19. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Local Government: What is the current
situation regarding the establishment of regional local government for Wellington?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): The present situation is that the
provisional scheme, promulgated by the Local Government Commission on 21 July 1977, is
still under consideration by the new commission. In terms of the Local Government Act
1974, as amended last year, the present commission may decide either to completely
abandon the scheme and start a fresh examination of the proposal or to continue with the
statutory procedures set out in the Act. If the commission decides on the latter course of
aotion, it must consider the objections lodged to the provisional scheme and take one of
several procedures, which are: (1) to abandon the provisional scheme and start the whole
process afresh; (2) to issue a final scheme either in the same terms as the provisional scheme
or as modified as a result of the objections; (3) to issue one or more substitute provisional
schemes, which again will be open to objection. The new commission has been in office only
since April of this year and is now examining all the provisional regional schemes on hand. I
understand that the commission has not yet taken a decision as to which of the available
options it will take in regard to the Wellington regional provisional scheme.
Mr Brill: Does the Minister propose to exercise his power to order the commission to
abandon the earlier Wellington provisional scheme?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: No, I do not intend to exercise that option. I am confident that
the new Local Government Commission will consult all parties. I am quite happy to leave it
to act as it considers appropriate.
Exports to Chile-FOL Ban
20. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) to the Minister of Labour: When will he take action
against the Federation of Labour to have it remove the ban on New Zealand exports to
Chile?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): As the member probably knows, the ban on
Chilean trade originated from a decision of the International Confederation of Free Trade
Unions, The Federation of Labour is affiliated to this organisation, and Mr Knox, the
Secretary of the Federation of Labour, is an executive member. Despite my personal efforts
and the Government's persuasion, the Federation of Labour at its last conference decided to
continue the ban at least in the meantime. However, Mr Knox, who is at present in Europe
attending ICFTU and International Labour Organisation meetings, was asked to make an
assessment of the situation following any discussions on the issue at those conferences. In
these circumstances I believe it would be advisable to await Mr Knox's return to New
Zealand before consideration is given to any action that might be appropriate.
Mr Downie: Could the Minister tell me whether or not all the countries that are
signatories to the agreement are holding out on exports to Chile?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I cannot be emphatic, but I think most of what we would call the
Western democratic countries have some degree of trade with Chile. The latest move I know
of from overseas was a recent action by the Australians to restore a degree of trade with
Chile.

Mr SPEAKER: I have to inform the House that I have received a request from the
member for New Lynn to move the adjournment of the House in accordance with Standing
Orders 89 and 90. The request, which was received this morning within the required time,
reads as follows: "In accordance with Standing Orders 89 and 90, I propose this day to move
that this House do adjourn to discuss an urgent public matter of recent occurrence which
requires the immediate attention of the House and the Government and which involves the
administrative responsibility of the Government-the disclosure of serious discrepancies as
reported on page 1 of the Auckland Star of Wednesday, 14 June 1978, in the electoral rolls in
many Auckland seats. In addition, Mr Speaker, there have been reports from many other
parts of New Zealand which all add up to the question of the compilation of the electoral
rolls.
"It has usually been argued that because the House is in the middle of the Budget
debate there is the opportunity for members of Parliament to raise nearly any matter which
would therefore void this particular request, but I would like to submit that there are two
special grounds for this adjournment motion to be granted-first, I have already spoken in
the debate as have a number of my colleagues, all of whom are directly affected by the
revelations of discrepancies in the electoral rolls; secondly, this matter is of such immediate
concern to Parliament involving as it does every member of the House and, indeed, the
whole political process.
"Democracy in New Zealand, as in every other country, is a fragile instrument. It rests
on a number of principles such as the consent of the governed, the responsibility of the
executive to Parliament, and the existence of an impartial and efficient civil service. I would
submit that in this particular case the efficiency of a Government department, the head of
whom is directly responsible to a Minister in this House, is at stake. I would therefore ask
your approval to have this matter discussed as one of the greatest importance at the earliest
possible opportunity. Practical suggestions may then be made to deal with a problem which
threatens to disenfranchise over 400 000 adults in the forthcoming election." The letter is
accompanied by a copy of the article from the Auckland Star dated 14 June 1978: “Minister
calls heads to unscramble roll mess."
Standing Orders 89 and 90 enable the House to debate some particular event of recent
occurrence that demands the immediate attention of the House and of the Government. The
requirement for a particular case or event rules out debates on general continuing matters-
for example, the cost of living, or unemployment as such. Also the event must be of recent
occurrence. It is not the announcement of an event that the House debates under the
Standing Orders, but the event itself. I dealt with cases of this kind towards the end of last
session. In the present case the announcement is of recent occurrence-last night's
Auckland Star. It also deals with events of recent occurrence-reports of problems arising in
the course of the past few days, following the distribution of cards to electors.
With regard to the question of whether I should allow this debate to take place during
the Budget debate when many members are still awaiting the opportunity to speak, I point
out that this is not necessarily a predetermining factor. In this case, 40 members have spoken
or are in the process of speaking in the Budget debate; so about half the House has had the
opportunity to speak, while the other half, or probably less than half, still remains. It seems
to me that this matter does require the immediate attention of the House because of the
considerable public concern, and accordingly I am prepared to accept the motion. Are there
any other members who would support it?

the Minister of Justice has called a meeting of electorate and Department of Justice officers

Every day hundreds of people are in despair because of the problem. I want to refer to
some specific examples. Mr Jack Ridley, the member for Taupo between 1972 and 1975,
went into the Tokoroa Post Office 6 weeks ago. There were no forms, and it was suggested
that he should write to Wellington. Cards were then found, and he was given 100. In the

is addressed to Mr E. G. W.-I can supply the name and the document to any member on
request. The address is given, the number in the electorate, and then the word "Auckland",
and underneath that "Christchurch".
Thousands of electors who were correctly on the roll in 1975 have now received cards
indicating that they are not on the correct roll for 1978. My next-door neighbour, who has
given me authority to use his example, was married towards the end of 1972. In both 1972
and 1975 he and his wife voted, and the address on the rolls was the same as that where they
now live. They have now received cards indicating that the address for both of them has been
put down as that of the husband before he was married.
The new boundaries were proclaimed on 20 June 1977-a year ago next week. If the Act
is being applied, within 3 months- and that means 20 September 1977-the electoral officer
is required to complete the roll and to notify electors that they are on the roll, and thereafter
to notify any new enrolment within 7 days after the event taking place.
The Minister recently answered a question in the House, and produced a press release
dated 27 April 1978, from which I quote: "New electoral rolls are presently being compiled
and notices to electors advising them of registration details already held and the names of
their new electorates where there have been boundary changes will be distributed about the
middle of May." That is a month before they were actually distributed. "At the same time an
advertising campaign will be mounted to explain the steps being taken to encourage those
not enrolled to do so." My first question to the Minister is: when have advertisements
appeared on television or radio backing up the statement that he released on 27 April 1978? I
have not seen one, nor have any of my colleagues.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is the press not doing its job?

terms of lot numbers and would not be clear even to an expert.
I remember a meeting held in the Prime Minister's office in late 1975, when the Labour
Government passed the Electoral Amendment Act. That was one of the most forward-
looking steps that had been taken on the matter, but the consent and the co-operation of the
Post Office was required to ensure that the system worked. We talked to Mr Reddish, who
gave us every indication-and I accepted his word completely-that there would be no
difficulty in meeting the requirements of the Act. I know that the then Prime Minister, now
the Leader of the Opposition, will corroborate that statement.
What were those requirements, and why did we choose the Post Office? We chose the
Post Office because, of all Departments of State in New Zealand, it has the most up-to-date
and accurate record of where people live. The postie's walk book is the most accurate
indication that anyone can have, because it is changed daily whenever a person moves from
one place to another. Postal staff were promised that, if they did their part, there was no
reason why some financial incentive should not be offered them; and I think that was a
reasonable quid pro quo. They would be required to pass out the enrolment forms so that
they could be filled in, and to pick them up the next day, so that within 2 days of a person
moving into an electorate that person would be automatically put on the electoral roll.
That is the proper system, and I do not have any sympathy for the person who
deliberately trys to avoid being put on the roll. He or she should be prosecuted, no matter
who they are; and the fact that no prosecutions have been made since the inception of the
Electoral Act 1956 is an indictment of all five Governments that have been in power since
then. I stress that, as far as the Act is concerned, and in common justice, people who take
the step to fill the forms out must be entitled to a valid vote on election day if they have
completed their side of the bargain.
I have examples of the present rolls that have become available to members of
Parliament. I could use my electorate, but I choose instead to use the electorate of the
member for Manukau, who is now to stand for the seat of Manurewa. I have a sample that I
am prepared to give to the Minister, if he wishes. It includes the names of voters on the
Manurewa roll who should be on other rolls. Eight people who should be in the Papatoetoe
electorate, three who should be in the Hunua electorate, two who should be in the Mangere
electorate, and twenty-five who should be in the Papakura electorate are listed here. That is
a total of nearly 50 mistakes from a sample of only 20 pages-and that means 2000 names,
because there are usually 100 names to a page. On that basis, there are more than 1000
mistakes in every electorate, and probably 3000 to 4000 in those electorates where new
boundaries have been drawn.
About five or six electorates have had no boundary changes. Why could the people in
those electorates not have received their cards early so that new rolls could be made
available? On 17 August 1977, 9 months ago, the Minister was recorded in Hansard, Volume
412, at page 2232, as saying that a street index would be available in June 1978. I asked a
supplementary question on the same subject the other day. My colleague the member for
Onehunga, who has done a magnificent job, contacted the electoral officer on the
understanding that the street index would be available much earlier than it now is. We were
told yesterday that it would not be available until October. That is scandalous, because it
means that many people will not be entitled to a valid vote even though they have taken all
the necessary legal steps to be on the electoral roll.
Democracy is a two-way process: the voter has responsibilities, as does the
Government. I refer specifically to the example given me by the member for Manukau, in
which 50 people who have gone to the trouble legally to fill out the forms and do everything
required of them have been wrongly entered on the Manurewa roll instead of the other rolls.
One person, a Ms H., who was wrongly entered on the Manurewa instead of the Mangere
roll, is listed as living at 46 Ventura Street. Anyone with a knowledge of Auckland would
realise that that street is nowhere near the electorate of Manurewa, but is in the centre of the
city, probably in either the Remuera or Auckland Central electorates. All electorates have
their difficulties, but none more so than the new electorates, which deserve special and
urgent consideration. If the electorate is the same as it was in 1975 there is at least a base roll
on which to work. However, new electorates such as Albany, Kaipara, Papatoetoe, or
Helensville deserve special additional treatment.

of the Statutes Revision Committee. However, I hope that the use of information gleaned by

The Chief Electoral Officer should have got his men into gear, should have had electorate

gazetted nearly a year ago and when the Boundaries Commission had completed its job. I
have been told that one of the reasons this was not done was because there might have been
no by-elections. With the new computerised system it is only a matter of pressing a button to
have an old electoral roll set up, if the tragic need for a by-election arises. However, that will

safeguarded by the opinions of one's own caucus, and that there was no need to express

I do not want to be purely critical of a failing machine so I shall give a solution to the
dilemma in which the Minister now finds himself. The solution will ensure that every New
Zealander, whether he is well or badly organised, or whether he has moved into an

vote will be validly counted. Every New Zealander will have a vote by virtue of the fact that
he is a New Zealander, not because someone has entered him correctly on the roll. The
present position makes a person's right to vote dependent on the efficiency of the Civil
Service. The efficiency of the Civil Service is dependent upon the amount of money the
Government will give it for the job and the amount of pressure the Government puts on the
Civil Service to ensure that it is efficient. A person's right to vote is now dependent on the
Government of the day-that is an administrative reality for a great number of people.
I shall give the Minister an answer to his problem, but I am sure it will not appeal to the
Government. My answer has all the elements of real democracy. This afternoon
Government members have said nothing that would indicate they are anything but
frightened of total democracy. Every person should be allowed to vote validly at the
election, whether the roll is good, bad, or indifferent, and I shall not argue about that. At the
time the person votes he would fill in an enrolment form. The computer would produce a
further supplementary roll so that dual voting could be checked in exactly the same way as
the roll is now checked. The necessary prosecutions could take place. Dual voting could be
traced and the number of dual votes subtracted from the validly cast votes. All the
safeguarding machinery imposed in the present roll system would be maintained in the
future. But the one thing about it is whether someone's vote is valid. In actual fact, whether
voters take part in a democratic process will not be decided by the whim of someone running
the electoral procedure; it will not be decided on arguments over legal technicalities or
residential qualifications. The whole thing can be checked perfectly accurately, just as it is
now, but it will have the very great danger for the present Government of everyone's vote
being counted.

the situation. As he has just rung me, it is the most relevant illustration I can give. When he
received a Porirua general electorate card he rang the registrar's office to complain, but was
told to ring back in 3 weeks as they were very busy. He rang back today, 3 weeks after his
first inquiry, only to be told that he must have been careless since apparently he had not
correctly registered during the census. This person is intelligent, and a senior public servant,
and is absolutely confident that he made the correct registration at the time of the census. He
now finds that he is on both the Porirua general roll and the Southern Maori roll. What
happens if he votes in both electorates? What would happen to him under the system of
justice at present prevailing? This situation is the result of the Government's ineptness.
Section 7 of last year's Electoral Amendment Act provides that henceforth no person
may cast a valid ordinary vote unless he or she is correctly enrolled, thus repealing Labour's
legislation which permitted any unenrolled elector to cast a valid ordinary vote providing he
or she made an attempt to be registered. The previous Labour Government gave that person
the right to cast a valid ordinary vote. Section 7 of the amendment Act removes that right,
thus adding to the confusion that exists today. That legislation is not only elitist and
discriminates against the less well-educated and sophisticated elector, but also imposes

NORTHLAND HARBOUR BOARD EMPOWERING BILL
Second Reading
Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. The
purpose of the Bill is to authorise the Northland Harbour Board to have industrial premises
erected at Onerahi, in a Whangarei suburb, for Bradbury, Wilkinson, and Co. Ltd., for the
establishment of a security printing works; and to borrow money for that purpose. Many
members will realise the importance of the Bill to me, to the Northland Harbour Board and
to the people of Whangarei and Northland. The enactment of this empowering legislation
will result in the establishment of the first major industry in Whangarei for 10 years-a
factory which will employ up to 200 persons, and will be of great importance at a time of
significant unemployment. I am proud to tell the House that I have been associated with the
project from the start.
Two directors of Bradbury, Wilkinson (UK) Ltd. came to New Zealand in May 1977.
Bradbury, Wilkinson is a world-wide concern engaged in the printing of bank notes,
travellers' cheques, and other security documents. They were investigating the possibility of
establishing a security printing works in New Zealand. The Minister of Regional
Development referred those men to me, and I invited them to Whangarei. They had already
investigated sites in other parts of New Zealand.
They spent half a day in Whangarei, and talked with Mr Jim Carney, a member of the
Regional Development Council and Chairman of the Northland Harbour Board, and Mr
Howard Mullinger, the Northland Manager of Winstones. Mr Mullinger discussed transport
details, while Mr Carney showed them possible harbour board sites for the factory. The next
day I received a letter of thanks from the two gentlemen and was told that they had decided


## p. 927 (#37) #############################################

15 June
927
Northland Harbour Board Empowering Bill
to go to Wiri in Auckland, and were not interested in Whangarei. At that point we were sure
we had lost them, but I underestimated the ability of Mr Carney and the harbour board.
They put together a package deal which so impressed the company that the managing
director came out from London and agreed to reconsider Whangarei.
As a result, an agreement has been entered into between Bradbury, Wilkinson, and Co.
Ltd. and the Northland Harbour Board embodying a firm arrangement for the establishment
of the industry at Whangarei. The proposal is that the harbour board will lease to Bradburys
a suitable site situated in Onerahi, Whangarei, comprising about 13 ha. Security premises
are proposed for this site, to be built within a security fence bounding an area of
approximately 2.4 ha. The harbour board will construct an access road from the public road
to the site, which will cost the board some $160,000. The security printing factory, the
security fence, and ancillary buildings will be erected on the site under a contract entered
into and supervised by Bradburys. The factory buildings, security fence, and roading will
cost nearly $3 million, and will be paid for by the harbour board. Bradburys will, under a
lease, pay an agreed land rental of $12,500 per annum for the first term of 21 years,
amounting to $262,000 over that period. At the end of the first period of 21 years, Bradburys
will have the right to purchase the land at valuation.
The building will be sold on a table basis of 21 years to Bradburys. This will repay the
cost of the building to the board and the interest incurred by the board in borrowing this
sum, plus a premium of 2 percent additional interest over and above the rate at which the
board borrows. The board calculates it will receive about $750,000 from this premium rental
for the first period of 21 years. At its own cost, Bradburys will install all plant and machinery
in the building. The company will be wholly owned by Bradburys (UK) Ltd. to 70 percent,
and by the Bank of New Zealand to 30 percent. As the projected work is not harbour work
the board will need statutory authority to implement the arrangement, and the board,
therefore, seeks that statutory authority to have the building erected to borrow money for
the cost of erecting the building and the security fence, and to construct the access road; and
to lease the land and sell the buildings on a long-term basis to Bradburys.
To outline the Bill briefly, clause 1 is the short title. Clause 2 is an interpretation clause.
Clause 3 gives the power to have industrial premises erected. Clause 4 gives the power to
borrow. Clause 5 gives authority for the board to refund to its harbour fund account the
amount of any money expended. Clause 6 gives the power to lease or sell the industrial
premises. Clause 7 relates to the application of the Public Bodies Leases Act 1969. Some of
the provisions of that Act would be quite inconsistent, unless specifically modified with the
proposed agreement in lease. Clause 8 refers to the application of the Land Settlement
Promotion and Land Acquisition Act 1952. It is submitted that it is appropriate in this case
to exempt the lease and any disposition of the land by way of a sale under the powers
contained in the Bill from the provisions of the Land Settlement Promotion and Land
Acquisition Act. The land is not farmland, although it is technically so, being over
2.02343 ha.
Clause 9 validates prior agreements entered into by the board. It has been necessary to
enter into agreements incorporating the arrangement between the board and Bradburys well
before the bill could be passed into law. Agreement has, therefore, been made subject to the
passing of the Bill. A copy of the main agreement has been available to members of the
House who have expressed interest, and a careful perusal of the agreement will show that the
Northland Harbour Board has been meticulous in its attention to detail in agreements
entered into. Neither the Audit Department or Treasury, nor the loans board, has shown
any concern about the agreements involved. Clause 10 states that other Acts are not
affected, particularly the Town and Country Planning Act, the Municipal Corporations Act,
the Water and Soil Conservation Act, and the Local Government Act.
I am particularly anxious to have Bradburys established in Whangarei, and so is the
Northland Harbour Board. The industry is non-noxious, and Whangarei wants such an
industry. It will employ up to 200 people, and it is ideal for the local employment pattern, as
80 percent of the employees will be female. In future, young people will be able to secure an
apprenticeship and learn the skills of a specialised industry. The benefits to Whangarei and
Northland of the establishment of the Bradbury Wilkinson bank-note firm will be
considerable.
In conclusion, I thank all those who have been involved in securing the factory for
Whangarei-the Minister of Regional Development; other Ministers who have been
involved in negotiations; the Northland Harbour Board, and particularly the Chairman,


## p. 928 (#38) #############################################

928
15 June
Northland Harbour Board Empowering Bill
Mr Jim Carney, who has done a fantastic job in wooing Bradburys to Whangarei; the select
committee and chairman, who supported the Bill; and, finally, in anticipation, all members
of the House, who I know, will support this excellent proposal. I cannot promise any sample
notes to any of my colleagues, because factory production will be wholly in foreign currency
at first, and so pretty hard to cash in New Zealand.
Bill read a second time.

young New Zealanders. The Government has wrecked the private mortgage market,
allowed mortgagee sales to increase dramatically, and destroyed the land bank, which was
the best guarantee for stabilising land values. The Government has permitted private
mortgage interest rates, particularly on second and third mortgages, to run riot, so that
interest rates are now between 18 percent and 23 percent. The Government has lifted the
Housing Corporation private interest rate from 5.5 percent to 8.5 percent. The
Government's housing policies have caused 10 000 fewer homes to be built in New Zealand.
When the Government was in Opposition prices were another feature of its policy. In
1975 the National Opposition said it would bring down the cost of living to single-digit
figures within its first 12 months in office. The consumer price index is still a long way from
that goal.
During the Budget debate certain Government members placed great weight on the fact
that during the first quarter of this year the consumer price index decreased. They claimed a
victory. I remind those members that 1 year ago the Prime Minister hailed the March quarter
2.6 percent increase in the consumer price index as the best news on the economy for some
time. He said, "I think we can grab our inflation rate." I shall now discuss his method of
grabbing the inflation rate. In the next quarter the increase in the index was 4.8 percent-the
biggest increase in the history of the index. In the third quarter the increase was 3.8 percent,
and in the final quarter the increase was 3.5 percent, giving an annual increase of 15.3
percent in the consumer price index. So much for grabbing inflation 12 months ago. I predict
that the Government will be no more successful in grabbing inflation this year than it was last
year.
The Labour Party has some very real alternatives that should be incorporated into the
Budget. When the Labour Party becomes the Government it will introduce its policy of a
basic income free of tax, which will assist people who are being punished at present. The
amount of tax-free income will increase with the number of dependants. All dependent
children, including teenagers, will qualify for the dependant rebate, which will assist families
with teenagers. People with teenage children know that the teenage years are the most
expensive when bringing up children.
A Labour Government budget will include a new tax structure to help people on lower
and middle incomes. The tax paid by people on the top scale will remain relatively
unchanged. Overtime will be taxed at a standard rate, and in future rates will be indexed to
wage rates. Those are the measures that a Labour Government would introduce in its first
Budget, and those are some of the measures that one could have expected this Budget to
grapple with.
I want to say a word or two on energy. The most significant feature of the Budget
relating to energy was the increase in the petrol price. The cost per gallon has gone up by
approximately 14c to about $1.50. Of course, that does not come to charge now- 9c of it
does, but the remaining 5c will be imposed after the election. That is the Government's
strategy. It will delay the impact until after the election. The sum total taken from motorists
this year will be $51 million, and $65 million in a full year.

As for oil and gas prospecting over the past 22 years the Government has a very

The Labour Government bought the right to half the field for $30 million. If we had

signed and sealed energy prices would have hit the world and the asking price would have
doubled or quadrupled. In reply to a question the other day the Minister said that the value

subsequently, to be one-third bigger than was initially believed.
The Government has a very bad record indeed on oil prospecting. Both on-shore and
off-shore drilling are almost at a standstill. There are no private on-shore prospectors at
present, and even the Government's own rig is in mothballs. The Penrod rig is being kept
going only because the Government has decided to take the sole risk and to spend $15
million of taxpayers' money to keep it here. As the Government has just concluded a tax
regime for oil prospecting, one could very well ask whether the Sea Hunt group, the owner
of the Penrod rig, is to be signed up as part of that regime. It would be a tragedy for the
country if we lost the Penrod drilling rig, and if the Great South Basin were not investigated.
The Government should give the people some information about this. It makes loud noises
when it is dealing with multinationals. It tells us how strong it is, and how it can stand up to
and control the multinationals, but it has been silent on the terms of the agreement with the
oil prospecting industry.
In fact, the central part of the Government's new tax regime was negotiated by the third
Labour Government. It was for a 51 percent right to any successful discovery for 40 percent
of the exploration costs. The Government has said that that is the central part of the
agreement, and that the other details will not be announced. They will be kept secret until
such time as the legislation is introduced into the House.
I want to discuss electricity costs, which should concern all members. They bring home
forcefully the high cost of the Government's interest-rate policy. I ask members to turn to
page 51 of this year's Budget, table 4, and look at the cost of interest on energy. In the year
ended 31 March 1977 the Government had to find $77.1 million to meet interest charges on
energy. Now, after 2 years, because any control over interest rates was abandoned, energy
consumers-and in particular electricity consumers have to find $178 million to meet
interest charges, an increase of $101 million in 2 years. Is it any wonder that power bills have
more than doubled? The reason is the high interest rate charged by the Government. In fact,

existing housing stocks, make it possible for people to acquire and occupy existing houses,
make it possible for present owners as well as new purchasers to improve their houses, add to

In 1972 the National Government introduced home improvement loans. These are now
beginning to be really effective-well recognised and used. Last year, 731 such loans were
made by the Housing Corporation, and applications have considerably increased this year.
In fact, in the 12 weeks that followed the announcement of the February package, there were
613 applications, compared with 225 in the same period last year. The February package was
also effective in stimulating activity in the building industry. Housing Corporation lending in
the 12 weeks following the announcement of the package increased to 3 600 applications to
erect new houses, compared with 2 100 for the same period last year. That further indicates
that the Government's housing policies are working well.
The Housing Corporation is also setting a good example by encouraging State rental
house tenants to transfer to smaller houses as their housing needs grow smaller. Last year we
saved an estimated $6.5 million that way. There were 544 voluntary transfers affecting State
rental houses, which made a further 680 bedrooms available—another indication that we can
and must make better use of our resources.
It is wise to consider the role of the building industry as we move into the early 1980s.
That industry is a service industry. It is there to provide for the needs of home seekers, and
to satisfy demands which the country can afford. It is not there simply to build houses
regardless of demand. The National Government wants to see a strong, profitable, viable
building industry-one that is geared to the real needs of the country, not one that is used
continuously as some kind of political football.
Not one builder I have met or spoken to condones the policy of the Labour
Government, particularly in 1974-75. They all know that the industry was subjected to
intolerable pressures; that the failure of the Labour Government to control land and house
prices put housing further and further beyond the reach of the average New Zealander. In
fact, there is no doubt that the Labour Government's policy was part, if not all, of the cause
of the building industry's difficulties today.
The Government wants to see the building industry settle at a level where employment
is reasonably constant, where the work load provides it with a level of activity that can be
maintained, and where the fluctuations that are certain to occur in the future can be
absorbed without unnecessary disruption. That was the situation before the disastrous 3
years of the former Labour Government, which completely destroyed the steady progress
then being made and completely disturbed the balance necessary in any industry. But the
industry's work load does not come from new house construction only. It is obvious that in
future, new house construction will form a smaller proportion of the building industry's
activity than it has over recent years. The emphasis, at least in the immediate future, will be
on improving the overall standard of our housing stock.
Of course new houses will be built. Of course new houses are needed, but they will not
be built simply to satisfy a demand that grew as a result of excessive immigration and
shortages resulting from the second world war. They will be built to replace ageing and
obsolete units; people will build new houses because they want to trade up to something
better than their present circumstances. Houses will be built to satisfy changes in needs and
demand for types of dwellings that are not readily available; they will be built to correct
imbalances in the distribution of our housing stock, and to make better use of our land and
existing facilities. What that means, of course, is best described by the term "urban
renewal". To many people urban renewal conjures up visions of slum clearance and a
scorched earth approach, when an area near a city centre is flattened and medium- or high-
density accommodation subsequently emerges.
Urban renewal is much more than that; it really means community regeneration. It
means constant regrowth, rehabilitation, and improvement inside the developed town and
city environs. It already occurs naturally, without prompting or Government help. It occurs
not only a stone's throw from the city centres, but out in the suburbs as well. At long last we
are able to do something positive about the urban sprawl. I believe we can develop within
existing city and town boundaries, generally speaking. More attention will be given in future
to additions and alterations to sound existing homes, and to the better use of land. The social
cost-that is, the provision of schools, kindergartens, parks, shopping centres, libraries,
transport, and the reticulation of power and sewerage of a new subdivision or new suburb
must be enormous, in the long run.

Zealand has nothing to worry about from the proposed sheepmeat regulations, but they
point out that the same assurances were offered when the regulations for butter exports were
drawn up a few years ago. The result has been a steady decline in New Zealand butter
exports to the British market." Members will have seen in the Evening Post of 14 June 1978
comments by Sir Harold Wilson, former British Prime Minister, and Dr David Owen,
British Foreign Secretary, about New Zealand's position. Sir Harold hit very hard at the
EEC, and accused the nine member States of letting New Zealand down. In fact, in a
separate conversation with New Zealand officials later Sir Harold said, "We've ratted on
you." He believes this, because he was, and still is, a good friend of New Zealand. We
found, in talking to parliamentarians, there was a general lack of knowledge of the
seriousness of New Zealand's situation. If the regulations are approved, establishing what is
known as a harmonising of prices for lamb among the nine member States, this could
effectively make New Zealand lamb too expensive for British housewives to buy. The cost of
food in Europe is unbelievably high, and any move to find a common price will mean a
substantial increase in the price to the British people.
Let us consider exports of lamb to the United Kingdom to 30 September 1977. Out of a
total of 311 380 tonnes to all destinations, 210 067 tonnes or 67 percent, went to the United
Kingdom. Ninety-five percent of our lamb going to the nine EEC countries went to the
United Kingdom. Greece is traditionally a good market for our lamb going to countries
outside the EEC. In the early 1970s Greece was our second largest market, but by 1976 it
was our fourth largest. It is an important market, but it tends to fluctuate. However, the
European Parliament has decided, in principle, to allow the entry into the EEC of Portugal,
Spain, and Greece. The entry of Greece concerns New Zealand most, because this could
become a threat. Each country we visited gave us the impression that, although they would
like to help us, their main concern was for their own farmers. This was particularly so in
Ireland, where many farmers have had a very hard time. I think I am correct in saying that
almost all Ireland's lamb production is sold outside Ireland.
The Dutch adopted a pretty hard-nosed approach in the discussions. They made it clear
that lamb is not a favoured meat in their country, and they tend to regard it as inferior. The
Dutch asked why we were not selling more lamb and mutton to Japan. The Japanese market
has grown steadily, but only 14 000 tonnes of lamb were sent to Japan in 1977. The Dutch
failed to understand the dietary habits of Orientals, whose main food intake is fish and rice.
The Dutch also asked why we were not expanding our manufacturing base. We were able to
point out that our manufacturing exports had risen considerably in recent years, but that we
would not replace meat and dairy production as major sources of income. With our small
population we do not have a large domestic market and, consequently, small runs of
manufactured products are costly to produce.
Our second problem is New Zealand's distance from world markets. The Belgians
listened to our case with sympathy, but again we had little success. In Belgium our name
stands very high because of the contribution made by New Zealand in World War I. It was
sobering for the five-member delegation to see thousands of Commonwealth war graves in
Messines, Ypres, and Paschendale-graves of soldiers aged 18, 19 and 20. That really
emphasised the futility of war. The Belgians were keen to talk, but we did not get very much
from the discussions. In Luxemburg the Minister of Agriculture promised to help us where
possible.
Although Belgium is a small nation, it is still a member of the EEC. In Denmark our
arrangements were interrupted by divisions in the Chamber of their Parliament. The
highlight of the tour was a session of dialogue with Geoffrey Rippon, the vice-president of
the European Parliament, Senator Yeats, and other members of the European Parliament at
Luxemburg. Geoffrey Rippon made it abundantly clear that he is biased in favour of New
Zealand, which brings me back to my original statement, and the Otago Daily Times
comment that Britain said that New Zealand had no reason to worry about her dairy
products. I think we do have reason for concern, because Britain is only one of 9, and before
long it will only be one of 12. Then we will have more difficulty. I hope the Deputy Prime
Minister can secure some assurances from EEC countries other than Britain, because this is

Having witnessed proceedings in the Mother of Parliaments, I feel sure that your period

that this House is a perfect example of exemplary behaviour-if I can mix my metaphors—

order. That should be of interest to some members in the House.
The Budget has been presented against a backdrop of an uncertain world, with all the
attendant problems. When in Los Angeles en route to London I had the opportunity to
attend a luncheon for 63 trade delegates stationed in that city. It became clear that problems
of recession, stagnation, and inflation-complex in varying degree-release old hatreds into
the world, as indicated by the troubles in Lebanon, in Ireland, in other countries. The
problems of trade surpluses that have arisen from the energy price crisis in 1973, and perhaps
more importantly the desire by many countries to raise protective barriers in trade, could
create some difficult challenges for New Zealand in the year ahead. These are the problems
to which I referred when I commenced my speech. There are no traditional answers to these
problems anywhere in the world. New Zealand is fighting for her survival. I want to quote
the opening statement in the Budget: "International trade is much more important to New
Zealand than to most other countries in the world, and, as a result, the international
economic situation affects New Zealand more than it does most other countries." Having
been overseas, I now know that that statement underlines the situation, but I doubt whether
it brings home to us, isolated at the bottom of the world, the seriousness of the situation. The
Budget makes big strides in removing some disincentives that have hindered the efforts of
our work to increase productivity. I shall come back to that if I have time.
I wish to talk on international trade, and, in particular, on the proposal by the European
Economic Community to introduce a regime for sheepmeats. That subject is referred to on
page 3 of the Budget: "The proposal of a Community regime for sheepmeats represents a far
greater danger to the New Zealand economy than anything that we have faced in the field of
dairy products." I doubt whether the seriousness of that statement is fully appreciated.
Having been overseas, I can vouch that we are very much at the mercy of greater powers
than we have previously faced. The value of our sheepmeats to the EEC-and it depends on
which year we talk about-runs between $250 million and the most recent figure of $320
million a year; and a tonnage that ranges between 200 000 tonnes and 240 000 tonnes. We
export 70 percent of our lamb to Europe, and most of that lamb goes to Britain. This is the
key element in our agricultural trade.
Our fear is that the proposed regime will do what it has done to other products inside
the EEC—that is, push up retail prices and depress consumer demand. Already we pay a 20
percent tariff to enter the EEC. It is a community that is less than 65 percent self-sufficient in
sheepmeats. Britain, our biggest market, is only 55 percent self-sufficient. If we consider
those figures against the fact that we supply about 85 percent of EEC markets-and about 65
percent of that export total goes to Britain-and the fact that we have diversified into new
markets, it can be understood that there is no immediate market for the very large tonnage
we send to Britain. New Zealand is well respected. There is a history of orderly trading in its
products, particularly in sheepmeats.
During my visit I was very pleased to be associated with the member for Grey Lynn. At
a number of seminars, meetings, and other functions with 90 British MPs and others, we
discussed the radical changes that would develop if the sheepmeat regime came into being.
There is no doubt that British members of Parliament, and in particular those who have
responsibility for sitting on the select committee that deals with European legislation, not
only want radical changes to the regime as proposed, but they doubt the wisdom of it.
Today, the Secretary of State for Agriculture, Mr Silkin, has confirmed this in discussions

There is a lot of sentiment for New Zealand in Britain. It is noticeable, when talking to
members of Parliament, to the people you meet in the streets, in the English pubs, and in
taxis. There is no doubt that that sentiment is there. But the strongest thing we have going
for us is the solidity of the supplier-consumer relationship, and the fact that we offer a good
product at a good price-one that cannot be matched anywhere. We can count on the fact
that the British have investments in the shipping lines that serve New Zealand, and in some
parts of the freezing industry. This is important when our case is considered. There is also a
great deal of disenchantment in Britain with the effects of the EEC agriculture policy on the
prices of consumer goods. We were not led to believe that Britain would opt out of the EEC,
but at all levels there is disenchantment with high prices.
There will be changes forthcoming in the parliamentary scene in Britain. The devolution
of Scotland and Wales is at present being considered. Next year there will be the first direct
elections for the European Parliament. New Zealand thus faces a new challenge. We shall
have to lobby elected members from all of the European countries, particularly those
members who represent rural areas. No matter what political allegiances there may be within
the new European Parliament, there will be further grouping of interests, and the rural
interests will be well represented in the new Parliament. We shall have to consider the
relationship of a new elected European Parliament to the present commission-in other
words, the Council of Ministers. I can liken it only to the situation in the United States,
where the Executive sits separately from the House of Representatives and the Senate.
What influence the members of this new Parliament will have on the Council of
Ministers, we have yet to learn. If our case is understood in Britain, it is not so well
understood in the European Parliaments, and so we have a lot of work to do there. That is
why the Deputy Prime Minister is now in Europe. I do not doubt-and I believe the member
for Grey Lynn, who was with me, would agree that Britain is better inside the EEC arguing
our case than she would be outside, and that our best influence is exercised through London.
However, I also believe that we should make a practice of sending members overseas each
year, in groups at least 10, to the capitals of the EEC to put our case, because it is on this
basis that we can get our argument across. It cannot be left only to Ministers, or indeed the
political level. It was good to talk to butchers and to the customers in the market place on a
face-to-face basis. It was clear that they liked the product we send to Britain. There are many
indicators from those people that our products will still be required in 10 to 20 years' time.
Will the sheepmeat be required leaner rather than it is at present? Will it be required to be
processed into cuts, or demanded in carcass form?
After visiting places such as Llangollen and Abergavenny in Wales, Bristol in England,
St. Heliers in Jersey, and Glasgow and Edinburgh in Scotland, I concluded that it would be
unwise for anybody in the House to tell the meat producers what they should sell; in fact, it
would be very dangerous indeed. We have to produce products for markets, and if the
British market is to be retained, and if it requires carcass meat, then that is the meat we shall
have to send. I was interested to hear, after I had returned to New Zealand and made
comments to this effect that were reported in the newspapers, that a letter had recently been
sent to all members of Parliament-and I confess that it must be at the bottom of my 4-ft pile
of accumulated correspondence-from Mr Hilgendorf, the Chairman of the Meat Producers
Board, explaining the position. I have not seen it yet, but it is pleasing to learn that the Meat
Producers Board is in touch, and is using sophisticated market research techniques that
cover the supplier, the retail supplier, and the customer.
The news about dairy products is not so good. I think it is unlikely that we shall achieve
any further large quantity of cheese exports to the European Community. The machinery

make the cheddar cheese that is produced in New Zealand. As a consolation I believe our
machinery suppliers did very well to sell that machinery. The outlook on butter, however, is
different, and I believe we can be quite optimistic that further access for our butter to a level
of about 100 000 tonnes will be achieved. I hope the Deputy Prime Minister can report
further on this when he returns. It was interesting to hear of the anger felt by British MPs
about the EEC dumping its dairy surpluses into the diversified markets that they asked us to
open. This is a matter for concern. It is receiving attention, and it was good to hear them
bring the subject up.

applicants took only $3.4 million. În 1976-77, 17 applicants took $2.6 million. In the 1977-78
year to date, 12 applicants have taken $3.38 million. Figures can be used selectively to prove

from Labour, but it required new initiatives, and they were undertaken-establishment and

Housing Land Sales, Taupo and Tokoroa
1. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Housing: What is he doing to ensure that
the land purchased in Taupo and Tokoroa for housing is made available at prices that will
keep the price of building sections down and allow the less well-off members of the
community to build their own homes?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Any sections made available for sale in
Taupo and Tokoroa, as with sections in all other centres, are made available at their current
market value. All sections suitable for modest to low-cost housing are offered to the public
by way of ballot, and preference is given to landless first-home seekers intending to build
within 12 months. In this way, corporation sections are directed to those persons with the
greatest housing need.
Mr Hunt: What percentage of the sections to be set aside will be for people on low
incomes, and will some remission be offered?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I cannot say what percentage will be set aside. As I said in
answer to the question, all sections available for modest and low-income housing are offered
to the public by way of a ballot, which I think is fair, and are given to landless home seekers
intending to build within 12 months. I point out to the honourable member who referred to
giving a concession that it is not necessary in today's context to give a concession. In 1973
under the Labour Government section prices increased by about 42 percent, and in 1974 by
about 53 percent. Today section prices are increasing annually by about 8 percent only.
Mr Hunt: If, as the Minister said, section prices were increasing at that time and
apparently are not now increasing, why are so few houses being built in that area?
Mr SPEAKER: That has nothing to do with either the original or the supplementary
question.

have been told by his department that they are better off on the benefit they are receiving
now than they would be on national superannuation?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: It is the Government's policy to let people, particularly war
pensioners, choose for themselves. If a person approached the department he would be told

Industrial Legislation
3. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of Labour: Has he read the
statement of the executive director of the Employers Federation as reported in the
Employer, No. 49, May 1978, which reads "Ultimately it is only by the exercise of mutual
responsibility and trust that we can hope to achieve happier industrial relations and a better
future", and, if so, can he indicate how the numerous penalty provisions directed against
unions in his Government's industrial legislation serve to further this goal?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I have read Mr Rowe's statement, and
would fully endorse much of what he says. It is my belief that the offences provisions in the
industrial relations legislation will ultimately lead to more stability. I am interested to
observe that the New Zealand Planning Council's discussion paper also accepts the need for
"well-framed industrial laws to define acceptable responsibilities and reduce the risk of
disruption". I should add that the offences provisions referred to by the member for Roskill
are by no means as onerous as critics of the Government make out. Two of the provisions
simply reinforce the dispute settlement procedures in the Industrial Relations Act, and in
essence were incorporated in the Act passed by the Labour Government in 1973. The law
was being defied without penalties. I can inform the member that in an increasing number of
cases the law is now being observed, particularly with regard to notice of intention before
ceasing killing at freezing works.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can I take it from the Minister's reply that the increased and
record level of industrial stoppages has not been brought about by anything other than the
Government's economic policies?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: No, the member cannot take that from my reply. In several
instances-I believe too many-industrial stoppages have taken place because of safety
factors and management muddlement: in a case reported in last night's newspaper an
employer incurred a penalty because he was in error.
Mr Latter: Is it correct to say that the penalty provisions are directed against unions, or
is it more correct to say that they are directed equally against unions and employers?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: As the law was written by both the Labour Government and this
Government, the penalty provisions apply equally where possible, with a heavier impost in
the size of fine on an employer than a union member.

State Insurance Fund for Securitibank Ltd. Liquidation
5. Mr LANGE (Mangere) to the Minister in Charge of the State Insurance Office: Will
the State Insurance Office establish a fund to meet the contingency of a claim by the
liquidator of Securitibank Ltd. against shareholders on behalf of creditors?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister in Charge of the State Insurance Office): No, it is not
seen as being necessary.
Mr Lange: As the deficit is about $50 million and the State Insurance Office is a
substantial shareholder, why does the Minister not consider that move necessary?
Mr SPEAKER: That is really seeking the Minister's opinion. Perhaps the member could
rephrase his question.
Mr Lange: Why is it not thought necessary, and what are the reasons that led the
Minister to that conclusion?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The key to the action is contained in section 364 of the
Companies Act, and section 126 of the Insolvency Act. Those sections provide for the
recovery of funds from shareholders if it can be established that they solicited funds from the
public when they knew their firm to be insolvent. It must be shown that shareholders knew
the firm was unable to pay its debts on the due date, and that they willingly continued to
solicit funds from the public. This was taken up by the insurance company, which advised
Securitibank that it would not permit its name to be used. Its name was used once in 1974,
and the general manager of Securitibank wrote to the insurance company apologising for
using its name.
Mr Lange: Does the Minister acknowledge that shortly after he became the Minister he
was made aware of the fact that Securitibank was unable to discharge its liabilities, and was
still borrowing money?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes. I shall give one or two brief points to clarify the position.
The investment board of the Government Life and the State Insurance Offices decided to
commission an independent appraisal of the company before subscribing to the new capital
issued in 1973. The report prepared by Barr, Burgess and Stewart was favourable. On the
basis of that report, the Labour Government doubled the investment to $102,000. Up until
that time the investment board quite rightly believed that Securitibank was a good
investment. It was not until a report appeared in Truth that there was any suspicion that the
company might be in financial difficulty. Immediately the Wellington shareholders called the
general manager of Securitibank down to Wellington. It was then realised that the company
was in difficulty. At no time was money invested when there was any doubt about the
company's ability to meet its liabilities.
Arapawa Island Goats
6. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Lands: Has he seen the two reports
