meeting of the Marlborough Sounds Maritime Park Board held on 31 May, a wild animal
control programme prepared by the New Zealand Forest Service, and involving both private
and reserve land, was formally adopted by the board. The meeting which was attended by
the major organisations and individuals with differing points of view on the control
measures, unanimously agreed with the board's proposal to carry out a three-phase control
programme commencing this month and finishing in February-March 1979. The board's
decision to adopt this control programme is recorded in the second article referred to, which
was published on 1 June. I do not propose to interfere with this decision.
Mr Latter: Is it a fact that the third phase, which does not start until January next year,

and second phases involve private land in the north and south of the island?

Electoral Rolls
7. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Justice: Were the new electoral rolls
compiled entirely from the enrolment cards distributed with the census, and, if so, how is it
that persons who had died before the census, or had left New Zealand before the census, still
have their names on the roll?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The electoral rolls for the new electoral
districts were not compiled entirely from the re-registration forms collected at the last
census. They also include residual names of persons who were on the 1975 rolls, but did not
subsequently re-register. I should observe that this information was indicated in paragraph 7
of the instruction that I circulated to all members of Parliament a month ago. Since it was
known that many people did not return the re-registration forms after the census, it was
thought preferable to retain their names on the roll in the meantime, and send cards to all
who were on the roll in 1975. The 1975 roll was, of course, not perfectly up to date.
Mr Hunt: Is it a fact that the point made by the member for Onehunga in his question
refers to people who were not on the 1975 roll, but who had died between 1972 and 1975 and
had received cards for the 1978 roll?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Goodness knows what point the member for Onehunga was
trying to make. I merely answered the question that was asked.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Is the Minister satisfied that the Chief Electoral Officer was acting in
the best interests of all voters by taking the steps he adopted?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I am confident that that was so. The 1975 roll has been
included so that the people who were on that roll, even if they did not return the census re-
registration card, will at least have the right to vote because they were on the 1975 roll.

Industrial Legislation
11. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: In view of the report in the
Evening Post of 13 June 1978, in which he is reported as saying that "he was contemplating
legislation to combat illegal strikes", will he outline what he means by illegal strikes, and


## p. 955 (#65) #############################################

16 June
955
Questions-Oral
legal strikes?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The Industrial Relations Act 1973 and the
Commerce Act 1975 specify various offences in relation to a strike or lockout. Under the
Industrial Relations Act, a stoppage is illegal in the following circumstances: if claims have
not been withdrawn from the conciliation council-section 81; if the matter is within the
disputes procedure deemed to be in every award or collective agreement-section 124A; if 14
days' notice of intention to strike or lockout has not been given in respect of a stoppage in
specified essential industries-section 125; and if 3 days' notice of intention to strike or
lockout has not been given in respect of a stoppage in meat export slaughterhouses-section
125A. Under the Commerce Act, a stoppage is illegal if it is over a matter that is not an
industrial matter-section 119B; or if it is in defiance of a resumption of a work order by the
Arbitration Court under section 119c. In some of these it would be a defence if safety and
health were involved.
Mr Isbey: Is a stoppage still permissible in a dispute of interest as against a dispute of
right?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Only in unique circumstances would such a stoppage be legal.
Tourism-Lamb Chop Values
12. Mr BELL (Gisborne), on behalf of Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of
Tourism: Has the Tourist and Publicity Department ever calculated the relative value
between a lamb chop exported for consumption overseas and a similar chop consumed in
New Zealand by an overseas tourist?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Tourism replies: "I do
not know about the Tourist and Publicity Department, but when I addressed the Cookery
and Food Association in Wellington last July, I had a suggestion to make to them. As I told
them, ‘A quick calculation on a scrap of paper this afternoon suggested to me that, while we
might sell a lamb chop overseas for 35c, if we can sell that same lamb chop to an overseas
visitor in a New Zealand hotel the value is most likely to be about $1.50. These figures might
not be accurate to the nearest cent, but they make a point for all of us. In fact, if we can
follow this through to a logical conclusion, the most profitable way of selling all our export
foods would be to serve them to tourists in our own hotels', and I still think this is true."
Mr Bruce Barclay: How does the Minister of Tourism calculate that a chop would be
worth $1.50 if consumed in New Zealand by an overseas tourist? Does he suggest that the
26 000 000 lambs that New Zealand normally exports should be consumed in New Zealand
by tourists?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The supplementary information I have is that the new lamb
chop pack being promoted by the Meat Development Company in North America is
returning 35c a chop on an f.o.b. basis before freight and other overseas costs. The figure of
$1.50 is based on a $6 lamb chop dish. The meat is half the cost of the food content, returning
$3, and there are two large chops, so each is worth $1.50.
Mr Quigley: Can the Minister confirm that the cost to visitors to New Zealand would be
much less if New Zealand could purchase the chops and then give them to visitors?
Mr SPEAKER: That is going a bit beyond the scope of the question.

Maori Housing

this financial year?

houses were built so 1000 people were settled through the Department of Maori Affairs. Of
course, they were equally eligible to be settled through the Housing Corporation, but I do
not have those figures.
Mr Couch: Would the Minister agree that many marriages between Maoris and pakehas
have led to housing applications being channelled through the Housing Corporation instead
of through the Department of Maori Affairs, thus reducing the amount voted for Maori
housing?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Obviously a large number of Maoris including those with mixed
marriages, are settled by the Housing Corporation, and this has reduced the number who
would otherwise have applied for Maori housing loans.

Squid
18. Mr BELL (Gisborne), on behalf of Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua), to the Minister of
Fisheries: How much research has been done on surveying the potential supply of squid in
New Zealand's 200-mile fishing zone?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): Research has been carried out mainly in
two ways. First, from 1970-72, Japanese scientists carried out extensive jig-fishing surveys
around the entire New Zealand coast. The results of these surveys have been published in
Japanese journals and have also been made available to the Ministry of Agriculture and
Fisheries research division. Secondly, the fisheries research division is at present observing
and collecting larval and juvenile squid, and is looking at the relationship between the
distribution of New Zealand squid and oceanic water currents.
Mr Bell: Can the Minister confirm that this is a continuing research programme that will
not cease at the end of the year?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: I can confirm that the programme is continuing, and is likely to be
expanded.
Mr Courtney: Now that Japan has been excluded from the 200-mile economic zone,
the Government still receiving data on squid and other species as in the past?
is
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: Japanese fishing vessels have been excluded only for a very short
time, and to date this has had no effect on the research information received from Japan.

22. Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) to the
Minister of Education: What provision is being made for training in the teaching of English

Wellington has offered a 1-year diploma course in teaching English as a second language to
selected teachers, technical institute tutors, teachers college lecturers and Department of
Education advisers. An extramural university diploma course on English as a second

Educational Resource Centre in Auckland provides courses and resource material in English
as a second language. Other in-service courses-national, regional, and local-are held to
train teachers in teaching English as a second language. Department of Education advisers
assist teachers with language programmes in schools, and in Auckland and Wellington.
Volunteer home tutors are being trained to teach communication English to migrant
families.

APPROPRIATION BILL-FINANCIAL STATEMENT
Interrupted debate on the question, That this Bill be now read a second time.
Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru): When the House rose last night, I was talking about the
background to the 1978 Budget, the third Budget in the first 3-year reconstruction plan. I
explained that the first two Budgets were designed to cool the heat of inflation and to restore
some balance to the balance of payments, and, those measures having been largely achieved,
I was describing the Budget as expansionary and designed to encourage the use of
underutilised resources and to reduce the numbers of unemployed, while encouraging the
movement of resources into exports through the farming industry, and from the State to the
private sector through the $530 million total tax cut.
I also spoke about Government moves to stimulate farm production, many of which are
outlined in the Budget. In general, cropping farmers have not really benefited from the
Budget, although they have benefited from the fertiliser subsidy and the provision of
$5 million through the Rural Bank for the financing of machinery. Because the country has
not reached self-sufficiency in wheat there will be a need to import some, and within the next
few weeks the Government will need to consider seriously the application for an increase in
the wheat price to be paid to farmers next year. The wheat farmers are now deciding whether
to sow wheat or buy sheep, and, with the Budget incentives for sheep farmers, the wheat
acreage may well be reduced, thus necessitating further wheat imports. The Government
should seriously consider the application for an increase in next year's price, so that this
winter's planting can be reconsidered by wheat farmers.
There is no doubt that poor industrial relations are the main reason for the reduction in
stock numbers. Everyone is an expert on industrial relations, including the Planning
Council, which, a few days ago, issued a useful paper putting forward some ideas. However,
in the end it is the employers and the employees in the industry who will make the decisions
to effect the necessary improvements before the next season starts. At the Labour Party
conference the president of the Labour Party, the member for Roskill, said the popular
thing, and no doubt he got an ovation for his statement that all penalty clauses and all
industrial legislation would be effectively removed from the statute book should Labour
become the Government. I wonder whether he said that because he meant it, or because he
thought he would get a cheer from the conference, or because he did not think he would ever
be faced with that situation, and could thus get away with an irresponsible statement.
The farming industry's concern at what is happening in the freezing industry and the
servicing industries generally is reflected in the fact that 7500 farmers have committed their
support to the Ravensdown company in its bid to take over, rationalise, and improve the
Kempthorne Prosser fertiliser company. In some districts these farmers represent 92 percent
of the farming community; therefore, 92 percent of all farmers have stated their support for
the takeover of the Kempthorne Prosser fertiliser industry by the farmer-owned
Ravensdown organisation.
Trade negotiations with the EEC, Japan, and the United States are obviously vital to
our economic recovery, and in the last few days there has been action on all fronts as a result
of recent initiatives by the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister. Yesterday we
heard that Mr Silkin, the British Minister of Agriculture, has conceded that the EEC
sheepmeat regulation will be an election issue.
Yesterday, the Meat Board representative told the select committee that the increase in
price to the British housewife would be approximately 30 percent. Mr Callaghan, the Prime
Minister, also accepts that the sheepmeat regulation will be an issue in the forthcoming
British elections because of the increase in the price to the housewife.
Our beef quota on the United States market has been removed, and there has been
official confirmation that the 24 member countries of the OECD have accepted that
agricultural products should have the same recognition in dealings and negotiations as
industrial products. That came about because of the initiative taken by the Prime Minister
and by New Zealand, and was one concession among many as a result of our high profile and
aggressiveness in negotiations with our trading partners.

and especially the two Dunedin members-when comparing the South and the North
Islands. I do not think these comparisons are very intelligent. The South Island has fast and
slow growth areas, as has the North Island. However, the South Island Labour members
have been saying that the South Island has been undernourished during the term of the

Government its responsibility for the disastrous state of our economy. In the Budget the

provide building contractors, manufacturers, and others with the opportunity to work and to
produce in the right economic atmosphere.
The decisive action needed now is missing from the Budget. Every week, almost every
day, in some New Zealand centre, major manufacturing establishments and long-established
commercial enterprises are going to the wall or reducing working hours. Last week I
approached the Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Industry about the serious
plight of engineering establishments in Christchurch, the possibility of more skilled
tradesmen being laid off, and the cutting back of production. This week we read in the
Christchurch papers about the serious plight of the building industry and about builders
being forced to submit uneconomic tenders to keep their industry intact and their people
employed.
The Government knew exactly what it was doing when it adopted its inflationary policy
and withdrew support for the economy. It was told what would happen, not only by the
Opposition, but by other informed people. It went ahead, and the Budget indicates what has
happened. Already this year, expenditure on unemployment and relief work, and the loss to
the Government of tax on incomes and profitability that otherwise would have been
available, is running at around $200 million. Would it not be sensible to spend an equivalent
amount, to get the country moving again?
Let us think what the expenditure of $200 million committed firmly by the Government
would do. It would put efficient organisations to work, create optimism, create enthusiasm,
create agair confidence to invest, and create confidence in the business community. Instead
of pursuing a planned unemployment policy and paying out unemployment benefits, and
presiding over the demise of our manufacturing and commercial sectors, the Government
should spend an equivalent amount to get the country moving again. The fact is that all the
Government's efforts to reflate the economy-and it has spent about $700 million since
October in tax cuts, in relaxing credit, on the import deposit scheme, and in relaxing the
wool retention scheme and hire purchase terms-have been to no avail, because the
Government has not been able to command the confidence of the commercial community.
Labour's alternative-which provides for a responsible approach to funding taxation
reform of placing a surcharge on the use of overseas exchange has important advantages
for the country. It would deter the expenditure of vital overseas funds and help us to ease the
pressure on the balance of payments. It would deter the purchase of imported goods and, in
that way, create a demand for the products of New Zealand industry thus making work for

factories and employment for people, and would help to restore confidence to the business
community. That is the approach needed at present.
That brings me, at this stage, to the performance of the member for Rangitikei in the
two major debates so far in the House. He came into the House as the leader of a party with
the prized possession of a financial theory-it is called the A plus B theorem-which, it was
alleged, would cure the country's ills. In the two major debates in the House so far-the
Address in Reply and the Budget debate-he has not put forward specific detailed proposals
or programmes to put the country on its feet again. Would you not think that a member who
claimed to have the answers to the country's ills would have taken the very first opportunity
to tell Parliament about them, and keep on repeating what he had to say? But the member
for Rangitikei did not do that. People are wondering why they have heard no detailed
proposals from him. The fact is, of course, that the party, with its discredited theory, has
nothing to offer.
In his contribution to the Budget debate the member for Rangitikei made an astounding
statement; he said he would support Labour's surcharge on foreign exchange if the proceeds
were used to repay the overseas debt. He appears not to understand that, while the
surcharge would have the effect of discouraging the expenditure of overseas funds, it does
not produce overseas funds as such for the Government's use. That levy will be paid in New
Zealand dollars. What the member for Rangitikei said is similar in principle to the
impression that, it is claimed, Social Crediters have been leaving with people throughout
New Zealand—that credit can be created through the Reserve Bank and used to pay other
countries for the goods we buy from them. One cannot create dollars, sterling, marks, yen,
or any other overseas currency through the New Zealand banking system, and those who
give that impression are misleading people.
Then, of course, the Minister of Customs reported that the Social Credit Political
League has been circulating a document in Kaipara that stated that the league would
withdraw all controls and props for the economy to boost and protect high-cost secondary
industries. That is reminiscent of statements made by National Government members, and
such an action would be comparable to the actions of the National Government, which has
withdrawn regional development support and support for industry throughout the country.
It shows that the Social Credit Political League and the National Party follow identical
courses, and are opposed to the development of industry.
Labour Governments have a record of achievement in financial affairs. Under previous
Labour Governments New Zealand has led the world with financial innovations. A Labour
Government made the Reserve Bank of New Zealand a public bank, and through it created
credit, within justifiable limits, for public benefit. A Labour Government asserted the
sovereign right of the Crown to create credit and currency, but that provision was repealed
by the National Government. I point out that that National Government was elected as a
result of the vote splitting caused by the Social Credit Political League and, as a result,
important financial policies have been frustrated. No wonder Mr Chapman, President of the
National Party, recently said that the Social Credit Political League could, by splitting the
Labour vote, help the National Party retain seats it holds with small majorities. People are
awake to the National Party and the Social Credit Political League. They will not be fooled,
and will not forget that the first time the member for Rangitikei voted in the House he voted
with the National Government for the introduction of a tax on the cost of fuel, which
increased the costs to family men and workers of running their cars.
The 1978 Budget has many surprising features and many omissions. The Prime
Minister-the Minister of Finance- said that he had the choice of increasing Government
expenditure or reducing taxation. If Government support for the economy had not been
withdrawn, business confidence and growth in the economy would have been maintained,
and the heavy cost of unemployment and loss of income would have been avoided. The
Government would have received a higher income, which would have given it the resources
to initiate some tax reform and to provide for an increasing level of Government
expenditure. I notice that Government expenditure as a percentage of the gross national
product is at an all-time record level. In 1976, Government members talked about the large
increase in Government expenditure during the last year of the Labour Government, and
claimed that the Labour Government had moved a part of the national product from the
private sector to the Government sector. The Prime Minister described that move as
"socialism by stealth". I remind him that Government expenditure is now at its highest level.

says that the course the Government is following leads to a communist State. The
Government is hoist with its petard.
In the Budget the Government also tries to justify its actions, and in particular the
major Budget deficit, by saying that the overseas deficit and the rate of inflation have been
cut by half. That is quite incorrect. If the present rate of inflation is computed on the same
basis as it was during the term of the Labour Government, the rate for the year ended March
1978 would have been 14.6 percent-not very much lower than the rate for the previous
year. We should look at the balance of payments figures rather than at those for overseas
transactions. The former correctly record New Zealand's external position; overseas
exchange transactions merely record cash remittances.
The balance of payments records show the economic transactions between New
Zealand and other countries on a gross basis, and give a correct measurement of New
Zealand's external position. The balance of payments deficit in March was $810 million, not
very much lower than the highest level under the former Labour Government-and we must
remember that export earnings since have almost doubled. In the 2 years the National
Government has been in office it has received an additional $2.9 million in export earnings;
yet the reduction in the balance of payments deficit has been relatively negligible. Of course,
the Government had to find some excuse for justifying its actions, and has used figures in a
misleading way.
The Government has also been trying to justify its unemployment policy by saying that
productivity and output have been higher because of unemployment. The latest figures
available from the Government Statistician show that the real output for each member of the
labour force has in fact fallen under this Government. Unemployment has not increased
productivity for each person in the labour force, and it is disastrous for the country. It means
that we lose output, wealth, and opportunities for our people.
In its 1975 policy the National Party promised the Racing and Trotting Conferences 0.5
percent of on-course and off-course turnover. In 1976 the Government gave the conferences
0.5 percent of the on-course turnover, by raising the punters' costs, but the 1978 Budget still
makes no provision for paying the conferences 0.5 percent of the off-course turnover. That
promise has not been redeemed, and the racing fraternity throughout New Zealand will not
forget that. I know that in the election stakes in November they will back a winner-the
Labour Party.
Government members have spoken a great deal about the effective disinheritance of
people as a result of the impact of estate duty. The inflationary policies followed by the
National Government have increased the cost of properties by 40 percent, but the 1978
Budget provides no relief from the payment of estate and gift duty. The Government has
failed to help the people it claimed were being disinherited. No matter what is said in the
Budget, total taxation is now more than $5 billion-an all-time record. Total taxation, at
37.6 percent, is also at an all-time record level as a percentage of the national income. The
total tax take under this Budget is an all-time record, at $1,628 for every man, woman, and
child. This year, the tax take overall is up by more than $500 million, or more than $160 for
every man, woman, and child. Income tax alone has been increased by almost $400 million
to an equivalent of $120 a person.
The Government may have given some relief to the middle-income group downwards,
which the Opposition said was necessary, but it has given no relief to those on the lowest
incomes. In fact, the tax those people pay has been increased. For instance, apprentices,
widows, and the family man on the average weekly wage claiming young family rebates, will
pay on a higher proportion of their income in tax. The married couple on national
superannuation with little or no additional income, will also pay more.
The statement in the Budget about what has been done for national superannuitants is
quite misleading. The Minister of Social Welfare knows that the tax for married
superannuitants, with little or no additional income, will be increased. The tax on part-time
workers, such as mothers desperately trying to earn a little money for their families, or to
pay off mortgages, has been increased. Everyone earning $57 a week or less has had his tax
increased under the Budget.
At a time when the country needed statesmanship, leadership, and decisive action to
overcome its problems, the response of the Government-the economic Neros sitting
opposite-was to opt out of its responsibilities, and engage in a lolly scramble in the hope of
stalling the inevitable defeat it will now suffer. It is a thoroughly bad Government, and New
Zealand cannot afford to delay any longer the return of the fourth Labour Government.

4 percent and 7 percent. New Zealand has 1.3 percent. That is a success story, because we

countries have, plus the fact that our economy is largely agriculturally based.
Our economy lacks the flexibility to give us a degree of choice in manufacturing,
particularly with metals and non-agricultural products, so our difficulty is much greater than
theirs. New Zealand has attacked the problem sensibly. The Government is implementing

As I am about the fortieth or the forty-fifth person to speak in this debate many people
have already mentioned the information contained in this small blue document. Opposition

important points are not the little rows of figures at the back, the easily identified lists of
handouts, or the support given to social welfare. The main thrusts of the document are its
premises, principles, and statements about the problems facing New Zealand and the
policies necessary to overcome them. Only by reading the declarations and recognising the
criteria can we identify the principal direction in which we as a country must be moving.
Every member in the House should work towards that policy.
The Budget tells us something we all know-that New Zealand faces an economic
battle. Today's greater international pressures, compared with those of 1973, have placed
trade restrictions on this country. Trade barriers are being built up by countries that were
once traditional buyers from New Zealand, but who have now turned into competitors. The
aim of the Budget should be to overcome the problem of access to international markets and
to project New Zealand into the 1980s. A combination of those forces will determine
whether or not the nation survives, whether it can continue with an acceptable standard of


## p. 982 (#92) #############################################

982
16 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
living, and continue to pursue its trditional forms of industry, manufacture, service, and
employment. It is true to say that those same forces and the manner in which we are
prepared to cope with them will determine the degree of change necessary and the extent to
which we must restructure and reshape our livelihood to accommodate that change.
One of the phenomena rightly pointed out on page 1 of the Budget is the large trading
surplus at present in the hands of a few nations, especially the major oil-exporting nations.
We should all support the performance of those New Zealand exporters who have developed
contacts and substantially increased their volume of trade with countries such as Iran and
Bahrain. I mention those two countries as examples because they illustrate one of the
practical measures New Zealand must pursue in future, because the future of the country
depends on our ability to get access to overseas markets and to trade there profitably. That is
the whole purpose of the exercise. I am pleased that the Government has decided to enter
into a bilateral joint venture with Bahrain, giving New Zealand the opportunity to set up and
establish a facility in a free port area. That is a practical step on the road to a new and
exciting market.
People, especially Opposition members, speak blithely about social policies. No country
can afford to pursue extravagant and costly social policies unless it also has a strong and vital
economic base which provides the means and the wherewithal to finance them. What we
have to do is look for the criteria to contain inflation and keep the cost of production relative
to that in the countries with which we compete and trade. More than anything else, declining
terms of trade are working against New Zealand. Recently a well-known economist, a
financial adviser to the Bank of New Zealand, said: "Nothing helped New Zealand more—
and it was probably the only major factor that allowed us to pull our socks up-to come out
of the 1930 depression than an improvement in the terms of trade overseas." Frankly, we
cannot look forward hopefully to that happening in the next few years, so other measures
have to be taken. The answer, of course, is simple, but it might not be achieved easily. We
must increase productivity.
Export year, a promotion of this Government, is one of the exciting projects aiming in
this direction. We are strengthening our trade posts overseas, in the Middle East, and,
specifically, in Vancouver, San Francisco, and Singapore. Just recently we had a trade fair in
Auckland, but, perhaps more exciting, just on the horizon is the all-New Zealand trade fair
to be held in Los Angeles in October. The United States of America, is, of course, becoming
a prominent influence on New Zealand's terms of trade. Only last week the United States
Government relaxed its tight and stringent conditions for beef imports—and there is a very
wide unsatisfied market in that country for a wide range of our products. I believe these
dense and populated markets of Western America are those to which we can readily gain
access. We are taking the right to promote the trade fair in Los Angeles. In addition a trade
fair will be held in Kuala Lumpur in November. The Government is giving practical financial
support in the promotion of these trade fairs.
In the few moments I have left, I want to say that New Zealand must pursue three
objectives: agricultural support, the development of primary industries like fishing, and
manufacturing support. If the Government continues to encourage manufacturers as it has in
the past and as is spelt out in the Budget, and if it continues to support farmers and
fishermen, the country will soon be well on the way to overcoming the economic problems
that beset it now.
Debate interrupted.

Mr SPEAKER: It would be more helpful if the notice of motion was presented to the

Leader of the Opposition was anticipating the lodgment of that notice of motion.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): This is a procedural notice of
motion, and I thought the time most appropriate to raise the question of how it should be
dealt with was when you call for notice of motion. I merely sought your advice on the most
appropriate way of dealing with this procedural matter.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The point of order is invalid, because
there is no procedure under which advice on a notice of motion may be sought. If the Leader
of the Opposition wants advice, he should call privately on either Mr Speaker or the Clerk.
The method used by the Leader of the Opposition does, of course, give publicity to the
proposed notice of motion. Senior members usually have a reasonable knowledge of the
Standing Orders, and what is or is not appropriate by way of a notice of motion.
Occasionally something out the ordinary may occur, but this matter does not seem in any
way to be extraordinary. If the member feels able, he should present his notice of motion. If
the member feels unable, he should seek advice privately from Mr Speaker rather than take
up the time of the House by putting to Mr Speaker a matter that would need thinking about,
and on which Mr Speaker would later have to rule. This procedure is unusual, and should
not be encouraged.
Mr SPEAKER: The matter was drawn to my attention just before the House met. The
Clerk came to my office, and said that he had been approached by the member for New
Lynn on another matter. As I understand the point raised by the Leader of the Opposition,
notice has been given that leave will be sought to move a procedural motion. Ministers may
move a procedural motion without notice, but members may not. A motion relating to the
business of a select committee is a procedural motion, and a member must give notice of his
intention to move it. If the notice of motion had been lodged with the Clerk's office, the
member could have given notice of his intention to move next sitting day that a certain
procedure be followed. The member may do that tomorrow, but not today.

their proceedings or on their report, the Committee shall instruct the Chairman to move in
the House to that effect."

whether these or those proceedings, all of the proceedings, or any of the proceedings, should

committing a breach of privilege.

Tax Comparison
1. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department: What will be the amount of tax payable after 1 October on weekly earnings of
$140 by (a) a married man (single-income family) with three children aged 13, 14, and 16,
and (b) a married man (single-income family) with one child aged 2?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): The Minister in Charge of the Inland
Revenue Department replies: "The weekly tax payable by the married man in the first
example would be $29.48, and in the second case quoted would be $20.48..In addition, the
married man with a 2-year-old child would be entitled to claim the single-income family
rebate of $260 in his end-of-year tax return. These figures do not take into account the family
benefit payable in respect of the children."
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Why has the National Government made a deliberate decision to
tax a married man with three teenage children $14 more than a married man with one 2-year-
old child?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: A number of factors are taken into account when deciding on
the current arrangement. First, a family is generally not so well off financially when the
children are young. Secondly, it is unusual for a man to be still on the average wage when he
is old enough to have three children. Thirdly, when the children are older the mother is
better able to work. It is open to Opposition members to contest this with figures if they
wish, but the Inland Revenue Department has very good reason for coming to these
conclusions.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: What measures were taken by the Labour Government between
1972 and 1975 vis-a-vis a married man with children aged 13, 14, and 16?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The member may not ask that question.
Mr Prebble: In his reply to the supplementary question the Minister said that a man
with one child under the age of 2 years was usually worse off than a man with three teenage
children. Is this comment as a result of a Government survey, or of conclusions drawn by the
Minister?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The observation is borne out by the Inland Revenue
Department, which has considerable experience in these matters.
Mr Falloon: Could the Minister advise the tax cut both categories will receive from 1
October as a result of the Budget's provisions?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: I cannot give the exact figures, but to the best of my memory
each category will be $4 a week better off.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: The Minister gave a number of reasons why the Government made
a decision to tax a married man with three children $14 more than a married man with one
child. Did these reasons include the fact that one 2-year-old child ate more than three
teenage children, and possibly cost more to clothe?

Foreign Exchange Surcharge
6. Mr BIRCH (Franklin) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: Has he read of the Labour
Party proposal to impose a surcharge on the purchase of foreign exchange, and, if so, has he
asked his department to consider whether this proposal if implemented would offend any
trade pledges, international undertakings, or General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade to
which the New Zealand Government is a party?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade): Yes, I have
read of the proposal, and my department has looked into the sort of implications mentioned
in the question. I am informed that a tax on foreign exchange would probably conflict with
Article VIII of the International Monetary Fund Articles of Agreement. In addition, there is
a strong presumption that a tax on foreign exchange would place New Zealand in breach of
(1) the IMF Articles of Agreement; (2) the specific Government undertakings in relation to
borrowing from the IMF oil facility; (3) the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade; and
(4) the OECD trade pledge, which the Labour Government adopted in 1974, and which the
Deputy Minister of Foreign Affairs has recently renewed. The Labour Party proposal to
impose a surcharge on the purchase of foreign exchange would invite immediate retaliation
from our principal trading partners. This could well take the form of recourse to the IMF,
GATT, and OECD provisions that I have mentioned.
Mr Hunt: Can I take it from the Minister's reply, and his use of the words "probably"
and "strong presumption", that he is not prepared to be more definite than that about this
question?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: There was one case involving GATT some time ago,
and I think it concerned Greece. That country proposed a similar surcharge, but withdrew
the effect of it by devaluation before GATT and the IMF could adjudicate on it. But the fact
of the matter is that the official advice the Government gets from its advisers is that this is
dangerous and would be very likely to result in retaliation from our major trading partners in

7. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Justice: Is it correct that he replied to me on

changed to October 1978?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): The Minister of Justice replies: "It is
correct that the member was so informed on 17 August 1977, but I emphasise the words
"likely to be available by June 1978". My reply also pointed out that the index of places and
streets was a by-product of the print-out of the electoral rolls. The date has now been
changed, because of the need to complete the roll preparation first. The index of places and
streets is not thought to have the same urgency as the printing of the rolls."
Mr Hunt: In view of the fact that, legally, under the Electoral Act, this roll was
supposed to have been prepared by September 1977, or, in other words, 3 months after the
boundaries were gazetted, could the Minister explain why we are not likely to get an index of
streets until about 13 or 14 months after the actual legal limit for the time of the production
of the roll?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: All I can tell the House is that on the last occasion there was a
boundary change the index was not made available until about September or October,
before the election. This timing will be in line with that, and I do not recall the member
challenging the legality or propriety of that timing back in 1972.
Mr Hunt: In view of the fact that in 1972 the main roll was out considerably earlier than
at present under the programme, that the Act has been changed since that time to require
the Chief Electoral Officer to have the roll out 3 months after the boundaries have been

think I can none the less make the general comment that, apparently because of the new
computer arrangements, it has been necessary to put the whole programme back. This will
entail the rolls being out by about August, and the index by about October.

State Rental Applications-Criteria
20. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) to the Minister of Housing: Is it correctly
stated in the New Zealand Law Society's newsletter Law Talk that his department has
decided, as a matter of principle, to reject applications for rental accommodation from either
party to a matrimonial separation involving the sale of the matrimonial home?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I have read the article in Law Talk 74,
and neither it nor the letter from the Housing Corporation on which the article is based
states that the corporation has decided, as a matter of principle, to reject applications for
rental accommodation from either party to a matrimonial separation involving the sale of the
matrimonial home. When a husband and wife separate and there is a family home owned by
the husband, or if a suitable home has been sold with the agreement of the applicant, or
because the applicant did not desire to pursue legal avenues for obtaining possession for the
benefit of, say, herself and her children, housing allocation committees reasonably take the
view that the housing difficulties are self-created and that an allocation, when considered in
relation to the needs of other applicants, is not warranted. Nevertheless, while this
represents the general attitude of the corporation, it is not an inflexible policy, and each
applicant's circumstances and needs are taken into account.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Am I not to conclude from the Minister's answer that whether or
not a decision has been taken in principle to the effect mentioned in the substantive
question, in effect it has been operating in practice?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: In practice, people in these circumstances stand in exactly the
same situation as those in other circumstances. They are pointed according to their needs,
and the housing allocation committees make their allocations of State rental housing
according to the assessment of those needs.
Mr Lange: Would the Minister accept that applications for rental accommodation, as a
consequence of matrimonial separation, have been declined by the Housing Corporation
without reference to the housing allocation committees?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I have no doubt that this has happened, in the same way that
applications from other people have been declined without reference to the housing
allocation committees if the circumstances are such that there is no chance of their being
allocated a State rental house. For example, the application of a person who has been
pointed with 20 points is not referred to a housing allocation committee because it is well
known that such a person would not be allocated a State rental house.
Mr Prebble: If the Housing Corporation will not even accept applications at the
counter, as I understand is the case, how can the Minister say that the corporation's attitude
is flexible, when the housing allocation committee does not even see the application?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: Clearly, the honourable member does not understand the
procedure for allocations. If the application of a person applying to the Housing Corporation
for a State rental house has merit, it is pointed and considered, and then handed to the
Housing Corporation should there be a reasonable possibility that a State rental house will
be allocated. As I explained to the member's colleague the member for Mangere, there is a
limit below which-in most places, if not all—the number of points allocated could preclude
an application for a State rental house. The system has not been changed. I concede that the

allocation, as indeed to the corporation's lending aspects. In fact, that is being done.

I want to turn briefly to our main exporting industry, agriculture, and to mention some
of the measures introduced to assist it. The Government's approach has been quite simple. It
has given some short-term assistance where necessary by way of cash grants, and has
initiated longer-term programmes to give greater security and stability by underwriting
minimum prices across the board—a measure that was welcomed up and down the country.
The Government also picked up some costs—for instance, meat inspection fees. We have
taken the industry one stage further. Much land in New Zealand is capable of development.
Development is expensive, so we introduced grants to allow farmers to apply for interest-
free suspensory loans of up to $250 a ha for developing land, with 50 percent of the loan
written off after satisfactory development.
The Government also introduced a new policy to encourage more intensive use of small
holdings. There are 27 000 small holdings, many of which are underused. Those with small
holdings are encouraged to develop them more productively, to plant crops, or to find a way
to produce a greater return to New Zealand from 100 000 ha held in small holdings.
Another policy designed for the better use of land lies with the improvement of
irrigation subsidies. This improvement in irrigation subsidies ties in with the Government's
concept of regional development. Land-based industries are to be expanded so that they
contribute more to regional districts and country towns. The Government has dealt with
something that has annoyed the West Coast for a long time. The east coast has been able to
get irrigation assistance, but the West Coast has not been able to have drainage assistance.

sure that even members opposite will agree with that. I am sure they will also agree that it is

productivity of West Coast land, which is what we are sure will follow from our Budget
policies.

The Budget that has been debated over the last few days is the best Budget this country
has had. It is designed entirely for the times that New Zealand faces at present. It assists the
agricultural sector to produce the exports that are at the basis of our economy, and gives
incentives and support over a whole range of areas. It acknowledges and recognises the
limitations of working within the tight financial constraints we now have. It did not throw
away the constraints we have had to place on the economy since the National Government
took office in 1975. What it said to New Zealand was that we can now look forward with
some greater optimism, we can now give some support where previously we were unable to,
and we can now pick up some of the problems we were unable to attempt to deal with
before. Members have listened to a debate on a document which I believe will be
acknowledged by all New Zealanders as being one designed for the times. In this major
debate the Opposition has had its last opportunity to explain to the country what it would do
should it be elected as the Government at the end of the year. Members opposite have failed
miserably. They have not touched on exports—although they did make some glib comment

was spoken of briefly by the member for Mt. Albert. In matters of social concern members

I want to comment on the Budget provisions for the Maori people, and to examine what
has happened to them during the past 2 years. Young Maoris have become very vocal, and
many non-Maori New Zealanders who have become accustomed to Maori hospitality and
generosity have branded these young people as stirrers, and perhaps racists. They forget that
social patterns are changing in New Zealand, and that new policies are needed at both
central and local government level. Young Maoris are, more often than not, vocal about
land issues, where there is a common interest and a common ground.
In the last 6 years, although the amount voted has doubled from $24 million to $48
million, the amount provided for the needs of young Maoris has barely risen from the
average of 5 percent of the total Maori Affairs vote. At the moment the Maori population
comprises 70 percent of young people under the age of 20, yet the Budget appropriation for
their needs is only 5 percent of the total vote. The vote has doubled in the period I have
mentioned, but there has been a minimal increase of only about 0.1 percent for youth. Is it
any wonder that today young Maoris are more vocal about their frustrations and grievances
than ever before in our history? The country itself is to blame if they become impatient. The
results of that neglect are hardly surprising. Since the new Secretary of Maori Affairs took
office a few months ago he has publicly expressed his desire to move more and more towards
the provision of funds for people-orientated programmes. He should be given every
encouragement, but I fear that those changes in attitudes will not be made under the
provisions of this Budget.
Three-quarters of the Maori population now reside permanently in our towns and
cities—a complete reversal of the position 25 years ago. That, among other things, has
caused many changes, including increased social difficulties and more problems for
individuals and families. During the last 2 years, employment opportunities have
diminished. Housing provisions, which should have improved under the Budget, have been
slashed by $1 million. How can we expect an improvement in living conditions? Health care
is unsatisfactory, and family ties and community disciplines have weakened.

built, or double the number built under the previous Labour Government. The best that
Government could do was to build 52 in its last year.

industry. Do members opposite agree that the increases in the dairy marketing guaranteed

These and many other measures in the Budget have passed unnoticed, but I should like
to pick out two in particular. Page 22 of the Budget deals with the commercial trials of new
horticultural crops. It points out that the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research
and the research division of the Ministry of Agriculture are continually striving to produce
strains of well-known horticultural crops. I should like to deal for a moment or two with the
tremendously important work being done by scientists in the Department of Scientific and
Industrial Research and in many other research organisations, such as those in the
universities, and in research associations. Those programmes, dealing with the development
and production of new crops, will mean that New Zealand's place in the world in this field
will be even more sure in the near future than it is today.
Apart from the use of biological products in the development of an oil-based industry,
one thing that requires attention is the development of wood burners that, although small,
can obtain complete combustion, and at the same time enable us to overcome some of the
heating problems in the home. A simple example relates to the question of complete
combustion. The Department of Scientific and Industrial Research has developed a burner
that is almost 100 percent efficient. By its burning 10 kg of wood-a relatively small
amount-we could obtain sufficient heat to maintain the full heating requirements of a
house.
The department is also greatly involved with research into horticulture in general, and
this will lead to great diversification and intensification of agriculture. Some of the things we
shall be doing will take some of the traditional products of this country away from traditional
areas of agricultural production. If we are to continue to maintain our place in the world we
have to maintain the levels of traditional agricultural production. I am not suggesting that we
diminish them. The Budget makes provision for a move towards greater productivity in hill-
country areas such as those in Rangitikei and Manawatu, where there is a possibility of
greater use of higher-producing country. Therefore, the provisions in the Budget for
subsidising commercial trials of new crops is already of extreme importance.
It may surprise members to know that we have already evolved a great variety of new
crops. Forward estimates of food production on present prices show that by the early 1980s
kiwi fruit will have displaced pipfruit as our most valuable horticultural crop, even though
the production of the latter crop is expanding rapidly. In the last 10 years the value of exports
of kiwi fruit has increased from nil to $13 million. While we have been slow to be involved in
fruit processing, that should also be undertaken, and activity in the Department of Scientific
and Industrial Research is increasing accordingly. Over the last 20 years the production of
pipfruit—that is, apples and pears-has more than doubled. During the same time the
amount of pipfruit processed has risen from nothing to about 20 percent of production.
That is what we are doing with our traditional crops, but in other areas the potential is
almost as great. We have a variety of climates suited to horticultural crops, and only a small
part of the soil resources suitable for horticulture is being used for that purpose. We have the
expertise in growing traditional crops such as pipfruits, stone fruits, citrus, grapes,
berryfruits, and kiwi fruit, and so our research is centred on the intense production of
superior varieties and stocks while improving and increasing the number and variety of other
products. So that item in the Budget, which appears to have gone unnoticed so far, is of
tremendous significance to New Zealand's total agricultural production.

that has been arousing interest in the last year or so and has been tending to come to a head
just now. I am thinking of the upsurge in interest in what is being taught, and of the question
constantly being asked, whether standards are changing, for better or for worse. This has
been a continuing preoccupation of mine, as it should be, because as Minister I have the
ultimate responsibility in these fields. To be certain of whether there has been any change I
have taken several important steps, and I shall remind the House of them tonight. Last year I
asked the department to look at educational standards in State schools. The department was
asked to prepare a report, I have it with me now. It is a good report. It has only recently

In the judgment of the inspectors standards in the basic subjects are generally being
maintained, and that in face of a great many influences that impede the progress of some

prepared for citizenship and work. Changes in competency can be measured only by a
massive long-term objective research programme. This is of little value in a short-term
objective research programme. However, the research that is available does confirm the
judgment of the inspectors.
The survey found that in most subjects standards were being maintained. There is no
doubt that some of the less able students are better prepared than were their counterparts of
30 years ago, but let us not forget that the complexity of our modern society is placing a
greater demand on basic skills and creating many new problems. I was concerned to read in

able students than among the less able. The difference between the able and the less able
student is wider, and appears to be widening further. The report also confirms outside
comment that students are having difficulty with computation, particularly long division,
and, to a lesser extent, long multiplication. Some of us might ask ourselves when we last did
long division or long multiplication calculations without the use of the small computers most
of us have on our desks. The report also draws attention to other school activities that are no
less important to the education of effective citizens, workers, and parents. The report states
that art and outdoor activities are generally satisfactory, but that physical education and
music cause the writers of the report some concern. I am sure that when the report is
released it will contribute greatly to a public discussion on educational standards.

Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I shall deal with some of the basics. Reading is a basic subject,

becomes less and less. Between 1500 and 2000 teachers volunteered to take part in the Early
Reading In-Service Course, sometimes referred to as ERIC. Two long-term courses for

individual weaknesses, and to provide programmes suited to individual needs.
Recognising that parents have an important role in helping children to read, the

A similar course was held last year in Feilding. I believe it was valuable, and I should like to

Last year Government approval was given for a programme designed to improve
mathematics textbooks used in primary schools. Between $1.5 million and $2 million will be
spent on this programme, and over the next few years the new textbooks will be introduced
into the schools as they become available. The new textbooks will replace those introduced
during the 1960s, which have served schools well but are no longer adequate. Those
textbooks taught children a range of mathematical topics that went a long way beyond the
simple arithmetic we knew. The new books will place more emphasis on computation than
do the books they are replacing, and the content will be more relevant to New Zealand.

What worries me about this call for "back to the basics" is the implied criticism of the

profession than this country is. I wish every critic of the system would take the opportunity to
visit the schools, to talk to teachers, and to see what is being done.

educational standards will concern itself less with recrimination, name calling, and a search
for scapegoats, and more with what needs to be done to ensure that children and young
people whose educational standards are less than satisfactory are better equipped through
their schooling to face what may well be a very uncertain future. But whatever direction the
public debate takes, it is hoped that one thing of the greatest importance can be accepted
without further question: a concern for educational standards is a central concern of the
teaching profession. It always has been. It is no less a central concern now than it ever was.

The hard reality is that Auckland is not as pleasant a place to bring up children as it was

The stock explanation is that the deterioration in the quality of life is an inevitable
consequence of size, and in terms of area Auckland is a big metropolis. It stretches for 60
km, from Albany in the north to Papakura in the south. On a world scale Auckland City
covers one of the largest areas, but with a population of only 750 000 it is not a large city. I
reject the argument that Auckland's problems are an inevitable result of size. Size does
present challenges, but they are not insurmountable. If size alone caused the deterioration in
life, then crooners would not sing about Paris, San Francisco, and London.
The quality of life is not changing because of Auckland's size, but because of the
problems of growth and social change that have been neglected for the 22 years since the
second world war that the National Party has been in power. I was born when the first
Labour Government was in office. That Government faced up to the challenges of
Auckland's rapid growth. What was done by the first Labour Government is an inspiration
to us all. Model suburbs such as Tamaki, in which the Prime Minister resides, have high
quality State houses. In 1950 Auckland was basically a port, and its largest industry was the
freezing industry.

Auckland stagnated through the 1950s. The quality of State housing declined the
moment National came into office. In that period houses deteriorated; they were not as good
as the first houses that were built. The second Labour Government came in, and in only 3
years laid the foundations for the manufacturing industries of Auckland. Those
manufacturing industries, founded under the second Labour Government, are now
spearheading the export drive. The success of those Auckland companies says much for the
planning initiatives of the second Labour Government and for the entrepreneural skills and
the hard work of Aucklanders. It was clear then that whole new suburbs had to be planned,
and the second Labour Government went about buying land in an ambitious programme to
found new model suburbs to emulate the first ones.
Unfortunately for Auckland, the National Party came into office and foisted on my
home city some of the biggest disasters in town planning. The National Government built
Otara and Mangere, which in town planning terms can be regarded only as disastrous. Every
single rule of town planning and every single lesson for building a good neighbourhood were
broken. Houses were built without thought, and there was no adequate preparation for
schools, transport, and community facilities. In Otara today two completely portable schools
are built on reserves because the National Government in the 1960s could not do its
arithmetic and work out how many children there would be. The fact that Otara has
managed to build neighbourhoods and a community spirit is a tribute to its people, and no
thanks is owed to the National Government.
National's planners added difficulty to Auckland by actively promoting the so-called
elite social suburbs of North Shore and Pakuranga. These suburbs have social problems of
their own. They are typified by extraordinarily high mortgage debts and high rates of
marriage breakdown. These suburbs have as many social problems as the new suburbs of
Otara and Mangere. North Shore and Pakuranga would have been better suburbs if they had
had the same cross section and social mixture that typified the first model suburbs built in
Tamaki by the first Labour Government.

Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora): The Opposition appears to have given up its fight in this
debate, which is an ideal opportunity to compare the economic policies of the National
Government with those of the Labour Party. The Opposition put forward what it called "an
alternative budget", and no doubt it will argue its merits during the election campaign and
expect to be judged on it by the electors. From a philosophical point of view, the
Government's Budget and the Opposition's alternative budget illustrate the wide gulf
between the two parties, particularly in the attitude to taxation. The National Government,
both in the past and more particularly in this Budget, has made substantial progress towards
restructuring taxation. The change that will take effect from 1 October 1978 does away with
the present 19 steeply rising progressive tax scales, and substitutes five plateaus.
Two basic problems are associated with the present tax scales. First the tax on additional
earnings and I am thinking particularly of overtime-is far too high. If a person moves
from $85 a week to $155 a week, the tax rises from 19c in the dollar to 46c in the dollar. The
second basic problem with the present tax scales is that far too much tax-about 25
percent is taken from the average taxpayer. The five plateaus to be introduced will tax up
to $4,500 of taxable income at 14c in the dollar; from $4,500 to $10,000 at 38c; and the three
further steps will be at 48c, 55c, and 60c in the dollar, at which rate the taxable income will
be over $22,000. This tax change will substantially lift the tax burden on the lower middle-
income earners.
The extent of this change and of the changes that have taken place during the last 2
years are clearly demonstrated by a comparison of a person who earned $6,000 of taxable

What is the Opposition's attitude to GATT? The member for Kapiti has spelt out in
considerable detail some of the GATT provisions. Its obligations are binding, and in the past
New Zealand has not been slow to remind other member countries of the provisions. I refer
particularly to the sheepmeats regime. Perhaps a future Labour Government would attempt
to rely on article 25 of GATT, which allows the use of multiple currency exchange fees for
balance of payment protection with the approval of the International Monetary Fund. Some
South American countries have relied on multiple currency exchange fees and they have not
been particularly successful in dealing with their overseas exchange problems or with
inflation.
Leaving aside the question of illegality, if the Labour Party was able to introduce the
surcharge on foreign exchange, would it receive the $400 million in revenue that it would
need? The total exchange payments for the year ended March 1978 amounted to $4,652
million, and 10 percent of that amount is a little more than $400 million. That is the figure
the Labour Party is discussing. It has introduced exceptions, so the foreign tax will not be an
across-the-board imposition. Some of the exemptions that have been mentioned are
exports—both primary and secondary-freight, inputs into farming, and selected travel.
Apparently New Zealanders who have not travelled overseas within the past 5 years will be
exempt. Surely people who are travelling overseas to sell New Zealand products will be
exempt from the 10 percent imposition.
What goods are left? What items can be taxed by a future Labour Government to obtain
the $400 million that has been referred to? Private payments other than for imports for the
year ended March 1978 totalled $1,263 million. Only three types of payments could be taxed.
Overseas fares, which amounted to $133 million, could be taxed, but the Labour Party has
said that some fares will be exempt. Payments for travel amounted to $298 million, but travel
is to be partially exempt too. A likely item is the $61.9 million of remittances sent home by
Islanders. If a future Labour Government imposes a 10 percent surcharge on remittances it
will not be profitable for Island people to work in New Zealand. By the time the exemptions
have been applied it is unlikely that a future Labour Government would receive more than
$25 million on private payments. Opposition members say private imports can be taxed. For
the year ended March 1978 private imports amounted to $2,900 million, representing a
potential tax of $290 million.
What items are likely to be taxed? Agricultural machinery and plant will be excluded.
Transport and communication items amounted to $524.3 million for the year ended June
1977, but part of the freight content would be excluded. Finished goods and components are
classed as consumption or capital according to the type of buyer, and for the same year
amounted to $434.2 million. The two major items in that category are assembled and
unassembled motor cars. Will a future Labour Government impose a 10 percent tax on the
cost of motor vehicles at the point of entry? What about the Government content of overseas
payments? Surely a future Labour Government will not impose a surcharge on Government
borrowing or interest payments.
When it is all added up, the only item left is consumer goods, and Italian shoes were
specifically mentioned. I wonder how many millions of dollars were spent last year on the
importation of Italian shoes. Other items mentioned were toys, tea, and china. Will the New
Zealand consumer be pleased to find a 10 percent increase on those commodities at the point
of entry? If a 10 percent tax is imposed on a commodity when it enters New Zealand, the cost
to the consumer will be substantially higher. That assumes that a future Labour Government
could obtain enough money to bridge the gap it would need to bridge.
We will not be faced with a 10 percent imposition. Labour would be lucky to be able to
tax more than $200 million on the list that I have outlined. That means that if it wants to get
$400 million worth of revenue it will have to impose a 20 percent surcharge on foreign
exchange. The Deputy Leader of the Opposition has already admitted to a likely increase of
2 percent in the consumer price index, and that was only on a 10 percent imposition. We
know how wrong the member has been in talking about inflation on previous occasions. It is
a gigantic fraud, and a cover to introduce after election year-if New Zealand is unfortunate
enough to have a Labour Government—some other form of tax, probably a capital gains tax.

Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga): I think all members would agree with the remark made by

The final comments made by the Minister of Finance in the 1978 Budget are, "This is a
generous Budget, but no more generous than economic realities require." Over the past 12
months there has been a serious stagnation, as I am sure everyone interested in economics
would agree. It is extremely difficult for a Government to slow down the activities of the
community within a short term. Indeed, it is a little like slowing down a large steamship
when it has a full head of steam. The ship travels many miles before it reacts to the controls.
In the same way, Government moves will not result in positive reactions in the short term.
Towards the end of 1976 the economy received a greater stimulus than it was felt by some it
could stand. However, over the past 12 months a serious stagnation has affected
unemployment in a way that has been unprecedented during the past 25 years. As a
consequence, some action has to be taken not only to stimulate the economy, but also to
ensure that we achieve the exports on which the country is so vitally dependent.
There are three main ways of achieving efficiency. The first, I suggest is that the
Government has a responsibility to ensure maximum efficiency in the expenditure of
Government revenue-in other words, to ensure that every taxpayer's contribution to the
public purse is spent wisely and in the best interests of the country. The second is that there
must be maximum efficiency within the private sector, particularly to ensure that all business
activities increase productivity. An increase in productivity is one of the greatest needs
today. Productivity per head of population in New Zealand is frighteningly low when
compared with that of other countries that share what is commonly called a Western-style
civilisation. Productivity must be increased if we are to maintain our present living

1030
20 June

standards, let alone improve them; and improve them we must. The third point is the need
for much greater flexibility in our exports of primary produce, which account for 80 percent
of New Zealand's overseas earnings.
I go back to my first point, the Government's responsibility to ensure maximum
efficiency. The Government made a sound move in calling for a report by the Controller and
Auditor-General on the financial management and control in administrative Government
departments. That report sent shockwaves throughout the country, and certainly throughout
the bureaucracy. The summary of conclusions includes this statement: "Financial
management in administrative departments is mediocre and lacks positive leadership. The
focus of attention has been confined for too long to the narrow purpose of keeping
expenditure within estimates." The more we think about that statement, the more we realise
that the Government has a major responsibility to take notice of the report to ensure greater
imagination and greater competence.
The summary of conclusions also states: "There is a serious shortage of competent
accountants able to provide a proper financial management service." Departments, such as
the Ministry of Works and Development and the Department of Social Welfare, have
tremendous responsibility for expenditure in their respective areas. Though the report may
highlight such facts, it will be of no use if it gets buried or is put on the shelf to gather dust
over the years. The Government has responsibility to act on the report.
In view of the difficulties facing New Zealand at present, great care must be exercised in
the expenditure of Government revenue, but this must not be done at the expense of our
education, health, and social welfare services. At the same time, while the public should get
what it is entitled to, there must be no abuses. For instance, there must be no irresponsible
and unnecessary expenditure on education. Educational aids and equipment are no
substitute for sound teaching methods, although frequently they are imagined to be.
Spending large sums in this area of education will achieve little. We have heard criticism of
the frighteningly low standard of fundamental education, and must look hard and long at
this.
We must ensure that there are no rip-offs, as they are commonly termed, in social
welfare expenditure, while making sure that money is available for where it is needed. The
average New Zealander accepts this, and, understandably, is angry when he sees
unnecessary Government expenditure. It is all very well to promise money for this and that,
but we must bear in mind where Government revenue comes from. Most people think of the
Budget in terms of what it will do for them personally. How much will my taxation be
reduced? That is what the taxpayer wants to know, and reduced it must be, as it has been,
even though many anomalies remain. The fact remains that a deficit of $1,000 million is
budgeted for. That shortfall has to be picked up somewhere along the way, and naturally the
public wants to know where it will come from.
That is why my second point-the maximising of efficiency within the private sector-
must be taken into account. After all, Government revenue comes from the private or
trading sector. It comes from the taxpayers. Over $3 billion of taxpayers' money is used by
the Government to discharge its responsibilities. When there is a down-turn in business, and
company profits drop, the shortfall of funds that would normally come from company profits
must come from each and every taxpayer's pocket. When company profits or trading are
down, both young and old must pick up the shortfall. That is why the Government stated
that it would be no more generous than the economic realities required; and economic
realities dictate that we must stimulate the economy to ensure that there is profit in the
private sector, because only then can we make the advances that are so necessary.
The Government recently introduced legislation that I consider to be of the utmost
importance, although I am not entirely happy with the way it is being done. I have said that
before, and will say it again. I am referring to the small business administration that was
mentioned in the National Party's 1975 election manifesto. It was recognised that over 95
percent of New Zealand businesses can be classed as small businesses. A small business is
defined as one in which one or two people make all the major decisions, as opposed to the
multinationals, which employ full-time professionals in each section of the enterprise. The
definition of a small business also covers manufacturing enterprises that employ up to 50
people. They represent approximately 95 percent of all businesses, and the difficulties they
face are the same as the difficulties that are being faced by small businesses throughout the
world.
In America the SBA, which has been operating since the early 1940s, has saved many

businesses from failure, and has made it possible for many small businesses to grow into

The third point to which I draw attention is overseas marketing of our produce, and
