Internal incentives are vital to encourage the growth that everybody knows is there.
When one is considering the drop in imports, one must remember that a part of that drop
represents raw materials that would, in normal circumstances, be exported. Therefore, there
must be stimulation to increase exports. Firms must realise their potential. All too often,
however, we ignore the "sacred cows"-the producer boards-and do not ask whether they
are working to their full capacity. Meat exports totalling $903 million and wool exports
totalling $612 million are a tremendous achievement, and the recently announced increase in
United States beef imports is a welcome step. The producer boards have a tremendous
potential for diversifying food products, but we must also encourage private entrepreneurs
to enter this field, because the time has long passed when our exports could be marketed
through a single channel.
The world is wide open for many of these diversified products. Markets exist in the
Caribbean, South America, South-east Asia, and many other countries, and small though
many of them are, collectively they represent substantial business for New Zealand. With a
population of only 3 100 000, it should not be difficult with modern technology and skills to
raise our standards substantially. This can be done if we encourage the people who are active
in many fields. All too frequently members hear of instances-and I have come across some
myself of exporters receiving the opportunity to export products controlled by producer
boards, only to be told that they cannot export the goods. This dampening effect is not in the
best interests of New Zealand. Primary products have almost a 100 percent New Zealand
content, and are the easiest way of increasing our overseas earnings. Tourism and the
airlines, which come under the heading of overseas trade, are similar. Increases in these
areas are necessary if we are to improve our terms of trade and increase our productivity.
We must prevent the further disappearance of skilled people. Incentives must be
created. One of the objects of Export Year is to give incentives to bring people back to New
Zealand and to encourage the people to strike out and find new markets. The people must
not see the disadvantages of living in New Zealand, which they often do in times of economic
hardship. They must see the advantages and shoulder the responsibility to ensure that the
country grows and does not continue to lose momentum. Once momentum has been lost it is
difficult to regain it. In Government administration the departments closely linked with
trading-particularly the Department of Trade and Industry and the service departments—
must pay particular attention through the trading commissioners, the High Commissioners,
and the embassies to ensure that staff are fully professional in their approach. The idea that a


## p. 1032 (#142) ###########################################

1032
20 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
position overseas is a perk must be forgotten, and staff must realise that their work is vital to
New Zealand.
We must break the all too frequent insular attitude of New Zealanders, which they
cannot afford to have. We must reach out to the world markets and find out precisely what
they want. We must produce what they will buy. It is no good presenting the countries in
South-east Asia with thumping big blocks of butter and stating that that is what New Zealand
markets. We must find out what packs those countries want, and produce the butter in that
form. It must be flavoured as those countries want it, not as we want to dump it on them.
Greater emphasis must be put on market research.
I welcome the statement by the export guarantee office that it will consider providing
100 percent unconditional guarantees on pre-shipment finance and trust that it will work
effectively. The statement includes the words "in such cases". How this will work out in
practice remains to be seen, but the export guarantee office is giving consideration to the
tremendous amount of expenditure necessary by exporters, potential exporters, and
entrepreneurs to find, establish, and sustain markets. Unless we are able to do that we
cannot hope to build the healthy export' industry that we are capable of supporting. We have
our first foot on the ladder, but in terms of markets we have not gone much beyond that
point. We are moving in the right direction, but the need is desperate, and there is no
evading that fact. Overexpenditure has had a seriously dampening effect over the last 12
months. Therefore, the necessary stimulation must be applied and, at the same time,
directed towards overseas earning capacity. Industry must be encouraged and I was glad to
see incentives for industry in the Budget. But putting them in the Budget is one thing; acting
on them is another. We trust that action will be properly carried out and that the
Government departments responsible will apply satisfactory and proper management.
I refer to aid for developing countries. It must not be the type of aid given shortly after
the war. Today, it must be linked with trade. We cannot continue to vote moneys to certain
countries and tell them that they have so many million dollars to spend on some worthy
project. We should work for the betterment of those countries. Nothing is gained by giving
food if we do not show the people how to grow it for themselves. I think it was Ghandi who
was supposed to have said: "Give a man a fish and you have fed him for a day; teach him to
fish and you have fed him for a lifetime." That is the underlying principle that must be
applied to all aid for development countries, and to any country to which the Government or
the people of New Zealand see fit to give aid. Our ability to give aid is governed by our
prosperity, which brings me back to the three main points.
First, the administration of Government expenditure must be managed responsibly, and
the Government must look carefully at the calibre of people in high places within the
bureaucracy. Secondly, proper, careful, and effective incentives must be given to ensure that
the level of productivity we need is reached, and substantially increased. Thirdly, we must
ensure above all else that our exports increase more than our imports, including the invisible
payments in the form of insurance, freight, and the repayment of loans, which are a serious
drain on our economy. If we apply these principles, and adopt the positive elements of the
Budget to encourage exporters to work to their utmost, I am sure New Zealand will advance
as it should.
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.

Domestic Purposes Benefits-Terminations
1. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) to the Minister of Social Welfare: How many domestic
purposes benefits were terminated in the 1976-77 and 1977-78 financial years by the spouses
reuniting, what percentage of the total was this, and how many were the result of the
counselling of the marriage guidance service?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): During the year ended 31 March
1977 a total of approximately 11 500 domestic purposes benefits were cancelled. The
corresponding figure for the year ended 31 March 1978 was 13 400. No detailed statistics are
available as to the precise reasons for termination, but it is estimated that approximately 25
percent of cancellations are the result of reconciliations. On this basis about 3350
beneficiaries reconciled with their spouse in the year ended 31 March 1978 compared with
about 2850 in the previous year. It is not known how many of the reconciliations were
directly due to the counselling of marriage guidance officers.
Mrs Batchelor: Since the introduction of the new regulations, how many people on full
domestic purposes benefits have become reconciled, and also how many on the limited rate
of domestic purposes benefit have become reconciled?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: We do not have statistics to show that, but a sample was taken of
the benefits that ceased between January and May 1978, and it worked out that about 25
percent of the beneficiaries had been reconciled. The only other information I can give the
honourable member is that the rate of increase in applications for the domestic purposes
benefit has decreased from 23.2 percent in the year 1976-77 to 10 percent in the last full
financial year.
Mr Lange: Of the 25 000 disclosed by the survey earlier this year, how many have been
referred to a conciliator?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Here again, the scheme has not been going long enough for
precise statistics to be available. Before the scheme was introduced, marriage guidance
councillors said that they were able to give positive help to about 30 percent of the people
referred to them. They now say they are able to give positive help to about 60 percent of
those referred.
Mrs Batchelor: Do the figures the Minister quoted include the emergency maintenance
allowance, and does the figure used for the domestic purposes benefit include those people
who are on the emergency maintenance allowance?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: There is a difference between the emergency maintenance
allowance and the domestic purposes benefit, but I understand that the figure does include
those who are or were in receipt of the emergency maintenance allowance.

Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui): Opposition members have been speaking about regional

at the end of 1975, at best, regional development has stood still, and at worst, in many areas
it has lost ground substantially. I wish to refer to questions 77 and 120. They refer to my
electorate and the area surrounding it.
Under the Labour Government between 1973 and 1975 there was considerable
expansion of established local industry in the Wanganui region and in other regions around
the country. In some instances new industries were established under the Government's
regional development policy. A certain amount of decentralisation took place, and there was
a boost in housing as a spin-off from that industrial development. Above all, and most
important, there was a revival of confidence in many of the provincial towns around the
country. That confidence came mainly from the establishment of regional development
councils, and from the restructuring of the Development Finance Corporation. Before that
of course, we had years of neglect by successive National Governments, with years of reports
and research, but no activity.
The Wanganui region particularly, benefited from the Labour Government's policy. A
regional development council was established within 6 months, and the answer to question
120 shows the enormous boost that came to the Wanganui region from the restructuring of
the Development Finance Corporation. In the 9 years from July 1964 to June 1973 only 9
companies received assistance. In the 5 years following, the Development Finance
Corporation was reorganised and 81 companies have received assistance amounting to $11.4
million. The bulk of that assistance to most of those companies was given under the Labour
Government, at least until the middle of 1976. That, of course, was the major reason for the
boost in confidence in the Wanganui region. Fortunately, thanks to the quality of the council
appointed by the member for Mt. Albert 5 years ago, and to the qualities of that council's
executive officer, Wanganui has continued to receive a spin-off from that activity, and has
survived relatively well in the 2½ years since the change of government, although at a rather
reduced level of activity.
We need a revitalisation of regional development policies, and more active
encouragement from the Government. We also need more imagination in the development
of new policies to take us on to the next stage. I make a particular plea for the plight of the
smaller towns, the Taihapes, the Woodvilles, the Eketahunas, and the Pateas. The time is
overdue for an overall policy which will give extra assistance to encourage industry to stay in

Electricity-Loss in Transmission
3. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Energy: Can he give any precise estimates
of what proportion of power transmitted from the South Island to the North Island is lost in
the transmission process, and an estimate of the approximate value of power lost in the
transmission process?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: During the year ended 31 March 1978, the
amount of energy sent from the South Island was 1349 GWh and the amount received in the
North Island was 1244 GWh. The transmission loss was therefore 105 GWh or 7.8 percent of
the energy sent. This compares with a loss in the same year over the whole NZE system of
the order of 6 percent. The approximate value of the energy lost is $1.46 million or 0.5
percent of the estimated $292 million electricity revenue in the year ended March 1978.
However, the value of the energy received in the North Island must be assigned a value on
the basis of thermal station replacement costs. The value of energy received in the North
Island, based on replacement at Meremere costs, is $17.35 million.

(1/6/78)
International Energy Agency
5. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Energy: Can he state how the
International Energy Agency is financed and what contribution, if any, New Zealand paid in
the last and in this financial year, and did the experts reporting on the New Zealand energy
scene come as a result of an invitation, or as part of the agency's duties?
Hon. G. F. AIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The International Energy Agency is
financed by member countries according to a scale of contributions determined according to
the principles and rules set out in the annex to the "OECD Resolution of the Council on
Determination of the Scale of Contributions by Member Countries to the Budget of the
Organisation". In effect, members contribute to the agency an amount determined


## p. 1053 (#163) ###########################################

21 June
1053
Questions and Replies
according to their GNP figures for the preceding year. New Zealand's contribution to the
IEA was $47,873 in 1977-78. An appropriate provision is being made in the 1978-79
estimates. Every year the International Energy Agency reviews the energy policies of
member countries on the basis of responses to questionnaires prepared by the agency. The
agency also conducts "in-depth" reviews of members on a 3-year cycle, which involves a
team of three to five officials visiting the country being reviewed. Energy measures in place
are examined thoroughly, and some consultations held with the energy industries. New
Zealand was one of the countries selected for in-depth review in the first year of the cycle,
and there were no grounds for asking for deferment.

Wine Resellers-Sale by the Glass
12. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Justice: Does he intend this year to amend
section 156 of the Sale of Liquor Act 1962 to provide for the sale of wine by the glass by those
holding wine resellers' licences?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: I do not propose to introduce any
major liquor amendments into the House this session, and this would clearly be both a major
and contentious change. I am not unsympathetic to the concept in principle and will consider
it, along with the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Liquor on this topic, for
possible legislative action next year. I told this to representatives of the New Zealand Wine
Resellers Association when I met them on 10 March, but pointed out to them the difficulties
that we may run into because of our GATT obligations. A provision in the 1962 Sale of
Liquor Bill to allow the establishment of licensed restaurants selling New Zealand wine only
was withdrawn following a Crown law opinion that it would breach our obligation under the


## p. 1055 (#165) ###########################################

21 June
1055
Questions and Replies
GATT treaties to treat imported products in the same manner as we treat our own. The
association claims that other countries have the facility that they are currently seeking. If, as
I suspect, these facilities (like our current wine resellers' licence that permits the sale of New
Zealand wine by the bottle) were in existence before countries entered into their GATT
obligations, then their continued existence does not constitute a breach of GATT. It is the
creation of new facilities that could constitute a contravention. However, I have asked my
department to look into the matter further and it is currently awaiting a further opinion from
the Crown Law Office as to whether implementation of the royal commission's
recommendations on the sale of wine by the glass would constitute a breach of our GATT
obligations.

Freezing Works-Export Standards
25. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of Agriculture: (a) Can he list each of
the freezing works in New Zealand, together with the export kills in each case over the past 5
years; (b) How many of these works have been delisted for particular export markets, which
are these, and for which markets have they been delisted; and (c) in each case under (b), can

taken by the companies concerned to meet the hygiene requirements of the countries for
which they have been delisted?

divulgence of the names of the companies removed from the export lists of certain countries
or the time span of such delistments is contrary to policy, and, in the interests of the
companies concerned, is not made public. In most cases individual companies have moved
expeditiously to correct the operational defects involved. However, where problems relate
to constructional work, there are some companies which have responded more slowly. No
New Zealand meat export premises comply with the E.E.C. requirements at present.

Electricity Users-Connection Deposit
26. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Energy: (a) Can he list each of the district
electricity and gas supply authorities that apply a policy whereby tenants, but not home
owners, are required to pay deposits of $20 before their power supplies are met; (b) can he
give an estimate of the amounts currently being held by supply authorities in this fashion; (c)
can he indicate what proportion of the total amount held in deposits has been returned to
tenants after a 2-year period by any typical electricity or gas supply authority; and (d) what
steps do power supply authorities take to ensure that (i) tenants are compensated for their
loss in the value of their deposits held over a 2-year period as a consequence of inflation, and
(ii) tenants who are entitled to a refund after 2 years do in fact get that refund?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: (a) No. Each gas undertaking and
electrical supply authority is free to set its own conditions in regard to the amount of the
deposit, whether it should apply to tenants only or consumers generally, and the length of
time for which it is held. (b) No. Gas undertakings and electrical supply authorities statistics
do not show this as a specific item. (c) No. (d) (i) In accordance with normal business
practice, I would not expect any compensation for the effects of inflation. (ii) I am not in a
position to know how gas undertakings or electrical supply authorities ensure that refunds
due to tenants after 2 years are in fact made.

(6/6/78)
Honey Returned from Japan
31. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt Albert) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: What was the
reason for the return on the ship Aotea, which arrived in Auckland from Kobe on 6 April
1978, of seven drums of local honey consigned to the Honey Marketing Authority, what was
the total weight and value of the consignment and the cost of freight to and from Japan, and
who carried this loss?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied: The seven drums of
honey returned on the ship Aotea from Japan were refused entry by the Japanese authorities
because the honey was discovered to contain slightly more than 5 percent sucrose, this being
the maximum permitted level set by the Japanese. Climatic or seasonal factors occasionally
result in honey from certain floral sources containing more than the usual amount of sucrose,
but, because this seldom occurs, little research has been done on the problem, and the
reasons why the sucrose level of some New Zealand honeys occasionally exceeds 5 percent is
not known. To avoid any further shipments being returned from Japan, consignments of
bulk honey to Japan are now being sampled and analysed for their chemical composition and
an accompanying certificate is being supplied. The total weight of the seven drums was 2.142
tonnes, valued at NZ$2,467.50. The total freight to and from Japan was $612.76; the return
freight of $387.88 being higher than the outward freight because the seven drums had been
part of a total consignment of 56 drums. In addition to these freight costs, the customs,
inspection, and analysis charges in Japan amounted to a further $873.50, making a total cost
of $1,486.26, which was borne by the New Zealand Honey Marketing Authority. The honey
is now back with the authority, and as the sucrose content has no effect whatsoever on its
flavour or suitability for human consumption it will be perfectly acceptable for use within
New Zealand.

Abortions-Dr Peter Willcox
46. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Justice: Is he aware of the grounds
on which the supervisory committee declined Dr Peter Willcox's application to become a
certifying consultant; what rights of appeal or challenge has Dr Willcox got against this
decision; and, if he has no rights, can the Minister advise of any other decision by any
statutory body for which he has responsibility which can be made in camera, decided without
reasons being given, and is not subject to appeal?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: In exercising its statutory functions
under the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977 the Abortion Supervisory
Committee had declined to appoint a number of applicants as certifying consultants. In
doing so the committee has thought it proper not to give reasons for its decisions, and it does
not intend to depart from that practice in the case of Dr Willcox. The statute does not confer
a right of appeal upon a person whose application is declined by the committee. Regardless
of the existence or otherwise of appeal rights, every statutory body is required to act within
the law. If it does not do so then the Supreme Court in the exercise of its supervisory
jurisdiction may review the decision to which objection is taken. This is a principal of general
application, but the outcome of such proceedings, if they were to be taken by Dr Willcox,
would be for the court to determine, not the Minister.

Energy-Intensive Industries
51. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Energy: (a) What are the recognised
criteria for classifying industries as energy intensive, and (b) what proportion of the
industries that fall within this classification and are heavily dependent upon (i) coal, and (ii)
hydro-electricity, are located in close proximity to the source of energy upon which they
depend to produce their products?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: (a) The major criterion is the amount of
energy used by an industry per unit of output. Another important factor in considering
energy consumption by industries is the total amount of energy used. For example, the
cement industry has a high energy input per unit of output, but the meat-processing industry
is a larger energy-user in terms of total energy consumption. (b) In answer to the second part
of the member's question, it is possible to give examples only: (i) coal-the Westport
Cement Works and New Zealand Steel's iron and steel plant at Glenbrook, South Auckland;
(ii) hydro-electricity-the Bluff aluminium smelter. Energy is, of course, only one of the
factors that determine the location of a particular industry. For example, the major factor
determining the location of the large forest-processing industries has been the source of the
timber they require rather than their source of energy. Also, most energy-intensive
industries were established before the upsurge in energy prices in 1973.

(8/6/78)
Police J-Team, South Auckland
58. Mr LANGE (Mangere) to the Minister of Police: What were the establishment figures
for J-team police work in the South Auckland division in 1975 and 1977?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied: In early 1975 one J-team was
based in the south Auckland division, and later that year a second team was formed and
operated from Papakura. There were six J-teams covering the whole of New Zealand in
1977, two being in the south Auckland police division. Additional youth aid officers have
been appointed to that division also since 1975 and, in all, 12 members of the Police are now
employed on youth aid, J-team, and law-related education duties. The complement of a J-
team is a social worker, a Maori community officer, a community volunteer, and a
policeman from the youth aid section.

Arapuni B Power Station
64. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Energy: When is it proposed to
proceed with Arapuni B, and what is its energy potential?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The 1977 report of the Power Planning
Committee recommended that approval to proceed with Arapuni B be sought by October
1978. It is already apparent that this date will not be met and at this stage it seems likely that
this project will need to be rescheduled for a much later completion date The Arapuni B
station is intended approximately to double the maximum throughput of water at this point
on the Waikato River. This approximately doubles the peak power generation and, because
of improved machine efficiency and the development of some additional head, provides an
additional energy potential of 142 GWh (million units) per annum.

Exports-Commodity Percentages
66. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) to the Minister of Statistics: Can he provide the House
with the percentage composition of the main export commodities for trade years 1975-76 and
1976-77?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Statistics) replied: The percentage contributions of
main commodities to New Zealand's total exports in 1975-76 were: meat and meat
preparations, 25 percent; dairy products, 16 percent; wool, 19 percent; hides and skins, 3
percent; forest products, 6 percent; chemicals, 2 percent; non-ferrous metals, 3 percent;
other manufactured products, 9 percent. The percentage contributions of the same main
commodities for 1976-77, stated in the same order as I have used in the first part of my reply,
were: meat and meat preparations, 24 percent; dairy products, 14 percent; wool, 20 percent;
hides and skins, 4 percent; forest products, 6 percent; chemicals, 3 percent; non-ferrous
metals, 4 percent; other manufactured products, 9 percent. A miscellaneous list of other
commodities as well as re-exports made up the balance of 17 percent in 1975-76 and 16
percent in 1976-77.

Australia-New Zealand Defence Production
86. Squadron Leader DRAYTON (St Albans) to the Minister of Defence: What extensions
of reciprocal activities under the Memorandum of Understanding on Australia - New
Zealand defence production have there been since March 1976?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence) replied: Following the initiatives taken
by the Prime Ministers of Australia and New Zealand, initially at Rotorua in 1976 and in
Canberra in March 1977, the respective Ministers of Defence met in Canberra in April 1977
to pursue proposals for further developing Australia - New Zealand defence co-operation.
At that meeting the Ministers agreed that steps should be taken to improve co-ordination
and rationalisation, particularly in such areas as defence production and supply co-
operation. An Australia - New Zealand policy group, supported by a supply working group,
is examining ways in which opportunities for joint production and supply may be developed
to the advantage of both countries.

LPG-South Island Costs
100. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What will be the
estimated expenditure on the South Island freight subsidy for the transport of LPG, what
will be the average selling price per litre of this fuel in the South Island, and how does this
compare with the average North Island litre cost?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The expenditure on the temporary freight
subsidy is estimated to amount to $200,000 in this financial year. The selling prices by
producers, wholesalers, and retailers vary over a wide range depending on the amount of
LPG purchased. It is not possible to calculate average selling prices. The most meaningful
comparison is in the bulk (8 tonne tank) selling prices; this amounts to 11.4c a litre in the
North Island, but has yet to be fixed for the South Island. However, it is expected to be of
the order of 16c a litre in the South Island when the special trailer units are brought into
operation in the near future.
(9/6/78)
Blood Plasma
101.
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Health: How much of New
Zealand's blood is turned into plasma in this country and how much overseas, and, if any is
processed overseas, why is this done?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: An exact figure of the quantity of New
Zealand blood turned into plasma is not at present available because the separation of
plasma from donated blood is performed at blood transfusion laboratories at all major
hospitals in New Zealand. No plasma is prepared from New Zealand blood overseas. In the
year ended 31 March 1978 approximately 10 000 litres of plasma were forwarded to
Commonwealth Serum Laboratories in Melbourne for fractionation into such products as
albumin, various blood-clotting factors, and specific immunoglobulins. Commonwealth
Serum Laboratories undertake fractionation of New Zealand plasma at present because New
Zealand has not yet established a fractionation plant in this country. Studies into the
feasibility and economic viability of the establishment of a New Zealand fractionation plant
are at present being evaluated.

Television-Children's Programmes
102. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Broadcasting: What proportion of the
programme budget of TV1 and TV2 respectively is expended on children's programmes?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: I am advised by the
Broadcasting Corporation that such proportions are not easily determined, because the
amount of television time devoted to the various programme categories is determined on
programme values and fluctuations in viewer interests. Budgetary allocations are dictated by
the form and content of the programmes themselves, so that budget figures do not
necessarily indicate the importance or effectiveness of a category of programmes, especially
those of a specialised nature.

Overseas Students-Bilateral Aid Scheme
108. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Can he list
separately the number of university students, technical institute students, and teacher
trainees who were in New Zealand under the bilateral aid scheme during the years 1975,
1976, 1977, and 1978?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS- SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: The total
number of students in New Zealand under the bilateral aid scheme during 1975 was 567. Of
these, approximately 443 were university students, 68 technical institute students, and 56
teacher trainees. In 1976 the total number of BAP students was 703. Of these, approximately
579 were university students, 80 technical students, and 68 teacher trainees. In 1977 the total
number of students was 412. Of these, 331 were university students, 50 were students at
technical institutes, and 31 were teacher trainees. As at 1 June 1978 the total number of
students studying under BAP was 396. Of these, 284 students were studying at universities,
91 at technical institutes, and 21 at teachers colleges.

Deportation Appeals
110. Mr LANGE (Mangere) to the Minister of Immigration: Has he determined any
appeals against orders for deportation under recently awarded powers, and, if so, what were
the numbers and the outcome?.
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied: From 1 February 1978, I received 133
appeals against deportation under the new provisions of the Immigration Act. Of these, 55
were received during the month of May. As at 7 June, 15 cases had been approved, 37 had
been declined, and 67 were still under action. Fourteen of the appeals could not be
considered, as they did not fall within the criteria laid down by the Act.

grounded as an economy measure, and, if so, how much will it save the Government, and
when will the service be reinstated?
Hon. W. L YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied: Magnetic sweeping of
all State highways in the South Island was discontinued by the National Roads Board in the
1977-78 financial year. The relatively small quantities of metal collected (64 ounces per mile
of road swept) were not considered sufficient to justify the $12,000 cost for full annual
coverage of these highways. Since then, coverage of parts of the highway system has

(14/6/78)
Depository Library Scheme
115. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) to the Minister in Charge of the Government Printing
Office: Has the Government Printing Office received any complaints from libraries or from
the New Zealand Library Association on the running of the depository scheme for
Government publications, under which certain libraries are designated full or selective
depositories to receive all or some publications; are all publications issued for sale listed on
the notices sent to libraries concerned for selection; are sufficient copies withheld from sale
to ensure that libraries requesting copies from the list receive copies, and are libraries
notified if copies are not available; and are publications requested as standing orders sent
regularly to the depositories without further request?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister in Charge of the Government Printing Office) replied:
The Government Printing Office has received complaints from individual libraries about the
operation of the depository library scheme. The complaints generally have been about the
delayed receipt or non-receipt of particular publications rather than criticisms about the
operation of the depository scheme itself. Requests have been made for improved
bibliographical information and, where possible, these have been met. Not all publications
issued for sale are notified on the weekly depository list sent to the libraries participating in
the scheme. The list is restricted to those publications published by the Government Printer
and those departmental publications for which he is the sole commercial distributor.
Publications bought in for sale from the DSIR or Department of Lands and Survey are not
included. Sufficient copies of all publications to meet the needs of depository libraries are
held in a separate area for approximately one month after having been notified on the list.
This allows sufficient time for selective depository libraries to make their choice and inform
the Government Printing Office. Publications on standing order are sent automatically
without libraries having to make further requests. A notification to this effect is appended to
every list.

Christian Medical College, Ludhiana, India-NZ Aid
121. Mr LANGE (Mangere) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: When did the Government
of New Zealand commit itself to providing aid to the Christian Medical College at Ludhiana,
India; to what sum is it committed; and how much had been paid as at 28 February 1978?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: In May
1975 the Associate Minister of Foreign Affairs, together with the Minister of Finance,
approved the disbursement, over a period of 2 years, of $500,000 to the Christian Medical
College at Ludhiana, India, to help in the construction of a new obstetrics and gynaecology
wing. As at 28 February 1978, because of the delays the college had encountered in securing
contributions from other sources and in beginning actual construction, only $250,000 of the
New Zealand Government grant had been passed over. The final payment of $250,000 was
made to the Ludhiana (N.Z.) Fellowship in March 1978.

132. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Health: Is he aware that the Department

has said that Oamaru's water supply is completely unsatisfactory and a danger to health. This

proposes to construct a water-treatment plant to improve its supply, and has obtained
sanction to raise a loan of $1.1 million towards the estimated cost of $1,521,000. The project
will be eligible for a Government subsidy at the rate of $1:$2, and the Department of Health
has advised the borough council that a subsidy of $457, 546 has been approved in principle.

Emigration Loss
133. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Immigration: Has he seen a statement in
the Auckland Star of 25 May 1978 that "New Zealand has lost the equivalent of New
Plymouth through emigration in just two years. . . The 1976 census gave New Plymouth a
population of 37 711", and, if so, is this statement correct?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied: I can confirm that the results of the
1976 census showed that the population of New Plymouth City numbered 37 711. I can also
confirm that the statistics of external migration, which include passengers, through
passengers, and crews, recorded a net loss of 38 987 for the 2 years ended April 1978.
However, I am surprised that the member for New Lynn should use these figures as he must
be aware that they include temporary movements of population, and that permanent
migration is only a small part of this total movement. I suggest the appropriate figures are
those of permanent immigration and emigration which were released by the Government
Statistician on 25 May and which show a net loss of only 4 828 for the 2 years to April 1978.

Cyprus-Withdrawal of Foreign Troops
135. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is the Government
taking any steps to assist in advancing the UN call for the withdrawal of foreign military
forces, namely Turkish, from their occupation of 40 percent of the territory of the
Commonwealth country of Cyprus?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied: New
Zealand voted in favour of the resolution on Cyprus at the most recent session of the United
Nations General Assembly. This resolution referred specifically to a previous United
Nations decision calling. for a withdrawal of foreign troops from Cyprus. The Government
takes the view that the key to progress in Cyprus lies in the resumption of the negotiations
between Turkish and Greek communities. At the Commonwealth Heads of Government
meeting held in June 1977, New Zealand joined the consensus statement reaffirming support
for the United Nations General Assembly resolutions seeking, among other things, the early
removal of foreign troops from Cyprus. This statement was endorsed by the New Zealand
permament representative to the United Nations in November 1977, when he expressed the
hope that the resumption of talks would lead to progress on the question of troop
withdrawal. In keeping with the Government's concern over the territorial integrity and
stability of a fellow Commonwealth member, we shall continue to work for the
implementation of resolutions aimed at achieving progress on the Cyprus problem.

Wellington Teachers College Library Grant
137. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Education: In view of the ever-
increasing price of books, and the fact that they are a vital tool in the training of teachers,
can he explain the reasons for the 58 percent cut in the Wellington Teachers College library
grant this year?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): There has been no cut in the Wellington
Teachers College library grant this year. In each of the last 7 years special grants, in addition
to annual per capita grants for library purposes, have been paid to the teachers colleges to
enable them to bring their library book stocks up to an acceptable level. The grant paid last
year completed the programme for upgrading the library stocks at a total cost of nearly
$68,000 over the 7-year period. There was, consequently, no commitment on the part of the
Government to continue with the special grants in addition to the annual per capita grant of
$35.80 per student for teaching and library purposes. Wellington Teachers College will
receive $26,500 in the 1978-79 year from its annual per capita grant.

Golf Balls Imports

situation regarding the importation of golf balls from overseas, and how does it affect the
golf ball manufacturing industry in New Zealand?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): There is token
provision for the importation of golf balls under basic import licences issued under successive
Governments, both Labour and National. Because of rising overseas prices and a policy of
holding the value of basic licences to 100 percent over the last three licensing periods, the
volume of imports of golf balls has been reduced by about 50 percent during the last 3 years.
Imports of golf balls amount to less than 5 percent of total sales in New Zealand.

Immigrants-Resettlement
145. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) to the Minister of Immigration: What action is the
interdepartmental committee on resettlement taking to assist immigrants to adapt to
conditions in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): The resettlement of migrants is an important
priority in our immigration programme. The interdepartmental committee on resettlement
groups a number of departments with interests in the area. At present the committee is
concentrating its attention on providing accurate information about New Zealand both to
prospective migrants and to recent arrivals. The interdepartmental committee supported a
pilot course on public counter attendance for basic grade public servants, focussing on
Polynesian cultures and on general problems of migrant settlement in New Zealand. The
committee has also commissioned the preparation of scripts for two films for screening to
migrants before they depart for New Zealand. The first film will show day-to-day living here,
and is intended to be suitable for migrants from all countries. The second film will be
designed specifically to help migrants from the South Pacific.

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): In order to locate overstayers as quickly as
possible, arrival and departure information was computerised in October 1976. In addition,
a number of extra field officers have been appointed to combat the problem of overstayers.
Since the computer system of recording overstayers was introduced, the total number of

figures are: January, $33 million; February, $65 million; March, $103 million; and April, $59
million—a surplus for the year of $261 million, compared with $160 million for the same 4
months of 1977, and a deficit of 216 million in the first 4 months of 1975. I do not have
information on trade volumes for the early part of this year, but for the June years 1974-77
the volume of imports has fallen and the volume of exports has increased.

Ministerial Speeches Press Publication
183. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Will he
elaborate the statement he made to the New Zealand Press Association on 25 May so that
journalists receiving the text of a ministerial speech before delivery may know exactly what
procedure to follow before: (1) they transmit that text to their papers; (2) their papers set it
in type; (3) the text may be published?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): I can elaborate as
follows. Journalists receiving the text of a ministerial speech before delivery should, it is
suggested, check the speech against delivery if it is intended to report the actual content of
the speech. Checking against delivery becomes particularly important if it is intended to
subject the content of a speech to a careful analysis. If arrangements cannot be made to
cover the speech in person, journalists are, of course, free to use the material, provided they
make it clear that their reports are based on notes that have been prepared for a Minister,
rather than on the speech itself.

Taneatua Food-processing Factory
187. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manakau) to the Minister of Labour: Why was special
dispensation not given by the Secretary of Labour to allow the 15 women at the Taneatua
food-processing factory to work after 11 p.m.?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): Saxpack Foods Ltd in Taneatua had applied
for approval to employ women 24 hours a day, 12 months a year, to process vegetables that
were subject to rapid deterioration. The company was informed that approval of its
application could not be granted as such approvals were limited to specific situations that did
not occur on a regular or continuing basis. The night work provisions in the Factories Act
accord with ILO convention 89, which New Zealand has ratified. The Federation of Labour
supports that convention. To renounce it unilaterally would be a very serious step and is not
recommended by constitutional lawyers or the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. It is to be
reviewed in 1981, and New Zealand can move then.

Education-Maori Language
192. Mr ELLIOT (Whangarei) to the Minister of Education: Apart from his personal rapid
progress with the Maori language, what developments have occurred in the teaching of
Maori language in our teachers' colleges and in our schools?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The teaching of Maori has increased
considerably in the last 2 years. The appointment of 30 itinerant teachers of Maori in 1975
enabled support to be given to policies for the inclusion of Maori language and studies
integrated into the programmes of primary schools. Some 250 intermediate and primary
schools have programmes involving more than 46 000 pupils. The Budget allows for the
appointment of 10 additional itinerant teachers and for the provision of resource materials to
assist teachers. A programme in which the Maori language as well as English is used as the
medium of instruction was begun at Ruatoki School in 1977. In 1974, 96 secondary schools
taught Maori to 9000 pupils. In 1977, 153 secondary schools taught Maori to more than
13 000 pupils. All teachers' colleges offer selected studies in the Maori language with 19
Maori studies lecturers involved in teaching those courses.

Maui B Construction
206. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Energy: Has he been correctly
reported as stating that a decision was made to use steel for Maui B because a concrete
platform would have meant a delay of a year or more in production, and, if so, would he
elaborate on the investigation made which resulted in this decision?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): It is correct that investigations made showed that a
concrete platform for Maui B, when compared with the steel alternative, would have meant
a delay of a year or more. Comparative studies of the costs and timing of construction of
both alternatives were undertaken by the Maui Joint Venture and independently by
Offshore Mining Co Ltd, the Government-owned company in the Maui field development.
MR A. G. Stirrat, Chief Civil Enginer of the Ministry of Works and Development, along
with Shell International Petroleum Co. provided advice to the Joint Venture on both the
technical and economic feasibility of a concrete platform, while offshore Mining engaged a
firm of United Kingdom consultants well experienced in offshore construction in the North
Sea. The decision to proceed with a steel tower was made on the basis of the report made by
these consultants.

Law Society. However, the Law Practitioners Act is not within any of my portfolios and I am
not aware of the actual amount of the annual fees involved. There is clearly no power for the
Minister of Labour to require a ballot of the members of a District Law Society to determine
whether they wish membership of the society to be compulsory. Because a District Law
Society is not an industrial union of workers, and because it has not got the unqualified
preference clause in an award that requires membership of the society, the question of
compulsory membership cannot be the subject of a ballot under the Industrial Relations Act.
(8/6/78)

Food-Exporting Countries-Price-Fixing Cartel
227. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt Albert) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: Has he seen the
report in the Evening Post of 1 June 1978 in which it is claimed that the world's four major
food-exporting countries are moving closer to the formation of an OPEC type price-fixing
cartel, and, if so, has New Zealand been consulted by the nations concerned and is the
Government in support of the proposal involving Canada, the United States, Argentina, and
Australia?


## p. 1118 (#228) ###########################################

1118
21 June
Questions and Replies
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade): Unhappily, I am
not able to be as brief with this one as with the previous question. It is rather complex. I did
see the report in the Evening Post of 1 June 1978. I also read the report in that same
newspaper on 2 June 1978, which reported the strong denial of the United States that it
would back any world food price-fixing cartel. New Zealand has not been approached by the
Governments of any of the four countries mentioned to support any OPEC-type price-fixing
arrangement, and I do not think that we would support such a proposal if one were received.
We have, however, been concerned at the effects of subsidised exports of dairy products on
world prices, and we are currently members of agreements on minimum price levels for some
dairy products. We hope that these arrangements will be extended in the current GATT
multilateral trade negotiations. The intention is simply to allow a reasonable return to
efficient producers, in the face of heavily subsidised exports. It is not to set prices at any
unreasonable level, which would obviously be impossible when the international market has
in fact a surplus of such products. We have not made any such proposals on beef. Generally I
would regard OPEC-type proposals on beef or dairy products as impractical, given the
international market situation.

## p. 1120 (#230) ###########################################

1120
21 June
Questions and Replies
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): Progress has been made on
the lake level control structures for both Lake Rotorua and Lake Rotoiti, on the Utuhina
Stream flood control works, on the design of upper catchment soil conservation works, and
on negotiations with landholders affected by the works. Water rights have been obtained by
the Bay of Plenty Catchment Commission for the lake level control structures, and detailed
design is proceeding. Approval of the Utuhina Stream flood control works has been given,
and works are about to begin. Soil conservation works to reduce erosion by retiring stream
edges and tree planting have been designed for some of the tributaries, and negotiations with
the farmers concerned have started. Discussions have been held with the Tauranga County
over likely offset works required in the Lower Kaituna River as a result of the upper
catchment works. Future progress with implementing the comprehensive scheme will
depend very largely on the availability of favourable rates of grants for the works, and that,
in turn, depends upon local authorities demonstrating their practical acceptance of the whole
scheme. So far Rotorua City has shown no positive indication that it will accept and promote
works to remove its sewage discharge from the lake. The discharge contributes a significant
and growing proportion of nutrient material to the lake, and its removal is a vital part of the
comprehensive scheme.

Shipment of Meat-Cost
256. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Transport: Has he read the statement
of Mr Gerdelan, Secretary of the Harbour Board Employees Union, as reported in the
Gisborne Herald of Tuesday, 9 May 1978, that “it costs $17 per tonne to ship meat overseas
from Gisborne as opposed to $65 per tonne for railing it to Wellington and putting the meat
on a container ship to Europe", and can he tell the House (a) whether the quoted figures are
correct; and (b) who pays?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I have read the statement by the
secretary of the Harbour Board Employees Union on the cost of shipping meat to Europe
from Gisborne and from Wellington. I am not aware how Mr Gerdelan derived his figures,
nor am I aware of any freight rate existing for meat shipments from Gisborne as, in fact, no
such service exists. The comparison is merely hypothetical and assumes that there is a
conventional shipping service operating with the required frequency to move the relatively
small quantities of meat that would be exported through the port of Gisborne. In drawing
any comparisons it must be realised that it is not economic to maintain a large fleet of
conventional ships which are both time and labour intensive to uplift relatively small
quantities. The principle behind New Zealand's entry into containerisation has always been
to reduce the number of vessels servicing our trade. On the question of who pays in Mr
Gerdelan's example, under the scheme aggregating meat cargoes to the container ports, the
meat trade as a whole, through the freight rate, pays.
(13/6/78)

field when it comes on stream?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): The Minister of Energy replies:
Maui field production builds up gradually. It also displaces part of the existing temporarily
accelerated production from the Kapuni field. Over the next 2 to 3 years, therefore, oil
import levels can be stabilised, with reductions in oil use by power stations and some large
industries being offset by possible growth from the transport sector. At an equivalent import
value of around $2/GJ, the Maui-Kapuni field production is estimated to be worth about

Counselling Service. That service does not meet the required conditions for residential as

Unemployment Statistics
279. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Labour: Can he confirm that
the method used to measure unemployment in most OECD countries, such as Australia and
the United States, is by a sample survey technique, while that used by New Zealand relies on
registration, and so no real comparisons can be made?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Labour replies:
Unemployment statistics are available from household sample surveys in most member
OECD countries. Almost all member countries also collect employment service registration
or unemployment insurance statistics on a monthly or more frequent basis. The number of
registered unemployed in New Zealand can be compared with the registration statistics
available for other countries. For instance, registered unemployed expressed as a percentage
of the labour force stood at 6.4 percent in Australia and 6 percent in Great Britain at the end
of March 1978. This compares with a corresponding rate of 1.7 percent for New Zealand. At
the end of March 1978 the registered unemployed seeking full time work in Australia
numbered 409 994, whereas the household survey of registered unemployed also seeking full
time work numbered 345 300-a difference of 64 694.

new farmer freehold rural farm land sales last year was 22.6 percent. Over the previous 3
years it was: 1974, 21.9 percent; 1975, 23.4 percent; and 1976, 25.5 percent.

Vandalism in Schools
283. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Education: Has he read the front page of
the Auckland Star of 6 June 1978, which had the caption "Vandal raid forces new school shut
after 2 weeks", and, if so, what action is he taking to protect schools, particularly in the
south Auckland area?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): The Minister of Education replies:
I have read the article, and I am naturally concerned about incidents of vandalism such as
these. In January 1974 the Department of Education issued a circular to all school
controlling authorities detailing recommended security precautions for school buildings.
These included outside security lighting, alarm systems, and in extreme cases the use of
security patrols. This circular was re-issued in July 1976 stressing again the necessity for
security measures in school buildings. The Auckland Education Board has advised me that
approximately 80 percent of the primary and intermediate schools in the Otara area have
burglar alarms.

Farm Vendor Mortgage Scheme
284. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) to the Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and
Finance Corporation: How many farms have changed hands since the farm vendor mortgage
scheme was introduced?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister in Charge of the Rural Banking and Finance
Corporation): The farm vendor finance settlement scheme applied to sale and purchase
agreements entered into on or after 28 July 1977, but which had a date of settlement not
earlier than 1 April 1978. As at 30 May 1978 the bank had approved the following
resettlements under the scheme: bond option, 8 settlements valued at $683,400; gaurantee
option, 21 settlements valued at $1,236,760, making a total of 29 settlements valued at $1.9
million.
(14/6/78)
Immigrants-Knowledge of English
285. Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei), on behalf of Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister
of Immigration: How long has it been an essential requirement for intending immigrants that
they should have a knowledge of English; what section of the Immigration Act requires this;
and what are the criteria for adjudging adequacy of English, and who applies them?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): As early as 1899 New Zealand's immigration
legislation included a provision' that some prospective immigrants be required to pass an
English language test. Entry to New Zealand is now governed by the Immigration Act 1964
and there is now no such requirement in the Act, but this requirement has been accepted as
part of entry policy for some years. The Act does not prescribe details of immigration policy,
but directs that entry permits may be granted subject to any conditions which may be
prescribed by regulations under the Act, or which may be imposed by the Minister of
Immigration. The Act itself accordingly does not require immigrants to have an adequate
knowledge of English. Current policy for permanent entry to New Zealand accepts that one
factor that facilitates successful settlement in New Zealand is fluency in English. Where
possible, applicants for permanent entry are interviewed by an officer of the nearest New
Zealand overseas post, to assess this and other factors. If an interview is not possible the
assessment is made on the basis of the applicant's educational attainments and previous
employment history.
(14/6/78)

Air New Zealand—NAC Merger
286. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) to the Minister of Transport: What is the estimated cost of
the merging of NAC and Air New Zealand, and what is the estimated financial gain over the
next 5 years?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Defence): The Minister of Transport replies: It is
difficult to be precise in a matter of this nature as both costs and financial gains can be
influenced by decisions yet to be made by the Air New Zealand board of directors.
Notwithstanding, it is estimated that over the next 3 years the company will have to absorb
direct added costs attributable to the merger of the order of $1.5 million to $2 million.
Providing the market remains reasonably stable it is conservatively anticipated that by
March 1981 the financial revenue gains and cost savings directly attributable to the merger
will be in the order of $10 million to $12 million. It is difficult to be more precise on the levels
of benefits after that date. I should add that these benefits may not be reflected in increased
profits, but rather in more favourable fare and freight rates to the consumer.

288. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua) to the Minister of Fisheries: What is the value of squid

Zealand waters have increased each year, and in the last season some 70 000 tonnes were
taken. The actual potential is not precisely known but catches at this level do not appear to
damage the resource. As squid is an annual species, it is possible that there will be variations
in abundance seasonally.

Abortions Operating Surgeons
291. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Health: What plans has the
Auckland Hospital Board to provide an operating surgeon to perfom the abortions for those
women holding the necessary legal documentation entitling them to abortion and whose
plight has now become desperate and urgent as a result of the decision of the supervisory
committee to decline Dr Willcox's application as a consultant and to operate on other than
the seven or eight cases he had personally interviewed prior to the committee's decision not
to appoint him as a certifying consultant?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The situation in Auckland does not result from a
decision of the supervisory committee. The medical superintendent-in-chief of the Auckland
Hospital Board advises that Dr Willcox has agreed to perform the seven or eight abortions
on the patients he has seen. I can only appeal to operating surgeons in Auckland to deal in a
normal manner with cases referred to them for abortions, and not to discriminate against
them because their cases have been considered by certifying consultants who have certified
that such abortions would be lawful. Operating surgeons owe this to the patients, and I
appeal to them again not to withhold their services. It would assist the board if Parliament
passed quickly the Bill now before the House to amend the Contraception, Sterilisation, and
Abortion Act.
(1/6/78)
Abortions-Certifying Consultants
292. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Health: Did the Minister hear the
reported comments on "Morning Report" today by the Chairman of the New Zealand
Medical Association that he can see no reason why Dr Willcox cannot carry out operations
for abortion in spite of the fact that he has not been appointed a certifying consultant, and is
this the same advice that the Minister has received from his medical advisers?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): My answer to this question must necessarily be
brief. I issued a press statement on 20 April 1978, and copies of this are available in my
office. There is nothing in legislation which requiries an operating surgeon at an abortion
hospital to be a certifying consultant. My medical advisers agree that an operating surgeon is
entitled to have before him all the medical advice and information available on his patients
and to interview and examine the patient before he makes the decision as to whether or not
he will operate. In the event that it has already been agreed by two certifying consultants that
the operation would be lawful, the operating surgeon can proceed in the knowledge that
what he is doing is within the law. In the event that the case has not been certified as lawful
by two certifying consultants, the operating surgeon must ensure that such certificates are
issued before he operates. Since there is some doubt in the minds of some doctors as to the
legal position, the legislation currently before the House should be passed quickly to ensure
that the unsatisfactory situation that has developed in Auckland is cleared up quickly in the
interests of the patients.

Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): I move, That this House notes the recent assessment of
the Minister of Labour that "public emotion gets stirred by this sort of talk, but communists are
not dominant elements in industrial disputes, probably less than 1 percent", and draws
attention to those disruptive elements in the Government caucus who use the 1 percent as a basis
for propaganda purposes, anti-trade union statements and diversion from the underlying issues
of inadequate wages, lack of job opportunity, and rising prices, and therefore calls upon the
Government to review industrial law as proposed by the New Zealand Planning Council in its
discussion paper Working Together.
I tabled this motion in order to advance the discussion paper of the New Zealand
Planning Council. That planning council was set up by the Government, and has people on it
appointed by the Government, but none of the positions are elected positions. Its considered
opinion must be taken seriously, particularly in industrial relations. The National Party has
for at least two decades, if not more, used industrial relations as a weapon in the pursuit of
political attention, which has been detrimental to the welfare of our country. Now, we have
an impartial body appointed by the same Government and advising the Government to stop
doing what it is doing in industrial relations. I hope that the disruptive elements, who have
over the last 2 years made the job of the Minister of Labour a hell on earth, will take aboard
what Sir Frank Holmes said in a foreword to that document. It is not a Labour Party
utterance, but a statement from the Government's appointed chairman of the Planning
Council.
He says: "It is already found that there are habits of labelling, which are at present
seriously clouding the issues"-and the leaders of that clouding are the National
Government's maverick members. "Ideally, we aim to help people on both sides of the
fence; to see people and situations as they really are, rather than in terms of stereotypes."

country more concern than they need, even if the situation is serious. At a time when the

ranting that inflates the communistic influence to a bogy of fearsome size is a timewasting
exercise that undermines public confidence. It must encourage unsavoury reactions. We

helping their electorates or the House, and the newspapers imply the Labour Party is a party
to it. This impartial body that they set up tells them to breathe through their noses a little
more often on this matter-one that they have made a mess of.

Government members do not help their Minister, the Government, the constituencies, or
the country by their attitude. In the Planning Council's report it seems that the
Government's economic policy underlies much of our industrial trouble. What does it say? It
says: "Present trends potentially threaten our economic well-being as much as the great
depression of the 1930s." What a reflection on the Government! "Heavy Government and
private overseas borrowing has delayed the worst effects of an international recession which
still lingers on." Further on the report states: "New Zealand's problem is aggravated by the
very high inflation which exceeds the inflation rate of most of our trading partners." Those
are the facts of the current economy underlying the cause of industrial feeling and of
industrial and employment insecurity-all under the National Government. The
Government's own Planning Council tells it where it gets off plump and plain in a non-
political document.
The report continues: "It would be naive to expect an absence of tension between
labour and management at a time like this. However, the negotiated solution of tensions can
often be productive. New Zealand cannot afford destructive conflict that undermines our
struggle for recovery." Those members who go to the Government caucus to put pressure on
a Minister in difficult circumstances should be told not to aggravate the position, which the
Planning Council sets out clearly in a non-political document tabled a few days ago.
The council's report continues: "Leaders in management, unions, politics, and the
media have a particularly important part to play in improving the process of communication.

public statements." During the last 2 to 3 years this Chamber has too often been a vehicle
for what can be described as impetuous and irresponsible public statements dealing with our
most precious resource, the work force. It is the work force that creates the real wealth. The

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): I thank you, Mr Speaker, and the House. I support the
motion before the House, and in doing I commend the authors of the paper Working
Together for outlining the problems of industrial relations. However, I must express regret
that its suggested legal changes are merely playing with the symptoms of industrial unrest
and, even if implemented, would achieve very little. Transferring disputes from one court to
another will do little, if anything, to resolve the causes of those disputes. The present
industrial unrest will not be resolved by ad hoc measures, or fiddling with a law here and the
fine tuning of another there. A fundamental restructuring of New Zealand industry is
required to remove the causes of present problems and unrest. Unfortunately, the paper
Working Together does not suggest a way of achieving this critically necessary restructuring
of New Zealand industry. It is not enough to urge the Government to review industrial law,
and to believe that a solution can be found this way.
I commend and congratulate the Minister of Labour for his sense of political
responsibility in stating that communists are not dominant in industrial disputes, but are
probably fewer than 1 percent. This approach is in marked contrast to that of other National
members, who are using the theme of "a red under every trade union bed" as a political
tactic to divert public attention from the failures of the Government's industrial relations
policy. Some National Party members have embarked upon a planned strategy of emotional
red-baiting in an attempt to force confrontation and polarisation of public opinion for
political advantage. The strategy is to show National as the saviour of New Zealand from a
communist threat. That sort of political scaremongering does not produce the environment
in which rational and reasonable discussion can take place-discussion that would allow the


## p. 1139 (#249) ###########################################

21 June
1139
Discussion of Motions
public to examine alternative policy options.
The present industrial problems are the culmination of a little-broken period of three
decades of National Government. However, it must be said that the two short periods in
which Labour controlled the Treasury benches over that period saw little significant attempt
to reform industry and remove the causes of the problems that have reached crisis point
today. I cannot see that the call for a review of industrial law proposed by the Labour Party is
more than a first step. I rather doubt that Labour does, in fact, have an industrial relations
policy substantially different from that of the National Government, apart from the removal
of some penalties. The basis of any review of industrial law must be to recognise that
industry must become self governing. That is the core of my party's policy, and the paper
Working Together reinforces this view. It states: "The objective should be to downgrade the
adversary concept inherent in the present system of industrial relations and substitute
measures which encourage general problem solving by the parties themselves."
Disputes are better solved in the work force than in the courthouse. For example, the
industrial crisis within the freezing industry in Southland could be resolved by workers at
each works forming one works council to represent all workers, irrespective of occupation.
This reform would prevent friction arising between present unions, and stop the formation of
an industrial aristocracy of members of the strong militant unions such as the meat workers,
who are able to hold to ransom the country and their fellow workmen. One bargaining
organisation, democratically run, would protect the interests of all workers and would stop a
handful of members of one union denying everyone else work and income. The new works
council would hammer out a contract within each freezing works for each season's kill, with
agreed margins for skill and details of working conditions. It would also self-administer the
working contracts, recognising that it would initially have to be subject to legal recourse,
until profit sharing provided the incentive for self-discipline to apply and be applied.
Workers could also have representation on the board.
An Hon. Member: Theory.
Mr BEETHAM: It is not theory. It works in some countries. Workers would also have
representation on the board of directors, as a prelude to converting each works to a full co-
operative.

is in sharp contrast to the negative and destructive statements being made by South Island
Labour members, who in recent weeks have been endeavouring to undermine the dramatic
progress being made in the South Island under National's regional development policies.
The rallying call for rugby in Otago-a style of rugby that is respected throughout the
sporting world for its attention to basic and attractive style—is "C'mon Otago". Otago has
had a proud record of innovation in many fields, none more so than in rugby, and one poor
season does not mean we damn the team for the next. But, apart from that, Otago has been
innovative in health, education, social welfare, and manufacturing. The present regional
development programme is a counterpart to those earlier programmes. It stems from
recognition in the early 1960s of the changes that had occurred and the need to reassess what
those changes meant to Otago. As the focus for regional development moves from short-
term to long-term resource-based incentives, the need for wider understanding of the
region's relative strength in various basic resources is increasing. The motion is based on a
very factual and positive article prepared by the chief executive of the Otago Council, Mr

the single most important component in our export income, or about Otago's share of total
livestock units having increased from 8 percent to 9 percent; that our irrigation-the
Maniototo, for instance-and the rural water supplies are the biggest programmes to be
undertaken in the province in 40 years; that our share of irrigation has gone up from 41
percent to 53 percent; that our farm development capital investment expenditures have
increased from 7 percent to 9.1 percent; that our forestry plantings have gone from 12
percent to 15 percent; that our export shipments through the container port of Port

be able to take part in the challenges and decisions on how that power will be used. Our
share in housing is up, and our tourism is up. Our annual population growth is in line with
that of Southland for the first time since 1945. The rate of migration to the north has
diminished-and I have here a chart that shows this. We are on the way back.
We hear a lot from the Opposition about freight, but mainly about its cost. We hear a
lot about subsidies, but we do not hear about the freight rebate. In the first 2 years of the
National Government expenditure on freight had already exceeded that during the 3-year
term of the former Labour Government by more than $500,000. The National Government
has also instituted the Cook Strait ferry concession, which gives a 25 percent advantage to
north-bound traffic from the South Island. It is a fact that not one company that has moved
or closed had a suspensory loan, but two companies that shifted and the one that closed had
freight subsidies exactly as given to them under the former Labour Government. That is an
indication of the effectiveness of suspensory loans versus the freight subsidies.
