The problem of prescribed drugs has to be looked at closely. More than $90 million a
year is spent on drugs in this country. Most of those drugs are excellent, the vast majority
being the sort that keep people alive, fit and well, out of hospital, and on the job. Some of
them however, are being overprescribed and some of them are not good. I refer to drugs
such as barbiturates. We have been trying to do something about barbiturates for some time.
We spent all last year trying to educate the medical profession in the prescription of
barbiturates, and trying to discourage doctors from prescribing them for new patients,
because they are vicious, addictive drugs, and there are not many complaints for which a
barbiturate is the right answer. Too many people, old people especially, become addicted to
barbiturates, and, not knowing they are addicted, get into extremely serious trouble. We
should all agree that drugs that are abused most be tackled on a wide front. By that I mean
we must tackle them through education, prevention, enforcement, cure, and rehabilitation. I
am talking about the full spectrum of drugs: hard drugs, soft drugs, alcohol, tobacco, and
prescribed drugs. If we in the House are determined to do something about this problem, we
will conceivably make some progress—and that progress is overdue.
I should like to spend a few minutes talking about immigration. The effectiveness of our
administrative machinery for coping with the immigration problem, which to a large extent,
in terms of time, is the overstayer problem, has been greatly improved and increased.
Amendments to the legislation were introduced in 1976 and passed in 1977. An amendment
to the Act requires people to have specific authority if they are going to work when they
come here. In the past we did not have that; people were given a temporary permit when
they arrived and they were not required to have an authority to work. It is necessary for us to
protect the employment opportunities in this country for our own people, so we have
introduced work permits for people coming here, no matter where they come from.
The right of appeal against deportation has been introduced. That was a problem that
the previous Government, as well as preceding Governments, must have faced. Although we
had rights to deport people, there was no machinery for appeals against decisions.
Undoubtedly, 90 percent of the people deported needed to be deported, but every now and
again the odd one appeared who perhaps had a very good, solid reason for his actions that
could not be properly investigated until after the legal charge had been heard. We have put
that right, and also introduced appeal procedures, which will become law this year, to give
rights of appeal to a tribunal-or, failing a tribunal, to the Supreme Court-for permanent
residents who have to be deported. We hope that these measures will cope with the
overstayer problem. There is reason to believe they will, because in the last 4 months the
number of overstayers, according to the computer, has gone down from about 5800 to 5000,
and is being reduced month by month. There is reason to believe that we now have a grip of
the problem.
I have been asked several times-and I have also seen the question raised in the
media-why so many Polynesians are prosecuted as overstayers. I do not know the answer.
However, I can say that nothing in the regulations or in the training and briefing of the
enforcement officers discriminates on the grounds of a man's race, colour, or creed. One of
the reasons more Polynesians are prosecuted is that, generally speaking, they tell tales on
one another. A Polynesian will ring up and say that so-and-so works at such-and-such a job
and lives at such-and-such an address; he is here illegally, and ought to go home. A Niuean
will perhaps put up the weights of a Samoan, or a Tongan will put up the weights of a Fijian.
When a complaint has been made that the law has been broken it has to be followed up for
example, by the Customs men or police. When a complaint is followed up it might be found
that not just one, but two, three, four, or five people are involved.
Another possible explanation is that Islanders who come to New Zealand and overstay
have very little cash, whereas people from the United States or Great Britain who overstay
after a holiday do not look for a job and are not detected. I can assure the House that
nothing in the regulations, instructions, legislation, or practices of the department
discriminates racially against those people who break the immigration laws.
I recently saw a programme on TV1 in which people were allowed to say that the staff of
the immigration division were cruel and ruthless. Because I thought those comments about
dedicated public servants who, perhaps do not have the best job in the world, were ill judged
and ill balanced, I made a formal complaint. Those officers do their job very well. It is time
that people gave them credit, and ceased to make snide comments about them.
The Belgian millionaire who was sent home is always being mentioned. As far as I


## p. 1152 (#262) ###########################################

1152
21 June

know, the extent of the fortune he brought to this country was $30,000. He had a wife and
children back in his home country. All the countries that administer immigration laws accept
that they are not havens for deserters or for people who walk out on their marriages and
other responsibilities. So long as people are legally married, divorced, or separated, they will
be admitted to this country. However, if they have responsibilities in their own country they
will not be admitted. That is why the Belgian was not allowed to stay.
Recently, there have been newspaper articles about a Samoan boxer who came to this
country, but overstayed. I should have thought that his trainers or those who selected him
for the Commonwealth Games would have made some inquiries about him. When it was
learned that he was an overstayer, he was prosecuted. He appeared before the court, and
was ordered to be deported. His appeal against deportation was not accepted because such
deportation has to be considered unduly harsh or unjust, which in these circumstances it was
not. However, we amended the legislation last year, because after the Freddie Fender case
the immigration division was castigated. The law made no provision to allow a prohibited
immigrant, such as Freddie Fender, into the country. As we thought it was unduly harsh to
stop somebody visiting New Zealand for a short while, it was decided that it would not do
much harm to allow such a person into the country because we would know about him and
could keep our eyes on him. The same principle was applied to the Samoan boxer. He will be
allowed into the country on a short visit to train, but will be returned home as a deportee.
An article in one of today's newspapers headed, "Immigration lowers population",
mentioned the outflow of people from New Zealand. Every 2 months for the past 2 years I
have been saying that the figures issued by the Department of Statistics are confusing and

1976 there was a net gain of 12 738 permanent arrivals over permanent departures. In 1977,
the net gain was 352, and in 1978 the net loss was 4148. The newspaper clipping I referred to
earlier mentioned that nearly 60 000 residents had left New Zealand permanently or for a
long term. As I said before, last year there was a net loss of 4148. However, for the past 3
years there has been a net gain of 8942. I wish people would study the statistics seriously, as
it does not do the country any good to continually drag out misleading figures.

intentions. It can point to shortcomings in anticipated performance, based on past records,

aspire or perspire to office or to be Cabinet Ministers. We have no axe to grind; we speak on

If I am in the wilderness, as some people who are seeking to come in from the

We of the third force can also be dispassionate throughout the coming lengthy debates
on the estimates. I am not an economist, as has always been obvious. New Zealand politics
are plagued with the idea that only the experts can be administrators, and only the experts
can be judges. New Zealanders think that generals should be Ministers of Defence, that
lawyers should be Ministers of Justice, and that engineers should be Ministers of Works.
That attitude is reflected in local bodies throughout the country, but the fundamental
principle of democracy is that the ordinary people should make the final judgments. The
layman must again be on top. The old saw is that expert advice should be available, but the
experts should not be on top.
I have heard it said, particularly in the East, that economists inhabit cloud-cuckoo-
land-that they try to operate theories and laws that are nothing more than mere puffs of air
in the face of the anarchy, banditry, greed, and corruption that hold sway in the pecuniary
affairs of the real world.. Perhaps economists are like conservationists. The Chinese say that
conservationists preserve wild species in order that they can eat each other. I am not an
economist, but a layman who knows the needs of the people. I certainly know the needs of
the people in my electorate, and I do not need outsiders coming into my electorate and
telling me what my constituents need. The Government's job is to share the wealth
produced to apportion it and to distribute it equitably. It must do that, not by right, but on
the delegated authority of each and every citizen. The Government should never exercise
power in its own right; it should always recognise that the power exercised is delegated to it
by the people.
Over the next few weeks we will be discussing the Budget and asking how the
Government has performed before we vote the money it has asked for. We will ask how it
has performed in the management of inflation and in the management of our terms of trade.
In the Budget the Government talks of halving the inflation rate and also of halving the
overseas deficit. I believe those statements are of doubtful validity, and I am surprised to see
them in a document presented to the House. Professor Galbraith might say that those
statements are fraudulent, because they are clearly untrue. The Government has not halved
the inflation rate; it has not been reduced to 8 percent, or anywhere near that. The inflation
rate is still the same as it was last year.
I do not want to look too far; I do not want to do what everyone else is doing, and talk
about what is wrong. I want to look for solutions, if I can. The public is fed up with the
gobbledygook on reflation, deflation, and inflation fed to the people by jargon peddlers. The
people are as fed up with that as they are with the two-party "your turn, my turn" political
system. The public is not as gullible as the leaders of the major parties think. The people
question the appearance of an inflationary Budget at this time. They question terms like
"fine tuning", and the juvenile jargon that disguises the budgetary manipulation taking place
in this country. No housewife in New Zealand believes that one can spend more than one
earns. No housewife believes that she can live on borrowing unless she is in love with her
moneylender. The only justification for an expansionary Budget at this time lies in the belief
that we have, as they say, turned the corner, or that we have seen some light at the end of the
tunnel-some light other than that of a train coming in our direction.

The oft repeated claim that we have turned the corner is the result of a euphoria that the
Government is in some way entitled to, having won the fish-for-beef battle with Japan. The
Prime Minister gambled, and I think he has probably won that battle. New Zealand has the
potential to sell an additional $42 million worth of beef to the United States. Consequently,
there will be no beef surplus to sell to Japan, but, in fact, the Prime Minister's gamble has
paid off. I might have believed in the logic of the trade war against Japan if it had been based
on motor vehicle imports. It would have been far less of a gamble if it had been based on
motor vehicle imports rather than raw materials-in this case, fish. We need motor vehicles,
and we need not have gambled to anywhere near the same extent as we have done.
It seems that the additional $42 million worth of beef sales to the United States is the
sole significant factor in reflating the economy; it is the sole justification for the reflation the
Budget provides. Goodness me, that amount represents only 4 days of borrowing at the rate
the National Government is borrowing at present-and it considers it is time to reflate the
economy! I mention in passing that the $42 million represents 6 days of borrowing at the rate
at which the former Labour Government borrowed, and, I presume, at the rate at which it
would continue to borrow if it was again elected to the Treasury benches. We really need a
great deal more explanation for reflation at this time.
My constituents, when they were asked to offer suggestions for a new social order, said
to me, "Why don't we in New Zealand consider advances that should have been made 120
years ago, like a 6-hour day? We have had an 8-hour day since 1840. Why don't we consider
a 6-hour day in two shifts, which would free women to pursue their own creative activities
and would give men obligations to the home that currently they do not have? It would give
them obligations to the home equal to those they feel they have to the football field and the
pub." My constituents offered those suggestions in response to my inquiries. They want to
change the social order. They want to change our mental attitudes-attitudes that see
women only as serving and not as creating.
My constituents also believe that there should be a greater use of existing community
assets, such as schools. Instead of having the schools in my electorate burned down by the
idle, unemployed victims of the present economic system, the people in my electorate would
rather see those assets used as cultural centres right around the clock. The unemployed
would no longer be denied the right to work if the position of night watchman was reinstated
at schools. If the care of community assets again became a source of employment I am sure
my constituents, besides questioning the basis for expansionary policies at a time when
inflation is still rampant, would accept the logic behind what the Government at least says it
is trying to do.
My constituents criticise not only the philosophies behind the Budget; they criticise the
organisation and the administration. They are critical of the kind of philosophy that has New
Zealanders farming money, not grasslands. Sixty-five percent of our people, euphemistically
called employed, work in the servicing industries. Those people should be engaged in
productive industries, not in moving money from point A to point B. My constituents are
critical of the organisation of the Government system, and question whether the
Government's share of the national income, which is increasing at a rapid rate, is being
handled wisely. They referred me to the fact that the devaluation that took place in Britain
when Mr Callaghan was Chancellor of the Exchequer was unnecessary, and was simply the
result of an inaccuracy in the statistics provided by Treasury. There is wide room for
administrative change, particularly in Treasury. A report on this by an American
Presidential exchange scholar has disappeared into some sort of nether world. It should be
made publicly available so that everyone in New Zealand can examine what is happening
with our administrative structure.
My constituents are critical of the administrative structure. They see, perhaps as I do,
room in Cabinet for a Minister of Co-ordination, a job similar to that held overseas,
generally by the Deputy Prime Minister, whose responsibilities are to co-ordinate the
activities of central government. They see disadvantages in the Prime Minister being
Minister of Finance, in as far as he cannot really co-ordinate the activities of various
ministries because of his duties as Prime Minister. The Prime Minister's control of Treasury,
as everybody admits, appears to give him power; but does it? Does it not just make the
holder of the highest office in the Government a prisoner of Treasury?
My constituents have noted that, according to the Budget, the world's money system
has broken down. The Bretton Woods Agreement has disappeared into eternity. For the
first time, the collapse of the International Monetary Fund is mentioned on page 1 of the

Capitation grants in all children's homes have been increased from $12.60 to $25 a
week. As well, children's homes will receive the normal family home board rate of $24.35 a
week for all State wards resident in such homes. These grants have been made possible by
the research and joint work of the New Zealand Council of Christian Social Service and the
Department of Social Welfare.
The Labour Government's 1972 Budget had a plank which no doubt gave it support, but
having received the support, it failed to implement the improved family benefit capitation
scheme. The allowable income under this scheme has been increased in this Budget from $95
a week to $125 a week for couples with one child, increased by $5 for the second and
subsequent children, with an increase in the upper limit from $2,000 to $3,000. This move
will materially assist young people wanting to buy their own homes. The former Labour
Government promised that increase, but never implemented it. The National Party thought
it was a good idea and the Government decided that young people today deserved the
increase. The items I have mentioned are in addition to tax cuts of about $520 million. The
Government has also introduced the young family rebate, the single income family rebate,
and a wide range of measures to assist home owners and the building industry. The Budget
has increased the allowable income for widows and people on social security benefits. These
measures provide concrete evidence that the National Government is working in the
interests of the country.

have nothing but the rule of force, which means we lose all protection for the weaker
members of society. Protest is a legitimate democratic right, but deliberate trials of strength
between small sections of the community are neither responsible nor constructive, they are a
step backwards from civilised living. This continuing problem is as important to our future as
the economy, overseas markets, or industrial relations. It is one that we must solve. It is

There have been too many confrontations recently that could have been settled

reasonable, lasting agreement. First, there must be good will on both sides; secondly, once
an agreement is reached, neither side must break it. Often, recently, we do not seem to have
had either of those essentials. We have had one side that will keep no agreement that does
not let it have things all its own way. As there are reasonable men and women in any group,

licence by the defendants. There is no vagueness in the decision, and no trace of doubt. It
was a legal ruling binding all New Zealanders of whatever race.
This National Government is the first Government ever to have recognised, not a legal
point, but the moral right of the Ngati Whatua people of Tamaki. The legal right is clear-it
is Crown Land. The Maori owners-not, it may be recollected, the original owners, who
were defeated and exterminated by the Ngati Whatua—were, at their own request, given
permission to sell the land. Times and minds change. The children repent of the bargains of
their fathers. They wanted the land back. The National Government, working with the Ngati
Whatua elders, came up with a scheme that Mr Justice Speight described as a handsome
remedy of long felt wrongs, whether real or imagined. The elders and most concerned
Maoris agreed; a minority, supported by some others for their own ends, did not. The result
was mostly unnecessary and was a cause of further division between the races. The worst
aspect is the way this episode is being used to divide people by race.
Racism these days has only one definition-it means anything done by a person with a
white skin. Anything done to a white-skinned person is right, honest, and moral. Neither
New Zealand nor any other country will get very far on a diet of racial hypocrisy. We need
overseas markets and full employment, we need to make this a prosperous and friendly
country to live in, but, most of all, we need good will between races, tolerance of the other
person's point of view, and a willingness to see the worth of others-the other man's cause
and culture. That is the only way we can build a nation.

Mr LATTER (Marlborough): I think it is essential to consider the Budget, not just as
the Budget of this year, not as the Budget of this Government, and not even in the light of
the 6-year period going back to 1972. We must look at it over 11 years to remind ourselves
that when the late Harry Lake died in 1966-67 a new, fairly junior Minister of Finance was
appointed. The man was Robert Muldoon, and he inherited a dramatic turnround in New
Zealand's terms of trade-about a 40 percent drop in our wool exports overnight. New
Zealand fought back from 1966 to 1972, when Labour took over. That man, and the
National Governments over that period, spent all that time righting the economy and getting
inflation back to 5 percent, a figure we would love to have now. What happened? New
Zealand dropped the pilot in 1972 and during the next 3 years moved towards a moment of
truth.
I will not talk particularly about 1973, except to call it the inheritance year, because that
was the year the incoming Labour Government had everything for its comfort. It had a
sound economy, and it started to blow the lot. I would call 1974 the prodigal or locust year. It
was the year of going through the lot until there was nothing left. And so, if one looks at the
history of those 11 years, one comes to 1978.
Members do not have to take my word that 1975 was definitely the gathering storm. It
was there, and even the Labour Party could see it. There is no need for me to convince those
opposite. I shall simply quote from the 1975 Budget, because the effects of the recession
were apparent in that year. This is what the present Deputy Leader of the Opposition said in
opening his 1975 Budget: "The last 12 months have been a period of deepening recession".
That, of course, was May 1975, so he acknowledged that from May 1974 to May 1975 was a
period of deepening recession, a particularly difficult time for New Zealand. Then he goes
on-and this is a good one: "Most of the major economies nevertheless chose the
conventional route of restraint on their expenditure." He is pretty fair, and he says, "The
conventional ones have succeeded in reducing their balance of payments deficits." Then he
says, "This year great weight has been placed on the expenditure programme." This was
1975, after 12 months of seeing the deepening recession when the conventional economics
were taking a conventional approach and starting to beat the battle-but not the Labour

Minister of Finance in 1975. He went on: "The Government is not prepared to compromise

Budget, but it is this process of looking at the economy over a decade that sets the scenario
for a Budget like this. It is not a "oncer", and its provisions are not made because it is
election year; they are made at the end of a 3-year programme that is coping with problems.

Vandalism in Auckland Schools
1. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Education: Has he read the article in the
New Zealand Herald of 15 June 1978 which said that the Auckland Education Board was
deeply concerned about increasing vandalism in Auckland schools and would ask him "to
offset the fall in morale of staff and parents by urgently considering erecting Government
pool housing on or adjacent to school sites for caretakers or school staff", and, if so, what
action is he taking, particularly in the south Auckland area?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I have read the article and share the
education board's concern at the vandalism in Auckland schools. The provision of housing
on primary sites has been considered, but the cost is quite prohibitive when contemplated on
a national basis. The Auckland Education Board is to meet the regional superintendent of
education in Auckland, the Otara Principals Association, and the Police Department in the
near future and I hope this meeting may produce some new practical suggestions for dealing
with the problem.

or 33.56 percent of her income she would have paid under the last Labour Government.

$9 a week in the case of the first man on $120 a week, and $3 a week for the second man.

NEW ZEALAND PORTS AUTHORITY AMENDMENT BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to
present the report of the committee on the New Zealand Ports Authority Amendment Bill.
The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That
the report do lie upon the table. I should like to record the thanks of the committee to all those
who presented submissions. In all, 17 submissions were received, and 13 organisations
appeared in support of the Bill. All who asked to be heard were given the opportunity to
appear.
It is worth recording that, in addition, the Local Bills Committee asked the New
Zealand Ports Authority to appear. A useful morning was spent cross-examining the
chairman and members of the board, including the chief executive officer. It was obvious at
the beginning that at the heart of all submissions received was a questioning of the definition
of a national ports plan. The definition had been taken from the principal Act, passed in
1968, and it was obvious that doubts had existed since then on the role of the New Zealand
Ports Authority.
A number of parties obviously had come to their own conclusion that by "plan" we
meant a blueprint. Others acknowledged the dynamic changing character of such a plan, and
realised it was not pertinent to require the Ports Authority to bring down a blueprint. This
latter view prevailed. While conceding that the authority had to be given some flexibility in
tackling its task, the unanimous view of the select committee was that the authority would
have to work towards a plan even given its dynamic nature.
One of the supporting papers presented by the Ministry of Transport stated: "It seems
that in the past emphasis on the word 'plan' has conjured up the idea of a very definitive
chart or piece of paper containing a positive indication of precisely what cargoes will be
handled at which port over the next 5 or 10 years. Such a document is not desirable, and not
intended by the words 'national ports plan'. . . National ports planning is proceeding, but
the Ports Authority believes that with a wider appreciation of the dynamic nature of the
plan, the process should be facilitated." In acknowledgment of that, clause 4 dealing with
section 11 of the principal Act has been rewritten and the purpose behind the rewording is
the acknowledgment of the select committee's decision.
The rewritten clause 4 will read: “Functions of the Authority. The authority shall have
the following general functions: (a) to foster an efficient and integrated ports system for New
Zealand; (b) "—and this is the substantive change-"for that purpose to undertake the
processing of a national ports planning by developing progressively and keeping under
continuous review a national ports plan". We believe this goes all the way towards meeting
the reservations presented to the select committee. Clause 4 also spells out further: "in the
performance of this function the authority shall have regard to the following matters: (a) the
export, import, and coastal trades of New Zealand and related matters; (b) the distribution
of the population of New Zealand; (c) the transportation system of New Zealand; (d) the
resources, industries, and commerce generally of New Zealand; (e) national, regional, and
local economic and transport planning; (f) ship design, cargo handling and related matters;
and (g) such other considerations as the authority considers to be relevant to the purposes of
the Act."


## p. 1179 (#289) ###########################################

22 June
1179
New Zealand Ports Authority Amendment Bill
Consequential amendments are also included in clause 5, which deals with section 12
relating to the national ports plan itself. It is the accepted view of some organisations that
took up the question that there is a need for public notice, and similarly that is acknowledged
in clause 5 as reported back. There it states the authority shall "give public notice of the
decision in daily newspapers circulating in Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch and
Dunedin, and in a daily newspaper circulating in the area in which the port is situated".
Again, that is an acknowledgment of the fact that on a number of occasions a decision in
respect of a particular harbour board has some ramifications far beyond the immediate area.
That was spelt out in many of the submissions.
In addition, the clause shortens the time for the appeal from 2 months to 14 days. The
reason is obvious. Such decisions are made only after a great deal of consideration, and
obviously it is not in the interests of anyone to have matters dragging on. This at the same
time acknowledges the right of interested parties to lodge their appeals. The amended clause
further spells out the manner in which the Minister shall hear an appeal. For instance, he is
required to give public notice of the time and place of the appeal.
The appropriate subclause states, "the Minister shall give public notice of the time and
place so appointed so that the last date of publication is no less than 14 days before the date
of the hearing, and otherwise in the same manner as specified in subsection 3(b) of this
section." I have already referred to that, and shall not cover it again. The subclause further
goes on to state that on hearing an appeal the Minister may confirm, modify, or reverse a
decision appealed against, or shall refer the matter to the authority for reconsideration, in
which case, following reconsideration by the authority, the matter shall proceed again as if
the decision was the initial decision of the authority. This is spelling out what we have always
understood would be the position if this circumstance arose.
Subclause (1) of clause 5 states that in any such appeal the Minister's decision shall be
final. While we appreciate the very heavy burden that such appeals place on respective
Ministers of Transport, it was the unanimous view of members of the committee that it could
not be otherwise. In taking into consideration all factors, including the national interest, the
Minister must finally be the appeal authority— even though one or two of the submissions
suggested that it should be otherwise, and that there should be an appeal authority divorced
from the Minister.
The operative clause states at subclause (12), "Where the Minister approves any
proposal submitted to him in subsection (11) of this section as part of the national ports plan
he shall cause it to be published in the Gazette... and may also cause it to be published in
such other manner as he sees fit." This recognises the importance of trying to ensure that
decisions are widely distributed and advertised.
Clause 6 deals with the control of capital expenditure, a matter which exercised the
minds of members of the committee quite considerably. The limits provided for in the Bill as
introduced were the same as those set down in 1968, and in all instances they have now been
doubled. In addition, we have moved the two container ports of Lyttelton and Otago into
the big league with their Auckland and Wellington counterparts.
Subclauses (d) and (e) also introduce the overview by the Ports Authority of other
boards and organisations that may have anything to do with harbours or harbour works.
That is an improvement on the existing position, and adequately spells out the important
function of the New Zealand Ports Authority. I believe that all interested parties will be
satisfied with the committee's recommendations.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): The chairman of the Local Bills Committee has
given a full report on the Ports Authority Amendment Bill, but, because the committee has
made some significant recommendations, I think I should comment. I agree with the
chairman's report, and agree also that the committee was unanimous in recommending the
amendments he referred to. The chairman said that 13 organisations appeared before the
committee, and that a total of 17 organisations had presented evidence. The Opposition is
pleased that those who wanted to give evidence were heard, and hopes that the practice will
be followed at all select committee hearings in future.
The committee spent some time considering the definition of the national ports plan.
When the Bill was introduced I asked the Minister whether the amendment meant that a
fixed national ports plan was no longer thought desirable. He was less than clear in his
answer. However, as a member of the committee, I now realise that this is the intention of
the Bill. The original objective of the Ports Authority was to bring down a fixed ports plan.
That is the view clearly expressed in the evidence presented by the harbour boards, and is


## p. 1180 (#290) ###########################################

1180
22 June
New Zealand Ports Authority Amendment Bill
the correct interpretation of the functions of the authority as laid down in the New Zealand
Ports Authority Act.
I agree that this is not a contentious measure, but I do think some clarification of the
proposed amendment is needed, in case people get the wrong idea of the committee's
recommendation. The stated function of the Ports Authority to prepare a national ports plan
has been reviewed by the Bill, and extensively revised. The committee decided that section
11 of the principal Act should be completely revised in the light of experience since the
passage of the Act in 1969.
It has been found that a fixed plan for the future is unrealistic. A plan could not be
devised until the issue of container ports was settled. Now that new multipurpose ships are
being designed and built for world trade, it would be ridiculous to insist that the New
Zealand Ports Authority should produce a fixed plan to meet New Zealand's obviously
flexible present shipping requirements, as well as its projected requirements. The committee
has acknowledged this, and has incorporated the provision in the Bill.
The New Zealand Ports Authority will still be required to have regard to a series of
guidelines, which are spelt out in the Bill, when considering applications from harbour
boards to proceed with harbour work. These guidelines have been outlined by the chairman.
If the basic function of the authority was to be changed, clear guidelines were needed,
because the committee did not want anyone to think that it would be open slather. We still
need a rolling plan, which will be flexible enough to meet the changing needs of New
Zealand and changing world trade. The committee has recognised this, and has
recommended that section 11 of the Act, which sets out the function of the authority, be
rewritten.
I join with the chairman of the committee in commending the Bill to the House, and
hope that when members study it they will see the wisdom of dealing with the matter now.
When the Minister introduced the Bill he said its purpose was to increase the degree of
control that the authority has over the expenditure of money on harbour facilities and
equipment. The Government obviously agrees with the findings of the green paper on
transport brought down by the Labour Government-one of the objectives of which was to
strengthen the Ports Authority.
The Opposition is pleased that the Government has accepted that section of the green
paper. The Minister said he had consigned it to the rubbish bin, but I forecast at that time
that he would be reaching for it if he was to make any progress on a total transport
programme.
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I thank the member for Timaru for his helpful
observations, although he was drawing rather a long bow when he suggested the
Government had reached into the rubbish bin and picked up the green paper on transport
brought down by the Labour Government.
When the Ports Authority appeared before the committee it indicated its intention of
designating certain equipment that would be taken beyond the prescribed limits laid down in
the appropriate clauses. The authority specifically referred to wharfside cranes suitable for
lifting containers on and off ships, transtainer cranes for shifting containers within a
complex, straddle carriers, bulk-cargo handling plant, and linkspan. With those functions
spelt out quite clearly, I hope that many of the objections to the prescribed limits in their
original or amended form will disappear.
Motion agreed to.
MASSAGE PARLOURS BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Massage Parlours Bill. The committee recommends that
the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. The committee further recommends that the
evidence of the two witnesses heard by the committee on 28 February 1978, the witnesses'
names, and any evidence that might tend to identify them should be treated as confidential,
even after the select committee has reported on the Bill to the House, provided that the
Clerk of the House may, with the leave of the House, divulge the evidence to any person
designated by the House. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
This Bill was introduced at the end of the last parliamentary session, and it is intended
to control the activities of massage or sauna parlours. In the period immediately before the
introduction of the Bill, considerable concern had been expressed about the activities of


## p. 1181 (#291) ###########################################

22 June
1181
Massage Parlours Bill
some of these establishments-particularly about allegations of prostitution and drugs.
The committee received 14 submissions, 8 of which were heard in person. These
submissions can conveniently be divided into five groups. First, the New Zealand Law
Society and the Council for Civil Liberties, while not opposing the Bill, questioned whether
it was really necessary. The Law Society expressed the view that if, in fact, massage parlours
are operating as a front for unacceptable activities such as prostitution, then an extension of
Police powers and an extension of the substantive criminal law would be more appropriate.
The Council for Civil Liberties expressed the view that the operation of a massage
parlour is a legitimate business activity and the right to carry on the business should be taken
away or denied only for grave and weighty reasons, and also said: "Prostitution will continue
regardless and no doubt continue in massage parlours. The only really effective method of
control would be to license brothels, which continue to operate, sanctions notwithstanding."
The Committee, understandably, does not accept that view.
Furthermore, on the basis of the evidence received by the select committee, members
are satisfied that there is a need for some measure of control, although not precisely in the
form envisaged in the Bill as introduced.
It is clear from the evidence heard by the select committee—much of which was
undisputed—that some massage parlours have been actively engaged in prostitution and
brothel keeping. In fact, a number of recent court cases and convictions have arisen from
these activities. Furthermore, although to a much lesser degree, there was evidence that the
opportunity to engage in prostitution in some parlours-and thereby to earn a substantial
income, which would not otherwise be available to them- does attract some drug users to
this type of employment as the only means of sustaining a drug habit.
In considering the Law Society's suggestion that rather than introduce a licensing system
the existing criminal law should be strengthened, the committee concluded that the only
effective change in the law would be to impose some sort of "vicarious liability" on the
owners of establishments for the criminal actions of their masseuse employees. In other
words, if a masseuse performed or offered to perform an act of prostitution on the owner's
premises the owner would be criminally liable for her action. Sections 148 and 149 of the
Crimes Act provide for terms of imprisonment of up to 5 years for such offences, and the
select committee was not prepared to contemplate the possibility of imposing vicarious
liability on owners for such offences. Accordingly that suggestion was rejected by the
committee.
The second group of submissions came from the New Zealand Sauna Bath Association,
representing 24 proprietors of massage parlours who saw their business operations as being
somewhat threatened by the Bill, and also from a section of the same association
representing the interests of the employees—the masseuses. Although the submissions were
separately presented to the committee-and separately represented-the committee found it
difficult to distinguish between the two sections, and their evidence was heard together. In
fact, their four witnesses were heard on two occasions-some months apart-the committee
having heard other evidence and taking the view that persons with such a direct interest in
the Bill as these people had, should be entitled to clarify any matters that had arisen in
subsequent evidence.
In essence, the evidence from the proprietors and masseuses was to the effect, first, that
there were some massage parlours and masseuses that did engage in prostitution. However,
they claimed that this did not apply to their 24 members. They said that anyone convicted of
or suspected of engaging in prostitution was dismissed. Secondly, a number of non-member
massage parlours-some of which were named in evidence-were suspected of or had been
convicted of offences involving prostitution. They also conceded some general knowledge of
involvement of particular individuals from non-member parlours with drugs. Thirdly, the
association itself acknowledged that there was a need for some control of the industry, but
argued strongly that that control should be exercised by the association itself rather than by
some external authority, and also claimed that they were regulating themselves by excluding
unsatisfactory operators from membership of the association and blacklisting unsuitable
employees. Fourthly, in answer to a question from a member of the select committee as to
whether they acknowledged that some cleaning up needed to be done across the massage
parlour industry one of the association's witnesses replied, "Most definitely, we were aware
of that in 1973 or 1974 when we first formed the association." Finally, the association's
witnesses all expressed confidence that if the Bill became law they as proprietors would have
no difficulty in becoming licensed.


## p. 1182 (#292) ###########################################

1182
22 June
Massage Parlours Bill
Overall, this evidence, while tending to exculpate those witnesses who appeared before
the committee and the fellow members of their association, also tended to confirm the
general trend of evidence before the committee that some parlours were engaging in
prostitution and that control was needed. The select committee was not, however, prepared
to accept the association's contention that it-the association-should itself exercise this
control. Such control is given usually only to very long-established and experienced
professional or trade associations. The third group of witnesses were proprietors of what
they described as legitimate massage establishments. They claimed that the pressure of
illegal activities, particularly prostitution in some of the less reputable parlours, was
imposing on them a pressure they could not resist.
The fourth group of witnesses are those whose evidence the committee has suggested
should be treated even now as confidential. The first was a police officer who gave the
committee a large amount of background information of a confidential nature. That
information has not, in itself, been used by the select committee in reaching its decisions, but
it did provide a very useful basis for the questioning of other witnesses who appeared before
the committee. The second witness-whom I shall refer to simply as Miss X-was a former
masseuse. She told the committee that at various times, and often with the active
co-operation and knowledge of her employers, she had engaged in prostitution while
working in massage parlours. She also gave other evidence of prostitution occurring in
certain massage parlours, which she named. This evidence was not necessarily in conflict
with that of the proprietors' association, which accepted that there was prostitution in some
parlours and accepted the need for control.
Miss X also confirmed that some masseuses, particularly those who were drawn to
prostitution, are also drug addicts, as she herself had been. She told the committee that it
cost up to $150 a day to support a heroin habit, and that in some cases girls were also
supporting their drug addict boy friends. She said that she and some other girls worked in
massage parlours, even though the basic wage paid by the proprietors was low, because it
was only in such places that they could earn sufficient extra money-from prostitution-to
support a drug habit. It must be emphasised that this particular witness's evidence does not
mean that every massage parlour is a brothel, that every proprietor is a brothel keeper, and
that every masseuse is a drug addict or prostitute. Furthermore, the committee would not
have been prepared to accept this girl's evidence by itself, but it was confirmed by other
aspects of evidence, including that given by the owners' association.
The final group of submissions came from groups and individuals who thought that their
activities as genuine masseurs, physiotherapists, or beauticians might come within the
provisions of the Bill, and who sought exemption.
I turn now to summarise, very briefly, the major changes to the Bill that are proposed
by the select committee. First, under the Bill as introduced, all masseuses had to apply to the
magistrate's court for a certificate of approval. Careful consideration of the evidence has
satisfied the select committee that this is unnecessary. The purpose of the Bill is to control
organised criminal ventures into prostitution, and that basic aim was obviously supported by
all those who gave evidence, so any necessary control should be exercised at the
management and ownership level rather than the employee level. An employer will be
obliged to keep a register listing the true names of all employees, and the Police will have the
right to inspect that register at all reasonable times. It will be an offence to employ a person
whose name is not entered in the register or to fail to keep such a register.
Secondly, while the committee recommends the deletion of the provisions relating to
certificates of approval for employees, it believes that both the evidence and recently
reported court cases indicate that employers must exercise more supervision in respect of
their staff. The committee therefore recommends that if an employee is involved in an act of
prostitution and there has been inadequate or negligent supervision of employees, or there
has been generally inadequate or negligent supervision, the Police should either be able to
oppose the annual reissue of the proprietor's licence or to apply for the cancellation of that
proprietor's licence. It should be emphasised that this proposed provision does not impose
any criminal liability on the proprietor-it would merely be a ground for complaint to have
the licence revoked. Whether a court would regard any incident, or series of incidents, as
sufficiently serious to justify such cancellation will depend on the facts of the case.
Thirdly, the Bill as introduced provided that the court could cancel a proprietor's
licence in an emergency without any notice to the licensee. The committee sees no need for
this provision and recommends its deletion. Fourthly, suitable amendments are

recommended to ensure that the Bill does not apply to registered physiotherapists,
beauticians, and those engaged as masseurs by sporting teams or cultural groups.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The form of the Bill before us is familiar enough.
Almost every year, Parliament is called upon to pass legislation that is industrial or
occupational in character, and sets out to regulate and discipline members of the occupation
with which the Bill is concerned. Sometimes it is by internal discipline and sometimes it is by
means of supervision from an outside body. This Bill adopts the second approach, but
whatever the mode, the result is to give members of that occupation, whether it be a
profession or otherwise described, a status that they would not have without the regulation.
In some other respects, too, it could sometimes give them an exclusive right preventing the
public from having certain work done either on it or for it, other than by members of that
occupation.
When I first saw the Bill, it seemed to me that while there was some merit in regulating
the affairs of physiotherapists-skilled professionals—as has been done, it seemed an odd
way of going about licensing massage parlours as such. As the evidence unfolded before us
and we heard comments on that evidence from the Department of Justice and the Police
Department, my fears mounted, and my suspicion that the Bill would not achieve its object
in the proper way tended to be confirmed. I concede that some of the worst aspects of the
original Bill have been mitigated, but I still find it heavy-handed and inept, and I would
prefer other alternatives. I am not at all happy about some of the amendments. I made my
views clear at an early stage of the proceedings, and little has happened since then to modify
them.
It appears from the evidence, and the gloss on it from the departments, that three
particular evils are thought to arise from the great proliferation of massage parlours in the
last 2 or 3 years: first, that they encourage prostitution; secondly, that they lead to
exploitation of young girls; and, thirdly, that they facilitate drug peddling. I would like to say
a word or two about each of these. The first-prostitution-is not a crime in itself. At most,
it is an ingredient in some other kind of offence-either keeping a brothel or soliciting or
importuning. To establish either of those offences it is necessary to know what constitutes
prostitution.
A form of words that has proved acceptable to the courts has grown up in English law,
and been adopted in New Zealand law. It should be clearly understood that this is judge-
made law and reflects the moral concepts entertained by English judges some 50 years ago.
At its last sitting the committee adopted this phraseology. I question its suitability, and I
await comments of other people who have practical experience in the social and sociological
field as to whether they think this is appropriate to the requirements of 1978 and the 1980s.
If these offences continue-and there is little doubt the community would want them
to-I believe it is desirable to give statutory expression to what constitutes prostitution, but
this should be in accord with 1978 attitudes and equally applicable to male and female
participants. This is an aspect of the law that should be made crystal clear. If I have time to
develop that, I propose to do so at a later stage.
Mr McLay: We have gone some distance.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: I know, and I appreciate that in a recent amendment the
committee has taken some steps along that line. A recent anomaly has developed, and it is so
recent it has become evident since the Bill was referred to the committee: that is, whether or
not a person practising prostitution, however it may be defined, is putting himself or herself
in the clutches of the law.
It depends whether this is on premises over which the person concerned has some
control. In other words, if the act is done in a massage parlour-in the case concerned, the
judge put it vividly by saying that the occupant has no greater security of tenure than one
entering a public toilet maintained by a municipality-the question is whether that can be
said to be keeping premises that are described as a brothel. The judge found it was not, but
the same act carried out in premises, however small, even a bed-sitter, but occupied by the
person concerned, would constitute keeping a brothel. A fine distinction like that clearly
leads to the potentiality of abuse and ought to be cleared up. The second danger, that of
exploitation, is a grievous wrong and one not to be tolerated, especially when it is susceptible
to organised exploitation at the hands of unsavoury characters.
The first step towards countering this would be to use the traditional way accepted by
trade unions and others in the past-namely, organising the people concerned and using
their combined strength. It is clear that an attempt has been made to do this, but it turned

22 June
Massage Parlours Bill
out to be ineffective. I am not persuaded that that is to be accepted as a final dismissal of
possible organisational protection under the aegis of the trade union movement, or
something of that kind. I was greatly disturbed and moved by an article that appeared in the
Auckland Star on 13 April. One could infer from that that whatever exploitation exists has
been or could be compounded by excessive zeal on the part of some policemen.
The third aspect, drug peddling, was supported by rather nebulous evidence. I am,
however, not dismissing that evidence, because it is inherently credible that these areas
should be a focus of drug trafficking, and for that reason it is not to be disregarded. But
again, I fear that just to eliminate this point of attack would have very little effect in
minimising or reducing the drug traffic, which has qutlets in many places other than premises
of this kind. It would not be over-pessimistic to believe that even if drug activity were
eliminated entirely from massage parlours we would still be left with a problem of massive
dimensions in the drug trade.
The simple remedy is to control the advertising that proprietors of massage parlours can
engage in. The committee was told that quite a number of newspapers already reject
advertisements, and others censor or vet them. Certain other newspapers have no control
and apparently accept anything at all. This propagation is the real evil. If that avenue were
cut off, the evil that people understandably see in these massage parlours would be mitigated
to a point at which they could be regarded as socially acceptable. Any efforts on the part of
newspaper proprietors should be supported and strengthened.
Let the problem lie there for a while and see if the social problem that has been
presented by the proliferation of these premises can be contained and reduced to acceptable
levels. The device adopted by the Bill of what I call sanitising the occupation and giving it not
only official status but some salable value, could increase the problem. Briefly, my view is
that the present law on prostitution is an uneasy compromise. It is partly or marginally
criminalised, and if the will of Parliament be that it be fully criminalised, then so be it. It
would be a great deal easier to enact that then to enforce it. However, if the preservation of
public order is the true objective, then the appropriate course would be to put soliciting or
importuning into the category of begging, obstruction, or disorderly behaviour.
If our aim is to repair the defects in the law as to brothel keeping, some of which have
become manifest since the Bill was referred to the committee, let us do so in contemporary
terms and in terms that emphasise that it is an offence involving more than one person, and
that any burden of culpability shall be borne by all persons involved, of whichever sex.

has gone through quite a few phases. It has come and gone on several occasions. It was
introduced because it would control the rackets, get rid of the unofficial brothels, get rid of
the underworld element that was running the rackets, and get rid of some of the crime
associated with brothels. It would bring all that under licensing. It was also said—and this

Any members associated with troops overseas, particularly those associated on the

parlours in his area, but that the party will not worry about it one little bit.
I must confess that I found the contribution made by the member for Southern Maori
difficult to follow. None the less, I agree with her very real concern about the exploitation of
young girls in these establishments. For that reason the age limit of 18 years was placed in the
Bill. When she spoke it was obvious-because she was not a member of the select
committee-that she did not know that fact. The Bill proposes a statutory prohibition to
prevent girls under the age of 18 from working in these establishments.
The proposal before the House is that the report of the select committee should be
agreed to, and it invites the House to accept the Bill in its amended and modified form. That
amended form ensures effective law enforcement legislation, but at the same time ensures
that those who engage in the legitimate operation of massage parlours-and there are many
who fall into that category-are not unduly inhibited. It places no greater onus on employee
masseuses than is at present contained in the law. It will require employers to exercise
proper supervision of their premises. That outlines the Bill the House will be asked in due
course to adopt after accepting the report of the select committee.
Motion agreed to.

Mr LATTER (Marlborough): Last night, I spent some time placing the Budget in the
context of 11 years' financial management of this country, making the point that, for 8 out of
those 11 years, the Budgets were brought forward by the present Prime Minister. It is
essential that the person who controls our finances has financial ability. I praised his role in
the years to 1972. I made the point that the country dropped the financial pilot in 1972, and I
dealt with the trends shown in the years of the Labour Government, quoting particularly
from the 1975 Budget. Tonight I want to talk about the 1978 Budget. I believe very few real
debating points have come from the Opposition. Perhaps one is the rather interesting figure
of a deficit of about $1,000 million. It is interesting because it is pretty close to the deficit at
the end of the last year of the Labour Government. When the National Government came
into office in the December and took some remedial action it prevented the deficit from
reaching $1,200 million and the projection of $1,400 million.
Hon. Michael Connelly: There was no such figure.
Mr LATTER: There was. It is in the accounts. The member for Wigram wants to argue
figures. If we are to talk about figures and Budget deficits, let us go back to 1975, when we
will not find a Budget deficit of $1,000 million—I did not say “would”. The figure will
probably be about $497 million, because the supplementaries of $50 million were not taken
into account, nor was other Government financing such as that for the Rural Bank and
housing. All of those are included in the figure this year. The 1975 figure did not show the
record unvalidated expenditure or the subsidies. The two figures are entirely different. To
begin with, the main difference, which will be seen by most people, is in the deficit budgeting
exercise. In 1975 the Labour Government, in desperation because it was election year, and
refusing to lift the freezes and acknowledge that something would have to be done after the
election-and we know that work was done on those figures-stoked a ship that was going
down. As I said last night, the present Deputy Leader of the Opposition said in May 1975,
"We refuse to compromise our social objectives."
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: It is worse now.

inflation increased to nearly 17 percent, but when a Government is elected at the end of a

where are you? You are in a completely unmanageable area, with inflation above 25 percent.

should be returned to office, is that it grappled with inflation, which is now coming down.

Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Oh!
Mr LATTER: O.K., under 5 percent, and, therefore, under 10 percent for the year.

Hon. W. A. FRASER: I want to highlight the bleak future that faces the building

5 permits were issued, in February the number increased dramatically to 8, in March it
reached 11, in April-the month the increased loan took effect-the number dropped to 5,
and in May it increased to 9. If those figures were projected over 12 months, 91 houses would
be built, assuming all permits were acted upon. Last year the number of permits issued
dropped to 135.

The Budget is a bolstering Budget and a booster Budget. It has bolstered and boosted
the farmers' confidence. As a city member I wholeheartedly approve of the assistance given
to the farmers. They are still producing 80 percent of our overseas income. After a disastrous
drought they deserve all the assistance that the Government can possibly give them. The
assistance has been appreciated by the farmers, as I have found when travelling throughout
the country.
The Budget has also boosted the morale of the worker, particularly the breadwinner in
the single-income family. I shall not blind everyone with figures as some speakers have done,
but I will put the facts simply. After comparing the figures with those under the Labour
Government, a married man with a family of young children under 5 years who earns $8,000
a year, or $160 a week, will now be able to save $1,000 a year, or $20 a week under the
Budget. The Budget has boosted the morale of the worker who has been discouraged in the
past from working over time or taking secondary employment because it has meant that he
has moved into a higher tax rate. The following example demonstrates the reduced taxation
as a result of the number of steps being reduced. Prior to the Budget, a person earning
$6,500, or $130 a week, could, by working overtime or taking secondary employment, be
taxed up to 48c in the dollar. Now he can earn an additional $3,500 per annum, or $70 per
week extra on overtime, and still be taxed at the same rate as if he was earning $6,500–
namely, 38c in the dollar. This will be a tremendous boost to productivity. No longer will we
hear the cry that it does not pay to work overtime. The workers are pleased with this Budget,
particularly those workers who are prepared to work longer hours to provide that little extra
for their wives and families. They are the New Zealanders that the Government wants to
help. The Government has helped them in a way they can appreciate most, and they
certainly have appreciated it.
I have two further points to make before I leave the Budget and talk about matters
affecting my portfolio. The action taken on estate duty is most humane. How many times
have we heard of a widow being embarrassed by an officer asking questions about the value
of her fur coat, her jewellery, her clothing, to say nothing of her furniture. That will not
happen anymore. From the date of the Budget all chattels left by a surviving spouse are
exempted from estate duty irrespective of value. There will be no more valuations and no
more distress to relatives assisting with them. Now, a woman knows that when her husband
dies she will not have to go through the dreadful indignity of having an officer value her
chattels. The $4,000 exemption applying in other cases will also be increased to $6,000. On
behalf of my constituents I want to thank the Prime Minister very warmly.
The other point I want to talk about is the aid for the parents of handicapped children.
From 18 October, at a cost to the Government of $1.5 million, there will be a payment of a
non-taxable allowance of $8 per week to the parents of seriously physically or mentally
handicapped children. Again, how many of us over the years have admired and wondered at
the courage and patience of parents who have insisted on keeping their handicapped children
at home and caring for and loving those unfortunate children. This small token from the
Government will let those parents know that the Government appreciates the caring and the
understanding that they show to their handicapped children and appreciates the costs
involved. I want to say to Opposition members who said that the Prime Minister had no
heart, that parents of handicapped children in my electorate have asked me to thank him for
this very heart-warming gesture. It is a bolstering, boosting Budget for the farmers and the
workers, but it is a very human, caring Budget for the bereaved, and those looking after the
handicapped.
Before turning to matters more closely related to my portfolio, I want to remind
members of the House and the public of the mess National inherited in 1975. It is so easy to
forget. National inherited an inflation rate of 15.7 percent, as against 5.5 percent when we
reluctantly handed over to Labour in 1972. We were reluctant because we feared the worst,
and our fears were realised. I confidently predict that, when the half-yearly figures are
available, inflation will be back to single figures-that is, under 10 percent on an annual basis
and under 5 percent on a half-yearly basis. Let me remind members of the overseas
payments position when we took over. In 1972 when we handed over to Labour there was a
surplus of $208 million. In 1975 when we took over from Labour there was a deficit of $1,000

I recently attended the annual conferences of the Municipal Association and the
Counties Association. Those two associations, representing the total field of territorial local
government, are very much in favour of the Government's action in restructuring the Local
Government Commission and in providing a more democratic process for changes in the
structure of local government. Sir Richard Webb, Mr Barry Hadfield, and Mr Keith
Dockery have already impressed everyone who has been associated with them with their
efficiency, there no-nonsense approach, and their enthusiasm. I am expecting great things
from them in the future. They have set a target for establishing the regions by the end of next
year at the latest. I am hoping that those regions will be established by June.
There was, it is true, some disappointment that the Government would not accept in full
the recommendations of the Local Government Finance Committee, particularly in respect
of revenue sharing. However, the issues at stake, both for the taxpayer providers and the
local authority spenders of such centrally collected revenues, are very great. It is in
everyone's interest that we should examine the issues dispassionately but with a great deal of
care and determination, to ensure that the ability of local government to grow into the role
of a full partner in the process of government is not frustrated by an inadequate ability to
raise the resources it needs in an effective and equitable way. I strongly believe that we have
to find an alternative source of income, other than rates, for local bodies. A way must be
found or permitted, in the larger urban areas in particular. Auckland is a case in point, and I
shall continue to impress on the Government the need to find this alternative source.
Despite the economic difficulties I have referred to, and despite the fact that we must
place curbs on Government spending, it has been possible to make significant progress in
those aspects of social and community policy covered by my portfolio. For this achievement I
want to thank my colleagues, who supported my proposals for developments in the fields of
culture, recreation, and youth affairs. I thank also such organisations as the Arts Council,
the Council for Recreation and Sport, and the National Youth Council. They have all played
their part in creating a climate of support for the development of the Government, for the
development of the con.mercial community, and for community activities in those fields.
I have been interested in obtaining additional resources for cultural, recreational, and
youth activities because, as members know, Government assistance in those areas has a
multiplier effect. In almost all cases, Government finance provides a stimulating
contribution to the funds provided by local authorities or by the community. In very many
cases it provides encouragement and support to that enormous army of volunteer workers
who give their time freely so that others may creatively enjoy theirs. I refer to the mums and
dads who referee and act as linesmen and lineswomen at Saturday morning football matches.
I refer to the ubiquitous raffle ticket sellers, and to the factory worker who gives up his
evening to pass on his skills in first aid to the local evening class. I refer to the headmaster,
who not only allows his school to be used for community activities, but who goes along to
participate in the evening.
This sort of community involvement is as much a part of New Zealand as our bush and
our beautiful lakes and rivers, and is subject to degenerative pressures in much the same
way. Protection and enhancement of voluntary planning in our community development
programme is essential. We need the professional in our programmes to provide new skills
and new ideas. We need him to help co-ordinate and activate, but he must not be allowed to
usurp the role of voluntary workers. If we lose them we lose the spirit that has given special
intensity and meaning to our community life.
The total allocation for recreation and sport this year is $4,418,000, a large increase on
the $3,284,000 initially allocated last year. Last year's allocation was supplemented in two
ways. The Lottery Board of Control gave $400,000 for the provision of community facilities
at schools, and the Government provided a mere $1 million to provide employment
opportunities for young people who have special difficulties in the present circumstances.

This year the Lottery Board of Control has allocated $600,000 to establish a community
development fund. The community facilities at schools scheme will be funded from this,
together with other projects to promote stronger and more self-reliant communities. I have
already approved a grant of up to $19,000 from this fund to assist the New Zealand Council
for Recreation and Sport in its family recreation programme.
I want to thank all those people who invested in the half-million lottery. The extra
profits from those lotteries will provide more money for the arts, for medical research, for
housing for the aged, and for the welfare of the aged-to name a few of the projects that can
be helped. I thank warmly all those who have been purchasing tickets. Please continue to
invest. You might win a prize, but if you do not, you are still assisting very worthy causes.
Last year nearly $900,000 was spent on the student community service programme which
found employment for 2 000 tertiary students on a wide range of community projects during
the long summer vacation. If there is anything about which my department and I should be
happy, it is that scheme. Whether or not the Government repeats the scheme this year will
depend on the employment position later in the year, and the result of a full assessment of
the usefulness of the initial scheme.
The reports I have had so far from local authorities, community workers, and members
of Parliament show that the scheme was highly successful. Not only was the employment
market relieved of the impact of another 2 000 would-be employees, but the new jobs
created were of direct community benefit. The students earned money to help them through
the year, and in many instances they gained a new insight into community needs and how
they might be able to contribute to them. One of the thrills I had when this scheme was
operating was to visit the Fortune Theature in Dunedin, where I saw half a dozen students
working like Trojans. I am sure that by working on that project they would get into the spirit
of the theatre; and probably from now on they will be devotees of drama in Dunedin. We
should examine the possibility of establishing such a limited community service programme
on a more or less permanent basis, irrespective of the availability of other employment
opportunities for students in the future.
The full involvement of local authorities in recreation and sport and in community
development programmes is absolutely essential. They are in a much better position to help
find out local needs and assess community priorities. Therefore, I am delighted that last year
an additional eight recreational officers were appointed to local authorities, making use of
the $2 for $1 salary subsidy. Eighteen of these officers have now been appointed or
approved, and I am making provision in this year's estimates for the appointment of a
further 10 officers this year. The local recreation and sport programme scheme has also been
amended to increase the finance available to local authorities from grants based on 50c per
head of population to 75c per head in this financial year, and $1 per head next year. The
scope of the scheme has been widened to cover recreation and sport and community
development programmes and facilities generally, and I also have in mind-with the support
of the Lotteries Board of Control-making available a sum of approximately $700,000 per
annum to enable local authorities to sustain community buildings, such as town halls and
sports stadiums. I know this has been very well received by the various local authorities.
Finally on this theme, last year I introduced with the strong support of the Prime
Minister a scheme under which the salaries of detached youth workers could be met from
community and recreation funds. The salaries of 12 such workers are being paid at present,
and I propose to approve a further 8 this year if suitable proposals are submitted for my
consideration. This scheme is assisting in facing up to a real problem, and is proving to be
very successful. This is a completely new scheme, which I believe can do much to meet the
real needs of young people, many of whom are at risk and in need of a constructive purpose
to their lives.

can make this tour. The regional orchestras are performing well, even if they are facing
continuing problems at the administrative level, and are handicapped at times because of a
shortage of funds. I take my hat off to administrators and musicians who, by sheer

But, in the long-term, the most important and exciting development in the arts in the
past year has taken place in film making. For many years, the merits of establishing a fund to
assist New Zealand film makers have been discussed at all levels. Film is such an important
cultural medium, in my opinion the most important if one looks at the range of talents
employed and the vast audiences for the finished product. Film, of course, is much more
than a cultural icon; it is part of today's living culture. It has also a strong commercial and
industrial element. Films have a turnover of hundreds of millions of dollars on the
international market. As well as cultural benefits, therefore, local films can bring significant
economic benefits by way of both overseas sale and import substitution. The industry is
already heavily capitalised, and a small priming of the pump by the Government will see

One major factor in that cost is interest rates. The cost of money is killing housing.
