C.C. BEKAELET LIBRARY
MOUNT EGMONT VESTING BILL
Introduction
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): I move, That the Mount Egmont Vesting Bill be
introduced. The purpose of this Bill is the symbolic transfer of the Mount Egmont National
Park land to the Taranaki Maori Trust Board, representing the Maori tribes of Taranaki,
who then wish to formally gift the mountain to the people of New Zealand—that is to say,
the Crown. When this is done, the Maori people of Taranaki in particular and New
Zealanders in general will be able to say that this great public treasure, the mountain, has
been given to the nation by its original owners or, as a Maori might well say, by their
traditional caretakers-as a free and loving gift.
The subject of Taranaki land confiscations is not on this occasion under discussion, but
there are historical facts already made public that are worth recalling. Those members who
are interested can find an admirable exposition in Parliamentary Paper G. 7 of 1928. This is
the report of a royal commission on confiscated native lands and other grievances. However,
today we are discussing the attachment of the Taranaki people to their mountain. To the
Maori, the mountain is Taranaki. It is to be regarded almost with religious awe as having a
special relationship to them as a spiritual relative of Tupuna of great sanctity. Their pride has
suffered for generations in that they were deprived of their sacred mountain in a manner that
they consider unjust. As one who was brought up in Taranaki, I have for many years been
conscious of the land grievances of the Taranaki Maori people. Like many Taranaki people,
I have sensed the anxiety that has simmered beneath the surface.
To the east, the neighbours of the people of Taranaki, the Tuwharetoa people, gave the
nation their great mountains, now the heart of the Tongariro National Park. The Taranaki
Maori people have felt for some considerable time a burning desire not only to regain their
mountain, but also to fulfil that part of their history by making a gift to our nation that will
ensure the continuing reservation of their mountain, Taranaki.
The principles of the Bill have been discussed with representatives of the Taranaki
Maori people and members of their trust board. I can say without any question that the Bill
has their wholehearted approval. In the light of more recent events, it is perhaps appropriate
to add that the Taranaki Maori Trust Board has always been most proper in its approach to
the Government on this matter. For its part, the Government, in accepting the importance
the Maori people attach to the return of the mountain, has not acted under any duress or any
threat of action whatsoever. I should also say that these proposals were originally raised with
11-Vol 418


## p. 1220 (#330) ###########################################

1220
23 June
Mount Egmont Vesting Bill
my predecessor, the member for Northern Maori, who had proceeded some way with them
while holding the Lands portfolio.
For the benefit of the House, I will quickly run through the various clauses of the Bill.
Clause 1 relates to the short title. Clause 2 relates to interpretation, and defines the terms
"board", "Minister", and "the mountain". Clause 3 binds the Crown. Clause 4 excludes the
mountain from the Egmont National Park, and vests it in the trust board for an estate in fee
simple. Clause 5 gifts the whole of the interest in the mountain from the trust board to Her
Majesty the Queen for the purposes of a national park, subject to a special condition relating
to possible future exclusions of land from the Egmont National Park.
Clause 6 relates to the special condition that every future proposal to exclude any part of
the gifted land from Egmont National Park shall be referred by the Minister of Lands to the
trust board. This will give the board a reasonable opportunity to consider the proposal and
comment to him. Clause 7 exempts the gift of the mountain to the Crown from gift duty.
Clause 8 subjects the provisions of the National Parks Act 1952, Part XXI of the Maori
Affairs Act 1953, the Maori Trust Boards Act 1955, the Estate and Gift Duties Act 1968, or
any other enactment to the Bill. Clause 9 relates to the necessary savings to preserve the
need for an Act of Parliament to exclude land from a national park and to preserve the
validity of anything whatsoever done or issued under the provision of the National Parks Act
1952 or any other former corresponding enactment subsisting or in force on the date of the
Bill.
From time to time every Government must, with sincerity and determination, find a
way through land issues that have been inherited from past Administrations and times.
Today, the matter in question is the mountain in Taranaki. In am sure the House will
appreciate the significance of the Bill, not only to the Taranaki Maori people, but also to our
nation as a whole. It will remove a great shadow on the pride and the mana of Taranaki New
Zealanders. I am of the opinion that, when the Bill becomes statute, generations of New
Zealanders who follow us will look back to this dignified act with pride and satisfaction. The
Bill will, of course, be referred to the Lands and Agriculture Committee, and at the
appropriate time I shall move that the proceedings of the committee during the hearing of
evidence on the Bill be open to accredited representatives of the news media.

Railways-Modernisation of Da Locomotives
1. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Railways: Is it still proposed to
proceed with the original proposal to have 35 Da locomotives modernised in Australia, and
has a firm contract been entered into for this number or can any of these locomotives be
modernised here in New Zealand?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The Minister of Railways replies: "Yes, a firm
contract was let for the rebuilding of 35 Da locomotives in April 1977, and has since been
extended to include a further 19. The possibility of this work being done in New Zealand was
fully investigated before the contract was let."
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Was it possible to have some of the work done in New Zealand rather
than have it all done by contract overseas?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I am informed that, because the workshops were fully committed
at the time on locomotive repairs, and the building and maintenance of other rolling stock, it
was decided to have the work carried out outside New Zealand. I am further informed that
the rebuilding of the Da locomotives goes appreciably beyond repair, maintenance, or
overhaul. It involves, for example, the rebuilding of the cabs, and the rebuilding and
upgrading of the diesel engines.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: Is the Minister able to confirm that some of the work let out to
Australia will not be completed, nor will the locomotives be returned, until 1982 or 1983?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I am unable to confirm that.
Recreational Grants/Subsidies, Hastings
2. Mr FENTON (Hastings) to the Minister of Recreation and Sport: What grants and/or

Taxation Relief-Budget
5. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department: What tax relief will a married couple with no dependants and earning two
incomes of $200 and $180 per week receive from 1 October, and how does the amount
compare with the relief given to a family with 4 children aged 2, 5, 9, and 13 years, in which
the man earns $130 per week and his wife supplements that income on a part-time basis by
earning $20 per week?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue Department): On
a weekly basis the reduction in tax payable by the couple with no dependants and earning
two incomes of $200 and $180 per week, which will ensure an overall reduction in this
couple's tax requirements of 17 percent since the last Labour Government, is $14.52. On a
weekly basis, the reduction in tax payable by the man earning $130 and his wife earning a
supplementary income of $20 will, with these four children, add an additional $2.53 to their
income, a figure which will ensure an overall reduction since the time of the last Labour
Government of 50 percent in tax paid. In short, since the implementation of the 1975 Budget
the combined tax of the first couple will have fallen from $124.68 to $103.63—that is, by 17
percent; and the combined tax of the second couple will have fallen after 1 October 1978
from $35.11 to $17.52-a 50 percent reduction. In addition, the couple with four children
will continue to receive family benefit amounting to $12 a week, or $624 untaxed income a
year.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Would the Minister tell the House why the Government has
deliberately decided that a two-income family with no dependants and with a total income of

four dependent children with a total income of $150 a week will receive tax relief of $2.52?

realises that we are dealing with a 3-year budgetary programme that started in 1976 to give-
[Interruption.] If the member for Manukau wants to ask the Junior Opposition Whip a

Budgets the Government has moved to bring relief to the young family and the single-
income family, as the member is aware. I have given the House figures that show that in 3

Beef Prices
7. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Agriculture: In the
event of the minimum price for beef exceeding the "trigger price", will the Meat Board
receive 50 percent of this difference for its reserve funds?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): This is a hypothetical question. It is
quite obvious that the questioner does not understand the system of setting prices for meat,
and beef in particular, under the stabilisation scheme. The question asks: "In the event of
the minimum price for beef exceeding the 'trigger price' will the Meat Board receive 50
percent of this difference for its reserve funds?" The minimum price set for beef is 70c for
cow beef, and 80c for prime beef. The Meat Export Prices Committee has not met this year
to fix next year's "trigger price". The committee comprises an independent chairman, two
representatives from the Government, and two from the Meat Board. They will know what
the minimum price is, and would take into consideration that it would be somewhat stupid
for them to set the "trigger price" below the minimum price.
Mr Barclay: Can I take it from the Minister's excuses-
Hɔn. David Thomson: A point of order, Mr Speaker. The member for Christchurch
Central asked a question that was patently hypothetical, and now accuses the Minister of
making excuses. A hypothetical question cannot be answered except in a hypothetical way.
There is no question of the Minister making excuses, and I think that remark should be
withdrawn.
Mr SPEAKER: This sort of matter should not be brought into the question and answer
period. As to whether the question is hypothetical, I allowed it, of course, because I did not
think it was hypothetical, but thought it was a question that could be answered.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Is it a fact that the independent authority fixing the "trigger price"
for meat will be directed by the Government when it establishes as it does, the minimum
price?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: It is not a fact. The authority comprises an independent
chairman, two representatives from the Government and two from the Meat Board. The
Government has no power to direct the authority whatsoever. It may influence its two
representatives, but I remind the member that two out of five members are not a majority.

Overseas Students
17. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Immigration: Is it correct that
overseas students studying in New Zealand are now required to return home immediately
after their final results have been received, and before graduation?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Immigration replies:
"Student permits are issued for a period of 12 months, valid until 31 December of each year.
Successful students know by the end of the academic year that they have completed the
course of study for which they were permitted to enter New Zealand, and that the conditions
of their student permits have therefore been fulfilled. To enable a student to remain in New
Zealand legally until the following May, an extension of 5 months would be required. There
is no requirement that students attend the graduation ceremony personally. The
interdepartmental committee on private overseas student policy has recently reviewed the
necessity for students to remain for graduation and has decided that extensions of permits for
this purpose cannot be justified."

ROAD SAFETY COMMITTEE-INTERIM REPORT
Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West): I am directed by the Road Safety Committee to
present an interim report of the committee for the year 1978. The Road Safety Committee
has been concerned that in the face of a mounting road toll, prompt legislative action should
be taken by the House. The report sets out a number of recommendations that the
committee wishes to place before the House. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
Before I discuss the recommendations, I should like to pay appropriate tributes to
members of the committee, particularly the members for Lyttelton, Timaru, and Onehunga.
They have worked assiduously. The committee worked without regard to party line or
division in the pursuit of a common concern that action should be taken to diminish the road
toll that concerns all responsible people. Our main recommendations are set out in the
report, and, briefly, they involve a number of perhaps controversial suggestions but,
nevertheless, suggestions that the committee believes to be positive.
We recommend that evidential breath testing should be introduced, substantially to
replace blood testing. The main purpose of this recommendation, or the hope behind it, is
that present complicated technical procedures that keep traffic officers from the roads will be
simplified, and that enforcement will improve accordingly.
We recommend that the blood-alcohol limit should be lowered to 80 mg of alcohol per
100 ml of blood. We recommend further, as a simplification of procedure, that one screening
breath test should be required instead of the present two. We also recommend that the
grounds for requesting a breath test should be somewhat extended. At present a test may be
taken if a traffic officer or enforcement officer has reasonable cause to suspect the
consumption of alcohol. We suggest that a test be obtainable where a person has been
involved in an accident, or where there is reasonable cause to suspect the commission of a
culpable driving offence. As for the device used in connection with breath testing, we are
dealing here with rapidly evolving technology and it is suggested that rather than name a
particular device, a discretion should be vested in the Minister of Transport to approve


## p. 1233 (#343) ###########################################

23 June
1233
Road Safety Committee-Interim Report
devices from time to time on the basis of the most up-to-date technical knowledge.
We are concerned to improve the position concerning drugs. Not only alcohol may be
involved in a driving offence, and we suggest that where alcohol may be suspected but not
proved, suspicion may be aroused that drugs are responsible for a driver's condition. We
want a provision that blood or other body samples may be requested where a drug other than
alcohol is suspected. We wish the present unsatisfactory position concerning hospital
sampling to be improved. Accordingly, we suggest changes in the law or to the present
position in hospitals.
As to penalties, we see these as basic to the respect that the law requires in this area.
There are recommendations on limited licences. These recommendations will make it more
difficult to obtain a limited licence after a prosecution for a blood-alcohol offence. We
recommend certain increases in pecuniary penalties for alcohol-related offences. On the
question of penalties, we have been asked from time to time why we do not look more at the
rehabilitation of alcohol-impaired drivers. The committee has long regarded this as an
important aspect, and indeed in 1974, 1975, and 1976 the committee recommended an
investigation of possible programmes for the rehabilitation of alcohol-impaired drivers. The
result has been an experiment in Dunedin where there has been a course for alcohol-
impaired drivers since 1976. Drivers are referred to the course as a special condition of
probation, part of a periodic detention sentence, or under section 68 of the Transport Act as
a condition of licence restoration. It is too early to say how effective the course has been, but
after careful study of the results achieved it may be possible at some not too distant stage to
recommend wider implementation of the Dunedin operation.
The report contains significant recommendations concerning seat belts. In its last report
to Parliament the committee stated that great accident reduction would be achieved through
the seat belt regulations. We were satisfied that we had not extracted maximum value from
the seat belt, and accordingly we place before the House further recommendations for the
improved safety we believe can be achieved through the efficient and effective use of belts.
One startling aspect of the report concerns young drivers. Representations have been
made to us about the issue of licences and various other matters relating to youthful drivers.
The graph attached to our report illustrates the high incidence of accidents in the young
driver group, and quite clearly some investigation is required. Such an investigation is
proceeding. The committee hopes it will be able to report further on this matter before the
end of the year.
At the end of the report the problems of traffic enforcement are mentioned. I am sure
all members of the committee would agree that, no matter how stringent the law, it loses its
effectiveness if it is not adequately enforced. There has to be some reasonable certainty of
detection, and indeed certainty of detection is the greatest deterrent of all. As the report
points out, the committee has some reservations about whether we are achieving the best
possible results in enforcement. Various attitudes prevail, and I refer in particular to
remarks of the executive director of the National Society on Alcoholism and Drug
Dependence, who is reported recently as having said that the problems of road safety will
not be solved unless there are major changes in society's attitude towards drinking.
The problem will never be solved, in the sense that it will be entirely eradicated. What
the Road Safety Committee is consciously doing is seriously trying to restrain, and keep
some measure of control over, the threatened increase in the incidence of accidents
attributable to alcohol-impaired driving. That, in outline, is the report. That, in outline,
reflects the attitudes of members of the committee. I commend the report to the House.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): I support the chairman of the committee, the
member for Hamilton West, in his introduction this morning of the interim report of the
Road Safety Committee. He mentioned the work of the committee. I believe it would be
only right that I should also make reference to the chairman's work. He was determined to
make progress, and kept the committee working; witnesses who appeared before the
committee were held very much to the point, particularly expert witnesses who, when
appearing before committees, tend to lead into technicalities in the area of their expertise
They were kept to the point, and spoke in laymen's terms so that the committee could fully
understand the points that were made. While the report is not entirely unanimous in detail,
the members are in complete agreement regarding the general objectives of the committee.
We must make progress in the area of road safety. It will be appreciated that some
members have personal feelings, not only committee members but those in the House, as to
how this can be achieved. There was agreement that an early report should be made to


## p. 1234 (#344) ###########################################

1234
23 June
Road Safety Committee-Interim Report
Parliament expressing the Road Safety Committee's complete agreement that legislation is
imperative to tighten up the law relating to drinking and driving, the maximum penalties that
the courts can impose over the complete range of offences they are called upon to consider
and to action, and other related matters in which the committee is called upon to adjudicate.
The report makes recommendations for wide-ranging changes designed to simplify the
law and to make enforcement more effective. The committee has presented its report,
conscious of a background of increasing road accidents and fatalities, and the high
relationship of alcohol with that situation is causing much public concern. The position is
deteriorating. The record of driver behaviour on New Zealand roads is not good. I refer
members to the chart at the back of the report, and to the reference on page 5 to young
drivers. The committee will consider this aspect further. The Road Safety Research Council
has done considerable work on this, and produced some valuable evidence to the committee.
On page 5 of the report it is stated, "Basically the initial findings suggest that the
accident involvement of young drivers (15-19) is, if anything, worse than had been expected.
While this group accounts for only about 14 percent of the over-15 population, 13 percent of
drivers, and 8 percent of total annual mileage, it accounts for 27 percent of all drivers
involved in injury accidents." The position is clearly illustrated in the graph in the report. It
is dramatic. I hope members will take a good look at it, because the committee will be
making recommendations regarding young drivers.
Many suggestions were made that the minimum age for obtaining licences should be
increased from 15 to 18, and that a probationary period should be instituted. These
suggestions will be considered. The committee makes a firm recommendation for the
adoption of evidential breath testing, after foreshadowing this in the 1976 and 1977 reports.
The option for a blood test remains. Provision is made for a driver who disputes the result of
the evidential breath test produced to him by the device, whatever device might be approved
by the Minister. There is also provision for a traffic officer to require a blood sample in cases
of doubt arising from a breath test. The committee recommends broader grounds for
instituting breath tests but stops short of random breath testing in all cases. This was given
considerable consideration by the committee.
I regret to say that, in my view, it has been imperative to clarify this section of the
Transport Act resulting from the confusion that involved the Prime Minister earlier this year
when he appeared to misunderstand the provisions of the Act when, following the decisions
of Mr Justice Chilwell, he was reported in the Evening Post of 28 February as saying, “In the
past it has been understood that a traffic officer could not stop anyone for a breath test unless
he thought an offence had been committed." That is not correct. Under the law that has
applied since 1974, a traffic officer can stop any driver and request him to have a breath test
if the officer suspects that person has been drinking. In fact, a person does not have to be
behind the wheel of a car, if the officer suspects that person has been drinking. That is in the
existing law. A person could be going towards a car and, if the officer suspects that the
person intends to drive, he can require a breath test to be taken.
It is unfortunate that this confusion arises, and it is imperative, with this
recommendation from the Road Safety Committee, that we underline the fact that this is the
law, so that everyone understands it. We should recommend the additions outlined on page
1 of the report, paragraph 2.1.(d); that the grounds for requesting that a breath test should
be taken should be extended to include the suspected consumption of alcohol-that is
already included—when there is involvement in an accident by anyone, and when a culpable
driving offence is suspected. We have to underline this, and make sure that there is no
misunderstanding by anyone, including the Prime Minister.
Turning to the continuing abuse of the limited licence provisions, by people granted this
consideration to avoid hardship to families, it has been necessary to recommend more
stringent control over the issue of these licences. The committee advises that no limited
licence should be issued for a second offence or for subsequent offences. Unfortunately,
there has been abuse in this area. It has been drawn to our attention, and we make this
recommendation.
The committee members strongly and unanimously support any move by the Minister of
Transport to get the Government to increase traffic law enforcement. The committee was
disturbed to hear evidence from the Chief Traffic Officer, Mr Roxburgh, of a serious
reduction in the number of traffic officers now on the roads, and the number of traffic
officers that the department is permitted to recruit, train, and employ, because of staffing
levels and staffing-level restrictions. This is embarrassing the Ministry of Transport law


## p. 1235 (#345) ###########################################

enforcement section. We heard evidence about it, and the committee was disturbed, and is
making strong recommendations to the Minister in the hope that his Cabinet colleagues will
realise that the position is serious. When the Minister makes this submission, the committee
hopes that it will be received sympathetically and with understanding by his colleagues.
Unless our traffic laws can be enforced by the provision of an adequate number of trained
traffic officers, the Road Safety Committee will have wasted its time preparing and

We were set a job to do, we made recommendations as a committee, and we worked

about this, and we trust the Government will take note. Road deaths increased by 100 in
1977, or by nearly 17 percent. After 3 years with the road toll and the accident rate declining,
there has now been a swing in the other direction. The committee has done its job. I see this
report as the absolute minimum that we must do to improve road safety in New Zealand. I

recommendations.

Research, had this to say about evidential breath tests: "While experiments with the devices

23 June

successful in operating conditions." He said he is very cautious in recommending any system

According to Mr McDonald, experiments conducted by the Auckland City Council
were less than satisfactory. The 163 tests used in the study would have resulted in one driver
being incorrectly released, and three drivers being incorrectly presumed to have breath
alcohol levels above 500 mg per litre. He stressed however, that the 163 tests used in the
study might not accurately indicate what would happen under more varied conditions. To
introduce evidential breath tests now, without further tests under operative conditions would
mean that we were prepared to accept that some people would wrongly be accused of having
positive readings when, in fact, they should not have been classified. In these cases the onus
would be on the driver to seek a blood test to refute the conclusions drawn from the
evidential device. My personal opinion-and I stress this-is that we should delay the
introduction of the change until we have further evidence under operative conditions.
The second recommendation that I want to discuss is the reduction of the permissible
blood alcohol limit from 100 mg to 100 ml to 80 mg to 100 ml. Furthermore, if we seriously
want to stop people drinking to excess and then driving it would be more realistic and
meaningful to drop the speed limit from 80 km/h to 60 km/h. We need an effective law to
control the drinking and driving problem, and we need effective devices to measure alcohol
intake. Let us reduce the speed limit to 60 km/h and postpone evidential testing until
adequate tests have been completed on which to base any change.

Mr SPEAKER: I do not need any further assistance. The honourable member asked me
for guidance on this matter. It is a question of the interpretation of the Standing Orders as
they relate to the presentation or to the tabling of the report. Standing Order 366, which
deals with the publication or divulging of the proceedings of or evidence taken at a select
committee, states that such matters are confidential to that committee, in relation to the
deliberations at any rate, until such time as the report of the committee has been presented
to the House-not tabled, but presented. That means that the chairman of the committee
stands up and tells the House that he is in a position to report back to the House from the
select committee. At that stage the report itself-in this case, the interim report of the Road
Safety Committee-and the evidence presented to the committee are available to the House,

Dr WALL (Porirua): Thank you, Mr Speaker. That is what I understood to be the
position, and I am glad to have it clarified. I realise that a bipartisan approach has been
taken on the report and that both sides of the House agree on it, but some of its aspects
disturb me. I appreciate that the committee had to deal with a difficult problem, and that
there will be considerable disagreement about its technical implications. One or two
principles that apply to offending have not been weighed up adequately in the report. One is
that the severity of penalties appears to have little.effect on the rate of offending. This goes
right back through history. One thing that does have a major effect on the rate of offending
is the likelihood of being detected. The committee was right in its approach, because, by
setting out certain grounds for investigation of a possible drinking driver, it has increased the
possibility of detection. For that, I commend the committee but I think it could have served
us better on the technical problems associated with determining the level of blood alcohol.
Members of the committee took particular note of the degree of accuracy of the breath
testing machines, which, while having the advantage of being easily available and requiring


## p. 1238 (#348) ###########################################

1238
23 June
Road Safety Committee-Interim Report
limited technical knowledge for their use, have the disadvantage of not having quite the
reputed accuracy of a blood test. The courts and the House accept the accuracy of blood tests
done by the Government Analyst, the presumption being that everything is done correctly in
the Government laboratory on every occasion. This would be somewhat different from what
we know of normal human behaviour, but the presumption is there. If there was a known
range of inaccuracy to the order of, say, 20 percent, and the limit level were set at 500
micrograms per litre of expired breath with the provision that breath-testing apparatus
would be considered as evidence if it gave a reading about 700 or 800 micrograms per litre, so
allowing a range of experimental error wide enough to rule out the possibility that it was
caused by the inbuilt inaccuracies of the machine, this would very much increase the
likelihood of examination of suspected drinking drivers and increase the ease with which
evidence could be collected.
Those of us who have been involved in taking a blood test and its procedures realise that
they are time consuming and expensive. Any machinery which, while protecting the accused
from being unjustly convicted, could reduce easily the expense or manpower involved,
would be of great advantage. I do suggest that in the not too distant future the committee be
invited to look at this aspect again to provide evidential machinery, but with a tolerance
level, built into the evidential requirements, that would rule out any experimental error. I
think the committee could have served us better by making such provision. I am also
concerned about heavier penalties. Because these are financial, the effects are quite
inequitable when spread across the community. For a man on a low wage and with heavy
family commitments, an increased financial penalty can be almost a life sentence, whereas
for a wealthy man, particularly if his livelihood is not in the slightest dependent on his driving
capacity, the financial penalty is just an incident. This disparity in punishment depending on
the financial circumstances of the individual becomes more and more marked the greater we
make the penalty. Therefore, I cannot support the introduction of increased financial
penalties. They are intrinsically unjust in their incidence.
Hon David Thomson: What about the penalty for a murder offence?
Dr WALL: The Minister has raised a question about other penalties. I maintain that the
whole system of imposing financial penalties, irrespective of the income of the accused, is
intrinsically unjust. I have raised this matter in the House previously and therefore do not
depart here from my view that the penalty should be related to income if it is to be equitable.
I am concerned about the provisions for cancellation of a licence. I am not opposing these in

able to continue with his bus driving, which has been without fault, but it would be perfectly

not categorised to fit the individual, it is quite inequitable. The punishment that would come
to a bus driver for a drinking-driving offence after a social occasion would be much more
severe than for a managing director of a company.
Society has not yet faced the fact, and certainly the Government shows no indication of
doing so, that the law has a different application for people on different income levels. That
will continue until we provide for financial penalties to be related to the financial resources
of the people affected. These matters do concern me.
To sum up, I suggest that at some not too distant date the Road Safety Committee look
at both these aspects: to make the punishment not fit just the crime but also fit the criminal;

Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I have previously been a member of ad hoc
committees set up to consider road safety. This has now become virtually a standing
committee and I am no longer a member, so I was not privy to the discussions or findings of
the committee before they were summarised by the chairman.
I have two comments on those findings that I hope the Government will take into
account when it prepares the legislation that the Prime Minister has forecast. The first relates
to the permissible level of alcohol in the blood stream. It is certainly a fact that the present
figure of 100 is higher than that prevailing in most comparable countries. By reducing it to 80
we shall be following a pattern established elsewhere. I question, however, whether this will
bring many more cases before the courts; and I await the outcome of this inquiry because a
stubborn and troublesome fact is that a high proportion of those who now come before the
courts have a reading of blood alcohol that does not hover around the 100 mark, but
approaches, and even exceeds, the 200 level. When that is what we are faced with the


## p. 1240 (#350) ###########################################

1240
23 June
Road Safety Committee-Interim Report
situation calls not just for a penalty, but for treatment, because a person with that level of
alcohol in his bloodstream is potentially, and more likely to be, an actual alcoholic, not only
requiring treatment but also with a propensity to reoffend with a higher and even more
dangerous level of alcohol in his blood. So I believe we should give more thought not just to
whether the permissible blood level is low enough, but to whether people who come before
our courts are not exceeding any possible level that could be taken into account as permitting
safe driving, and also whether we should not be looking just at the penalty provisions that
the committee recommends altering here, but to treatment which may be called for on a high
alcohol reading.
My second point relates to the large number of disputed cases that come before the
courts, and in which the only issue is really a plain and uncomplicated yes or no. Far too
much of the time of our appellant courts, let alone courts of originating jurisdiction, is taken
up in interpreting law that is essentially simple in character. It is not complicated by any
question of intent or other matters that would normally make up the ingredients of a criminal
offence. It is simply whether a quantity of blood is determined by proper analysis and at a
given time is higher than the law states it should be. That is all there is to it. It is simple. It is
dangerously simple, and it is certainly deceptively simple in the sense that it has been called a
statutory lie, because the time the assessment is made is not the time at which the offence
occurred. It must necessarily be half an hour or so later. The level is then found to be either
higher or lower than that prevailing at the time of the offence. Hence the phrase "a statutory
lie". However, that very simplicity is offset by the excessive formalities required to be
observed in bringing these facts to the court. I read somewhere that about 70 steps must be
taken by a traffic officer in order to pursue the whole chain of investigation from the time he
first saw a motorist whose actions aroused his curiosity, causing him to entertain some
reasonable belief that an offence was being committed, to the time when the blood sample
was produced, or the analysis certificate was produced in court.
This provides opportunities for challenge all the way along the line. The legislature has
tried to minimise this by encouraging the courts to overlook minor irregularities. The courts
have found those prescriptions unsatisfactory, and the irregularities are still challenged. I
believe one reason is that defendants in these cases are drawn from the whole spectrum of
society. In most other offences the people appearing before the courts are-I hesitate to
say-from the criminal class. However, in the cases we are talking about, a large number of
people are able to pay generously for their defence. I am sure that is the reason close
attention is directed to technical defences, which so often succeed.
I am sure it is not beyond the capacity of law draftsmen to enlarge the area within which
the courts may disregard informalities. I would not want the court to disregard the possibility
of challenging the chemical or laboratory process by which the analysis is made a point on
which the member for Porirua has already spoken. It is possible that if breath testing were
introduced some of these formalities could be omitted, particularly if the acknowledged
margin of error was taken into account by an inbuilt acknowledgement that the error could
be there, with the benefit of any doubt given to the person charged. Those are some of the
factors we must wrestle with in trying to translate the committee's report effectively and
practically into legislation. The present law has a great deal wrong with it; it is too artificial;
and it take up too much of the courts' time. While there can be oversimplicity, I am sure
more could be done by simplifying the law. I hope that the Government, when giving effect
to the recommendation, will take my comments into account and give them considerable
weight.
Mr MINGOUE (Hamilton West); The member for Henderson has stated in his usual
lucid fashion the position as most of us would see it. He has stated that the law on this issue,
perhaps more than on any other, is bedevilled by technicality and petty point taking.
Everyone wants to see the law simplified, and the incidence of technicality diminished. In
pursuit of these objectives, the committee has placed considerable emphasis on the merits of
breath testing. Concern has been expressed about the unreliability of this technology. I need
say only that this technology is used in Australia and other parts of the world, and
stands on its own. As an additional safeguard, the committee has recommended that
individuals have the right to demand a blood test as a backup to, or a check on, the
technology. This is a concession to people who fear that the breath-testing machinery might
react in a way that is disadvantageous to an accused or suspected person. I repeat that the
technology is used in other countries without that additional safeguard.
The comment has been made-and I think it is perhaps a fair comment-that we seem


## p. 1241 (#351) ###########################################

23 June
1241
Road Safety Committee-Interim Report
to have been overly concerned to protect the interests of people who have offended, and
seem to have leaned over backwards to see what we can do to make the prosecution and the
conviction of offenders as difficult as possible. I agree with the member for Henderson that
these technicalities and this undue concern must be positively modified.
The suggestion has been made that the committee seems to be moving in the direction
of random testing. That is untrue. The committee has never been close to recommending the
introduction of random testing. To suggest otherwise is to do an injustice to the committee,
which has been conscious at all times of the futility, well emphasised in the 1976 report of the
Australian Law Commission, of pursuing the course of random testing. It should be noted,
however, that the powers of apprehension would be extended so that the police will not be
unduly hampered by technical or similar considerations. An accident or a culpable offence
will, in itself, be a ground for requiring a test. The committee believes those grounds,
together with the existing ground of reasonable suspicion, are sufficiently wide to enable the
police to enforce the law effectively.
Concerning the problem of enforcement, it needs to be emphasised that the committee
was concerned not only with the numbers of traffic officers in the enforcement section, but
also with the way in which these traffic officers spend their time. The committee felt that all
too often traffic officers who should be out on the roads were occupied with administrative
and bailiff-type duties, of which they could be relieved. If officers were relieved of those
duties, they could spend much more time on the roads enforcing the law. The committee is
investigating this at the moment. I thank the House for the reception it has given the report,
and I look forward to the day when legislation based on its recommendations is before the
House.

the House not sitting was to enable them to work in their offices, and so on. There is nothing
unusual about calling a select committee meeting at an odd time. It is entirely up to the
members of the committee whether or not they attend. The plain fact of the matter is that
the task of a member of Parliament is an onerous one. He works long hours, and expects to.
If he is not prepared to do so, thousands of people are prepared to take his place. I commend
that to the member for Mangere.
Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert): The Prime Minister was quite correct when he said
the matter is the responsibility of the committee. My colleague, the member for Roskill
raised the point of order because the committee has not been consulted, or has not made a
decision. The member drew attention to the fact that the procedures for the following week
are normally discussed early on Friday morning. As the notice had been distributed after
that discussion, which you permit every Friday, Mr Speaker, he felt the only alternative left
to himself and other Opposition members of the Statutes Revision Committee was to raise
the matter in this way. We agree with the Prime Minister: it is the responsibility of the
committee, which should have made a decision about meeting on a Friday afternoon.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): Speaking again briefly, the point I was
making was that the matter is not one for the House, or for a point of order. It is not even a
matter for the informal indication that the Prime Minister, or the Leader of the House, gives
on Friday mornings about the work-not of the committees but of the House-for the
following week. It has nothing to do with that at all. A practice is growing up this session of
introducing matters which are not really points of order. They are designed, for the most
part, to publicise political points. In the old days, these matters used to be settled between
the senior Opposition member of the committee and the chairman of the committee, and
were never raised in the House, but some of our younger members have now got into the
habit of raising matters that are not, in fact, valid points of order.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I cannot let those last remarks
of the Prime Minister go unanswered. This was not raised by a new member of the House; it
was raised by the member for Roskill. There was no discussion between the members of the
committee and the chairman. There was a discussion between the chairman and one member
of the committee, but no mention whatever was made of the proposal to sit on Friday until it
was received in the House in the form of a notice placed on the desk of the member for

1252
23 June
Select Committee Hearings
Roskill, who happens to be a member of the committee. This does relate to the business of
the House, because of the Prime Minister's statement that estimates would be discussed next
Thursday. It is pretty obvious that pressure is being put on to get estimates through the
committees, so that they can be available for next Thursday.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: That estimate isn't on for next Thursday. I made that clear this
morning.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD: The estimate is on a list for discussion in the committee on
Wednesday. It may be that an over-zealous member of the Government has decided to assist
his Prime Minister in shoving things through, but the action of the member for Roskill was
simply to show that this procedure being followed by the Government had not been
discussed with the committee.
Mr SPEAKER: Strictly speaking, this is not a valid point of order, and the honourable
member for Roskill recognised that when he raised it. It has been the custom-not only in
this Parliament; I have seen it happen in others-that when there has been a dispute as to
when a select committee should be called together for the hearing of submissions on a Bill,
for the matter to be raised in the House. The rules are very clear to me, in as far as once the
House has referred matters to a select committee, it does not want to hear from the select
committee until the committee has dealt with the business. As a general rule, the House is
not interested in the detailed disputes that may occur within the select committee. That is
over to the committee. The House says, "Deal with it yourselves; we do not want to hear
from you again until you have dealt with the business the House has referred to you." If, of
course, the select committee is in a position where it cannot resolve the matter it can come
back to the House for further direction, but this is not the case today.
The member for Roskill suggested that the matter should more properly have been
raised at the informal discussion before the commencement of the formal business of the day
on a Friday morning. In view of the way matters have developed that might well have been
appropriate then. There is a tradition of consultation between the chairman of the
committee and, normally, the senior member of the Opposition members on the committee,
and it is assumed that the information will percolate down. There was consultation, but,
obviously, not on the matter of the sitting. That is a matter for the committee itself to deal
with. It is outside my jurisdiction, so I will not adjudicate on it.
The chairman of the committee has a right to call the committee together at any time he
thinks fit to discuss the business referred to it by the House, provided that such time falls
within the Standing Orders of the House. Standing Order 351 is relevant. It states: "Unless
the House otherwise directs, no select committee shall sit during the sitting of the House, or
on any day on which the House is not sitting." Therefore, if the select committee is called on
Friday, and it meets on Friday and does not complete its businesss, it will have to adjourn at
midnight on Friday, because Friday is a day set down for a sitting of the House. It cannot go
through to sit on Saturday, unless, of course, the House has decided, by resolution, that it
will sit on Saturday, in which case it may direct that the select committee can sit on Saturday.
I cannot help honourable members much beyond that.
The House adjourned at 1 p.m.

aware of the convention and the Speaker's ruling as every other member is, if not more so.
Speaker's ruling 78/5 states: "It is a convention that we do not make reference to the fact that
a member is away or is not in his seat." The reason for that was touched on by the member
for Franklin, the Senior Government Whip, when he mentioned why certain Ministers were
not in the House. We do not know if a member is attending a funeral, if he is sick, or if he is

Speaker's ruling that we do not refer in debate to absence is that it is not really relevant to
the subject-matter. Whether a member or a Minister is in his seat is irrelevant to the matter
under discussion, and it could be offensive or lead to disorder. On none of these grounds
should we encourage references to absences.
I believe this is a different matter; it is a matter of Parliament calling the Government to
account, and this is the place in which that should be done. I shall certainly not take steps to
discourage that being done or the opportunity being given to members to do it, providing

in which members of Parliament can question the Government's actions, and in which
Government members have the right to defend their actions before Parliament. Therefore I
have allowed the notice of motion.

Accident Compensation Commission-Publicity
6. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel), on behalf of Mr MALCOLM (Eden), to the Minister
of Labour: How much has the Accident Compensation Commission spent in the last 12
months on educational safety publicity, and directly for the rehabilitation of accident
victims?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): For the year ended 31 March 1978 the
commission spent $1.15 million in safety promotion. The major items making up this total
were: salaries, transport, cost of equipment, and accident prevention operating expenses,
$741,000; administration of safety courses, $60,300; and financial grants for safety
promotion and research, $260,100. For the same year, expenditure on rehabilitation was
$983,500, of which the principal items were: salaries, transport costs, and operating expenses
of rehabilitation personnel, $742,400; research grants, $14,200; and cost of rehabilitation
items supplied to individual claimants—that is, alterations to homes, wheelchairs, vehicle
adaptations, etc., $220,300.
Housing Corporation Lending
7. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Housing: Can he confirm, as is stated in
the Housing Corporation's 1976 loans survey, that repayments that would exceed 30 percent
of a head of household's gross income are usually unacceptable to any reputable lending
institution, and can he indicate what proportion of the Housing Corporation's clients were
committed to mortgage repayments exceeding 30 percent of the head of the household's
gross income in 1976, 1977, and this year?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): No, the actual statement made in the
Housing Corporation's 1976 loans survey was "25 percent of the household's total gross
income is regarded as the maximum acceptable commitment to mortgage repayments by
many institutions". The proportion of Housing Corporation mortgagors committed to
mortgage payments exceeding 30 percent of the head of the household's gross income in
1976 and 1977 was: 1976, 37.7 percent, and 1977, 31.5 percent. No details are yet available
for. 1978. It is to be noted also that the 1976 survey showed that almost 60 percent of those
mortgagors paying more than 30 percent were two-income families. Consequently,
repayments as a proportion of total family earnings would be considerably less.
Mr Rogers: If 30 percent is incorrect, could the Minister give me the figures at 25
percent?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I do not think the honourable member understood me. I said
that the quotations he incorrectly used in his question mentioned 25 percent. The Housing
Corporation considers each loan application on the ability of the applicant to pay. There is
no hard and fast rule that the percentage will be 25 percent, 30 percent, or any other
percentage.

Broadlands Geothermal Field
8. Mr W. R. AUSTIN (Awarua), on behalf of Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth), to
the Minister of Energy: What are the Government's present intentions regarding the
timetable of the Broadlands geothermal field?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): In 1977 the Power Planning Committee
recommended a commissioning date for the first unit at the Broadlands geothermal power
station of October 1983, which would have required formal Government approval by
October 1978. Although the Power Planning Committee has not yet formally reviewed these
dates, it is already clear that they cannot be achieved. It seems likely that the dates for
approval and first commissioning should be set back by up to a year.

the company, in which he describes the energy resources levy as a "short-sighted tax" which

which, Mr Wilson said, precludes potential users in industry from properly appraising the
economics of the capital expenditure necessary for converting from oil to natural gas?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): I have seen the remarks referred to and do not

honourable member knows, the levy is paid into the Public Account, and from that account
Parliament each year votes considerable sums of money to research and development
projects that benefit the development and the exploitation of our natural gas resource.
Maternity Hospital Closures, Wellington
10. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen the article in the Evening
Post of 20 June 1978, headlined "St. Helens closure is forced by Health Department", and
can he advise whether his department has forced, or proposes to force, the Wellington
Hospital Board to close its largest maternity unit?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): I have seen the article referred to. The
Department of Health has not at any time brought pressure on the Wellington Hospital
Board to close St. Helen's, nor has it any intention of doing so in the future. The decision to
close any of its institutions is primarily the responsibility of the hospital board concerned. It
must then apply to the Hospitals Advisory Council, which will make a recommendation to
me. Confusion appears to have arisen as a result of the Wellington Hospital Board's
application for the purchase of new equipment for the obstetric and gynaecological block
now being built at Wellington Hospital. Before approval could be given the department
properly asked for further information from the board about the future use of existing
equipment at both Wellington Hospital and St. Helen's.
Mr Brill: Quite apart from seeking information, can I ask the Minister whether the
department has changed its policy affecting St. Helen's in any way since July 1977, when the
board resolved to maintain St. Helen's Hospital for at least a further 4 years?
Hon. T. F. GILL: There has been no change in policy, but this is not a matter of
departmental policy. These effects are clearly stated in the Act. The responsibility to open
and close hospitals lies with the board, except for a permanent closure, but the board at
some stage must get the Minister's approval. It can close the hospital for a 3-month period
without approval, but it is not a matter of departmental policy. It is a matter of law, and the
boards have their responsibilities.
Mr Hunt: When the Minister first replied he said that it is primarily the responsibility of
the board. Can he say in what area it is the responsibility of people or departments other
than the board? In other words, what does the qualification "primarily" mean?
Hon. T. F. GILL: A board must seek the Minister's approval for the permanent closure
of a hospital. This is for a number of reasons, the first being that some hospital boards serve
the requirements of other hospital boards and the Minister and the Government have a
responsibility to see that the overall health requirements of the country are met. Primarily it
is their responsibility, but they do have to get the Minister's approval for a permanent
closure. The Minister almost invariably grants this approval, but it has been my custom to
ask a board what other health purpose the hospital will be put to. Usually the hospitals
closed are small ones.
>> Mr Comber: Can the Minister say whether the final decision to close St. Helen's has yet
been taken by the Wellington Hospital Board?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The final decision will not be taken by the board, but by the Minister.
To my knowledge, nobody has sought approval.

Regional Development Special Projects Scheme
11. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Regional Development: What
projects did he have in mind in the press statement dated 4 June 1978 concerning the
regional development special projects scheme?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development): At the date of the Budget, the
Government did not have any specific projects in mind to which the special projects scheme
would apply. The Government was, however, aware that the work of regional development
councils, particularly their resources surveys, could highlight projects of critical importance
to a region whose needs, because of their size, were unlikely to be met by the normal
processes of private sector investment and could not be adequately assisted by other
incentive schemes. Action was therefore taken to provide a more flexible tool to respond to
the resource development initiatives of councils that have the primary responsibility for
identifying such special projects.
Mr Marshall: Should councils now feel welcome to at least apply for the kind of projects
that previously have not fitted into the criteria?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Yes, providing the proposals in mind comply with the criteria for the
special projects scheme. A copy is available in my office, and councils have been sent copies.
There are seven criteria, and some break down into subsections. They are all directed
towards the development of resources that hitherto did not apply.
Hon. W. W. Freer: The Minister said that at the time of the Budget the Government did
not have any particular project in mind. Has the Government now had any approach on a
particular project?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The Government has two under study now, and one is at an advanced
stage of study.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Where are those projects?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: One involves the West Coast regional abattoir and export packing
house that is at a stage of requiring a satisfactory proposal and a firm commitment by the
proponents before it can be completed, but this is a matter that I would hope would be
resolved within the next 2 to 3 weeks. The other, which is not so well developed although a
good deal of work has been done on it, is the East Coast stage 2 fertiliser works. It is being
considered at the cost-benefit analysis stage.

Indigenous Forests Management Policy
12. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East),
to the Minister of Forests: What aspects of the 1975 indigenous forests management policy
have still to be implemented?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The main areas of change in the new
indigenous forest policy involve giving greater emphasis to the setting aside of scientific
reservations, the introduction of selective logging systems to replace clearfelling, and
changes to the pricing of native timbers to ensure that their intrinsic qualities are put to best
use. A great deal of work has already been done in identifying possible reserves on a national
basis, and the proposals are being collated by a special scientific committee. The change
from clearfelling to selective logging systems has also been progressing rapidly. Since the
policy was approved, the Government has itself approved three price increases for the higher
grades of indigenous timber relative to the lower grades, aimed solely at encouraging higher
grade uses for domestic timber.
Radiographers

the hospital service, and the Hospital Service Committee, representing the Director-General
of Health, as employing authority for the hospital service. As a result of these negotiations,
offers in terms of the payfixing criteria laid down in the State Services Conditions of
Employment Act 1977 were made to the society. No formal response has yet been made to
these offers, but further negotiations are to resume on Wednesday, 28 June. In these
circumstances, with negotiations continuing, it is not appropriate for me to comment further.
Mr Hunt: Is it likely that the meeting on Wednesday will result in an announcement
being made?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I am sure the meeting will not make an announcement. Is the member
asking whether the Minister will make an announcement? I am not sure that a decision will
be arrived at on Wednesday. There might be a short period of grace after 30 June-I hope
there will be—and they might go to the tribunal or to conciliation. I have no idea what form
the negotiations will take. I do not wish to prejudice them in any way by commenting on the
likely outcome, even regarding timing.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can the Minister confirm that the details of the offer by the
Hospital Service Committee are as stated in the original question?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Whether or not I am in a position to do so, I do not intend to do so.
Mr Hunt: As the Minister has said that an extension beyond 30 June could be
considered, and as this is of vital concern to the radiographers, could he tell us whose
decision it will be to grant the extension?
Hon. T. F. GILL: It might be forced on the meeting by circumstances such as lack of
availability of some statistics, returns, or reports that are needed for a proper consideration
of the matter.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: "Unavoidable" rather than "forced".
Hon. T. F. GILL: Forced by circumstances that make it unavoidable.

I want to talk about democracy and how it survives. It survives by restraint. It survives
by properly elected Parliaments. It survives by the understanding and the acceptance of
other points of view. It survives by respect for laws. It survives by respect for the courts and
the rights of minorities. In which other countries are Opposition members sitting in
Parliaments, debating Government moves, and offering alternative policies? The answer is,
very few indeed. If I might use the word "bastion", New Zealand remains a bastion of
democracy-let us keep it that way.
I heard about some extravagant statements made by the member for Rangitikei. He said
he felt he had no impact in Parliament. Well, that may be correct. He felt that Opposition
back-benchers—and indeed its front-benchers-had no impact in Parliament. That also,

Parliament or on the Government. That is entirely incorrect. As a Cabinet Minister, I am
well aware of the strength of the National Government caucus in our party. It is the
combined effort and the combined thought of all National members that spell out and
implement the policies of this party in Parliament-and it will always be that way. In
democracies, discussion in Parliament must be on what is done by the Government. That is
what this debate is all about. The Government presents a Budget, and the pros and cons of
that document of financial policies are then debated. Political parties must base their policies
and programmes on this type of approach. There is little point in any party putting forward
policies that are entirely unacceptable to people. The policies of any Government worth its
salt cannot always be popular. There must be a strength of purpose and statements of
interest.

The Leader of the Opposition, in his concise and pointed attack on the Budget,
described it as a lolly scramble, and a vote-now, pay-later Budget. The object of the Budget
is to hold sufficient support to win the general election in November. It is a classic example
of blatant, deceptive packaging, and this has been revealed by Opposition speakers, who
have torn the document apart page by page and section by section.
The Budget has been called generous by its sponsor, but it is nothing short of political
fraud. This has been revealed by the questions on taxation asked daily by the member for
Manukau, which have been replied to by the Associate Minister of Finance. The Budget
conceals more than it reveals. It reveals highlights and attractive elements from which people
are going to get something, but it is not quite so revealing on the deficit before borrowing-
on which the Government has been so critical in the past. The Budget can be described as
one that giveth to he who hath the greatest amount, but it is unfair and inequitable in all
other ways.
The Budget is the most blatant political bribery package the country has ever seen. The
Minister of Finance has produced a blueprint for economic disaster, and has called it a
Budget. It has an admitted deficit of $1,050 million, which is likely in reality to be $1,600
million-a level vigorously attacked by members opposite. The Budget was intended to
placate vociferous, disturbed, ex-National Party supporters, and it has misfired.
While the Minister attempted to leave the impression that everyone would gain from the
Budget tax cuts-and there are some-a close examination of the tax rates reveals that many
who can least afford it will be worse off. The stock subsidy to be paid to farmers will amount
to $60 million. Was the member for South Canterbury referring to the farmers who get the
$60 million when he said in Parliament that people were leaning on the Government, and
that fresh attitudes were needed? Perhaps he had better remain silent before he puts his foot
in his mouth altogether.
Certainly, farmers have had a bad year with droughts and floods, and needed assistance.
I do not begrudge it to those who needed it; but a flat stock grant across the board means
more to the well-britched farmers who comprise the "squatocracy" of New Zealand, and are
represented by members opposite. Many of them have freehold farms. They are not in hock
up to their eyeballs to stock and station agents and finance companies. A very insignificant
part of the $60 million Budget handout to farmers goes to those in the greatest need—say,
for instance, the smaller farmer, or the mixed farmer; the man who runs perhaps 600 sheep
and a few cattle, and crops the remainder of his land.
In his 1971 Budget the present Prime Minister said that no Government could justify
extensive use of public funds to help farmers who were not in financial difficulty. He was the
Minister of Finance then, and he still is, after an interlude on this side of the House. Let him
explain why that philosophy has been jettisoned in a desperate plea for votes. It was all very
well to make a statement on philosophy in 1971, but, my word, he has moved well away from
that now, because he and his party need the votes of the farmers who are expressing such
discontent with his policies and his Government.
The younger farmer is disillusioned. More often than not he has a heavy mortgage, and
has been hit by rising costs. He is the man most likely to put any extra cash that comes his
way into development, rather than rushing into buying a car, a boat, or a new trail bike, or
having a trip overseas. But he gets so much less than the men with the larger holdings. They
are not so much the successful farmers; many of them have inherited their holdings. The
farmer will welcome the fertiliser rebate, but it returns him only to the position he was in
before the 1977 Budget.
This is a put-and-take Budget. Meat inspection fees are to be met by the Government,
because this is election year. In 1976, the Labour Government paid them, to encourage
increased production. What about the cropping farmers-the forgotten farmers-in areas
such as Ashburton, Timaru, Waitaki, and, to some extent, Rakaia, and Rangiora? They are
the men the member for South Canterbury had so much to say about when he sat over here,
and about whom he has so little to say now he is a member of the Government. They have
been inveigled into growing wheat to give New Zealand self-sufficiency, but the price they

I shall now turn my attention to transport. The Government's white paper on transport
could well be described as such-in fact it has no print and no policy. The measures taken in
the Budget are completely negative. The Budget has introduced a 12.5 percent increase in
rail freights and an increase of about 6.7 percent in the price of petrol. Since the Government
took office in December 1975, the compounded increase in long-distance rail passenger fares
has been almost 150 percent, suburban rail passenger fares 130 pe cent, and rail freight
charges about 125 percent. The fare on the Wellington-Auckland Silver Fern, if it keeps
running, will rise from $30 to $33.75. It is not much cheaper to travel the same distance by
train than it is by air. The increases have resulted in a decrease in the patronage of rail
services, which has meant the closing down of branch lines. One line has closed in the North
Island and four lines have closed in the South Island since the National Government took
office at the end of 1975. For the year ended 31 March 1978, the estimated total freight
carried by rail was 12 600 000 tonnes, a decrease of 1 000 000 tonnes or 7.3 percent compared
with the March 1977 figure.
The Government is running down the railways and the total transport system. The latest
increase in charges will mean the further decline of patronage on the railways, despite their
more efficient use of fuel. The Opposition must bring this point home to the Government
and the people. The Budget gives as the reason for the increases the need to reduce the
present unsustainable loss. The Government's method of reducing losses makes rail travel
too costly and unattractive to be patronised, thus providing an excuse for cutting services.
There is no alternative. Carried to its conclusion, the Government's policy will mean that
finally the books will balance at zero on either side of the ledger, and rail transport will be no
more than a trip down memory lane for many members.
Another measure in the Budget stems from an admission of the short-sightedness of
past measures. On page 18 the Budget states that the Road User Charges Act has had a
significant impact on the cost of transporting farm commodities. The Government has given
farmers transport subsidies on fertiliser and lime to offset that. I shall not repeat the figures.
The Government's transport policy is a shambles. It has now resorted to piecemeal patch-
ups to make its ill-conceived measures work. The measures will not work. Much has been
said about them, and time will not permit me to go into the subject in depth.
I ask the Minister what has happened to the paper on the financial objectives of the
Railways, which was promised in an earlier National Government Budget. The Government
has shown no signs of recognising any objectives. Where are the Budget measures? Where is
the report on the electrification of the rail service? It is in a pigeon-hole in the Minister of
Transport's office, with the report on the economics of the Railways. Where is the report on
coastal shipping? It was given to the Minister of Transport about 12 months ago. It is another
secret report. Where is the report about the justification for merging NAC and Air New
Zealand? It is in the Minister of Transport's office. Six secret reports are in safes. Where is
the report on provincial air services commissioned by Air New Zealand, and when will it be
produced? No one can get into the Minister's safe for secret reports that should be made
available to the people.
The Government's administration of transport is a shocking disgrace. The Minister
should be called on to account for his actions. The suburban railways are desperate and local
services will be reduced unless overhaul and maintenance work can be kept to schedule.
Why is this work also being kept secret? I have been informed that the Northerner service
must be reduced in about 2 months as the coaches need overhauling and bogey changes.

local government will require added resources to discharge its responsibilities, and unless its


## p. 1280 (#390) ###########################################

1280
27 June
Appropriation Bill-Financial Statement
future resources are defined it is idle indeed to talk of adding to the responsibilities of local
government.
The nature of the problem is well illustrated by the recent comments of the Auditor-
General on the accounts of a number of local authorities. He commented on the late
presentation of their accounts, and rightly so. That problem has bugged local authorities for
years. It is nothing new. It does not reflect any incompetence or dishonesty on the part of
local bodies. It represents a shortage of skilled people in the financial and accounting
fields a shortage that is real, and must be faced.
Another problem is the change in the interest rate, which has seriously and quite
detrimentally affected the quantum of capital works that local authorities can undertake. For
instance, $100,000 borrowed today by a local authority at 10.5 percent for 20 years requires a
total payment of $400,000 over that period of 20 years, and, as a result, many local
authorities with sewerage, stormwater, and water responsibilities have been given serious
pause as to the size and dimensions of the programmes they can sustain. This comes in
addition to the already substantial burden of rates. There is a problem in my own city
centred upon stormwater: $20 million is required over a 10-year period to establish a
stormwater system that will prevent flooding in a considerable area of the city. The
magnitude of that burden alone at 10.5 percent certainly gives considerable pause to the city,
its ratepayers, and all those associated with it.
We must come to grips with the financial problems of the cities. They will not go away,
neither will they be easily solved in terms of the general economic situation I mentioned
earlier. Indeed, it can be said that, over the years, there has been much acknowledgment of
the problems of local authorities, particularly municipalities, but not much action. A local
authority finance committee first reported on the problem in 1973. The committee had been
established in 1968 under the chairmanship of Sir Patrick O'Dea. It took 5 years to report,
and when it did report it recommended that some alternative source of finance must be made
available to local authorities. That committee explored a variety of alternatives: the
possibility of sales tax, accommodation tax, payroll tax, special taxes on such things as
electricity consumption, local income taxes, poll taxes, beer taxes, and a variety of special
taxes that might assist local government; but it came firmly to the conclusion that the only
alternative source of revenue had to be broadly based and related to the taxation system of
central government.
The 1973 committee, having reported after 5 years, disbanded. A further committee
reported in September 1977, and what it had to say had a familiarity about it. It repeated in
vital respects the conclusions of the committee that had sat from 1968 to 1973. Again, it
looked at various forms of raising revenue. Again, it came to certain conclusions, the most
central of which was that there had to be some redistribution to local authorities, based
probably on income tax. That problem has been much debated. Administratively, it does not
appear to present any great problems, any more than does the present regional distribution
of the petrol tax. It is said that a redistribution of taxation wuld detract from the
independence of local authorities. To my knowledge, nobody has suggested that the existing
distribution of petrol tax in any way detracts from the independence of local authorities.
The plain fact of the matter is that we must regard local government as being in
partnership with central government in the management of the affairs of the country, and the
greater and more diverse the responsibilities we can vest in local authorities the greater our
political and financial health will become. If we are to do that on a basis of sensible
partnership, there has to be some recognition of the fact that local government too needs
resources adequate to the tasks that are assigned it. Clearly, the resources available to it,
particularly in the major metropolitan areas, are not adequate now, and I am the first to
acknowledge that there are contradictory views as to how that problem might be solved.
Some turn a determined face against the idea of redistribution of taxation income. They see
the answer in terms of a local tax, but both committees commented about the administrative
difficulties of collecting local taxes, and upon the problem of creating new tax-collecting
bureaucracies. It is a matter of balancing the pros and cons, and coming to some clear
determination about how we must solve this problem, because solve it we must.
I believe that if the present policies and the present inclination to procrastinate-to
incur the state of paralysis by analysis, as the late Mr Kirk called it—continue, the problems
in the major metropolitan areas-and I quote metropolitan Auckland as a notable
example will within 5 years be quite unmanageable and probably insoluble in the short
term. We have to look as far ahead as that, and embark now on actions that will ensure that

the major metropolitan centres can begin programming for the financial solution to the
problems that are so obvious. It is fair to regard central government as a partner of local

income per annum, paid only $597, not $1,400.

I turn now to the third most important package in the Budget—the continuing changes
in the energy policy, and the need for those changes. Earlier this year I was in Europe on a
Commonwealth Office of Information visit, and had an opportunity to visit the International
Energy Agency in Paris. Shortly after the change of Government in 1975, New Zealand
became a member of the IEA, because the National Government believed that membership
would offer New Zealand's policy-makers opportunities for keeping up to date with changes
in energy technology and with desirable changes in policy that would allow New Zealand to
be assessed from time to time by the agency, as part of the total OECD effort to reduce
dependence on liquid fuels.
I also had an opportunity for high-level discussions with the British Petroleum Co. in
Britain, with the Dutch Shell Co. in Amsterdam and at The Hague. At present, we are
facing an on-going energy crisis. That is not an empty phrase; it is not something we can
manage ourselves out of. The oil companies, the energy agencies, and world oil experts who
have investigated deposits of crude oil have no doubt that by the mid-1980s the demand for
liquid fuels will outstrip supply. This year it is important for New Zealand voters to compare
