In 1978 there was a whole new package of energy conservation measures. They are far
too long for me to spell out in detail, but I shall give one or two at random. There were the
incentive for the LPG conversion of business vehicles; incentives for substituting motor
cycles for motorcars; incentives for the increased use of natural gas and related products; the

industries. Those are samples from a long list of policies introduced in 1978. More has been

Nobody has spelt out the policies on solar heating announced in the Budget, and I think
it might be worth while to consider them in some detail. Five new policies were announced.
First, businesses are being encouraged to install solar heating equipment in a scheme that
provides for the full capital cost of equipment to be written off in the tax year in which the
expenditure occurs. A 10 percent refund of sales tax and DFC loans will be available in some
cases. Secondly, interest-free loans for home insulation, and including solar water heaters,
will be made available. When the administration arrangements and performance
requirements have been finalised interest-free loans up to $500-which is not very much
short of the cost of a solar water heater-will be granted. Thirdly, the Government will fund
research into ways of reducing the capital cost of solar water heaters. Fourthly, the
Government is undertaking practical trials in schools, buildings, and houses. Fifthly, a solar
water-heating testing facility will be constructed to enable the DSIR to obtain reliable
comparative data.
I want to emphasise that this is a developing technology. Some people would say that
the National Government ought to sit tight and do nothing, as did the Labour Government,
until the technology has been developed further. The Minister of Energy has taken a bold
approach and provided the incentives while the technology is being developed. That is
characteristic of the Minister. The efficiency of these policies can be summed up by looking
at changes that have taken place in energy use. Tonight I have spoken about the changes in
energy policy. I should like the House to consider the effect of those policies on the quantity
of oil we are importing, the increased use of indigenous resources, and the effect on our
dependence on imported energy resources.
I have developed a table that goes back to 1973, the year of the oil crisis—to which the
Labour Government failed to respond. That table compares the use of coal, oil, natural gas,
and hydro and geothermal electricity in 1973 with the amounts used today. In 1973, New
Zealand was 60 percent dependent on oil, 18 percent dependent on coal, 4 percent on gas,
and 16 percent on hydro and geothermal electricity. Today, as a result of the policies of the
last 3 years, that pattern has changed dramatically. We are now 45 percent dependent on
imported oil, our dependence on indigenous oil has risen from 2 percent in 1973 to 8 percent
today-largely because of the condensate produced from the Maui field-our dependence
on gas has risen to 17 percent, our dependence on hydro and geothermal electricity has
dropped to 15 percent, and our dependence on coal is down from 18 percent to 15 percent.
We are now less dependent on imported oil than we were 5 years or even 2 years ago. The
Government's objective is to reduce that dependence further as rapidly as possible so that
we can become self-sufficient and reliant on local resources, which are many and yet to be
developed. Those are the developments that have taken place in the field of energy in the
past 5 years. It is easy to compare the performance of the National Government with the
dismal failure of the Labour Government in 1974 and 1975.

This year we looked at another aspect of death duties that I first dealt with some years
ago, back in the late 1960s or the early 1970s-chattels and personal possessions left in the
family home when one or other spouse dies. Distress is often caused by someone coming in,
listing them all and putting a value on them, and working out whether any were personally
owned, and the like. This year the Budget has made a change, and I have not heard any
Labour speaker say whether it was a good idea. Personal possessions and chattels left to a
surviving spouse are now completely free of death duties. On top of that $6,000 worth of
chattels and because they are secondhand their value is not the replacement value—will be
free of death duties regardless of to whom they are left. That means that, if the husband dies,
only in a rare case will any death duties be payable on the contents of the home of an
ordinary family. It will not be necessary to have a valuation and listing of all personal
possessions. I did not hear any Opposition member say that that was a good idea, although I
suppose if they were asked one by one they would say it is a good idea.

Budget are the words "Hon. R. J. Tizard". The cover is the curious colour that the Labour

Hon. T. F. Gill: Karitane.

for this figure in table 2. The 1975 Budget had a new table, table 6, which included a further
$270 million that normally appeared in table 2 as part of the deficit. Table 6 was entitled
"Miscellaneous Financing Transactions"-a new term. At that time it was agreed that that
figure should have been in table 2. Under the normal way of making up the tables the deficit
for the 1975-76 year was $767 million.
As has been customary, the Labour Government provided $50 million for the
supplementary estimates-the extra spending after the Budget and before the end of the
year. It must be provided for, and $50 million was set aside. Later in the year the correct
amount of $128 million was brought in, which increased the deficit to $895 million. In
October 1975 the House rose and members went away to electioneer, and low and behold
there was a change of Government. The new National Government was given a Treasury
report, which stated, to its horror, that it faced a deficit not of $895 million but of $1,200
million. Somewhere along the line, between the time the supplementary estimates were
discussed in October and the time the Government changed, the Labour Government
committed $300 million of extra expenditure for a year that ended on 31 March, a few
months later. The present Deputy Leader of the Opposition was the Minister of Finance,
and he signed all the papers to authorise the expenditure of the extra $300 million after
Parliament had risen, and without the authority of Parliament.
Mr Malcolm: Is that legal?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No, it is not legal. The National Government worked very
hard for 2 or 3 weeks to alter the $1,200 million deficit. It cut subsidies on rail fares, postal
charges, electricity, and milk. The Labour Government had hinted that it would cut the
subsidies, and in some cases had made the statement outright, but it had not made the cuts
before the election. By holding spending the Government managed to reduce the $1,200
million deficit to $1,002 million, which was the final deficit for the year. The following year
according to the forecast given to the Government, the deficit would have been $1,400
million if policy changes had not been implemented. The Government changed the policies
and the deficit was lowered. The $1,002 million deficit was 9.2 percent of the gross national
product by far the highest ever. The deficit was 9.2 percent of the figure that measures the
size of the economy. Someone asked whether that was legal. No, it was not legal until it had
been validated. In 1976 the Government had to pass legislation to validate the illegal
spending of $238.8 million by the outgoing Labour Government. That was the largest
amount ever to be validated by legislation, and the Bill was passed with the support of the
Opposition. It did not vote against validating its own spending.
This year table 2 shows a deficit before borrowing of $1,050 million. Table 2 is compiled
in the old way, with no fiddling about and no putting in of little miscellaneous financing
transactions. The Deputy Leader of the Opposition was gloating over the $1,050 million
deficit, because the figure in his Budget was $1,002 million. It would have been $1,200
million if the Government had not changed. The National Government has provided not $50
million but $250 million for the supplementary estimates. It has provided $200 million more
for the supplementary estimates than the Labour Minister of Finance provided in 1975,
because the Government knows that there will be further wage increases before the end of
the year and it is providing for them. That is a more straightforward way than putting in $50
million and having to validate the illegally spent $238.8 million the following year. We have
$250 million for supplementary estimates included in the $1,050 million, which is not 9.2
percent, but 6.4 percent of the gross national product.
Some people might say, what about it; what does it mean? It means that if deficits
before borrowing tend to be inflationary then the Labour Government's deficit before
borrowing 3 years ago was half as inflationary again as it is this year. As the Labour
Government boasted, its 1975 deficit before borrowing was at a time when the economy was
under pressure and running at full capacity, so it would have been inflationary. However,
this year's deficit is at a time when there is considerable slack in the economy. It is therefore
necessary to lift the slack and to fill up some of that capacity in order to diminish the rate of
unemployment. That is a sound and relatively easily understood economic move that is
supported by people from one end of the country to the other who understand these things.
Furthermore, it is at a time when the rate of inflation is running at about 10 percent per
annum compared with the figure 3 years ago of 15.7 percent and rising, and getting
completely out of control.
The final point is that the deficit this year comes about through a reduction in
Government revenue and taxing, whereas in 1975 it came about through an increase in

Government spending. There is a considerable difference between the two. In 1975 the
difference came about by moving a greater slice of the economy into the hands of the
Government-I think it reached about 42 percent of GNP, or something like that—whereas
this year it comes about by moving a greater slice of the cake back into the hands of the
people. The tax reductions this year bring about the deficit, which is a much better way of
doing it than in 1975.
There has been a lot of toing and froing about personal income tax. I have some figures
here that show that a solo mum with one small child, who is earning about $80 a week and
receiving the young-family rebate, will pay $320 a year, or $6.15 a week, in tax when our new
tables come into force. During the term of the Labour Government she would have paid
$795 a year, not $320. You can put that another way. A solo mother earning $80 a week will,
after October, pay week by week the same amount of tax that a woman earning $45.50 a
week would have paid in 1975 under the Labour Government's tax table. Members opposite
say that people earn more today, so obviously they pay more tax. In October, a solo mother
earning $80 a week will be paying $6.15 a week in tax, whereas in 1975 she would have
earned no more than $45.50 a week to pay the same amount of tax.
A married man earning a little less than the average wage of $120 a week is paying more
than $1,000 a year less tax than he would have paid under the Labour Government's table.
He is paying $338.50 as against $1,425 a year when the present Deputy Leader of the
Opposition, who has been gloating about this Budget, was Minister of Finance. Let us work
out the income that that married man would have been getting in 1975 to pay $6.51 a week in
tax. To pay as little tax as that he would have been earning not $120 a week, but $59.50.
Members opposite say that that man would be earning more now. However, I do not know
anyone earning $120 today who would have been earning $60 a week in 1975- not in the
same job anyway. I doubt whether he could have lived on that amount under a worker's
beneficent Labour Government.
The past three Budgets of the National Government have considered the single-income
family and the young family, because it is difficult for the wife to go out to work. All the
clever arithmetic from the Labour Opposition's tatty whizz-kid does not add up to a row of
beans, because he does not look at the principle behind the changes. The Government
realises that many wives go out to work and that the difference in living standards between
the two-income family and the one-income family creates a major social problem. For three
successive years tax relief has been concentrated on the one-income family and the one-
income family with young children, the mother of whom should stay at home if it is at all
possible.
The member for Manukau said it was terrible that other people did not get as big a
reduction. He is an inverted Midas; everything he touches turns to garbage. He made a mess
of broadcasting, of the transport paper he brought down, and of Labour's superannuation
scheme. Now he has made a mess of criticising the taxation reform introduced in this year's
Budget. No wonder the Opposition promoted the member for Northern Maori, the member
for Timaru, and the member for Petone to the front bench before it promoted the member
for Manukau. There is still a lot of common sense left on the other side of the House.
Some members opposite have made only passing reference to the curious document

foreign exchange. Education, health, and social welfare take up only two-thirds of that
budget. Members opposite say there is no scope in that document to discuss their policies on
education, health, and social welfare. A surcharge on overseas funds is the only item of any
consequence. Does the Labour Party intend to surcharge the paying of debt interest? Surely
not official debt interest; that would be a curious debt-out of one pocket into the other. But
Labour will put a surcharge on to private debt interest and private overseas borrowing. Will
it put a surcharge on the freight on exports and make the farmer pay a surcharge on what it
costs him to get his produce to overseas markets? Is that what Labour proposes? Will it put a
surcharge on the transfer of funds by migrants-Pacific Islanders, who come here to work
and send money home? The Labour Government would charge them 10 percent on the
money they send home to their relatives. My word, it looks as though it intends to!
Mr W. R. Austin: Every time they go home for a wedding or a funeral.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Yes, every time they go home for a wedding or a funeral,
or to attend a court case or to vote in an election, they will be charged 10 percent on the
funds. My gosh, they will not like that. Many New Zealand companies are spending a large
amount of money overseas organising trade and attending trade fairs. The member for

Some Labour members have talked about our external trade, and I want to finish on
that note, because I heard a report today that some unidentified EEC official had said that
New Zealand had overreacted to the sheepmeat regime. I do not believe that the
Government overreacted. I wish it had had a little more support from the Opposition on this
matter. I have not the slightest doubt that a sheepmeat regime is the writing on the wall for
the New Zealand sheep industry—not what might be in it at the beginning, but what could go
in it subsequently, as has happened with our dairy products. This unidentified official said
that there must be a sheepmeat regime under the Treaty of Rome. The Nine subscribed to
the Treaty of Rome, but every one of them also subscribes to the trade pledge of the OECD,
which pledges that the member nations will put no more restrictions on trade and, as a result
of New Zealand's initiative last year at a meeting that I attended, specifically on trade in
agricultural products.
If they go along with the requirement of the Treaty of Rome to put restrictions on trade
in sheepmeat, they are breaking the trade pledge to which they subscribe. Which is more
important—the Treaty of Rome subscribed to by the Nine, which can be altered by the Nine,
or the trade pledge subscribed to by the 26 members of the OECD and the EEC countries? If
they adhere to the Treaty of Rome they are sworn in terms of the trade pledge. Again, in this
year's OECD communique, as a direct result of the work of the Deputy Prime Minister, they
said they believed that they must retain stability in the economies of the industrial countries
and the countries dependent upon agriculture. I have solemnly signed that communique.
Are they going to be foresworn on that as well? There is nothing more calculated to damage
the stability of the country than a sheepmeat regime in the OECD. We have seen it with
butter, and we have very certainly seen it with cheese.
My old friend Roy Jenkins said—and he chooses his words very carefully because he is a
very experienced politician-that a sheepmeat regime will not necessarily harm New
Zealand. When I saw the word "necessarily", I said that that simply underlined our concern.
He said that the price increases will not be great, and I thought to myself, in brackets—
initially. We have very real reasons to be afraid of this, and I hope that we can get the
support of members opposite in fighting it totally. Contrary to what Labour's spokesman on
overseas trade has said, I hope that when we have a visit in the next few days from the
Japanese Minister of Agriculture, Labour members, if they cannot support the
Government's policy, will say nothing. The next 3 days are very important for our
agricultural trade with Japan. If Opposition members cannot support it, would they please
say nothing.

Mr SPEAKER: Before I deal with the matter of privilege raised in the House yesterday,
it is appropriate to deal with the technical point raised by the honourable member for New
Lynn, when he argued that, because words had been used outside the House, the Minister
had a remedy in the courts, and that, to allow him a remedy in the House also, would be a
very considerable extension of the doctrine of privilege. I have had an opportunity to
consider this proposition in the light of those extracts from Erskine May quoted by the
honourable member. They do appear to support his argument, but they are taken from a
section on general conclusions in which an attempt is made to encapsulate the law covering
the jurisdiction of Parliament and the courts.
I refer the House to a more specific reference in Erskine May's Parliamentary Practice,
in which, at page 172, it is stated: "Where the matter of complaint is a charge alleged to have
been made by one member against another in a speech outside the House, it is usual, if the
member admits the correctness of the report, and states that he is in a position to prove the
charge and is willing to attempt to do so, to give him an opportunity of establishing his
charge and with this object to refer the matter to a committee"-that, of course, would be
the Privileges Committee. This comment clearly leads to the conclusion that the privilege
jurisdiction of the House is not excluded by the existence of another remedy in the courts.
Indeed, we have had several matters of privilege brought before the House in recent years
when another course could have been taken.
I am strengthened in this view by the undoubted fact that a private citizen who makes a
defamatory statement about a member of Parliament may be summoned before the House
or before the Privileges Committee, and made subject to the jurisdiction of Parliament in
matters of privilege. Such a person is also liable for civil action in the courts at the suit of the
member defamed. There is nothing in the law of Parliament to exclude a member from this
dual liability. I therefore rule, on this point, that the privilege procedure is available,
notwithstanding the possibility of a remedy within the jurisdiction of the courts.
On the matter of privilege, when I was dealing with it yesterday I suggested that the
members involved should get together and try to resolve the differences that apparently exist
between them. That was one of my main reasons for adopting the course, under Standing
Order 430(b), of deferment of my ruling until the next sitting day, which, of course, is today.
In the meantime I have been approached by some senior members, who asked whether I
would be prepared to defer my ruling for a further 24 hours because of certain
circumstances. Unfortunately, in terms of the Standing Order, I cannot do that, but, I can,
of course, take the pleasure of the House that this course be followed. If there is no
objection, then I take the leave of the House, that Standing Orders be set aside sufficiently
to allow me to defer making a ruling on this privilege matter for another 24 hours. There
appears to be no objection. I thank honourable members, and shall follow this course.
PERSONAL EXPLANATION
Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui): With the leave of the House, I want to make a personal
explanation about remarks on a radio programme. Last night I took part in a Radio Windy
talkback programme. Toward the end of the programme a caller asked me a question about

reference to the Prime Minister's performance in the House. Since I made that remark I
have thought about it and have come to the following conclusion: first, that there is an
important distinction between believing something and saying it publicly on the radio; and,
secondly, that such remarks diminish the status of the House. Therefore, I apologise both to
the Prime Minister and to the House.

LAND TAX AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Land Tax
Amendment Bill be introduced. This is a short Bill of only six clauses, and makes
miscellaneous amendments to the Land Tax Act 1976. The main amendment is to extend the
concessional rate of land tax to racing clubs. Two other amendments of a minor nature bring
the provisions of the Act into line with similar provisions in the Income Tax Act 1976. None
of the clauses calls for detailed explanation, but I shall briefly outline the amendments to
indicate their effect.
Clause 3 provides that any annual Act fixing the rates of land tax for the year may be
repealed without affecting the validity of tax assessed or paid, or still to be assessed or paid,
for that year. Clause 4 extends to racing clubs the same concessional rate of land tax that
applies to other sports clubs. The concessional rate generally results in the land tax assessed
being 25 percent of the amount otherwise payable. Clause 5 is a machinery amendment to
enable officers of the department to take proceedings for offences under a general
delegation of powers rather than by specific authorisation of the commissioner. Clause 6
clarifies the right of the commissioner to institute proceedings for offences against the former
Land and Income Tax Act 1954, which was consolidated in 1976.
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): Clause 4 extends to racing and trotting clubs
the concessional rate of land tax allowed under the Act. I should like to know whether a
companion Bill will be introduced providing for a reduction of totalisator duty of 0.5 percent
on off-course betting, as promised in the 1975 National Party manifesto.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): This is the Land Tax
Amendment Bill, and clause 4 provides for a concessional rate of land tax to be allowed to
racing clubs, trotting clubs, hunt clubs, and greyhound racing clubs.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

INCOME TAX AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Income
Tax Amendment Bill be introduced.It is my pleasure to introduce the Bill, which gives
substantial tax benefits to most taxpayers-benefits that were acknowledged in very
generous terms by all sectors of the community when they were announced by the Minister
of Finance in the Budget on 1 June. As well as giving effect to the most comprehensive
review of personal income tax rates undertaken in our history, the Bill contains positive
measures of considerable assistance to a wide sphere of activites-manufacturing, exporting,
farming, fishing, and racing. In addition, there are important extensions to the types of
energy conservation expenditure that will now qualify for the 100 percent tax write-off in the
year it is incurred. Those extensions include certain capital expenditure incurred by taxable
enterprises engaged in gas distribution.
This is a forward looking Bill-a Bill for recovery and for confidence, and a Bill that,
with other measures announced in the Budget, will most definitely assist in restoring the
shattered economy the Government inherited a little less than 3 years ago. For ease of
presentation the Bill is in three parts. Part I contains the various personal income tax
amendments. Part II covers the amendments to the increased exports incentive scheme
announced recently. Part III includes miscellaneous matters, both budgetary and non-
budgetary.
I shall now deal with the individual clauses. Clause 1 is the short title. Clause 2 is the
application clause for Part I of the Bill, which covers clauses 3 to 14 inclusive, and, as I have
said, gives effect to the new personal income tax changes that were announced in the
Budget. Unless any clause provides otherwise, amendments made in Part I will first apply in
respect of the current income year. Clause 3 reduces the personal rebate from $155 to $77.50
for the current income year, and abolishes it as from 1 April 1979. Clause 4 introduces a new
tax rebate of $78 a year, which will be allowed for children under 15 years of age, or those
attending primary or secondary schools, as well as for handicapped children at special
schools. For the current income year, the rebate will be limited to $39, or one-half of the full
rebate.
Clause 5 makes minor drafting amendments to the principal Act consequent on the
abolition of the personal rebate and the introduction of the new rebate for children. Clauses
6 and 7 give effect to the changes to the spouse's rebate. The rebates will now diminish at the
lower rate of 25c for each dollar of income in excess of the allowable income limit.
Previously, the rebates diminished at the rate of 30c in the dollar. Clause 8 makes a number
of changes to the single-income family rebates. The amount of the rebate is increased from
$208 to $260, and the age of qualifying children is raised from 10 years to 12 years. In
addition, the spouse's income limit is increased from $1,040 to $1,144. Thereafter, the rebate
will diminish by 25c in the dollar, instead of the present 30c, so the rebates will not be
completely extinguished until the spouse's income reaches $2,184, against the present
$1,734.

1298
28 June
Income Tax Amendment Bill
Clause 9 gives effect to the Budget announcement to allow payments for pre-school
education at registered private kindergartens and play centres to qualify for the donations
and school fees rebate. It also adds three organisations to the list of approved organisations
to which may be made qualifying donations for charitable purposes overseas. They are:
Christian World Service; New Zealand Catholic Overseas Aid; and Raphael, the Ryder-
Cheshire Foundations of New Zealand.
Clause 10 increases the standard deduction for employment expenses allowed to wage
and salary earners to $52 a year, and extends entitlement to national superannuitants and
others in receipt of taxable pensions and earnings-related compensation payments. Clause 11
increases from $200 to $500 the amount of taxable income from rents, interest and dividends
that taxpayers, other than those in business, may derive before becoming liable to pay
provisional tax. This applies from the year beginning on 1 April 1979. Clause 12 substitutes a
new composite scale of tax rates for the 1978-79 income year. This combines both the current
scale and the new scale, as if each applied for one-half of the year. Clause 13 substitutes a
new scale of tax rates to apply from 1 April 1979. Clause 14 substitutes new PAYE tables
based on the new rates in clause 13. These will apply to tax deductions from payments made
for any period ending on or after 1 October 1978. The tables incorporate the standard
deduction referred to in clause 10.
In Part II of the Bill clauses 15, 16 and 17 deal with the changes to the increased export
incentive allowances announced earlier this year. Clause 15 has the effect of discontinuing
third-party export arrangements after 31 March 1978. From that date, only the manufacturer
or processor of goods who exports those goods, or an export merchant, as defined, will
qualify for the incentive allowances. There is a further clarifying amendment to remove any
doubt that may exist that, when there is a transfer of export sales from one person to
another, the base period export sales of the former person must also be transferred. Clause
16 introduces the new tax credit scheme for exporters who are in a tax loss situation. The
deduction otherwise allowable will be converted to a refundable credit for tax, at the rate of
45c in the dollar, when an exporter would go into a tax loss and, therefore, get no benefit
from that incentive deduction. This will apply first to the 1977-78 income year.
Clause 17 validates existing third-party export arrangements to 31 March 1978, for the
purposes of the increased export incentive deduction, provided the third party does not
claim a greater deduction than the previous exporter would have been entitled to had he
continued to export those goods himself. There is provision for the commissioner to make
such adjustments as he considers equitable in cases in which the relevant parties have acted
under a genuine misapprehension about what constituted an increase in export sales. The
Government is confident that these measures, particularly the provision for the payment of
tax credits, will be of valuable assistance to exporters, and it is fitting that they should be
introduced during Export Year.
Clause 18, in Part III of the Bill, sets out the general application date for this part of the
Bill. Clause 19 is a machinery amendment to the section dealing with the retrospective pay
rebate, to take account of the new tribunal established under the State Services Conditions
of Employment Act 1977. Clause 20 makes three amendments to the section that exempts
certain income from tax. The first exempts greyhound racing stakes from tax; the second
exempts income derived by the New Zealand Racing Conference, the New Zealand Trotting
Conference, and the Greyhound Racing Association; the final amendment deletes a
reference to universal superannuation, because of the introduction of national
superannuation.
Clause 21 is consequential on the specified cost of motorcars for depreciation purposes
being increased last year from $6,000 to $7,000. The amendment in clause 22 is mainly of a
machinery nature, to confirm existing long-standing practice for the recovery of depreciation
when an asset is sold or disposed of at more than its book value. Clause 23 gives effect to the
Budget announcement of the inclusion in the fishing investment allowance of new motorised
boats used in the businesses of rock oyster or mussel farming. Clause 24 provides that plant
and machinery that are subject to a Government grant under the special hygiene assistance
programme for the fishing industry will not also qualify for an industrial development plan
investment allowance.
Clause 25 implements the Budget announcement of extensions to the kinds of capital
energy conservation expenditure that qualify for an immediate 100 percent writeoff for
income tax purposes. The extensions comprise certain capital expenditure on electricity
conservation and cogeneration, the distribution of natural gas and LPG, and the costs of

the benefit of the single-income family rebate. Why should the tax paid by this man be the
same on $121 as that for a widow with four teenage children who earns $100 a week? A
married man with one child aged 4 years is allowed to earn $144.73 a week before he pays
$17.28 a week in tax. Why should these four families all pay the same amount of tax?
I am sure the Government did its calculations before it introduced the Bill, but why did
it decide that this should be so? Why are the larger families discriminated against? Why
should a widow with four teenage children, and earning $100 a week, pay as much tax as a
married man with one child aged 4, but earning $144.73 a week? Why should a married man
with one child aged 4 need an extra $44.73 a week compared to a widow with four children?
Why did the Government decide that the more children one has the more tax one pays?
I believe this Bill is bad. A good tax system should have four components. It should be
simple, but this Bill is not simple. It should be fair and spread the burden of taxation, but this
Bill does not do that. It is not fair legislation, and the Government should have a look at it
again before introducing it. It should be honest legislation, and, in my view, it is not.

Student Numbers
2. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill), on behalf of Hon W. W. FREER (Mt Albert) to
the Minister of Immigration: How many private students were enrolled for the first time in
New Zealand primary, secondary, or tertiary schools or colleges this year; and how many
private students from overseas are at present training in New Zealand universities?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): I have interpreted this question to mean
how many private students from overseas were enrolled for the first time.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: I think that is what is meant, but I am not sure.
Hon. T. F. GILL: A total of 624 people were permitted to enter New Zealand this year
for their first year's study as private students. Of this total, 10 people are at primary schools,
293 are at secondary schools, 44 are attending technical institutes, and 277 are studying at
universities. For administrative reasons, the figures relating to the total number of overseas
private students studying in New Zealand each year are collated on the basis of the 12-month
period ending 30 September. I am, accordingly, unable to tell the member how many private
students from overseas are at present studying in New Zealand universities. As at
30 September 1977, however, a total of 2239 such persons was studying in New Zealand
universities-1904 at undergraduate level, and 335 at post-graduate level.

Electricity Tariff
24. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What has he done about
the promise in the 1975 blue National Party manifesto, which stated that “a more flexible
tariff will be considered to discourage the wasteful use of electricity and as a means of
reducing any hardship that may result"?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): As a result of the Government's pricing policy,
electricity tariffs are now at a level at which most consumers are careful to avoid wasteful
use. Electricity supply authorities have also reviewed their tariff policies and none now has
declining block tariffs for domestic consumers; a few have adopted the ascending block
system. The Government is investigating the potential advantages and disadvantages of the
system.
Hon. F. M. Colman: What has happened to the manifesto undertaking to reduce any
hardship that may result?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Although electricity tariffs have increased quite substantially, in real
terms they are about the same as they were during most of the decade of the 1960s.

DISCUSSION OF MOTIONS
Taxation Rates
Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth): I move, That this House commends the
Government on the major steps taken this year to reduce the percentage of personal tax paid by
the wage and salary earner, noting the dramatic across the board reductions, highlighted by the
fact that many married persons with families will pay $1,000 less per year in tax under
National's new tax scales than they did in 1975 under the last Labour Government. Many
groups within the community, including manufacturers, unions, and employers, have been
calling for tax reductions. It did not need a towering intellect to perceive that the tax tables
introduced by the Labour Government in 1975 were outdated. They were harsh at the time
they were introduced. At the end of its 3 years in office, the Labour Government introduced
very steeply graduated tax scales. When the National Government took office at the end of
1975 it found that the tax scales were causing considerable hardship within the community,
and so it began to take steps.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: It has taken 3 years.
Mr FRIEDLANDER: The member for Timaru knows full well that during the last 2
years of our term of office we have taken a number of major steps. Moves were made in
February, and this year's Budget provides for the largest ever tax cuts in New Zealand's
history. The member tends to forget the other tax cuts that have been introduced over the
last 2 years, which the Labour Government could not or would not give. With the February
package included, there will be a $520 million tax cut spread over most taxpayers. That was
welcomed by the population at large-by employers, employees, manufacturers, and
unions. The Labour Opposition is saying that is not enough, or it is not right, or it has not
been done the way Labour would have done it. In its first 2 years the Labour Government
did nothing to ease the tax burden on wage and salary earners. In its third year, coming up to
an election, it changed the tax scales in a minor way, which proved to be no more than a sop
to the wage and salary earners. Yet Labour is critical of what is being done now.
I suggest that the next Opposition speaker look at the tax scales and apply them to
various taxpayers in the community. A single person on $6,000 a year, who has the least
number of taxation concessions available, in 1975 would have paid $1,550 a year. As a result
of the Budget he will now pay $1,222— a saving of $328, or a 21 percent reduction. That
represents $6.30 a week that the person on $6,000 a year, with a take-home pay of $115 a
week, will get extra in his pocket as a result of the changed tax scales.
Rt. Hon. W. E. Rowling: It looks as if you'll have a bit of room in yours.
Mr FRIEDLANDER: I will be looking forward to my reduced tax rates, as will the
Leader of the Opposition. I wonder if he will give his extra back. I doubt it, because he will
need to build up a little nest-egg for next year, when, I understand, there will be a new
member for Tasman. A married person on $6,000 a year in 1975, under the Labour
Government, was paying $1,425 a year in tax. The Budget reduces his tax to $1,066, a saving
of $359, or a 25 percent reduction from the taxation rate that applied in 1975 under the last
Labour Government. A married couple with no concessions other than the married person's
exemption saves that amount of money. The young couple with a family is looked after by
the Budget. In 1975 a married couple with a single income and a young family, earning
$6,000 a year, paid $1,425 in taxation. The National Government has reduced that family's
tax to $338. The family will save more than $1,000 a year, or 76 percent of its earnings. It will
save $20.90 a week.


## p. 1314 (#424) ###########################################

1314
28 June
Discussion of Motions
The Opposition can say that a person earning $6,000 in 1975 would be earning more
now. I accept that. A person earning $6,000 in 1975 paid 22 percent of his income in
taxation. I know that that person's income would not have increased to $8,000, but if it had
he would have been paying 14 percent of his income in taxation. I hope that the next
Opposition speaker will explain that a person whose income has increased to $8,000 a year
will pay a smaller percentage of his income in tax under the National Government. Massive
changes have been made to the tax rates introduced this year. The tax cuts have been
acknowledged as the greatest tax cuts in the country's history.
I suggest that the Opposition looks very closely at the tax rates and explains its case,
because I believe it does not have a case. Despite the Opposition's claim to the contrary, the
Labour Government did not reduce taxation. The National Government has reduced
taxation; and the people will consider that when they vote in 1978. The tax cuts are no flash
in the pan. In 1976 the National Government introduced the young family rebate.
Opposition members talk about the sympathy they have for the young family and the single-
income earner. When the Labour Government was in power it did nothing for the young
family. The young family rebate, which applies to families with children under 5 years of age,
now amounts to $9 a week. It is phased out at an income of more than $240 a week. The
young family rebate is not a penalty to the families not eligible; it is a concession for the
families that are eligible. Families with no children under 5 years of age do not receive the
concession, but they receive a tax saving compared with the tax they would have paid under
the Labour Government's rates.
Families with children over the age of 5 have not been penalised. They receive
concessions, but the greater concessions go to the families with children under 5 years of age.
The Opposition is trying to create the impression that a family with children over the age of 5
are in some way penalised. They are not offered the same concessions, but the tax tables give
them greater concessions than applied under the Labour Government. As I have said, the
recent tax cuts are no flash in the pan. The single-income family rebate was introduced in
1977 to assist the family with children under the age of 10. The family can receive a rebate of
up to $260. The rebate has been welcomed by people with young families, because it assists
them to get started.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): We have just witnessed the
spectacle of the member for New Plymouth hailing an Irishman's rise for the taxpayer. He

Zealand"-I presume it meant New Plymouth-"to the news that New Plymouth had been
dropped from the regional development priority list." Two years later he is hailing an
Irishman's rise for the taxpayer. I hope the Irish will forgive us for the way we take their
name in vain, but members will know what I mean.
The member for New Plymouth said that Labour's changes were no more than a sop.
He should look at page 50 of the Budget to see what Labour's changes meant. The effects of
Labour's changes in 1975 were that in the following year income tax increased by only $160
million in round figures. What has happened each year since then? For the 1977 March year
income taxation increased by $532 million. In the next year the National Government did

substantial reductions to people on middle incomes. Let me give the two examples I gave last
night. In 1975 under the last Labour Government, a person on a taxable income of $6,000
would have paid $1,400 in tax. However, for the 1978-80 March year the same person will
pay $338. A person on a taxable income of $10,000 still in the middle income range-would
have paid $3,300 tax in the last year of the Labour Government. However, as a result of the
new tax codes, that person will now pay $2,078, a reduction of $1,300.
The 19 steps under the old Labour tax scale have been reduced to 5 simplified steps. It is
important to know what those steps are. Everyone will pay 14.5c in the $1 for the first $4,500
regardless of his or her total income. From $4,500 to $10,000 a person will pay 38c in the $1,
and from $10,000 to $16,000 the amount will be 48c. Those rates of taxation are marginal
rates. Members opposite are trying to convince the electorate that people pay more tax on
overtime earnings. They do not. Overtime taxation rates are the same as the rates on
ordinary wages providing they come within the five steps I have just mentioned.
I note that the honourable member for Southern Maori has been busy sending out

cyclostyled letter and the pamphlet as well. In that pamphlet there is a very misleading

Taxation Rates
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): I move, That this House calls upon the Government
to explain why, after 1 October, a married man with three teenage children on $140 a week will
be called upon to pay $14 a week more in taxation than a married man with one child aged 2,
and asks, is it that the child aged 2 eats more than three teenage children, or is it that the 2-year-
old costs more to clothe, send to school, the doctor, or the dentist, or is it that the Government
just does not want to give fair tax relief? This motion draws attention to the injustices and the
discrimination so apparent in the Government's taxation policy. A good taxation policy or
system must be simple, and it should be fair in the way it spreads the burden of taxation. It
should encourage people to work for the interests of their country and for the interests of
their families. Also, it should take into account inflation and the movement in wages. These
elements have been thrown out of the window by the Government.
I point out some basic facts of personal taxation: in 1969 the average wage earner paid
22.5c in the dollar on each extra dollar he earned. Today, that same person, still on the
average ordinary time, pays 45.5c in the dollar on each extra dollar earned. The percentage
of tax paid on the average wage in 1968 was 10.5. Today, in 1978, the percentage of tax paid
on the average wage is not 10.5 but 23.
There are five major weaknesses in the Government's taxation system. First, there is no
concept of horizontal equity at all. By that I mean that two families on the same incomes
would receive little or no recognition through the tax system for different family
commitments. Under the scheme it is possible for a married man with four children to pay
the same amount of tax as a couple with no children. There is very little recognition of
vertical equity. By this I mean that all those who earn less than $57 a week will pay more tax,
whether or not they have family commitments, or are on a low family income—that is unjust.
But, on the other hand, those earning about $200 a week will get the maximum tax
reduction, whether or not they have family commitments. Part-time earners who are
supplementing a family's main income will pay more tax under the National Government
regardless of whether that family is on a low overall income. This policy is anti-women.
National's taxation system gives insufficient protection against inflation. Overtime tax
rates for low and middle income earners remain far too high under this scheme. It is full of
injustices and discrimination, and I want to give some examples. A married man with 3
teenage children, earning $140 a week, pays $14 a week more in taxation than a married man
on $140 a week with 1 child aged 2. I ask the next Government speaker why a married man
with 3 teenage children should pay $14 a week, or 10 percent of his wages, more in tax than a
married man receiving the same wage but who has only one child aged 2. It is my opinion
that the three teenage children cost more to feed, clothe, send to school, and transport, etc.
A second case is a two-income family versus a one-income family. Under the taxation
provisions of the Government, a married couple who both earn $200 a week and have no
dependent children will receive in October a tax reduction of $15.44 a week. On the other
hand, a married couple with four children, the husband earning $140 and his wife
supplementing that income by $20 a week, giving a total family income of $160-not $400—
will, in most cases, get tax relief of $2.06 instead of a tax reduction of $15.44. In other words,
for the family of six on $160 the tax relief is $2.06; for a family of two on $400 the tax relief is
$15.44. Why should a family of six, with a total income of $160, receive less than one-fifth
the tax relief given to a family of two with a total income of $400? Where is the equity and
justice in that? What does it cost to clothe, feed, and send four children to school? Do

SPEAKER'S RULING-PRIVILEGE
Mr SPEAKER: I refer to the question of privilege raised on Tuesday by the Senior
Government Whip relating to words used in a press report issued by the member for
Manukau about the Associate Minister of Finance. As members will recall, there was a sharp
difference between the member and the Minister, and I deferred my ruling on the question
of privilege in the hope that the two honourable members would reach agreement on the
matter. Yesterday the House granted me leave to defer my ruling further since more time
was required to enable the members to complete their discussions. I understand now that the
honourable member for Manukau wishes to make a statement, and that the Associate
Minister of Finance would like to comment. Is it the pleasure of the House that this course
be followed? There appears to be no objection.
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): I wish to advise the House that I have held an
amicable discussion with the Associate Minister of Finance. Clearly my statement of 23 June
has been interpreted by the Minister as a personal accusation of blatant dishonesty. That was
never intended, and I regret that it was possible for the Minister to place such an
interpretation on my statement; and, to the extent that this interpretation is possible, I
withdraw it. Parliament demands that there should always be vigorous debate in the public
interest within and without the Chamber. Both the Minister and I acknowledge that this
should be so, and no doubt we will continue to disagree from time to time. Neither now nor
in the future will this be on a personal basis.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I thank you, Mr Speaker,
and the House for the opportunity to respond. May I simply say to the member for Manukau
that I am grateful for his courtesy in withdrawing his allegation of dishonesty against me.
Mr SPEAKER: I congratulate both honourable members on taking this wise course, and
I should like also to thank the senior members on both sides of the House who acted as
mediators on this occasion.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): In view of the two statements that have been read to the House,
I seek the leave of the House to withdraw my request for a ruling on a prima facie case of
breach of privilege.
Mr SPEAKER: I take the pleasure of the House that this course be followed. There
appears to be no objection. The breach of privilege will not be pursued any further.
ESTATE AND GIFT DUTIES AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Estate and
Gift Duties Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill is a short one of only five clauses, and the
main amendment is to give effect to the Budget announcement of exemption from estate
duty for certain personal chattels. The other amendments are of a minor nature and deal
with such matters as valuation of debts and shares.
Clause 2 is a machinery amendment to allow income tax on refunds from a deceased's
wool income retention account as a debt for estate duty purposes. Clause 3 provides that the
commissioner, when valuing shares, can ignore restrictions on the transferability of shares
contained in any document or imposed in any other manner, unless he is satisfied that those
restrictions are reasonable. At present the Act refers only to restrictions contained in the
memorandum or articles of association of a company.
Clause 4 provides that where a debt is owing to a company controlled by the deceased
and repayable at some time in the future, the commissioner can value it as if it were
repayable immediately. This brings their treatment into line with debts owing directly to the
deceased. Clause 5 gives effect to the Budget proposal to make personal chattels passing to
the surviving spouse of the deceased completely exempt from estate duty, and to increase the

exemption in other cases from $4,000 to $6,000. Clauses 2 and 5 will apply to people dying on
or after 1 June 1978, and clauses 3 and 4 will apply to people dying on or after 1 January
1979.

Labour Department Mirror, Auckland
4. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: Can he confirm that the Auckland
office of the Department of Labour has a mirror that greets the unemployed with a label
saying, "Take a good look at yourself", and, if so, what is its purpose?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): There are two mirrors in the Auckland
employment centre of the Department of Labour, which carry signs inviting job seekers to
"Take a look. This is how you would appear to a prospective employer. Does your
appearance enhance your chance of employment? If not, you are wasting our time and your
time. Thank you." The purpose of these signs has the effect of reminding job seekers that
they should be dressed neatly when presenting themselves for interviews with prospective
employers. This method of memory jogging is successfully used in other countries.
Mr Isbey: Will the Minister confirm that such a notice is considered degrading and
demeaning to those who are unemployed through no fault of their own?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: No, I do not. The aim of the Department of Labour employment
office is to get these unfortunate people back into a job. The purpose of this particular
psychological effort is to make people aware of their own handicap, if any.
Mr Malcolm: Has the department taken a particular interest in boosting not only the
presentation, but also the self-confidence of those seeking jobs?
Mr SPEAKER: That is not related to the question.
Mr Hunt: Does the Minister agree with the member for Invercargill that a lot of people
going into that office are barefooted and unwashed?
Mr N. P. H. Jones: That's right, I have seen them myself.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I endorse the interjection of the member for Invercargill as
accurate, because I have visited the Auckland office myself. The effort with the mirror is
designed to make the unemployed look at themselves. I had a group of unemployed in my
ministerial office, to try to give them confidence to go for an interview.
Mr Hunt: Were they decent people?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: They were relatively decent, but, regrettably, they could not look
me in the face, they could not answer a question, they could not read the Queen's English,
and they could not describe my model aeroplanes. However, it is one of the human tragedies
that a Minister of Labour has to suffer today. I believe that the use of mirrors, and any other
method of getting a message across to these unfortunate people, is to be commended.

Small Hydro Schemes
7. Mr LATTER (Marlborough) to the Minister of Energy: How many small hydro

there any estimates of their total generating capacity or total estimated cost?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): Eight small hydro schemes have been approved

estimated cost of $97.6 million.
Mr Latter: Would any of those eight have been started other than under the provisions
of the 1977 Budget?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: No. It was not until shortly before the 1977 Budget that negotiations

time to announce the provisions in the Budget.

the 1977 Budget, how many were actually under construction, and how many of the number

appreciate that any investigations that were being made before the 1977 Budget were of a
hypothetical nature, because they were predicated with “if”—if a satisfactory agreement
were consummated. A satisfactory agreement was not consummated until the middle of last
year.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: The Minister said that eight were under investigation at present.
How many applications have been made for small hydro stations over the same period?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I have not got the details in front of me, but I recall answering a
question along these lines earlier in the session. My recollection is that only one scheme has
been formally declined, and that, in addition to the eight for which there have been
approvals for either investigation work or design grants, about six or eight others are in the
pipeline.

question about small hydro schemes, approximately 19 stations; and, if so, what is the
difference between the 19 and the 8 mentioned this afternoon?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I gave a literal answer to the question asked this afternoon by the
member for Marlborough about the number of cases for which investigation and design
grants had already been approved. The reference to 19 was to the number of potential sites
for small hydro schemes that were then known to be under consideration. Many of those
were at the stage of the local supply authority considering the scheme, but there had been no
formal application to the Government at the time.

Plastic Road-Marking Paint
14. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga), on behalf of Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central), to the
Minister of Works and Development: In view of the criticism of plastic paint and the danger
of that to motor cyclists, what action is his department taking to find an alternative form of
road marking?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development): The paint used for
pavement marking is either chlorinated rubber, or alkoid based. Plastic paints are not used
for road marking, because they wear rapidly. The slippery nature of road-marking paint
when placed on smooth surfaces is recognised, and for this reason the area of paint applied is
kept to the minimum necessary for traffic guidance. In urban areas where the risk of
manoeuvring or braking on pavement marking is greatest, alternative materials such as pre-
cut sheeting with higher skid resistance, and thermoplastic materials, are being increasingly
used. Because of the high cost of these materials their use is limited to higher risk areas such
as pedestrian crossings, limit lines, and lane arrows. Pavement-marking materials used in
New Zealand are similar to those used in other countries. Overseas developments are
continually monitored and adapted in this country after evaluation, and if appropriate.

IMF Restrictions-Foreign Exchange
17. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Finance: Is the undertaking regarding
"restrictions on current international payments" given to the International Monetary Fund
by the Minister of Finance on 16 October 1974, and reaffirmed on three subsequent
occasions, still in full force and effect; and does that undertaking relate to impediments to
the purchase by New Zealanders of foreign exchange?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The undertakings given by the
previous Minister of Finance were made during a series of purchases of foreign exchange
under the International Monetary Fund's oil facility. I released the texts of those
undertakings in February 1976, and reaffirmed them the following month, when we made a
fifth and final purchase. They are still in effect and will remain so for as long as these
purchases, which amount to NZ$288 million, are outstanding. The undertaking is to refrain
from imposing restrictions on our current international payments that are inconsistent with
our obligations under the fund's articles of agreement, without prior consultation with the
fund. Article VIII prohibits the introduction of discriminatory currency arrangements or
multiple currency practices without the approval of the fund. The imposition of a tax on
foreign exchange clearly falls within the scope of this article. I cannot predict what attitude
the fund would take to such a tax, but an adverse judgment could lead to a request to repay
our oil facility drawings.
Mr Brill: Would the Minister confirm that New Zealand has had no previous
consultation with the International Monetary Fund about the imposition of a foreign
exchange surtax?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: As we do not intend to do that, obviously there has been
no previous consultation. We think the policy would be very bad, even standing on its own.

UN Declaration Against Apartheid in Sport
19. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Is it correct that New
Zealand abstained from voting last December at the United Nations General Assembly on
the issue of a United Nations International Declaration against Apartheid in Sport when it
was passed by 120 votes to nil, and, if so, what were the reasons for New Zealand's
abstention?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): It is correct
that New Zealand, along with 13 other countries, abstained in the vote on the Declaration
Against Apartheid in Sport when this was taken at the United Nations last December. As its
commitment to the Gleneagles Agreements shows, the Government supports the aims of the


## p. 1332 (#442) ###########################################

1332
29 June
Questions-Oral
declaration, which are the elimination of apartheid in sport. Unfortunately, the declaration
includes some specific ways of achieving those aims that are not in accordance with New
Zealand's laws and methods of administration. For this reason we were obliged to abstain,
along with a number of Western nations who shared our reservations about the declaration.
We remain, however, firmly committed to the basic principles of the declaration, which
parallel those of the Gleneagles Agreement.
Mr Isbey: What part of the declaration passed by the United Nations was in conflict with
the spirit of the Gleneagles Agreement?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I said that there were some additions to it over and
above the Gleneagles Agreement that caused us concern. An example is Article 6 of the
United Nations resolution that calls on states to deny visas and/or entry to representatives of
sports bodies, members of teams, or individual sportsmen from any country practising
apartheid. It also assumes that all sporting bodies are either inseparable from the
Government or, at the very least, subject to Government direction. Further, in a number of
articles in the declaration, the New Zealand Government was asked to accept applications
on behalf of international, regional, and national sporting bodies that it is simply not in a
position to do.
Mr D. M. J. Jones: Which Western countries abstained?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The nine countries of the European Economic
Community, and Austria, Iceland, Portugal, and the United States of America.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the reservations the Government had in supporting the
declaration, what if any steps did the Government take to initiate a move to subscribe to the
principles sought at the United Nations?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The Government is constantly taking measures, and
I have a file from the office of the Minister of Foreign Affairs of letters he has written about
the Gleneagles Agreement to sporting bodies in New Zealand. This is a constant and daily
operation by the Minister of Foreign Affairs.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Can the Minister indicate that the concern of the Government for the
international undertakings in the Gleneagles Agreement is less than the answer to question
17, which indicated that the Government's concern is for observance of financial
agreements?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: We are concerned, and have practised the spirit of
the Gleneagles Agreement, but we are also concerned with what we believe is the economic
trouble we would get into if we adopted Labour's irresponsible policy on finance.
Forests and Birds
20. Mr BELL (Gisborne), on behalf of Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua), to the Minister of
Forests: What is the area of indigenous nature forest at present not controlled by the Crown
that has a special forest and bird significance to New Zealand?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): There are some very important areas of
indigenous forest on privately owned land. In many cases the areas are relatively small, as
they represent remnants of forest types that existed on much of our developed farms lands.
At this stage their precise extent is not known, but the Forestry Council, on my request, has
set up a working group to examine the whole question of how incentives can be provided to
encourage private owners to retain indigenous forests.
Mr Bell: Can the Minister confirm that approximately 25 percent of New Zealand's land
area is covered with indigenous native forest?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: No, I cannot confirm that exact figure, but I can say that, of the
indigenous forest, approximately half is State indigenous forest and half is owned privately.
Of course, amongst the private owners, considerable areas of native forests are owned by
Maori people.

be audited by the Controller and Auditor-General in the same way as the Shipping
Corporation of New Zealand and most of the producer boards were.
The Controller and Auditor-General had pointed out in his report that there were
differences in the auditing systems of his office and of the private company that had been
auditing the records of Air New Zealand. He had also stated that the records of a public
corporation should be perused by his department, and that the easiest solution would be for
the chartered accountants to be employed by and to report to the department rather than be
appointed on the recommendation of the company's directors. Did the Minister agree with
that? The report had mentioned that an audit of the enlarged airline by the department could
result in disclosures that could harm its international competitiveness. However, that could
also apply to the Shipping Corporation of New Zealand, the Meat Producers Board, the
Dairy Board, and others. He was not implying that Air New Zealand was contemplating any
shady deal. However, it would be better to have the airline, a public corporation, audited in
the same way as other boards. QANTAS was audited by the Auditor-General of Australia.

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister in Charge of the Audit Department) said that
after Air New Zealand and the National Airways Corporation merged the Air New Zealand
company remained in existence. It could have become a public corporation, but it had
remained a company under the Companies Act. He said that he had not read the report of
the Controller and Auditor-General on financial management and control in administrative
Government departments because he had asked Treasury to report on it. The Treasury
report, he understood would be in his hands within a few days, and he proposed then to read
the Auditor-General's report and the Treasury comments. A decision would then be made
on any additional procedures that might be needed. If he were to comment on the report
before he had the benefit of the Treasury comments he might mislead the Committee.
If estimating procedures were eased up too much it could be said that the Government
would lose control, but he preferred to leave such comments until he had studied the details.
The Committee on Public Expenditure comprised permanent heads, who endeavoured to
programme departmental spending for the following 2 or 3 years. The committee met late in
the year, as the first of the processes leading up to the Budget. Since the change of
Government a Cabinet committee on expenditure had been introduced and it supplemented
the Committee on Public Expenditure. It performed effectively, and closely scrutinised
Government expenditure. It went through the estimates line by line in the presence of
departmental heads, Treasury officials, and the Minister if he wanted to be there. The
committee had had a considerable effect in helping and justifying Government expenditure,
and was a worthwhile innovation, although the work was time-consuming for the three
Ministers involved. The committee carried out a valuable task, and its recommendations or
minutes were put before the Cabinet in the following week for confirmation, and frequently
accepted.

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister) said that he deplored the personal attack

gathered information external to New Zealand that was extremely valuable, particularly on
the trade, geography, and economies of other countries. The bureau had wide contacts
around the world, and presented regular reports to the Prime Minister and to those
interested in New Zealand's economic relationships with other countries. Since the change
of Government, the work of the bureau had been upgraded. Giving the bureau more teeth
meant it could gather much more information. For example, in the present negotiations with
the Japanese, valuable information on details of the Japanese economy had been obtained.
The bureau had instituted some special work on South Pacific economies, and the newly
independent Island states and their relationship with New Zealand. He and other Ministers
appreciated the benefit derived from the bureau's work.
As was normal under successive Governments, the press section employed three men
on contract. Four of the eight members of the advisory group were also on contract. The
group's work had been widely applauded, particularly by those in industry and by various
organisations with which it kept the Government in touch. Four of the group were from
outside and four from inside the State services, and they did a magnificent job of liaison
between the Government and, particularly, the private sector. It was true that they did some
travelling to bring back to Wellington confidential information given to them from all types
of industry. That gave the Government valuable information, never before available, for its
economic planning. Time after time, leading people in trade, commerce, and industry had
said how much they appreciated talking in their own offices with members of the group,
thereby getting the feel of the Government's side of whatever the economic policy might be.
The information coming to Wellington supplemented other information given by various
departments, the normal source of advice. The departmental officers also appreciated the
liaison given. The Prime Minister's department had been used in all kinds of ad hoc
negotiations to supplement departmental sources, and its work had been much appreciated
by people inside and outside the House. He had not the slightest doubt that a Labour
Government, having seen how well the system worked, would use the same procedure. A
year ago Malcolm Fraser had been greatly interested to see what was being done in New
Zealand, and, as recently as this week, he had read of the Australian Prime Minister having
a similar advisory group in Canberra.

NEW ZEALAND NATIONAL AIRWAYS CORPORATION DISSOLUTION BILL
Introduction
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services):
I move, That the New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill be introduced.
This is a short and quite straightforward piece of legislation. Broadly speaking, its aim, as the
title states, is to give effect to the Government's decision to merge Air New Zealand and the
National Airways Corporation. Specifically, it covers the legal and fiscal aspects of the
amalgamation, and provides for the dissolution of NAC. The Bill contains only five clauses.
I shall briefly explain what is covered by each. Clause 1 deals with the short title and the
dates of commencement. Clauses 2, 3, and 5 are deemed to commence on 1 March 1978, and
clause 4, which deals with the actual dissolution of NAC, is deemed to commence at a date to
be fixed by Order in Council.
This is an appropriate time to make one or two comments on the timing of the
legislation and on the reasons for the commencement dates set out in the Bill. On 19
December 1977 the Government decided that the airlines should be merged, and made its
announcement. The merger itself was to take place on 1 April 1978. It came through loud
and clear from the investigations into the feasibility of an amalgamation that, if the
Government did decide to proceed with a merger, it should take place as soon as possible
after any announcement. The Ministry of Transport and both airlines were unanimous in
strongly advising against any delays in giving effect to a decision to amalgamate the airlines,
because of the effect of a delay on the morale of the airlines' 8600 staff. For that reason, an
early date was chosen. The date of 1 April 1978 was chosen because it left sufficient time for
the preparatory work to be done, and because it was convenient from an accounting point of
view.
The reason for the commencement date being set at 1 March 1978 for clauses 2, 3 and 5
is to place beyond doubt the validity of the preparatory steps towards the amalgamation
taken after the Government's decision was announced. As I said earlier, clause 4 of the Bill,
dealing with the dissolution of the National Airways Corporation, will come into effect on a
date to be set by Order in Council. The reason for this is simply that the corporation must
continue, as a legal entity at least, until consent is obtained to the assignment to Air New
Zealand of certain contracts that are governed by foreign law and cannot be affected by an
Act of the New Zealand Parliament. It is only a matter of time now before these formalities
are completed.
In the interests of simplicity all legal aspects of the amalgamation are dealt with in this
one Bill. Clause 2 simply defines "Air New Zealand Ltd." and the "Corporation". Clause 3
deals with the transfer to Air New Zealand of air service licences held by NAC. The clause
provides that Air New Zealand may maintain and operate domestic air services previously
run by NAC, and places beyond doubt the validity of the transfer of the licenses that took
effect on 1 April this year.
Clause 4, as I mentioned earlier, deals with the dissolution of the National Airways
Corporation. Under this clause the corporation is dissolved, its assets and liabilities,


## p. 1356 (#466) ###########################################

1356
New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill
30 June
including tax losses, are transferred to Air New Zealand, and its employees are deemed to
become employees of Air New Zealand on the same terms and conditions of employment.
The clause also provides for the repeal of the New Zealand National Airways Act 1945, its
amendments and associated regulations, and its bylaws approval order. This is the clause
which will commence on a date to be set by Order in Council. Clause 5 makes it clear that
Part III of the Commerce Act 1975 does not apply to the airline merger. The Bill is largely a
procedural one, designed to cover, as far as it is necessary and practical, all the legal and
fiscal aspects of the merger.
The decision to amalgamate the airlines has been widely debated already and the case
has been made. However, a number of responsible people have expressed an opinion on the
validity of some of the steps taken to effect the merger. I believe it would be irresponsible for
the Government to allow those doubts to go unresolved. The Bill removes all doubts and
provides for the final step in the merger, namely, the dissolution of the National Airways
Corporation. The merger has now been widely accepted.

Clause 4, which is the operative one, states that the takeover is to be given effect to, and

conditions of employment, including those applicable to salaries and allowances. It is
significant that those two are singled out, while there is no reference to superannuation. My
understanding is that different conditions of superannuation prevailed in the two airlines.
What happens to a person in NAC who had certain superannuation rights, when he becomes
an employee of Air New Zealand, whose employees have other rights? Do they all become
the same? Does each man continue to have the same superannuation structure related to a
salary structure which will certainly be different, because as aircrews graduate from the
biggest planes used in our domestic service to the bigger ones used overseas their salary
rights will certainly change. Their superannuation entitlements will differ accordingly. Can
the Minister explain what steps have been taken to overcome this?
Again, there are certain contractual rights involved. It is all very well for a Government
to deal with its own creations, but there are rights that have been assumed-for instance
insurance rights. Each of the companies has heavy insurance commitments and
responsibilities. What steps has the Government taken to make sure that the insurers of
NAC are willing to accept the continuation of the liability under those policies with a
different organisation? Moreover, the organisation, which is a statutory corporation, had not
limit to its liability; now it suddenly becomes a limited liability company. I am sure that the
Commerce Commission would have had something to say about that—and it is significant
that clause 5 exempts the merger of the two airlines from the scrutiny of the commission.
That body would in no circumstances agree to a merger enabling a company that had been
trading under an unlimited liability suddenly to become one with a specific limit to its
liability.
Mr Latter: Have a look at the date.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: It does not matter what the date is. That has nothing to do with
it. It suddenly becomes a company of limited liability, not one without limit on its liability.
I should like the Minister's view on the following point. While the accident
compensation scheme may have put out of consideration the possibility of an action for
negligence, there remains liability under a number of international air conventions that are
independent of negligence. The situation is possibly a hypothetical one and will not be real
once the Bill goes through, but in the meantime, assuming there is some mishap on a
National Airways Corporation aircraft while it is being run, as it is currently, by Air New
Zealand, who would be liable under any of the international conventions? Would it be the
nominal owner, the person in whom the licence to fly was originally vested and which licence
has been transferred without any statutory authority to another company, or would it be the
actual operator for the time being? To whom would a person look for redress under the
various conventions that establish a liability for that redress? Have these matters been given
thought, and what is the consequence? In other words, were all these matters covered in the
report? They are certainly not matters of confidentiality, but matters of public interest. If
they were covered in the report they should be made public.
Our view of this Bill is that it should not be our responsibility, and we should not be
called upon to give it any consideration at all without the benefit of knowing the grounds
upon which the Government made its move. If it feels justified in doing so, the Government
must tell us what that justification is. Without that justification, we are just arguing and
talking to no purpose in a vacuum, and the community will be no better informed when the
Bill goes through. All people can see is what will happen in the end. I concede that that may
be beneficial, but we are entitled to know why the step is being taken and how it is more
beneficial for the two airlines to be knitted together than would have been the case with
them continuing as separate identities.
