Dangerous Goods Amendment Bill
DANGEROUS GOODS AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That the Dangerous Goods
Amendment Bill be introduced. The primary purpose of the Bill is to facilitate the
implementation of a Government decision to transfer the administration of the Dangerous
Goods Act from the Department of Internal Affairs to the Department of Labour. This
transfer is part of a move to rationalise industrial safety inspection services provided by the
Government.
For some years there has been difficulty in staffing adequately the dangerous goods and
explosives branch of the Department of Internal Affairs, particularly scientific support
services. The changes to be authorised by the Bill will enable the dangerous goods
inspectorate to include an adequate scientific back-up service and to be fully co-ordinated
with the factory inspectorate in the Labour Department. The Bill in no way alters the role of
local authorities in connection with dangerous goods. I can say now that, while the Bill
provides that it shall come into force on a date to be determined by Order in Council, we are
aiming for a target date in the final quarter of this year.
Opportunity is also being taken to empower the chief inspector of dangerous goods to
regulate the type of pump unit to be used to supply liquefied petroleum gas to vehicle fuel
tanks. Because more and more vehicles will use liquefied petroleum gas it is desirable that
control should be exercised over the types of pumps to be used, in the same way that controls
already apply to the types of pumps for petroleum.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): What is the urgency for
introducing the Bill in this way? No copies were immediately available to members on this
side of the House, although that was remedied within a short time. Last night the Prime
Minister had much to say about undertakings between the Whips not being observed. We
were assured that only one Bill would be introduced today. I cannot see anything in the Bill
sufficiently urgent to necessitate breaching an undertaking given to the Opposition. If the
Prime Minister insists on the terms of undertakings being observed, he should back up his
assertions with his own actions.
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I want to answer the accusation simply and to tell the House that
about an hour ago the Senior Opposition Whip was informed that the Bills would be
introduced. That is more notice than is usually given on Friday mornings, when notice is
given at 8.30 a.m. At that time the Government intended to introduce only one Bill.
However, as two more became available, the Senior Opposition Whip was given one hour's
notice.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): I have had a brief look at the Bill and notice that
its main purport is to transfer the administration of one section of the Department of
Internal Affairs to the Department of Labour. That is very disappointing. For more than
34 years a specialist committee, comprising representatives from the Department of Internal
Affairs, the Department of Labour, the Ministry of Transport, and the Department of
Health, has been considering the transport of dangerous goods. However, on reading the
Bill it is apparent that no progress has been made. We find that officials from two of the four
departments concerned have been occupied in transferring responsibility, and in deciding
who should be responsible for the administration of dangerous goods. Are members
opposite prepared to allow injuries to continue to occur during the transporting of dangerous
goods while time is wasted in deciding which department should control what and which
departments shall have other responsibilities?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! Does this have anything to do with the question before the
House, that the Bill should or should not be introduced?
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: Yes, I am coming to that.
Mr SPEAKER: I should be grateful if the member would do so, because I have been
unable to follow his argument.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: We had been led to believe that the prime matter for

to that point. Has progress been made, and is the Minister able to say that the transfer of
responsibility will expedite the discussions that have been going on for 3 years?

EXPLOSIVES AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That the Explosives
Amendment Bill be introduced. The principal purpose of this Bill is to facilitate the transfer
of the administration of the Explosives Act from the Department of Internal Affairs to the
Department of Labour. Inspectors of dangerous goods at the Department of Internal Affairs
are also inspectors of explosives. Consequently, the administration of both the Dangerous
Goods Act and the Explosives Act must rest with the same department. The Bill also
provides that display fireworks may be handled directly across a wharf without special safety
requirements being laid down by the chief inspector.
The present law provides for that when consignments involve not more than 27 kg of
explosives, or when consignments consist of ammunition or of shop fireworks. Display
fireworks offer no greater hazard than goods that are now excluded. Parliamentary counsel
has asked for a clause to be included in the Bill providing that the United Kingdom
Explosives Substances Act 1883 shall cease to have effect as part of the law of New Zealand.
I am advised that this enactment has been overlooked during previous consolidations of the
Explosives Act, and that the provisions of clause 4 of this Bill should have been included in
an Explosives Bill as far back as 1887.
Dr WALL (Porirua): I ask the Minister again, what provision has been made in the
Department of Labour for better scientific and technical advice? Undoubtedly a new
category of person will be involved. Has the Minister solved the problem of establishing a
pay structure that will ensure the right people are attracted to the job? What will be done to
ensure that those appointed to advise and control will have genuine qualifications, not only
Public Service qualifications?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): The staff now engaged in dealing
with explosives in the Department of Internal Affairs will be transferred to the Department
of Labour. There has never been any suggestion that the present staff are inadequate.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): I move, That the Explosives Amendment Bill be
referred to the Labour Committee, and that the hearings of the committee be open to accredited
representatives of the news media.

list of names of persons suplied to him and certified as correct by the secretary of the union.

it is simply a question of whether the person is bound by the unqualified preference clause in

Electricity Charges, North Auckland
3. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Has he read the reports in
the Northern Advocate of 21 and 24 June on the North Auckland Electric Power Board's
intention, by using a second meter and higher charges, to increase charges to consumers who
have installed solar and chip heaters to conserve electricity, and, if so, can he state what
action he proposes to take to prevent steps such as this, which may frustrate energy
conservation?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): Yes, I have seen the reports the honourable
member is referring to. There can be no question of discrimination against those consumers
who are prepared to utilise the alternative renewable energy forms such as solar water
heating and solid-fuel combined space-heating and water-heating systems. I know that the
Electrical Supply Authorities Association accepts this principle, and it is noteworthy that this
has also been the general practice for many years with wetback fireplaces or chip heaters. It
is only with the advent of solar water heaters with seasonal characteristics that differ from
supplementary solid-fuel systems that this question has come up again. Because of variations
in supply authority situations, this is not a simple question, and I know it has been the
subject of some discussion between officers of my ministry and the Electrical Supply
Authorities Association. I am sure that this will lead to a satisfactory solution to the matter.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Should not householders who took steps at cost to themselves to
put in energy conservation installations, such as chip heaters and solar heaters, be rewarded,
and not penalised by the imposition of higher unit electricity charges, such as those proposed
by the North Auckland Electric Power Board?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: They certainly should not suffer from the action they are taking. This
was the burden of my answer, and it is the theme being taken up in the discussions between
the officers of my ministry and the Electrical Supply Authorities Association. The member
might be interested to know that a meeting of the conservation committee of the association
is to be held on 12 July, and my officers will attend. I think the matter can be sorted out
there.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Are the actions proposed by the North Auckland Electric Power
Board in opposition to the Government's policy on energy conservation, and, if so, what
action does the Minister propose to take in the foreseeable future?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I am sure the honourable member appreciates that the electrical
supply authorities have a measure of independence in their operations. The boards of the
electrical supply authorities are democratically elected, in the same way as are members of
local government organisations. Therefore it is possible for consumers or ratepayers to
register their thinking on the matter with the elected representatives concerned. Within the
broad parameters of the boards' functions, the individual electrical supply authorities have
some measure of flexibility in the way they apply their tariff proposals. The member should
appreciate that the boards consider that those who do not install solar water heaters should
not be placed at a disadvantage, either. That is why the North Auckland Power Board has
endeavoured to find, by a three-tariff system, a way of striking a balance between the
advantage given to those who have the cheaper water heating and those who must carry the
higher charge because they do not have solar heating.

5. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Has he seen the

"unconventional diplomacy" activity here in New Zealand; (b) the amount of funds
expended by the South African Department of Information in New Zealand; and will he
state what action, if any, he is proposing to take to put a stop to it?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): I have seen the
report to which the member refers. I am not aware that there is any such "unconventional
diplomacy" activity here in New Zealand. The minor New Zealand connection that was
referred to would appear to be no more than the transfer of an information official from the
consulate-general to his parent department in South Africa. I do not know the amount of
funds expended by the South African Department of Information in New Zealand.
Information work is a legitimate activity of a consular mission and the Government does not
intend to prevent the South African consulate-general from carrying out such activities. I
would, however, like to make it clear that if there is any question of the consulate-general or,
for that matter, the representative of any other Government in New Zealand undertaking
activities that are not legitimate then the Government will take appropriate action.
Hon. M. Rata: The Minister has said that some activities are carried out by the
consulate-general in the normal course of duties, and since some of the funds may have come
from an unconventional source as uncovered by the report, will he take the necessary steps
to advise the South African consul-general that New Zealand will not condone this action?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I see no need for me to interfere in the proper
operations of the representative of a foreign Government in New Zealand when those
operations do not infringe New Zealand's law or practice.
Rt. Hon. R. D. Muldoon: Is the Minister aware that one information activity carried out
by the consul-general of South Africa is the distribution of pictorial calendars, as is done by
many other diplomatic representatives in New Zealand, and does he regard that as
subversive?
Mr SPEAKER: The first part of the question is legitimate. The second part seeks an
opinion. The Minister may answer the first part.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am aware of this type of publicity activity carried
out by the South African consul-general, and that is a general kind of activity undertaken in
this field. I am not aware that he engages in any other type of activity.
Logging in State Indigenous Forests
6. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) to the Minister of Forests: At what rate is the extraction
of native logs from State indigenous forests being reduced?


## p. 1378 (#488) ###########################################

1378
30 June
Questions-Oral
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): The Minister of Forests replies: "The
reduction in the rate of extraction of wood from State indigenous forests can be illustrated by
the following figures. Total wood removals from State indigenous forests in the past 3 years
have been: for the year ended 31 March 1976, 529 000 m³; for the year ended 31 March 1977,
436 000 m³, and for the year ended 31 March 1978, 380 000 m³. This represents an annual
reduction of 15 percent. Removals of wood from State indigenous forests will continue to be
reduced at this rate or an even higher rate except on the West Coast of the South Island,
where the level of cut needs to be maintained at close to its present level for social reasons.
The aim is to bring the level of cut into balance with the growth of the managed native
forests."

Foreign Exchange Remittances, Pacific Islands
12. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Finance: What is his estimate of the amount of
foreign exchange remittance from New Zealand to the Pacific Islands, and what proportion
of this figure is estimated to arise from personal, as opposed to business, payments?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Total foreign exchange remittances
through the banking system to the Pacific Islands in the year ended March 1978 amounted to
$90 million. Of this total, remittances for imports were $28.7 million, and capital remittances
were $4 million. Total payments in the invisibles category amounted to $57.5 million, of
which travel remittances accounted for $28.7 million-largely the expenses of New Zealand
tourists visiting the Islands. Personal remittances—that is, gifts and similar transfers,
transfers by emigrants and temporary residents leaving New Zealand, and legacies-
amounted to $7.3 million. These remittances are for the following countries: Fiji, Tonga,
Western Samoa, Niue, Nauru, Tahiti and other French Pacific Islands, New Hebrides, and
other smaller islands in the general area of the South Pacific.
Mr Brill: Would it be correct that the imposition of a 10 percent surcharge on such
remittances would represent a payment of $730,000 by New Zealand residents sending
payments to Island people?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Yes, that would apparently be correct. The member said
New Zealand residents, but these are, for the most part, Pacific Island people from those
Islands sending part of their income back to their families.
Hon. M. Rata: Would it not be more correct to suggest that a reduction in the total
number of Island people entering and working in New Zealand would have a more adverse
effect?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: It depends on what the member means by a more adverse
affect. If he means an adverse effect on the relationship between New Zealand and the
Islands, I would say no. It would be a serious blow to the relationship between New Zealand
and the Pacific Islands if we literally taxed at a rate of 10 percent the money Pacific Islanders
earned and sent home to their people. That would have a much more serious adverse effect
than the changes in the number of people coming to New Zealand, which in each case has
been discussed with and agreed to by the Island Governments concerned.

QUESTION-URGENT
Children's Nightwear Supplies, Lower Hutt
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: Is he aware that there
are no supplies of children's pyjamas, nightdresses, or dressing gowns to retail shops in
Lower Hutt because of the failure of the Government to provide for testing provisions for
materials used in such manufacture in accordance with his legislation, the Safety of
Children's Nightclothes Act 1977, and will he take immediate steps to ensure that the
manufacturers can use the material they are holding, whether by postponing the date of the
application of his legislation or by establishing some authority to conduct the tests
immediately, as there is an urgent need now among families in Lower Hutt for these goods?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): Supplies of
children's nightwear are available in reasonable quantities in retail shops in Lower Hutt. The
short time available to prepare this answer has limited a survey to a few leading retailers.
However, even if there were some shortage of supplies it would not be a result of legislation
passed last year for the safety of children's nightwear. This legislation permits the
manufacture of any type of nightwear up to 1 January 1979 and its sale until 1 January 1980.
This would enable manufacturers to use current stocks. Moreover, provided garments are of
safe design, there are no restrictions on the materials that may be used. Arrangements for
the testing of materials have been made, and one New Zealand manufacturer has already
had one fabric tested and accepted as being of low fire risk. Details concerning testing
facilities have been advised to inquirers and will shortly be published in the Gazette.

NOXIOUS PLANTS BILL
Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture Committee
to present the report of the committee on the Noxious Plants Bill. The committee
recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie
upon the table.
The Noxious Plants Bill was introduced at the end of the 1977 session, and referred to
the Lands and Agriculture Committee for recess study. Some 63 submissions were heard,
and 20 of these were heard on 4 days of hearings. The committee spent a further 4 days in
consideration of reports and deliberating on the Bill. The amendments made to the Bill are
in most cases designed to improve on the detailed wording of the legislation, but some are of
more substance, and the following are the most important of these.
The membership of the regional co-ordinating committees, which a number of
submissions considered unsatisfactory, have been amended in clause 22 by adding the power
for the committees, with the approval of the Noxious Plants Council, to appoint co-opted
members to allow for a geographic spread of membership, or to obtain a reasonable balance
between the representatives of district authorities and Federated Farmers. The regional
committees shall also, in any region containing a substantial area of Maori land, appoint as a
member a person nominated by the Maori land advisory committee within the region. The
Bill is also amended elsewhere to ensure that Maori land is treated in the same manner as
any other land, and this provision for appointment to regional committees will ensure that
the rights of Maori landholders are not overlooked. I feel this is a very important
amendment, and one that is worthwhile.


## p. 1385 (#495) ###########################################

30 June
1385
Noxious Plants Bill
Clause 41, which covers the appointment by district authorities of noxious plants
officers, has been amended to make it clear that such officers will have to be employed full
time by a district authority unless the Noxious Plants Council agrees to a part-time officer in
special circumstances. To achieve this, local authorities are empowered to join together by
agreement to administer the Act and jointly employ a noxious plants officer.
Clause 42 relates to the payments by the Government of part of the noxious plants
officer's salary and expenses. This has been amended to make it clear that, in order to
receive this subsidy, the officer must not only be full time, with the exception previously
mentioned, but also be trained to the council's requirements, or be in the process of being
trained. A new clause 43A has been added to allow for officers of the Ministry of Agriculture
and Fisheries to be appointed as noxious plants officers to investigate plants that should be
declared class A, to ensure their eradication, and to carry out the provisions of the Act when
a district authority defaults under clause 32. A new clause 47A has been added to prohibit the
propagation, sowing, and selling of class A and class B noxious plants, but allows the council
to approve exceptions to this for scientific and other purposes. This was implied in the Bill
but not previously spelt out.
Clause 48, which deals with the responsibility for noxious plant control on roadsides,
attracted many submissions and promoted lengthy discussion within the committee. The
committee finally agreed to amend the Bill to remove the responsibility from the owner of
the road as provided in the Bill, and place it with the adjoining occupier as is provided in the
Noxious Weeds Act 1950. Provision is also made for the owners of roads-counties,
municipalities, and the National Roads Board-by agreement to take over control of
roadsides when they consider this desirable. In other words, this is a permissible clause.
Clause 50, which provides for appeals against notices served by district authorities, has been
amended to reduce the fee for filing an appeal from $50 to $10, to allow for more than one
arbitrator per region, and to set a time limit on when he must hear the appeal.
Clause 54, which provides for offences and penalties, has been amended in light of
submissions to provide for different penalties for offences against class A or class B noxious
plants, and for the level of penalties to be increased. A number of amendments have been
made to Part II of the Bill, which relates to the two nassella tussock boards, but these are of
an administrative nature and would make no major change to the tussock boards.
I believe the Bill, while retaining its basic elements and administrative structure, has
been improved by the amendments, and will prove to be effective legislation. The
recommendations of the committee were unanimous. I thank members of the committee
from both sides of the House for their co-operation, and also express appreciation to the
staff, parliamentary counsel, and others for their assistance.
Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central): I join with the chairman in saying that
members of the select committee worked together as a team to produce effective legislation
that will be in the interests of everyone. The Bill does more than set up a centralised control
of noxious weeds. It binds the Crown, something people in many parts of New Zealand have
wanted for a long time. Actually, the administrative side of the Bill has been in practice for
longer than 12 months, and, to a degree, the legislation is retrospective, although such a
measure was discussed by the last Labour Government with the idea of bringing in
legislation when it found the best way of making it work. It is working very well indeed, and
the Bill, after its consideration in the select committee and the alterations made to it, is even
better.
Essentially, there are two categories of weeds. Finance for control of class A weeds will
come from central government. In the case of class B weeds, there has at times been some
difficulty in establishing the ownership of properties, and, in particular, Maori land. Those
matters were dealt with very satisfactorily in the select committee. The central council, and
the regional committees-areas divided into regions, and divided further into district
authorities or local authorities-will provide the structure for noxious weeds control. The
result will be a tier system that will ensure a continuity of approach to noxious weeds.
Members on this side of the House are happy with the amendments, and hope that the Bill
operates in the way that everyone wants it to.
Motion agreed to.

QUEEN ELIZABETH THE
SECOND ARTS COUNCIL OF NEW ZEALAND
AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Mr COUCH (Wairarapa): I am directed by the Maori Affairs Committee to present the
report of the committee on the Queen Elizabeth the Second Arts Council of New Zealand
Amendment Bill (No. 2). The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as
amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. The Maori Affairs Committee heard
eight submissions on the Bill. They were from the New Zealand Maori Artists and Writers,
the New Zealand Maori Arts and Crafts Institute, the Race Relations Conciliator, the New
Zealand Polynesian Festival Committee, the New Zealand Maori Council, the Maori
Women's Welfare League, the Queen Elizabeth the Second Arts Council, and Pacifica,
whose submission was written.
It was obvious to the committee that there were three principal reservations: first, the
use of the words "traditional" and "Polynesian" in the title of the proposed council;
secondly, the need to specify that specific established Maori organisations should have direct
representation on the proposed council; and thirdly, reference to a possible clash of
functions with existing bodies concerned with Maori arts and crafts. A consensus decided
that the name of the proposed council should be "Council for Maori and South Pacific Arts”,
thus eliminating the title originally intended: “Council for Traditional Maori and Polynesian
Arts". As members can see, the words "traditional" and "Polynesian" have been omitted,
mainly because they were strongly opposed by those who appeared before the committee.
Regarding membership of the proposed council, several submissions suggested that
specified Maori organisations should have the right to be represented on the council.
However, this would not ensure that the distribution of members would bring about a
geographical and tribal spread, the knowledge and expertise of different art forms, or would
give adequate representation to young people and women. Pacific Island groups that are also
entitled to reasonable representation would not be represented. I am sure that when
appointing members to the proposed council the Minister of Maori Affairs and the Minister
of Internal Affairs will give careful consideration to making sure that there is no clash. It is
very much in the spirit of the Bill to engender co-operation rather than competition. The
council's function now is to receive recommendations on the distribution of funds from any
organisation concerned with Maori and Pacific arts.
The Bill should take an effective step towards guarding against the development of
cultural separation, and should ensure that Maori and Pacific arts flourish alongside New
Zealand arts of European origin. I am sure that each will benefit by this type of association,
and that they will derive greater strength from creative contact.
Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori): In commending the Bill and its amendments I want
to advise the House that any effort to expand and promote the cultural advancement of both
the Maori and Island communities in New Zealand has the wholehearted support of the New
Zealand Labour Party. The Bill arose from a grant of $50,000 made by the Government.
Although it is a oncer, I sincerely hope that that sum will be added to. This new council is not
being formed because of the absence of statutory authorities or bodies to cater for the
cultural needs or the promotion and advancement of the Maori people. This is something
new, and requires both the Maori and Island communities within New Zealand to advance
those things that they consider valuable. The council will also make available to Maori and
Island people the administrative and skilled resources of the Queen Elizabeth the Second
Arts Council. For those reasons, I suggest that the Council for Maori and South Pacific Arts
will be a challenge to the people who will administer it. The council will embrace and
embody both traditional and evolving Maori and Island art forms. However, the financial
resources must be given to enable the council to carry out its duties. The assistance given to
the committee by various organisations was valuable. The Opposition supports the
provisions in the amendment.
Motion agreed to.

Hospital boards recruit their own staff to such positions. When inquiries are received from
prospective applicants by the Department of Health they are channelled to boards that have
suitable vacancies.

Cook Hospital will shortly be without the services of an ear, nose, and throat specialist. In

2. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of State Services: Can he advise the House of the

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of State Services replies:
"A pilot study is being conducted by the State Services Commission, in conjunction with the


## p. 1390 (#500) ###########################################

1390
4 July
Questions-Oral
Public Service Association, of the feasibility of employing more part-timers on a long-term
or career basis as distinct from the temporary work usually undertaken. At least some of
those participating in the pilot study will be job-sharing; that is, one full-time position will be
shared between two persons. It is hoped that the scheme will be able to meet employment

Library. I have instructed that the results of this experiment be made known to other State
services and to private sector employers."

Sports Club Raffles
3. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Internal Affairs: Has he seen an article in
the New Zealand Herald of 20 June 1978 in which he was reported to have "advised sports
clubs to push ahead with quick-fire raffles in hotel bars, in spite of a police warning that they
may be outside the law", and, if so, does the statement correctly quote him?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): The article referred to by the
honourable member appeared in the New Zealand Herald on 26 June 1978, not 20 June as
stated in the question. It is generally in accord with what I said, but I did not advise sports
clubs to break the law. Rather, I pointed out that I had received advice that did not coincide
with the views held by the Police, and that in my opinion it was legal for sports clubs to sell
quick-fire raffles in hotel bars. I further expressed the view that, if necessary, I would
promote an amendment to the law to clarify the position. I believe that it was Parliament's
intention that quick-fire raffles, which are an important source of funds for sporting clubs,
should be permitted. I propose to introduce an amendment to the Act to clarify the law
beyond any doubt.
Mr Hunt: If the Minister introduces an amendment to clarify the law beyond any doubt
will the provisions be made retrospective, and, if so, does that not indicate that the quotation
shows that there might have been a breaking of the law before the amendment?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: It is obvious that there is a difference of opinion between my legal
advisers and those of the Police. As there is doubt, I intend to amend the Act to clarify the
position.
Mr Comber: If there is to be a delay in the amending legislation would the Minister give
individual societies an exemption from the conditions required to be fulfilled under section
34 of the Act-a power that he already has?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: If that proved necessary I would not hesitate to use the
legislation.

Abortions
7. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Minister of Health: How many abortions
have been performed in New Zealand hospitals since 1 January?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The following information is available. Between
1 January and 31 March, 96 abortions were carried out. However, the figure may not be
complete, as there was no requirement for notification. From 1 April to 31 May, 309
abortions were performed. Figures for June are not yet available.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can the Minister state which hospitals performed the abortions?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No, I do not have that detail with me. Although I do not have the
figures, I seem to recollect that they were given recently, hospital by hospital.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can the Minister give an estimation of the percentage of total
abortions in New Zealand that were performed in hospitals?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Since it is illegal to carry out an abortion other than in a licensed
hospital I should think the figures for April and May are accurate. I believe there was a
requirement in the Wall Bill, if I can call it that, to notify the Health Department of
abortions. However, that Bill was discarded earlier this year, and the new legislation
requires the supervisory committee to be advised on abortions. As the Health Department
needs to know the figures for its planning, I have asked that it also be advised. That is why I
can say the figures for April and May are accurate. However, the earlier figures may not be
accurate because there was no legal requirement for abortions to be notified.
Forest Service-Special Work
8. Mr BELL (Gisborne) to the Minister of Forests: What special provisions have been
made by the Forest Service to provide employment for special workers in the 1978 annual
tree-planting programme?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The Forest Service annually acquires and
prepares land additional to that necessary for its own approved programme to provide out-
of-season employment for workers under the temporary employment scheme. During 1977,
in anticipation of higher levels of unemployment in 1978, approval was given for the Forest.
Service to overexpend its vote. The total approval for overexpenditure was $800,000 on new
land purchase, and $620,000 on preparation for new planting. As a consequence, as at
31 May this year the Forest Service had already been able to increase its work force by 622
more than at the same time last year. As planting had not then commenced in several areas it
is likely that further substantial increases to the total work force will have occurred since.
Mr Bell: Could the Minister confirm that the special workers are employed as staff over
and above the normal requirements for the Forest Service?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: Additional special employment positions are being filled by the
Forest Service. In addition, because of the need for land preparation by wage workers, extra
workers are being employed by the Forest Service.

Foreign Exchange Charges and GATT
12. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Customs: Does the General Agreement on
Tariffs and Trade contain any provision for retaliation by other contracting parties in the
event of the New Zealand Government adopting fees or charges on foreign exchange?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs): Article XXIII of the General
Agreement on Tariffs and Trade specifically provides for retaliatory action if a contracting
party should consider that any benefit accruing to it directly or indirectly under the
agreement is being nullified or impaired, either as the result of the failure of another
contracting party to carry out its obligations under the agreement, or by the application by
another contracting party of any measure, whether or not it conflicts with the provisions of
the agreement. In the event of the New Zealand Government imposing fees or charges on
foreign exchange it would be open to any other contracting party to base its justification for
taking retaliatory action on this provision.
Mr Brill: Would the scope of retaliatory action available to other contracting parties
include the right to cancel the GATT bindings or to intervene with agreements already
entered into under GATT?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The scope for retaliatory action appears to me to be very
broad, and I would suggest that any Government contemplating action of the sort
contemplated by the Opposition would be taking a very great risk.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Has any contracting party been given GATT approval for such an
action, and would any general change in tariff or currency relationships be the cause of an
individual move for retaliation?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: This devolves on the question whether or not there is
provision in GATT for retaliatory action in the event of such a proposal being imposed, and
the answer is that there is, and any country that indulges in this type of measure runs the risk
of retaliatory action.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Can the Minister cite a specific example of retaliatory action being
taken, in order to give some evidence of his expressed opinion?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON: The evidence I offer is the wording of Article XXIII

Freezing Works Strikes, Southland
22. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) to the Minister of Agriculture: What was the estimated
loss in terms of overseas earnings caused by the Southland Freezing Works strikes during


## p. 1397 (#507) ###########################################

4 July
1397
Questions-Oral
1975, 1976, and 1977?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The Minister of Agriculture replies: "It is not
possible to provide the sort of estimate that the honourable member seeks. This is because
regionally-based industrial action in the meat industry does not simply translate into lost
overseas earnings. It may be possible for buyers to arrange for stock to be slaughtered at
other works, or the effect may simply be to delay the kill. Losses can, however, occur when
shipping programmes are disrupted or when the effect is to bunch shipments at ports of
destination, leading to an oversupply situation and lower prices. Furthermore, if stock has to
be removed from the works or held in a situation where the animals lose condition, or if
farmers avoid stocking their properties to an optimum level solely to provide additional feed
for stock for slaughter through strike periods, then the loss is obviously significant."
Mr Downie: Are any steps taken to bring to the notice of offending parties the
seriousness of the actions that bring about these losses that are difficult to determine in
detail?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The Government is always trying to impress on all the people
involved the fact that the losses caused by strikes at freezing works apply to farmers, freezing
workers, the industry, and the nation as a whole, and that they are quite substantial.
Mr W. R. Austin: Has the Minister any information of a meat order that has been
permanently lost as a result of industrial disruption?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I do have information that generally work stoppages mainly affect
buyer confidence in New Zealand's ability to supply on time. This often applies to the
supplies to Devco, particularly for the North American market.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Do I take from the Minister's vagueness in reply that the

Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council Amendment Bill

ALCOHOLIC LIQUOR ADVISORY COUNCIL AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. When I introdcued the Bill I explained that it had two distinct objects. The first
is to make several changes to the functions and powers of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory
Council. These changes have been sought by the council itself. The second is to make a
number of alterations to the sections of the principal Act providing for the calculation and
collection of the council's levy. While most of these alterations are of a machinery nature,
clause 11 is of particular importance because it authorises payment by instalments of the
council's levy by grape winemakers.
Rather than deal with the clauses of the Bill in strict numerical sequence, it might be
more helpful if I dealt first with the changes made to the functions and powers of the council.
Clause 3 provides for the incorporation of the council. At present the council is empowered
to enter into contracts under section 18 of the principal Act. However, difficulties arose in
respect of the registration with the district land registrar of a mortgage held by the council.
The district land registrar was not clear as to whether individual members of the council had
to be named in the mortgage, or whether it was sufficient merely to refer to members for the
time being. By providing for the council to be incorporated, clause 3 removes problems of
this nature. This change is being made at the request of the council, following a suggestion by
its solicitors. Clause 4 gives the council a more versatile role in respect of liquor advertising
by enabling the council to make recommendations on the need to regulate or restrict such
advertising to whomever it thinks fit. Until now the council has been required to make its
recommendations only to the Minister of Justice; again, the change is at the council's
request.
There is provision in Supplementary Order Paper 16 to ensure that the Minister is
informed by copy of any recommendations the council might make to any other people. This
was agreed with members of the Wine Institute at Auckland last week. Members of the
council feel that in some instances they might be able to obtain certain restrictions on a
particular advertisement or type of advertisement by persuasion without the need for
legislative proscription. Accordingly, clause 4 allows the council, for example, to approach a
publisher, broadcaster, or advertising agent, and make its views known. Where this course
meets with an unfavourable response, the council would have to take the matter up with the
Minister if it felt that legislative action was desirable.
Clause 5 authorises the council to make advances on such terms as it thinks fit to
organisations and individuals engaged in work related to the council's functions in the fields
of education, research, or rehabilitation. At present the council is limited to making grants
to such organisations or individuals. The amendment obviously gives the council far greater
flexibility when it wishes to underwrite a deserving project. For instance, if an agency such as
the National Society on Alcoholism and Drug Dependency sought to establish a detoxication
or treatment centre in an area and was unable to raise appropriate capital finance from
normal lending institutions, then the council may now choose to contribute to the necessary
interim loan finance to prevent the venture floundering, rather than to make a straight-out
cash grant.
Clause 6 is an adjunct to clause 3, and provides that, in the absence of negligence or bad
faith, members of the council are absolved from personal liability for their official actions.
The same protection is extended to officers and employees of the council and to those
persons whom the council co-opts. This reflects provisions in other Acts, and was sought by
the council on the advice of its solicitors. Clauses 7 and 8 are minor amendments of a purely
machinery nature that are sought by the Controller and Auditor-General.
I turn now to the second objective of the Bill and the clauses that make better provision
for the calculation and collection of the levy. The levy finances the council's activities, and is
payable by manufacturers of alcoholic liquor in New Zealand, or by importers. Clause 2
amends certain definitions found in, and adds new definitions to, the definition section of the


## p. 1403 (#513) ###########################################

4 July
1403
Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council Amendment Bill
principal Act. The term "beer" is redefined so that beer now has the same meaning for the
purposes of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council Act and the Beer Duty Act 1977. The
term "fortified wine" is defined to include any spirit-based drink, the strength of which does
not exceed 40 percent of proof spirit, while the term "spirits" is redefined to mean any
alcoholic drink produced by distillation and exceeding that strength. Members will be aware
that, for the purposes of the levy, liquor is divided into four classes-namely, beer, spirits,
fortified wine, and unfortified wine. The basis of the division is the alcohol content of the
liquor.
Mr Marshall: A point of order, Mr Speaker. It seems there is not a quorum in the
House at the moment.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I have a feeling there might not be. It would appear that 20
members are here now.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Since the levy provisions in the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory
Council Act have come into operation it has become apparent that a further type of alcoholic
drink does not fit exactly into any of the existing classes; I refer to the so-called bottled
"cocktail" concoctions. These drinks are usually spirit-based, but are in most cases below 40
percent proof spirit and therefore more akin to fortified wine in alcohol content.
There is a further complicating feature in that Customs duty is paid on a liquid litre
basis, while spirits pay duty on a proof litre basis. The basis for payment of the council's levy
is tied to the basis on which customs duty is paid for ease of collection. Rather than create a
new class of liquor, with all the attendant difficulties that would involve, it seems that the
convenient and equitable course is to regard these “cocktail” mixtures as fortified wines for
the purposes of the levy, provided that they are below 40 percent proof spirit, and are
classified as spirits when they exceed that strength. The new definitions of "fortified wine"
and "spirits" achieve this and are not objected to by the trade.
Other definitions contained in clause 2 that are amended or are new are described in
detail in the explanatory note to the Bill. Clause 9 is designed to put beyond doubt the right
of the council to accumulate surplus funds and to expend them in a subsequent year. At the
same time it is made clear that the Minister of Justice may, if he wishes, have regard to any
accumulated funds when fixing the amount to be raised by way of levy. Clause 10 provides
for the situation where an importer disposes of his interest in liquor before it has been
released from bond. It is plain that the person directly responsible for the liquor being made
available in this country is the person who enters it for home consumption. Accordingly, it is
upon him rather than upon the importer that liability to pay the levy is now imposed.
Clause 11, as I have already indicated, will enable a grape winemaker to pay his levy by
instalments throughout each financial year, if he wishes, while under the present legislation
he is obliged to have paid the full quantum of the levy early in the financial year. The Wine
Institute has informed me that that requirement could cause hardship to some of its
members. Therefore, the amendment authorises the trustee of the Wine Institute, whose
task it is to collect the levy from grape winemakers, to come to an agreement with individual
winemakers as to the method of payment of the levy during the year. It is also made clear
that a grape winemaker's licence will not be renewed unless he has paid the levy for the
previous year in full. When introducing the Bill, I indicated the need for urgency in regard to
the amendment made by this clause. If winemakers are to be able to avail themselves of the
provision for instalment payments in this financial year, the Bill must proceed as quickly as
possible.
Clause 12 specifically applies the enforcement mechanisms contained in sections 152 to
154 of the Customs Act 1966 to the levies under the principal Act which are collected by the
Collector of Customs. The levy is declared to constitute a debt due to the Crown
immediately it becomes payable, and that debt is recoverable by action at the suit of the
collector on behalf of the Crown. In addition, the levy is declared to be a charge on the
liquor, and the collector is empowered to take possession of, and to sell, the liquor to
recover the levy if necessary. Clause 13 is purely mechanical, and entitles the Crown to
recover from the council the costs incurred by the Department of Justice in the
administration of the Act. I commend the Bill to the House.
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): The principles in the Bill were spelt out in the principal Act of
1976, and were included in the Sale of Liquor Act 1962. Clause 21 of that 1962 Act provided
that profits from the licensing fund, through the Licensing Control Commission, could be
used by an advisory committee for certain purposes similar to those set out in the Alcoholic
Liquor Advisory Council Amendment Bill. The establishment of the council and its


## p. 1404 (#514) ###########################################

1404
4 July
Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council Amendment Bill
functions seem to have arisen from an investigation made by a parliamentary committee in
1960. That committee considered the proposition that it was the responsibility of those who
sold liquor to try to undo some of the mischief in the community.
Among the objects of the Sale of Liquor Act 1962 were the provision of vital
programmes on education, research, and, in particular, help and treatment for alcoholics.
Frankly, I am disappointed that clause 3 of the Bill now before the House provides that the
Liquor Advisory Council will be able to invest its funds in real and personal property. The
funds of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council should be directed to research and
education, and I regret that some of the funds will be invested. Knowing some of the people
in the liquor trade, who at present are on the advisory council, I foresee an effort being made
to invest in debentures in the liquor trade and elsewhere. That would be most unfortunate.
The proper function of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council is to make efforts to
deter people in the community from using alcohol, thereby lowering consumption and
reducing the business of liquor sellers. In the past few days I have come face to face with the
problem of funding research, and, because of that, I want to express my resentment at the
provisions in this Bill. A large research team at Massey University needs funds for an
important research programme. The team applied to the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council
for research aid, requesting $130,000 over 3 years. The team has been told that no assistance
would be available for that purpose. This team has won international acclaim for its
research, and the funds that are to be given to the council would be suitable for that sort of
research.
The council has received $1.5 million, and this year it has underspent its income by
$733,000. A continuing source of income comes from the licensed trade, and I believe that
the research efforts of the Massey University team should be given precedence rather than
permit the council to invest in real and personal property. It is stated here that the council
shall be a body corporate, with perpetual succession and a common seal, and shall be
capable of acquiring, holding, and disposing of real and personal property.
The research team at Massey University is working on breath-testing equipment and
believes that an accurate breath tester can be devised—a machine that could be used by
traffic officers. I understand that an electronics company believes that type of equipment, if
proved beyond doubt to be accurate, could be produced. The company has the equipment
under test and is collaborating with Massey University. A tremendous amount of research is
being undertaken to discover how alcohol can be measured on the breath. At present many
defective instruments are used. The research to which I have referred is important to road
safety, yet it does not receive the backing of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council. Until I
find that the council is more interested in vital research-for which its funds were
appropriated than it is in this wide area of investment, then I am sceptical of giving it that
right.
The council's annual report stated that the use of alcohol has contributed tremendously
to the rapidly increasing number of road accidents and road deaths. Money for education
and research into many subjects is needed, and I am disappointed that the council should ask
for the power to invest money in real and personal property, because it is an advisory council
and should not be encouraged to build an empire with large assets. I should like the Minister
to know that I would not be happy for the provisions in clause 3 to be extended to the Liquor
Advisory Council.
As the Minister has indicated, the other provisions are technical, and deal with the
calculation of levies based on certain alcoholic strengths. I wondered about the provision
allowing the council to make advances at specific rates of interest. However, I think the
Minister has given an adequate explanation, and, provided the funds levied and the work of
the council are directed to the ends for which the council was set up, I have no objection.
However, I shall be watching the performance of the council closely, and if an undue
proportion of the funds allocated are used for this type of investment, to the detriment of
education and research, I shall have something to say, because the council will not be
fulfilling its objective.
Dr WALL (Porirua): I also view the proposed extension of the council's powers with
some concern. The council was set up and promoted as an advisory council, but, once it is
incorporated and allowed to hold and administer property and to lend money, its advisory
function becomes secondary to functions that it may choose to take upon itself. If this is
allowed, its name, by the passage of one clause, becomes somewhat of a misnomer.
Over the last 20 years I have seen dramatic changes in the treatment of, and the


## p. 1405 (#515) ###########################################

4 July
1405
Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council Amendment Bill
attempts to treat, alcoholism. Most attempts have been good, but there is a trend, based on
economic rather than any other requirements, to promote assessment centres. It is no longer
possible to call for admission on the basis of good supporting clinical evidence or by taking
the case to court and having a patient committed to a psychiatric hospital registered under
the Alcoholism and Drug Addicition Act. It is no longer possible to be sure that a patient
will receive treatment, even though in his own and his family's interests urgent treatment
may be required. These changes have taken place in the last 3 or 4 years.
Quite recently, I had a patient who, because of the thought disturbance occurring in him
resulting from the disease of alcoholism, was intermittently a real physical danger to
members of his family. On two occasions, one on my recommendation, he was submitted to
Porirua Hospital for admission. On both occasions admission was declined and he was asked
to attend an outpatients' department for assessment. That request was made to a man who
was quite convinced that there was nothing wrong with him, and that the fault lay with the
unreasonable behaviour of his family and the stupidity of the doctors who had been conned
by his stupid wife into believing phoney stories. Because of his disease, he has black-outs and
is unaware that he has ever inflected any real violence on his wife, although she has physical
changes associated with that violence. Circumstances such as that are becoming increasingly
widespread, and those who desperately need compulsory treatment are unable to get it.
The standard of treatment may not have been as high 3, 4, or 5 years ago, but, at least at
that time, if a person, for his own or his family's protection, needed to be committed to the
custodial care of a hospital, it was possible for that to be done. It is no longer possible. I
know that is not entirely the responsibility of this Minister-it is more particularly the
responsibility of the Minister of Health-but the Liquor Advisory Council intends to foster
further and assist financially the development of these assessment centres, and I find that
approach most pernicious.
If institutions want to be able to publish good results for the treatment of alcoholism
they will not accept difficult cases of the type of which I have been speaking, because the
proportion of recovery in those cases is low. They very much prefer to have an institution
that people can come to, and leave as they like, those who will recover easily being chosen
and admitted so that a paper on how good the results are can be published later. That sort of
professional approach to the problem is unfortunately becoming widespread-and I make no
bones about saying that. But the really difficult cases, when patients are so disordered in
their thinking at the time of referral to the hospital that they deny they have any alcoholic
problem, and take 2 to 3 weeks to withdraw sufficiently from the effect of alcohol on the
brain to allow them to make even a reasonable assessment of their own state, are being
denied admission to hospital, simply because they themselves do not request it. They are
incapable of making a proper assessment and thus to make the request.
The problem is widespread and people are moving from being recoverable to being
hopelessly irrecoverable, simply because the hospital system and the approach to alcoholism
that is being encouraged at the moment are not providing for their compulsory restriction to
allow them to recover. They are drifting in and out of institutions voluntarily for a day or
two, or at the most 4 days. After 4 or 5 days they are sufficiently recovered to go out. This
continues for 3 or 4 years, while they become irrecoverable. The problem is difficult. The
Liquor Advisory Council should concern itself with this problem and not with the problem of
quasi-social drinking, when people who still have control attend assessment centres or day
centres and have their hands patted by a social worker, who encourages them to drink a little
less.
If the council was more concerned with the hard core of alcoholism that is causing social
disruption in our community I would have more sympathy with its approach to the problem.
I am concerned that the council will be a body corporate, which can be a law unto itself,
instead of being a purely advisory body. The council will be a body of considerable
independence, with much financial support. At the moment its constitution is fixed to
include many conflicting groups concerned with the production and consumption of alcohol,
which has disastrous effects. Only three problems are associated with alcohol in the
community: the problem of the alcoholic, the teenage drinker who is not used to alcohol,
and the drinking driver. If those three problems could be removed society would not have
the problem of alcoholism. The member for Hutt has shown that the advisory committee is
reluctant to deal with one of the problems, so I find its approach to alcoholism
unsatisfactory. I must have evidence to show that the council has an educative approach to
the teenage drinker. In the light of our present experience I am reluctant to say that the body

repay or refinance the loan. In other words, they were not asking for a grant, but for a loan.

council has the right to make grants or loans, whether secured or unsecured, on such terms
as it thinks fit. The effect is that the council's money can be used twice. I should have thought
members opposite would have been delighted to know that this was to be done, and that the
money being provided by way of loan and without interest was bridging or temporary finance
to further the purposes of the Alcoholic Liquor Advisory Council.
Mr Lange: Clause 3 is not limited to fulfilling the objects of the council, but is an

Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Yes, but under the Act the council is obliged to carry out its

Status of Children Amendment Bill
STATUS OF CHILDREN AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. When the late Ralph Hanan piloted the Status of Children Bill through the
House in 1969, he was breaking new ground for this country, and was proud of it. It is a
tribute to his far-sighted and humane thinking that the Act has been imitated in other
jurisdictions, notably Australia. By the same token, it is a tribute to all those concerned with
the framing of the Act that it has not caused problems in the courts, and that it has not
required any statutory amendments to remedy defects. Nevertheless, in the light of
experience gained in more than 8 years of the Act's operation, it is only natural to find there
are some areas in which improvements can profitably be made. The present Bill sets out to
pinpoint those areas, and to adjust the law accordingly.
The first problem is that the principal Act is silent on whether an applicant for letters of
administration has to make any inquiries about the existence of an ex-nuptial beneficiary
who might have an equal or prior right to a grant of administration. This submission has
caused difficulties, in the sense that the Supreme Court registrars, acting with the approval
of the judges, have had to devise a practice note to clarify the duties of an applicant for a
grant. In turn, the practice note suffers from certain deficiencies and, generally speaking,
there is an agreement that it would be best for the situation to be tidied up by legislation. The
new section 5A in clause 2 of the Bill sets out to say on the face of the statute what an
applicant for a grant of letters of administration must do. As reported back from the Statutes
Revision Committee-and I want to thank the members of the committee who worked on
the Bill-the new section 5A is somewhat modified.
The main change is the deletion of the requirement to make personal inquiries first,
from someone who may know about the existence of a child born outside marriage and,
secondly from the solicitor last known to have acted for the deceased in his lifetime. It was
felt, on balance, to be somewhat onerous to require these things to be done at the very early
stage when a grant is being applied for, and this was certainly the view expressed by the
Trustee Companies Association, which gave evidence to the Statutes Revision Committee.
Other changes in the new section 5A make it clear that a grant of administration may be
made in appropriate circumstances-for example, when it is necessary for the preservation
of the assets of the estate-even though reasonable inquiries have not been made. It is also
made clear that there is no duty to inquire simply because there may be a possible claimant
under the Family Protection Act 1955 or the Law Reform (Testamentary Promises) Act
1949.
The new section 6, also proposed in clause 2 of the Bill, is the vehicle for a
corresponding change. It has been broken up into four new sections, largely in the interests
of clarity. The basic object is still to remove the excessive protection given to trustees and
administrators under the present law, which provides that no inquiries whatsoever have to be
made about the existence of ex-nuptial beneficiaries before an estate is distributed. The new
section 6 provides that reasonable inquiries must be made before distribution, and the new
section 6A sets out the nature of reasonable inquiries that comply.
Paragraph (a) of subsection (1) of the new section 6A has been redrafted so that the
administrator no longer has to form an opinion about the person most likely to know of the
existence of someone who could claim an interest pursuant to the Status of Children Act. It
is sufficient if he inquires of a person whom he believes may have such knowledge. A further
point of clarification in the new section 6A concerns the search of papers required under
paragraph (c) of subsection (1). It is made clear that, where the duty arises to search papers
on more than one occasion, the duty applies only to those papers that have come to the
administrator's notice since the immediately preceding distribution of the estate or property.
The new section 6B contains an important addition by way of a proviso. The tenor of the
proviso is that if an administrator has acted honestly, albeit less diligently than he ought to
have done, the court may excuse him from liability that might otherwise arise from the
failure to make proper inquiries before distribution. This introduces a desirable element of
flexibility and is similar to provisions already appearing in the Trustee Act 1956. The new
sections 6C and 6D are virtually unchanged as to substance. They are supportive and
machinery provisions requiring no special comment.
I come now to clause 3 of the Bill, which relates to the recognition of paternity. It is
made clear that paternity admitted by or established against the father before the child is
born may found a claim to property. The present wording suggests that paternity must be
established after the child has been born. It is also provided that a Supreme Court


## p. 1408 (#518) ###########################################

1408
4 July
Status of Children Amendment Bill
declaration as to paternity, obtained after the death of the father, may found a claim to
property. Under existing law, paternity must in every case be established during the father's
lifetime in order to found a claim to property. There seems little merit in this rigid rule,
especially as the Supreme Court is specifically empowered to make a paternity declaration
whether the father, or the child for that matter, is living or dead.
The proposed new subsection (2) of section 7 of the principal Act was quite substantially
expanded and improved by the Statutes Revision Committee. The subsection still provides
that no distribution of property may be upset by reason of a further claimant having
established his right to a share in the property, and this is of course necessary. Largely on the
initiative of the Public Trustee, however, two changes have been made. First, the meaning of
the term "distribution" in relation to property forming part of the estate is made clear.
Secondly, a proviso had been added to the new subsection (2)(b), the effect of which is this:
if, after distribution of part of the property, a further claimant establishes his rights, the
earlier distributions are to be brought into account, so far as possible, in determining
respective rights in the property that has not been distributed. This will clearly lead to a more
just result than if prior distributions had to be ignored when ascertaining the proper share of
the new claimant. Nevertheless, to avoid problems for administrators, it is also provided in
subsection (4) that an administrator will be protected from liability for the way in which he
brings prior distributions into account so long as he has acted honestly.
Honourable members may feel that this is a rather dry and technical Bill, and in a sense
it is. We must look beyond the detail and the fine print towards the purpose of the Bill,
which is to secure greater justice in property matters for those who are unfortunate enough
to be born out of wedlock. It is not their fault. This is a very worth-while object, and one that
I believe commands support from most fair-minded people.
Honourable members will recall from the comments of the member for Birkenhead
when he reported the Bill back to the House that the New Zealand Law Society gave it
virtually unqualified support. The member added that the Trustee Companies Association
supported the broad principle of the Bill, though not all the details. I think this gives a
sufficient indication of the sound basis of support for the principle of the Bill among those
who will be closely involved in its practical operation. I commend the Bill to the House.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): The Opposition has been involved in the maturing process of
the Bill through the Statutes Revision Committee, and now seeks to endorse its principles
before the House. Quite simply, the Bill protects those who should have the opportunity to
make a claim on the estates of those who fathered them. In so far as that was the intent
behind the original piece of legislation, we welcome the opportunity of putting it into effect.
I expressed my accordance with the Minister's statement of the purposes behind the Bill,
rather than the mechanics of it, and acknowledge what I think is still an anomaly—that is,
that when letters of administration are sought certain extra burdens are cast on those who
seek the claim and letters of administration, a duty that is not to be found when probate over
a will is sought. It may be that eventually consideration will be given to alerting possible
claimants under the Family Protection Act to exercise their rights as people who were
fathered by the deceased. I welcome, as does the Opposition, the new principle of
determining paternity before and after the death. I am sure that removes an anomaly that
was not anticipated by those who drew up the original legislation. I welcome the opportunity
for the practice note of 1970 to be given statutory effect. The Opposition certainly does not
oppose the Bill.
Bill read a second time.
IMMIGRATION AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Second Reading
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. In doing so, I wish, first, to acknowledge the efforts of the Statutes Revision
Committee, which has spent some considerable time and effort over the recess studying and
improving the Bill, and I should like also to thank those organisations that made numerous
helpful suggestions on the Bill.
It says much for the deliberations of the Statutes Revision Committee that the
Opposition has indicated to the comittee that, while it reserves the right to comment on
individual clauses, it does not intend to oppose the passage of the Bill. This in itself is a
recognition that the Bill will do much to improve our immigration legislation. The most
important feature of the Bill is that it greatly rationalises and improves both parts of the


## p. 1409 (#519) ###########################################

4 July
1409
Immigration Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Immigration Act that deal with the deportation of persons who have been convicted of
criminal offences.
Members of the House will recall that, in legislation last year, the Government
established a procedure by which persons who have been convicted of immigration offences
and ordered to be deported may appeal against the sentence of deportation, and, if on
humanitarian grounds it is considered that sentence is unduly harsh or unjust, they may be
permitted to remain in New Zealand.
The Bill gives another new right of appeal by establishing a Deportation Review
Tribunal to which persons who have been ordered to be deported following conviction for a
criminal offence may appeal on humanitarian grounds. The tribunal will be able to quash
deportation orders in cases in which it is satisfied that it would be unduly harsh or unjust to
deport the person, and if it is satisfied that it would not be contrary to the public interest to
allow the person concerned to remain in New Zealand. Several matters are set down in the
Bill that the tribunal must look at it in making any decision.
The Bill inserts a completely new Part IV into the principal Act, and incorporates the
deportation provisions of the Aliens Act in the Immigration Act. Henceforth, aliens and
Commonwealth citizens will be on an equal footing in so far as immunity from deportation is
concerned. The position of Commonwealth citizens will, in fact, not change in any
appreciable way. The difference is that aliens will now become immune from deportation
after serving what can loosely be termed a probationary residence period of 5 years. That
contrasts with the existing position, in which they can still be deported on conviction for
certain offences, irrespective of how long they have been living in New Zealand. So there is
no reduction in privileges of Commonwealth citizens. Aliens will now be, for want of a better
phrase, equally privileged. All persons who are not New Zealand citizens will be treated in
the same way.
There are further provisions that will result in improvements to our deportation
legislation. At present, for instance, the period of residence that qualifies a person for
immunity from deportation is calculated as from the time of his last arrival in New Zealand.
This can have the strange result that a person who has lived here for many years but has not
become a New Zealand citizen can become liable to deportation on commission of an
offence merely because he left the country for a holiday in the previous 2 or 5 years, as the
case may be. To overcome this obvious injustice, the period of residence will now be
calculated on the basis of residence since the person's sixteenth birthday, irrespective of
intervening absences from the country. For example, time counted for these purposes will
even include any period or periods not exceeding a total of 30 days in any year during which
the person is absent from New Zealand. This is to allow persons to go away on holidays or
business trips of up to that duration and still have that time contribute towards the period of
residence that they must serve before they are immune from deportation. They may, of
course, leave New Zealand for trips of longer duration if they wish, but any such longer time
would not be counted as contributing to the 5 years they must reside here before being
immune from deportation.
There are also more liberal, but in my view far more practical, measures relating to
persons who are ordered to be deported for matters relating to national security and matters
relating to terrorism. At present, for instance, under the Aliens Act, a person can be
deported if it is considered that it is not conducive to the public good that he remain in New
Zealand. This is too vague and too wide, with insufficient safeguards. In this Bill, therefore,
we have restricted deportation specifically to persons who constitute a threat to national
security, or persons—and here we are talking of terrorists—who constitute a threat to public
safety. Persons constituting a threat to national security will be subject to deportation, and
may be ordered by the Governor-General by Order in Council to leave New Zealand. In
such cases, when the issue is one of national security and the decision is made at the highest
possible level, there is no right of appeal. Persons who are considered to constitute a threat
to public safety may be deported on the order of the Minister of Immigration. However, they
will have the right to appeal directly to the Supreme Court.
We have also made provisions under which a person who arrives at a New Zealand
airport or seaport and who wishes to enter, but who, we believe, may commit an offence or
be a threat to public safety, can be held in custody if he cannot leave New Zealand the same
day. Obviously, if we can make such persons leave New Zealand immediately—for instance,
on the next aircraft out-we shall do so. However, if this is not possible, we can hold the
person in custody until he can leave. This is merely a common-sense arrangement as we


## p. 1410 (#520) ###########################################

1410
4 July
Immigration Amendment Bill (No. 2)
cannot allow a person to enter the country and move about freely if we have evidence that
such a person is likely to commit an act that will endanger human lives.
persons
As the Bill has been so thoroughly examined by the Statutes Revision Committee, and
as its provisions will so obviously improve the Immigration Act, I need say no more in
elaboration. I shall therefore simply explain the individual clauses of the Bill. Clause 1 is
related to the short title. Clause 2 is an interpretation section. Clause 3 provides that
who are refused permission to enter New Zealand may be detained by the police pending
departure of the next aircraft or ship. Clause 3a, inserted by the select committee, sets out
the procedures to be followed when a person is detained under clause 3, for more than 24
hours. Clause 3b gives the Minister the right to revoke, in respect of any person, any
exemption that he has given under the Act if he believes that person to be a terrorist or to be
likely to commit a drug-related crime if permitted to enter New Zealand. In the Committee
stage I intend moving a further amendment to insert a new Clause 3c. This is merely
consequential upon the 1977 amendment of the Act, and will remove an anomaly that has
crept in.
Clause 4 repeals Part IV of the Act, which at present consists of only one section, and
replaces it with a new Part containing 10 sections. The whole part is concerned with the
deportation of non-New Zealand citizens for commission of offences, or for constituting a
threat to national security, or for being involved with terrorist activities. The Deportation
Review Tribunal and rights of appeal are set up under this new Part.
Clause 5 inserts a provision which, as well as giving a police constable immunity from a
civil or criminal claim for wrongful arrest under the principal Act, gives that constable wider
powers of entry. In the committee stage I intend to move the addition of a further sentence
to part of that provision. In effect, it will ensure that a person wrongfully arrested will still
have a right of redress even though the police constable is protected. Clauses 6 and 7 are
consequential drafting provisions. Clause 8 adds two new schedules to the principal Act.
These schedules set out matters of administration and procedure relating to the Deportation
Review Tribunal.
