people locked up without recourse to a court, simply because they do not have a temporary
entry permit? That sort of thing brings the law, immigration officers, and police officers who
are enforcing the law, into disrepute. It does nothing to uphold law and order. I would love
to see the Minister when some grandmother from Bradford arrives over here, and somebody
mucks up her temporary entry permit and she ends up in Mt. Eden.
Hon. P. I. Wilkinson: What happens if they're terrorists?
Mr LANGE: If they are terrorists there will be powers under the Act to take steps
against them. I wish the Minister, who is also the Attorney-General, could grasp the concept
I am putting forward. I am asking for some form of judicial review, but the Attorney-
General, who is Her Majesty's principal law officer in New Zealand, is content to see people
in prison without a judicial review and without the review of a quasi judicial tribunal. That is
where he has arrived at his upholding of the rule of law in New Zealand. I repeat, for his
benefit, that this clause provides, on the say so of a police officer or a registrar, for the
detention in a prison for an indefinite period without the right to go to the court of a person
who is not alleged to be a terrorist but who does not have a temporary entry permit.
Hon. P. I. Wilkinson: What would you do?
Mr LANGE: First, I would give those people the right to representation-as the United
Kingdom has done for donkey's years-and, secondly, I would give them the right to the sort
of review that the Minister is giving convicted criminals in the second part of the Bill.
Hon. P. I. Wilkinson: Then you would let them go.
Mr LANGE: The Attorney-General suggests that I would let them go. He is degrading
the judiciary in the eyes of the public if he thinks any judicial officer would let a terrorist go.
The Attorney-General, who is charged with upholding the rule of law, is taking the liberty of
the people away from the courts or from any review. That is typical of the way the Attorney-
General has discharged his high office. He ought to think again.
Hon. P. I. Wilkinson: You will let them go.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! If the Minister wants to address himself by way of interjection to

Immigration Amendment Bill (No. 2)
the member for Mangere, he should refer to him as the honourable member.

Income Tax-Opposition Proposals
2. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Finance: Has he seen the report in the
Dominion of 7 June 1978 in which the Deputy Leader of the Opposition describes the
proposed income tax steps espoused by the Opposition, and, if so, can he state whether his
department has calculated the revenue cost of those proposals as against (a) the tax tables
adopted by the last Labour Government in 1975, and (b) the tax tables described in the 1978
Budget?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): No, I have not seen the Dominion
report; I got someone to look it up for me. The income tax steps outlined by the Deputy
Leader of the Opposition were somewhat imprecise, but he indicated that they would cost
about $600 million a year compared with the existing rate structure. It is not possible to
calculate the revenue effects without fuller details, but as far as is possible to gauge from the
information given in the article it appears that $600 million would be an underestimate.
Using the same assumptions underlying the Government's Budget forecast, Labour's
alternative rate structure would cost about $700 million. However, a $100 million error is not


## p. 1415 (#525) ###########################################

5 July
1415
Questions-Oral
unusual for the people on the other side of the House. The present rate structure is based on
the tax rates introduced by the Labour Government in 1975, and incorporates a 5 percent
reduction from February 1978 costing $200 million a year. Therefore, Labour's alternative
system would currently yield about $900 million a year less than the tax rates introduced in
1975. By comparison, the Government's new rate structure, which will take effect in
October, will yield about $500 million a year less than the Labour Government's 1975 rates.
It appears, therefore, that in current annual terms Labour's tax rates could reduce income
tax by $400 million more than the Government's new rate structure. Of course, this would
not represent an overall tax cut, as the Opposition proposes to recoup the revenue from a
foreign exchange surcharge. These figures take no account of the family tax rebates
introduced by the present Government, which reduce annual tax payable by a further $120
million. The Opposition has not yet given specific details of any proposed tax exemptions for
dependent children.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Can the Minister outline the steps by which he could say in the first
part of his answer that there was insufficient detail to enable him to make an estimation and
then assert that the costs would be $100 million more than the Labour Opposition claimed?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: Yes, it is really very simple. I said in my answer that the
missing detail had been supplied by using the rate structure of the new tax tables. If any
changes caused people to pay more income tax, then they would affect the $100 million
miscalculated by the Labour Opposition and the member. However, on the face of it, no one
will pay more additional tax than that set out in the member's article, so we made that
assumption.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Is the Minister now prepared to admit that his assertions are for
political purposes, based on nothing better than guesswork?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No, they are not for political purposes based on nothing
less than guesswork, but are an estimate by Treasury officers on information available, and
using the assumptions I set out. As the member knows, Treasury officers do not make
estimates for political purposes. If the member would disclose any people, not yet disclosed,
who will pay more tax, then we will see if they add up to the extra $100 million.
Accident Compensation Act
3. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: Has he read the article in the
Evening Post of 29 June 1978, which states: "An anomaly in the Accident Compensation Act
is highlighted in a Supreme Court judgment released today"- dealing with the fact that a
self-employed person who suffered a heart attack during his work was not covered, but an
employee in the same position was—and, if so, will he take the recommendation of the judge
that it is a matter for the Legislature"?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Labour): The provision in the Accident
Compensation Act giving cover in respect of heart attacks applies only to employees, and
even that is subject to certain qualifications. The self-employed are not covered for heart
attacks unless the attack is a consequence of an injury or accident. This is not considered to
be an anomaly. The distinction was deliberately made when a partial definition of the phrase
"personal injury by accident" was introduced by the amending Act of 1974. There is a
variety of reasons for this distinction, which would take too long to give at this time. The
Accident Compensation Commission would, on request, gladly give a statement on those
reasons. In the Supreme Court judgment referred to, the judge made no recommendation
for change, nor did his judgment use the word "anomaly". As a matter of interest, I have
asked the commission for a report on the case, but am advised in the meantime that the
commission sees no reason for recommending any change in the Act.
Mr Isbey: In his reply the Minister stated that as a result of a personal injury at work an
employee could receive compensation-
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No, I did not.
Mr Isbey: The Minister stated that an employee, not an employer, could receive
accident compensation if he suffered a heart attack at work. However, the Minister would
agree that the circumstances would be the same.
Mr SPEAKER: Was the honourable member asking a question, or just making a
statement? I was not aware of any question-mark at the end of his comment.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: It might help if I repeated my reply.
Mr Isbey: I could rephrase my question.

Foreign Exchange Surcharge-Revenue
4. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) to the Minister of Finance: Have his departmental advisers
estimated the amount of revenue that would be raised by a 10 percent surcharge on (a) all
payments for imports, and (b) all foreign exchange payments including invisibles?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): The amount of revenue that would
have been raised by a 10 percent surcharge on all payments for imports in the year to the end
of March 1978 is $307 million. A 10 percent surcharge on all foreign exchange payments,
including invisibles, would have raised $529 million in the same period.
Mr Brill: Does the $307 million that could arise from a surcharge on all imports include
Government imports as well as private, and, if so, what proportion of those imports are
Government imports?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No, I would think that this does not include Government
imports, because Government imports could not attract a 10 percent surcharge levied by the
Government, but I am open to correction on this. I have not a split-up here, but if I was
giving an answer to the question I certainly would have ignored Government imports.
Dairy Farmers-Diversification
5. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Agriculture: Is it

particular farm situation some diversification into crops may be more advantageous than
increasing a dairy herd's size, but this always depends on the circumstances of the case."
Mr Bruce Barclay: Has the Minister taken any action to correct the heading that

Post. If I endeavoured to alter the headings I disagreed with in papers around New Zealand I
would have a full-time job.
Mr Couch: Does the Minister agree that any experienced dairy farmer would take the
necessary measures to provide crops for any increase in stock numbers?
Hon. J. B. BOLGER: Yes, I am sure that any dairy farmer would provide the crops he
considered necessary. Also, any competent and forward-thinking dairy farmer would
consider crops as a cash-producing alternative.

Indigenous Timber Use
10. Mr H. N. AUSTIN (Hobson) to the Minister of Forests: To what extent is sawn
native timber from North Island indigenous forests being processed into high-grade end
uses?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): From Forest Service field studies it would
appear that a major part of the volume of higher grades of sawn native timber from North
Island indigenous forests is being processed domestically into high value end uses, such as
furniture, joinery, and finishing timbers for decorative purposes. With the current weak
demand for indigenous building grades, most sawmillers and merchants are carrying out
some upgrading of this timber into high-grade shorts with a view to channelling this class of
timber into manufacturing.
Dr Shearer: Is that answer in conflict with the assertion made in the House by the
member for Auckland Central that the industry was downgrading timber?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The member for Auckland Central made the assertion that the
Forest Service was downgrading timber, and that assertion was not correct. The industry,
which does the grading, is upgrading the timber into higher value end uses.
Mr Wetere: Could the Minister specify the types of indigenous timbers that are being
used, as mentioned in his original answer?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I can specify the types of indigenous timber that are being milled in
the North Island, obviously for these higher grade end uses. They are a limited sawing of
kauri, rimu, and tawa.

Working Together
15. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: What action is he taking to
implement the recommendation of the National Government-appointed New Zealand
Planning Council's report Working Together, which stated in reference to industrial law that
"the objective should be to downgrade the adversary concept inherent in the present systern
of industrial relations and substitute measures which encourage joint problem-solving by the
parties themselves. Disputes are better solved in the work place than in the Courthouse"?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Labour): It is debatable how far we
should attempt to suppress or eliminate conflicts that are inherent within our industrial
relations system. The aim should be to improve the management of conflict by providing
channels through which differences can be reconciled in a constructive way. It is the
Government's hope that the new arbitration system will achieve just this. I agree with the
general principle that disputes should be resolved as close to their point of origin as possible.
Many are, but the member well knows that it is not always possible to effect a reconciliation
at that level.
Mr Isbey: In view of the Planning Council's recommendation, will the Minister accept
that penalties should be replaced or substituted in industrial law by measures that encourage
joint problem solving by the parties?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No. If there were no offences, there would be no need for
penalties. As the report makes clear, respect for the law is basic to everything.
Mr Malcolm: Is there any evidence that insisting on a rule of law creates conflict in
industrial relations, or is that conflict more likely to be caused by people who promote
concepts of class warfare?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: It is obvious that the concepts of class warfare are not
conducive to co-operation or the resolution of conflict when conflict is inherent, as the report
recognises. When conflict occurs, the aim should be to improve the management of that
conflict by providing channels through which differences can be reconciled in a constructive
way, and the Government hopes that, with the present arbitration system, that will occur.

Hire Purchase Terms
19. Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) to the Minister of Trade and Industry: Will he take
steps to prevent advertised offers involving hire purchase such as the offer made by the
Farmers Trading Co. of no charge for terms better than a bank overdraft or a loan from a
lending institution, when in fact within the terms of the offer the true interest rate charged on
credit advanced is of the order of 45 percent?
Mr ALLEN (Parliamentary Under-Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Industry):
The Minister of Trade and Industry replies: "A bank loan or a loan from a lending institution
would need to be at interest rates of less than 10 percent per annum calculated on monthly
rests to be cheaper, over a 2-year period, than the Farmers Trading Company's offer. As
money is not generally available at 10 percent interest, I see nothing offensive in the
company's offer. Consequently, no action is necessary."
Mr Falloon: Does that mean that the claim that a rate of 45 percent is charged is
fallacious?
Mr ALLEN: Yes, the claim made that the rate would be 45 percent is not correct. If a
loan of $240 were obtained for a 2-year period on the basis of equal monthly repayments of
principal-that is, $10 a month-plus interest at 10 percent on the balance outstanding at the
beginning of each month, the total interest payable would be $25, or $1 more than the
Farmers Trading Company's offer.
Mr Beetham: I think somebody's mathematics are a little out, and they are not mine.
Will the Minister take action, in view of the fact that section 8 of the Hire Purchase Act
states: "Disclosure of cost of credit as an annual rate―(1) The financial details mentioned in
paragraph (c) of subsection (1) of section 6 of this Act shall (a) Except where credit is
extended through a variable credit account, show the percentage (correct to within 1
percent) that the total cost of credit bears to the amount financed expressed as an annual rate
applied to the unpaid balance of the obligation from time to time"?
Mr ALLEN: I am not immediately familiar with the subsection referred to by the
member, but I imagine it would apply to hire purchase agreements, and that agreements
drawn up by the Farmers Trading Company would contain the figures required by the Act.
URGENT QUESTION
Raffles-Quick-fire
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Police: In view of the fact that the secretary of
the Marina Sports and Social Club, Auckland, Mr W. Doccher, was told yesterday by a
senior sergeant at Takapuna Police Station that a police report held that quick-fire raffles
were illegal, would he confirm that no police action either had been or would be taken
against clubs on this issue, and, further, that he as Minister would take steps to inform clubs
immediately of what he sees as the legal position?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): No prosecutions have been brought
against any club under the new Act relating to the selling of quick-fire raffles. I have been
advised by the Commissioner of Police that no prosecutions will be brought without prior
referral to the legal section at Police headquarters. I should emphasise that in no way have
the police been searching for any such case on which to prosecute, but have simply given
advice in response to queries from sports clubs and hotels. The member will be well aware
that it is for the police to decide whether or not a particular prosecution would be brought.
However, the police have a discretion in these matters, and I have been advised by the
commissioner that, in any decisions made, considerable weight will be given to the fact that
differing interpretations exist, and, in particular, the fact that the law will shortly be clarified
in favour of such raffles.

Cheese, Exports to Japan
1. Mr LANGE (Mangere) to the Minister of Agriculture: What quantities of
New Zealand cheese were exported to Japan in the year to 31 March 1978 for
(a) further processing, (b) sale in natural form?
Answer
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: Shipments of cheese
to Japan by the New Zealand Dairy Board for the year ended 31 March 1978
totalled 18 200 tonnes. Japanese law requires all processing to be carried out in
Japanese cheese factories. Consequently, all the board's sales are of cheese in
natural form but approximately 10 percent of the sales in the year ending 31
March 1978 were distributed in natural form, the balance being sold for processing.

granted tenancies over areas of Crown land, and in each case the squatters had
been in occupation for some years and limited tenancies were granted on grounds
of hardship. Of these, four are within the West Coast electorate and the remain-

Ports-Downturn in Trade
7. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Transport: Has he
received any representations from the New Zealand Ports Authority regarding the
present downturn in trade and the resultant drop of income for New Zealand
ports?
Answer
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: I have not
received representations from the New Zealand Ports Authority regarding a


## p. 1426 (#536) ###########################################

1426
5 July
Questions and Replies
downturn in trade. In fact, information I have indicates that there has not
been any substantial downturn. While figures available for the last 2 months
do indicate a drop in volume at a few ports, there is no evidence that this
represents a sustained decrease in trade as opposed to the normal fluctuations
that are expected. What is showing up in the figures for some ports is the effect
of containerisation in terms of trading patterns. Although the income of ports
is affected by such changes in cargo volumes, it also depends on the level of
charges set by harbour boards. Harbour boards operate under the provisions
of the Harbours Act, and that Act lays down the procedures they must comply
with in setting their charges. These procedures do not require any approval
from the Ports Authority or the Minister when increases are imposed.

Containers-Cleanliness Procedures
8. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of
Agriculture: What measures are taken to ensure that shipping containers are
scrupulously clean before they are packed with primary produce for export?
Answer
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture) replied: The person in charge
of loading at the load-out point is responsible for ensuring that the containers
to be loaded are clean. Staff of the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries carry
out spot checks from time to time on cleanliness. Should by any chance a
dirty container arrive for loading, the container is returned to a cleaning facility
for cleaning. However, containers that show only localised contamination may
be cleaned at the loading point by using approved procedures, which may
include wiping, sweeping, etc. Only containers that are clean, dry, and free
from odours and chemicals and other residues may be loaded with export
produce. If a container has previously carried toxic or hazardous materials,
terminal operators give the container special attention to ensure that there are
no residues that could contaminate the product or packaging. The dangers
of contamination and the possibility of rejection of the contents of a dirty
container are well known to container operators, who realise the financial losses
that can occur when the product is rejected.
(15/6/78)
New Secondary School-Tauranga
9. Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori) to the Minister of Education: Can he
indicate what plans there are for establishing another secondary school in
Tauranga?
Answer
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: My department is
completing a survey of the need and best location for future schools in the
greater Tauranga area. When complete, the report will be discussed with the
controlling authorities of the existing secondary schools and then the public will
be given the opportunity to comment. At this point, therefore, no decision has
been made as to where the fourth secondary school for Tauranga should be pro-
vided. Current roll forecasts suggest a new secondary school will not be needed
within the next 5 years.

Accident Compensation Commission's Reserve Fund
11. Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury) to the Minister of Labour: How has
the Accident Compensation Commission's reserve fund been invested and does
it favour local body and other types of return, or is some used to assist with
the mortgages of rehabilitation accident victims?
Answer
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The commission does not
have reserve funds in the normal sense. The commission does not have the power,
as many private organisations do, of deliberately committing annual amounts to
reserves. At the close of each financial year (31 March), the commission's accounts
disclose the respective balances in the farmers' compensation fund and the motor.
vehicle compensation fund that are available to meet future liabilities of claims
registered with the commission to that date. Section 30 of the Accident Compen-
sation Act 1972 authorises the commission to invest its funds: (a) in New Zealand
Government securities; or (b) on deposit in any bank or banks approved by the
Minister of Finance, or in the Post Office Savings Bank; or (c) in any manner,
or in any securities, that may from time to time be authorised by the Minister of
Finance.
(16/6/78)

Trade Balance, India - New Zealand
13. Mr LANGE (Mangere) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: What was the
balance of trade between India and New Zealand in the year to 31 March 1978
(excluding aid payments or services), and when does he propose to appoint a
trade commissioner to the New Zealand High Commission in New Delhi?
Answer
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade)
replied: The value of New Zealand's exports to India in the year to 31 March
1978 was NZ$5,116,771 f.o.b. The value of New Zealand's imports from India
in the year to 31 March 1978 was NZ$20,093,893 c.i.f. The balance of trade
between India and New Zealand in the year to 31 March 1978 was in a ratio of
41 in India's favour. The question of the appointment of a trade commissioner
to New Delhi is currently under consideration.

Part-time Government Staff-Tax Adjustments
17. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Works and Develop-

tax, and will the department raise their salaries to cover the tax increase?
Answer
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied: There are 2006 part-
time staff, of whom more than 1000 are cleaners, employed in the public Service

case of cleaners and all others employees, whose pay rates are adjusted by the
ruling rates survey, the increase will be backdated until 11 October 1977. The
effective date of the half-yearly survey has yet to be finally determined by negotia-
tion, but is expected to be in late 1977. The numbers of staff by departments are
attached.

Subsidised Employment-Manukau District
18. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: How much money
was spent in the south Auckland district on job promotion and on subsidising
people on special work during the month of May 1978?
Answer
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: The south Auckland area
is covered by the Manukau employment district, which extends from the Waikato
River estuary in the south to the isthmus between the Tamaki River and the
Manukau Harbour in the north. The amount spent by my department on job
creation measures during any one month does not reflect the actual cost of the
programme in that month since, as a general rule, employing authorities do not
recover expenditure in the month in which it was incurred. However, based on
the number of persons employed in the job creation programme during May
1978, the costs for the Manukau district are estimated as approximately $240,300
for the temporary employment programme, which covers public sector job creation,
and approximately $29,000 for private sector job creation. Private sector job
creation includes the skill promotion programme, the first job programme, the
farm employment scheme, and the additional jobs programme.

Orthodontic Treatment for School Children
26. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) to the Minister of Health: How many school
children have required orthodontic treatment in each year since 1970, and how
many of these were paid for by his department or any other Government
agency?
Answer
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: It is not possible to state
the number of children who have required orthodontic treatment since 1970.
A recent survey of 13- to 14-year-olds in Canterbury confirmed estimates, based
on other surveys, that 31.5 percent could benefit from orthodontic treatment.
At this rate, 19,000 children would require orthodontic treatment each year.
Although this large number can be regarded as candidates for orthodontic treat-
ment, the major proportion would be for cosmetic reasons. There is no provision
for orthodontic services in the dental programme administered by my depart-
ment. School dental nurses merely advise parents that they should consult their
dentist when apparent abnormalities show up in child patients. Treatment can
be provided by hospital boards for children whose parents are unable to meet
the fees of a private dentist and when the treatment is required to prevent
physical or emotional handicap. The number of children who have received
such assistance since 1970 is not known.
(20/6/78)

31. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of State Services: How many
people have material recorded about them in the Wanganui Computer Centre,
and how many remote terminals are there?
Answer
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services) replied: It is not possible
to give an accurate count of the number of people who have information recorded
about them in the Wanganui Computer Centre without writing a special com-
puter programme to extract this information. The reason an accurate figure is
not available is because different master name indices exist for differing functions.
These indices will, of course, be overlapping-e.g. it is probable that the majority
of names appearing on the driver licences file will also appear on the vehicle
owners file. In regard to remote terminals, there are at present 284 visual display
units, and, of these, 210 have small printers attached to them.

Notes: (1) The data provided relates to amounts drawn and repaid in respect
of official overseas debt, and covers both loans and capital equipment credits. No
new official overscas loans or credits were arranged (or signed) in April or May
1978. (Amounts drawn but not amounts arranged may be properly compared
with amounts repaid.) The "loans raised" figures given therefore relate to
drawings under credits in those months. The "loans redeemed" figures comprise
repayments of loans and credits on due date in accordance with agreed repay-
ment schedules plus the prepayment of a US$60 million drawing under the 1977
Lloyds revolving credit. (2) Exchange gains and losses are usually measured
only towards the end of each financial year and in respect of the whole year.
They are determined by the movement between the exchange rates at which
overseas debt transactions are recorded during the financial year and the exchange
rates used for end-of-year accounting purposes. No exchange gains and losses
have therefore been calculated for April or May 1978. Full details for the
1977-78 financial year for the Public Account appear in the report of the
Controller and Auditor-General on the Public Accounts (page 74).

Overseas Students-English Requirements
54. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Education: Why do
overseas students who have passed New Zealand University Entrance examination
requirements have to sit the LATOS test, which is an overseas examination,
before they can be admitted to New Zealand universities?
Answer
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: Language achievement
test for overseas students (LATOS) was introduced by and is the responsibility
of the Universities Entrance Board, which is an independent statutory authority.
However, as I understand it, the New Zealand University Entrance Examination
in English is concerned with literature, linguistics, and other aspects of particular
concern to scholars of English. The LATOS test, on the other hand, is concerned
with English communication skills such as the ability to read textbooks and under-
stand lectures. When in 1971 an investigation into failure of overseas students at
university revealed a close link between the lack of communication skills in English
and failure, LATOS was introduced to exclude such potential unsuccessful students.
Similar tests are used for the same purpose in England, Australia, Canada, and
the United States. If further information is required the member should approach
the Universities Entrance Board. LATOS was designed and constructed in New
Zealand to meet New Zealand conditions. It is not, as the question suggests, an
overseas examination.
(22/6/78)

Gas Water Heaters-Interest-free Loans
57. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What is the
estimated cost for the balance of this financial year and for 1979-80 of interest-
free loans to assist with the purchase of gas water heaters?
Answer
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: The estimated cost of loans
for gas appliances (i.e., cookers, waterheaters, space-heating) in 1978-79 is
$100,000. This is for interest payments on the amounts advanced to the gas under-
takings for on-lending. No breakdown has been made of the total between the
three appliance types. Indications are that in the early months of the loan scheme
the number of loans for space-heaters was about a third of all loans. No
estimate has been made for 1979-80, but the amount is unlikely to be markedly
different from the cost in 1978-79.

Solar Water Heaters-Interest-free Loans
58. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: How many
solar water heating units is it estimated will be installed as a result of proposals to
provide interest-free loans, and what is the estimated cost to the Government of
this proposal for the current financial year?
Answer
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: It is impossible to gauge the
increased demand for solar water heaters resulting from the interest-free loan
scheme announced in the Budget until the scheme has been in effect for some time.
It is proposed that up to $2 million will be provided initially, but as this will be
repaid by the recipients the real cost of the scheme to the Government will be
the reimbursement of the interest payments and of the administration charges
involved. This would be no more than $65,000 for the current financial year.
(22/6/78)
Traffic Intersection Problem, New Lynn
59. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Transport: Has he seen a
report in the New Zealand Herald of 13 June 1978 about proposals concerning the
intersection of Rankin Avenue, Clark Street, and Totara Avenue in New Lynn,
which also has a railway running through the middle of the intersection, and, if
so, what is his department doing to solve what seem to be real difficulties in trying
to understand who gives way and who has the right of way at any particular time?
Answer
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: Yes, I have
seen the newspaper report referred to by the member for New Lynn. The inter-
section of Rankin Avenue, Clark Street, and Totara Avenue in New Lynn has
concerned traffic engineers in the area for some time, as the news report makes
clear. The body responsible for the traffic engineering aspects of the intersection is
the New Lynn Borough Council. On 13 June the traffic committee of the borough
council in fact recommended that "the intersection and the railway crossing be
investigated for the purpose of revising the design and layout and in this respect
that the borough engineer be urged to liaise with engineers of the Ministry of
Transport and New Zealand Railways". The borough council is to consider this
recommendation when it meets on 21 June. I can confirm that officers of the
Ministry of Transport and New Zealand Railways will co-operate with the borough
council in investigating improvements to the intersection.
(22/6/78)
FM Broadcasting
60. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Broadcasting: Are there any
proposals to introduce FM broadcasting in New Zealand this year, and, if not,
why not?
Answer
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting) replied: The various
considerations surrounding the introduction of FM broadcasting to this country are
still being examined by an FM planning committee, which is representative of the
various interests concerned. I have inquired, and am informed that the commit-
tee's report is not expected to be completed until later this year. The Government
will have to consider the report, and all other relevant factors, before any decision
is made on the introduction of FM. I am not in a position to indicate when this
will be.
(22/6/78)

Maui Gas as a Premium Fuel
61. Mr BIRCH (Franklin) to the Minister of Energy: How much natural gas
is to be supplied annually from the Maui gasfield as a premium fuel, and how
does the amount compare with that arranged at the time the agreement was
signed?
Answer
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: At the time the Maui agree-
ments were concluded in 1973 it was reported in the white paper (page 14) that
the domestic and industrial market for gas as a premium fuel, taking Kapuni
production into account, was not sufficient by itself to make the development an
economic proposition, and this remains correct today. Studies undertaken in 1973
showed it could be expected that up to about 10 percent of the Maui gas offtake
could be used in the domestic and industrial markets. Recently provision has been
made for the Natural Gas Corporation of New Zealand Ltd. to be supplied with
increasing quantities of Maui gas, rising from 13 percent of the take or pay volume
in 1978-79 (September years) to 20 percent in 1985-86 and 26 percent in 1992–93.
(22/6/78)

"Iron Bridge" Concept
64. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) to the Minister of Regional
Development: Could he clarify his comments made about the "iron bridge"
concept, as reported in the Evening Post of 29 April, which read: (i) “In particu-
lar, it would cause dislocation through the transport sector"; (ii) "South Island
manufacturers, other than those in Blenheim, would be placed at a disadvantage"?
Answer
Hon. G, F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development) replied: (i) Introduction
of an "iron bridge" would create dislocation throughout the transport sector,
because the combined rail/rail-ferry journey between the North and South Islands
would become substantially cheaper. Inter-island coastal shipping services would


## p. 1457 (#567) ###########################################

5 July
1457
Questions and Replies
have difficulty in competing, and some would probably have to be withdrawn.
Road transport servicing these services would face reduced volumes of traffic
accordingly. Railways, unless granted a substantial subsidy of around $20 million
to $25 million a year, would have to raise charges on its other hauls and would
become uncompetitive on them. (ii) For manufacturers closer to Cook Strait, the
ferry component is a larger sector of total journey costs. Blenheim manufacturers
would derive the greatest proportionate reduction in costs of any South Island
manufacturers. However, an "iron bridge" would run both north and south. Thus,
North Island manufacturers would have their transport costs reduced too. Many
of them, geared to service large local markets, would then be able to out-compete
South Island manufacturers in their own local markets.
(22/6/78)

for locating that officer at the Waihi Courthouse, which is in the western extremity

Answer
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: The Electoral Act

returning officer for the Kaimai electorate has not yet been appointed; this
appointment will be made by the Chief Electoral Officer.

Unions required to Ballot for Compulsory Unionism
74. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: Will he list the unions.
and number of people involved who would be bound by an award that would be
required to have a ballot for compulsory or voluntary unionism?
Answer
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour) replied: Ballots on the unqualified
preference provision are restricted to awards and collective agreements negotiated
by unions registered under the Industrial Relations Act. In December 1976 there
were 294 unions registered under the Act with a combined membership of 464 453.
These figures give only a very rough indication of the numbers involved in the

Secondary School Boards-Unauthorised Grants
76. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) to the Minister of Education: Has he seen an
article in the magazine the Capital Letter dated 13 June 1978 in which it is
claimed that it will be necessary to pass an Act to validate the unauthorised
payment of increased grants to secondary school boards from 1 February
1975 to 31 March 1977, and, if so, is this statement accurate?
Answer
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied: I have seen the article
referred to. It is true that legislation is being prepared to validate the payments
made to controlling authorities of State secondary schools for general expenses for
the period mentioned. The grants to be validated are those for the year ended
31 January 1976, approved by the previous administration in August 1975, and
for the period 1 February 1976 to 31 March 1977, approved by this Government
on 9 July 1976. The payment of grants is made under the authority of the
Secondary Schools Grants Regulations 1974, regulation 3 (2), and although the
requisite approvals were obtained the actual rates were not published in the
Gazette until last year. The Controller and Auditor-General considers that the
payment of grants in anticipation of the publication in the Gazette of the basis of
calculating those grants requires validating legislation, and an appropriate clause
is to be inserted in the Finance Act 1978.

Solar Heating Promotion
77. Mr BIRCH (Franklin) to the Minister of Energy: What action has the
National Government taken to promote the use of solar heating?


## p. 1462 (#572) ###########################################

1462
5 July
Questions and Replies
Answer
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: (1) Businesses are being
encouraged to install solar equipment through the tax write-off scheme. This
scheme provides for the full capital cost of the equipment to be written off for
tax purposes in the year in which the expenditure is incurred, a refund of the
10 percent sales tax, and Development Finance Corporation loans to be available
in suitable cases. (2) As recently announced in the Budget, the interest-free loans
scheme for home insulation has been extended to include solar water heaters.
Once the administrative arrangements and performance requirements have been
finalised, interest-free loans of up to $500, for a period of 4 years, will be
available to householders for the installation of solar water heaters. (3) The
Government is funding research into ways of reducing the capital cost of solar
water heaters and of improving their overall performance. (4) Practical trials of
the units are being carried out in several Government buildings, including office
buildings, schools, and houses. (5) Construction of a solar water heater testing
facility to enable the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research to obtain
reliable comparative data is expected to begin shortly. The project is being
implemented at the request of the Ministry of Energy. The test results should be
useful to manufacturers, to the consumer and to the Government.

War Pensions Medical Research Trust
90. Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) to the Minister in Charge of War Pensions:
What is the source of funds for the War Pensions Research Trust; what amount
of money is at present held; for what purpose is the money allocated; how much
has been distributed from the fund in the last 5 years; and what is the amount
and purpose of this year's allocation?
Answer
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister in Charge of War Pensions) replied:
The source of funds for the War Pensions Medical Research Trust is set down in
section 181 of the War Pensions Act 1954. The main source of funds is war pension
moneys unpaid at the date of death of the pensioner that are unclaimed by any
dependants of the pensioner for a period of 6 months after his death. During the
year ended 31 March 1978 assets held by the fund amounted to $294,340. Its
income for that year totalled $90,897. Funds held by the trust are available for:
research into mental disorder or other fields of medical research beneficial to former
members of the forces; the provision of fellowships to qualified persons who will
contribute to such research; and the costs of administering the fund. The amount
of money distributed from the fund in the last 5 years is as follows:

lished. So far this year the board has approved new research grants for the follow-
ing research projects that have recently commenced or are about to commence:
(a) a research grant of up to $20,000 over a 2-year period on a project entitled
"The Major Syndromes of the Elderly. Prevalence and Prognosis"; (b) a research

Farm Subdivisions-Sales
94. Mr FALLOON (Pahiatua) to the Minister in Charge of the Valuation
Department: What is the number of subdivisions of farm property sold after
an existing unit was divided, compared with the number of farm enlargements
in each year over the past 5 years, including family transactions?
Answer
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister in Charge of the Valuation Department) replied:
The Valuation Department receives notification of the sales of farm lands in New
Zealand and classifies these under a number of different headings, including the
type of farm and the buyer, but while its figures are recorded in several different
categories it is not possible to answer the question in the way in which it has been
asked. There are no figures that would indicate the number of farm properties
sold after an existing unit was divided. However, as an indication of the position,
the department has figures recorded under the heading of "new farmers" which
represents a buyer (not a businessman) who has not previously owned a farm.
Sales in this category include a new farmer buying both a new farm and an
existing farm. The figures over the last 5 years show the number of sales recorded
as: 1973, 2324; 1974, 1788; 1975, 1338; 1976, 1603; 1977, 1628. This includes both
economic farm units and other farm land. The number of economic farm units
sold to new farmers over the same period was: 1973, 803; 1974, 556; 1975, 332;
1976, 501; 1977, 569. There are also no figures for the number of farm enlarge-
ments but, as an indication of this, the number of freehold farm sales that
involved a farmer buying additional land to enlarge his existing holding over the
last 5 years is shown as: 1973, 2114; 1974, 1418; 1975, 776; 1976, 1025; 1977, 1148.
This includes both economic farm units and other farm land. The number of
economic units recorded as being sold for farm enlargement over the same period
is: 1973, 690; 1974, 443; 1975, 213; 1976, 287; 1977, 319. Family transactions and
sales of leashold land, which are not considered to be as reliable an indication of
the market as freehold sales, are not categorised to the same degree as freehold
sales and are not included in the above figures.

Private Mortgages
98. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St Kilda) to the Minister of Finance: How many
lending institutions in the private sector are currently offering (i) variable repay-
ment mortgages, (ii) indexed mortgages, (iii) low-start mortgages; and what
proportion of all mortgage finance comes within each of these categories respec-
tively?
Answer
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: I am unable to
give precise answers to the questions asked, because of the lack of firm information
available and the difficulties of definition of the types of mortgage. The terms
"variable repayment mortgage", "indexed mortgage", and "low-start mortgage"
are all capable of definition in many ways. A variable repayment mortgage could
include one on which capital repayments were set at a high or low level in the
early years of the loan, followed by equal payments over the balance of the
period. Also, the term could include arrangements whereby institutions offer a
prospective borrower a range of repayment terms from, say, 5 to 25 years depend-
ing on the person's ability to service the outgoings. And again the expression
could encompass loans for which the borrower can renegotiate the period of the
loan if he is unable to meet the level of outgoings because of some change in
family circumstances or employment. An indexed mortgage could be one for
which the outstanding principal of the loan was indexed by the rate of increase
in the consumer price index, or by a property price index, or it could be one
on which the rate of interest was indexed to the rate of inflation. A low-start
mortgage generally implies one for which the rate of capital repayments in the
early years, is lower than the average over the whole term of the loan; or is
nil-i.e., a flat loan for the first few years; or is negative-i.e., interest is capi-
talised and added to the capital value of the loan. In any event, a low-start
mortgage will also be a variable repayment mortgage. The loans that the Govern-
ment is encouraging the savings banks to make are of the low-start variety, and
could include any of the variations described above. Because of these difficulties
of definition, no statistics are available on the amount of mortgage finance
that is provided on the various bases, although I understand the Reserve Bank


## p. 1473 (#583) ###########################################

5 July
1473
Questions and Replies
is currently having discussions with financial institutions aimed at overcoming
these problems and obtaining worth-while information. What I can do is give
an indication of the lending policies followed by the major private-sector lending
institutions. To my knowledge no lending institutions make any form of indexed
loan, although I understand some are looking into the practicalities of this type
of loan. The trustee savings banks all provide low-start and high-start variations
(to meet the situation of a two-income family) in addition to their normal loans
based on a fixed annual repayment of principal. The private savings banks are
looking into ways of varying their normal table mortgages, and have begun to
make some loans on a low-start basis. The life insurance offices generally do not
depart from lending on a long-term table loan basis, although the major offices
are currently investigating ways of making variable and low-start loans. The
permanent building societies: almost all will give a borrower an option to take
a repayment period to suit his needs, the term ranging from 5 to 25 years. Some
societies offer low-start mortgages that are essentially a flat loan for several
years, then converting to a table loan for the balance of the term. The terminat-
ing building societies are usually very flexible on the term of repayment offered
and will accept higher repayment levels than agreed if the borrower so wishes.
Loans can also be renegotiated if a borrower gets into difficulties through changed
circumstances. The terminating societies are all looking into ways of varying
their repayment arrangements to suit the circumstances of the borrower, but few
specifically lend on low-start terms at the present time.

Teachers' Government Superannuation Fund Refunds
116. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Finance: Are there
delays in paying superannuation to primary school teachers who have given proper
notice of withdrawal from the superannuation scheme, and, if so, what is the longest
wait that teachers are having and what is the reason?
Answer
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: At present the
majority of teachers' Government Superannuation Fund refunds are being paid
out within 3 weeks of the documents being received from the education boards.
Inevitably some delays will occur for any of a variety of different reasons. The
fund receives a large volume of refund applications from throughout all the State
services and the tendancy has been to concentrate on processing as early as
possible the great majority that are routine, with the result that refunds that may
involve queries or require further documentation can take somewhat longer to
process. It is not possible to provide details of the extent of delays and reasons
for these in any general terms.

Kapuni Natural Gas Production
119. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What addi-
tional quantities of natural gas will be produced from Kapuni 'this financial year
and how much of this is expected to be available for householder use?
Answer
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: It is likely that gas off-takes
from the Kapuni field in 1978-79 will be less than those in 1977-78, as the field's
productivity is naturally declining. There is, however, no restriction on the amount
available for householder use. The actual growth in household gas sales will depend
on how successful the undertakings are at marketing and expanding gas sales in
the context of the 1977 and 1978 Budget assistance.

Auckland Harbour Board-Income
123. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) to the Minister of Transport: What is
the income for the port of Auckland this financial year compared with that for
the last financial year?
Answer
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied: Harbour boards
have a financial year ending on 30 September. For the last completed financial
year ended 30 September 1977 the annual accounts of the Auckland Harbour
Board show an income of about $32 million compared with an income of about
$25 million for the year ended 30 September 1976. The board had a surplus on
operations of about $2.8 million, which, after allowing for loan repayments,
capital expenditure, and reserve payments, gave the board a surplus of $630,000
for the year ended 30 September 1977. For their previous financial year the
board had a surplus on operations of about $2 million, which, after allowing
for loan repayments, capital expenditure, and reserve payments, resulted in a
deficit of $1 million, which was funded from accumulated surpluses.
(28/6/78)
Housing Mortgages
124. Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda) to the Minister of Finance: Did the
committee investigating sources of housing finance, made up of representatives
from Treasury, the Housing Corporation, and the Reserve Bank, estimate (i) the
number, and (ii) the dollar value, of short-term high interest loans that will
require refinancing in (i) the next 12 months, and (ii) the next 3 years, and what
were these estimates in each case?
Answer
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The committee the
member is referring to was an ad hoc committee formed in 1975 by representa-
tives of the three organisations specifically to investigate the workings of the
mortgage market, and the policies and procedures followed by the major partici-
pants in that market. The committee reported its findings to the Government in
mid-1976, and has not continued in existence. It was not the responsibility of
the committee to quantify any particular element of the flow of funds into mort-
gages, including the number or value of short-term mortgages maturing over any
particular period. The Reserve Bank is at present engaged in organising statistical
surveys that will obtain, among other things, further information on flows of
funds in the mortgage market. At present, however, no data exists that would
enable the amounts of short-term private loans maturing over a particular period
to be reliably estimated. Nevertheless, it is not expected that refinancing require-
ments will place any strain on the mortgage market in the near future.

Foreign Fishing Vessels-Tax
126. Mr COURTNEY (Nelson) to the Minister of Customs: Are foreign fishing
vessels that are licensed to fish in New Zealand waters subject to tax when calling
at New Zealand ports, or has this tax lapsed as promised in the 1976 Budget?
Answer
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Minister of Customs) replied: Foreign fishing vessels
that are licensed to fish in New Zealand waters are no longer deemed to be
"foreign fishing vessels" within the meaning of section 2 of the Customs Acts
Amendment Act 1976 (No. 15), and such vessels are therefore not liable to the
foreign fishing vessel tax. The need for the continuation of this tax is at present
under consideration by my department.

Abortion Procedures-Auckland
130. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Health: Will he outline
the nature of the temporary arrangements made for the 12 Auckland women
holding the necessary certificates entitling them to early terminations of pregnancy;
how did they get their terminations; where did they get them; who performed
them; and what was the cost to the State?
Answer
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: It was announced on 7 June
1978 by a spokesman on the staff of the National Women's Hospital that 6
specialists had agreed to assist with the 12 Auckland women referred to. Since
then, two have been operated on at the National Women's Hospital and eight at
the Epsom Day Hospital. Of the remaining two, one aborted spontaneously and
the other is due for admission to the National Women's Hospital this week. It is
not possible to say what the cost of these terminations was to the State, nor do I
consider it appropriate to name the operating surgeons who performed these
abortions.

(28/6/78)
Abortion Procedures
132. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Health: Can he explain
the procedure required of a woman who has obtained a certificate from two
certifying consultants, but is unable to find an operating surgeon; is it now her
responsibility to find an operating surgeon?
Answer
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: Section 33 (5) of the Contra-
ception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977 places on the two certifying con-
sultants the responsibility of satisfying themselves that an operating surgeon is
available to any woman authorised to have an abortion. It should not be the
patient's responsibility to find one for herself.

(28/6/78)
Abortion Procedures-Reimbursement of Expenses
136. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Justice: Is a woman
who has travelled a considerable distance to obtain a certificate, specialist assess-
ment, and/or the services of an operating surgeon entitled to claim reimbursement
of expenses incurred by the failure of the supervisory committee to provide those
services described in the Act?
Answer
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied: There does not appear
to be any provision authorising payment of the travelling expenses incurred by a
woman in visiting either a certifying consultant or an operating surgeon. The
Abortion Supervisory Committee is required to appoint sufficient certifying consul-
tants for every woman seeking an abortion to have her case considered without
involving her in considerable travelling or other inconvenience. As yet the commit-
tee has been unable to make sufficient appointments in all districts because not
enough medical practitioners have made themselves available for appointment. It
is hoped that the passage of the amendments proposed by the supervisory commit-
tee may overcome this difficulty.

Abortion Procedures-Auckland
139. MARILYN WARING (Raglan) to the Minister of Health: In view of the
statement in the New Zealand Herald of 8 June 1978 by Dr Frank Rutter to the
effect that general practitioners "can refer women for counselling but there are
no prospects for early terminations", what arrangements are to be made for
Auckland women in possession of the necessary certificates from certifying con-
sultants to obtain early termination of pregnancy to which they are entitled?
Answer
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health) replied: I am informed that counsel-
ling services provided by the Auckland Hospital Board at the Epsom Day Hospital
are being made use of by general practitioners, and an average of two women a
day are being counselled there. It is not the responsibility of the hospital board to
find an operating surgeon. This is the duty of the certifying consultants, in terms
of section 33 (5) of the Contraception, Sterilisation, and Abortion Act 1977.
Urgent cases referred to the National Women's Hospital direct by general practi-
tioners are seen on a case-to-case basis by consultants there. If termination of
pregnancy is considered medically necessary, the patient is then referred to two
certifying consultants for the necessary certificate before the operation is performed
by an operating surgeon at that hospital.

(28/6/78)
Overseas Debt
141. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) to the Minister of Finance: What was
the level of overseas debt on 30 November 1972 and 30 November 1975?
Answer
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance) replied: The level of official
overseas debt at dates other than 31 March each year is not made public. In the


## p. 1492 (#602) ###########################################

1492
5 July
Questions and Replies
case of the Public Account overseas debt, the main reasons for not disclosing debt
levels at other dates are that: (a) The data would be provisional. New mid-point
exchange rates are usually struck only once a year for the purposes of realigning
overseas debt in New Zealand dollar terms. As this is generally done towards the
end of each financial year, the level of overseas debt at other dates would not,
whenever exchange rates are fluctuating, reflect a current measure. (b) Only at the
end of each financial year is it possible to ensure that all overseas debt transactions
for the year are allocated in the Public Accounts. The overseas debt level of the
Reserve Bank, which together with that of the Public Account comprises official
overseas debt, is similarly released only as at 31 March each year. Överseas debt
levels for years ended 31 March are available in the Budget and Public Accounts,
and the annual reports of the Reserve Bank. The figure for 31 March 1973 was
$564 million and for 31 March 1976 it was $1,983.5 million.

## p. 1494 (#604) ###########################################

1494
5 July
Questions and Replies
Forty-three of the New Zealand tenable award holders are from Africa Of this
number, 18 are Tanzanians undertaking agricultural courses at Massey University
and Flock House. Five Sierra Leoneans are studying dental nursing training in
Christchurch, and one student a B.D.S. degree at Otago. A Zambian student is
enrolled in a B. Ag.Sc. degree at Lincoln. Twelve Rhodesian Africans are under-
taking such courses as engineering, town planning, science, and pharmacy, while
two students from Swaziland are pursuing certificate courses in forestry. Two
Kenyans are undertaking practical training in geothermal and geochemistry work,
and a Malawian is attached to Radio New Zealand for broadcasting engineering
training. For the first time this year the Government made available an award
for a Namibian student who is undertaking practical training before enrolling for
a Diploma of Farm Management at Lincoln College.
The most recent comprehensive figures available on private overseas students
are those for the year ended 30 September 1977. The number then was 3 967.
It is the Government's policy to concentrate on providing opportunities for students
from neighbouring countries in the South Pacific and South-east Asia. Last year,
for example, there were 2 195 students from Malaysia, 116 from Singapore, 47
from Thailand, 712 from Fiji, 555 from Western Samoa, and 162 from Tonga.
The balance of the 3 967 was made up mainly of students from other Asian and
Pacific countries. Over the past 2 years the Government has made some extensions
of the geographical area from which we accept private overseas students. For
example, a quota of 50 was set last year for students from Iran and Iraq. A
modest number of students should be accepted for study from those countries next
year.

Wairaki Coal Mine
148. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: Is it still
proposed to work the old Wairaki mine by the opencast and underground methods,
and, if so, what steps have been undertaken to: (a) divert the stream, (b) ensure
the safety from possible flooding of any mine shafts that were proposed to be driven
from the opencast workings?
Answer
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy) replied: It is still planned to open the

considered by the Southland Catchment Board. The Ministry of Works and
Development is involved with the stream diversion and the design of the new
opencast mine. This involvement will ensure that all factors are taken into account
to secure the workings against the possibility of flooding.

Chancery Building, New Delhi
149. Mr LANGE (Mangere) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Does the New
Zealand Government still lease land in New Dehli for the erection thereon of a
residence and chancery, and, if so, (a) when does the lease expire, and (b) when
will construction commence?
Answer
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs)
replied: The New Zealand Government still leases land in New Delhi on which
it is proposed to build a chancery, official residence, and staff houses. The lease of
the 4-acre site was purchased from the Indian Government in 1962 for a term of
99 years. The Wellington architectural firm of Gabites, Alington, and Edmondson
is currently working on sketch plans for the full development of the site, but
because of the total cost involved the project will need to be phased. Priority is
being given to the chancery and official residence, and construction is programmed
to commence in December 1979.

patients and families are forced to travel to Hamilton or to use the Matamata private
hospital?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): It is the responsibility of the Waikato

the hospital, and the surgical wards are now fully staffed.

analysed, and a decision to be available within the next 3 months.

Import Volumes
167. Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury) to the Minister of Trade and
Industry: Have the Government's fiscal policies been successful in reducing imports,
and can he give a comparison of the volume of imports since 1972 and predict future
trends?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): Yes, the
Government has succeeded in reducing the volume of imports through its fiscal and
monetary policies. The Government Statistician's index of the volume of imports
shows that the following changes have occurred since 1972: in 1973-74, an increase of
31.8 percent; in 1974-75, an increase of 2.6 percent; in 1975-76, a decrease of 18.7
percent; in 1976-77, virtually no change in the volume of imports compared with that
of 1975-76; and in the first 6 months of 1977-78, on provisional figures, a decrease of
around 9 percent. On the basis of a survey of forward orders, the Government
Statistician has projected a steady fall in private import payments each month
through to October of this year, which is an indication that the declining trend in the

Regional Local Government, Wellington
168. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Local Government: What
is the current situation regarding the establishment of regional local government for
Wellington?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): The present situation is
that the provisional scheme, promulgated by the Local Government Commission on
21 July 1977, is still under consideration by the new commission. In terms of the
Local Government Act 1974, as amended last year, the present commission may
decide either to completely abandon the scheme and start a fresh examination of the
proposal or to continue with the statutory procedures set out in the Act. If the
commission decides on the latter course of action, it must consider the objections
lodged to the provisional scheme and take one of several procedures, which are: (1) to
abandon the provisiona! scheme and start the whole process afresh; (2) to issue a final
scheme either in the same terms as the provisional scheme or as modified as a result of
the objections; (3) to issue one or more substitute provisional schemes, which again
will be open to objection. The new commission has been in office only since April of
this year and is now examining all the provisional regional schemes on hand. I
understand that the commission has not yet taken a decision as to which of the
available options it will take in regard to the Wellington regional provisional scheme.
(15/6/78)
Exports to Chile-FOL Ban
169. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) to the Minister of Labour: When will he take
action against the Federation of Labour to have it remove the ban on New Zealand
exports to Chile?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): As the member probably knows,
the ban on Chilean trade originated from a decision of the International
Confederation of Free Trade Unions. The Federation of Labour is affiliated to this
organisation, and Mr Knox, the Secretary of the Federation of Labour, is an
executive member. Despite my personal efforts and the Government's persuasion, the
Federation of Labour at its last conference decided to continue the ban at least in the
meantime. However, Mr Knox, who is at present in Europe attending ICFTU and
International Labour Organisation meetings, was asked to make an assessment of the
situation following any discussions on the issue at those conferences. In these
circumstances I believe it would be advisable to await Mr Knox's return to New
Zealand before consideration is given to any action that might be appropriate.

169A. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Minister of Transport: In view of

downgraded air traffic control, with particular reference to Wanganui and Tauranga

air traffic control?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): There were 12 incidents

country. None of these, on investigation, was categorised as a near miss. Of the 12, 2

was not a factor. The ministry is satisfied that the level of air traffic services provided
at Tauranga and Wanganui meets the requirements of safe and orderly flying
operations. Therefore, I am able to give the member the assurance he requested.

Electoral Rolls
176. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Justice: Were the new
electoral rolls compiled entirely from the enrolment cards distributed with the census,
and, if so, how is it that persons who had died before the census, or had left New
Zealand before the census, still have their names on the roll?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The electoral rolls for the new
electoral districts were not compiled entirely from the re-registration forms collected
at the last census. They also include residual names of persons who were on the 1975
rolls, but did not subsequently re-register. I should observe that this information was
indicated in paragraph 7 of the instruction that I circulated to all members of
Parliament a month ago. Since it was known that many people did not return the re-
registration forms after the census, it was thought preferable to retain their names on
the roll in the meantime, and send cars to all who were on the roll in 1975. The 1975
roll was, of course, not perfectly up to date.

Industrial Legislation
179. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Labour: In view of the report
in the Evening Post of 13 June 1978, in which he is reported as saying that "he was
contemplating legislation to combat illegal strikes", will he outline what he means by
illegal strikes, and legal strikes?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The Industrial Relations Act 1973
and the Commerce Act 1975 specify various offences in relation to a strike or lockout.
Under the Industrial Relations Act, a stoppage is illegal in the following
circumstances: if claims have not been withdrawn from the conciliation council-
section 81; if the matter is within the disputes procedure deemed to be in every award
or collective agreement - section 124A; if 14 days' notice of intention to strike or
lockout has not been given in respect of a stoppage in specified essential industries—
section 125; and if 3 days' notice of intention to strike or lockout has not been given in
respect of a stoppage in meat export slaughterhouses-section 125A. Under the
Commerce Act, a stoppage is illegal if it is over a matter that is not an industrial
matter-section 119B; or if it is in defiance of a resumption of a work order by the
Arbitration Court under section 119C. In some of these it would be a defence if safety
and health were involved.
(16/6/78)

relative value between a lamb chop exported for consumption overseas and a similar
chop consumed in New Zealand by an overseas tourist?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Tourism
replies: "I do not know about the Tourist and Publicity Department, but when I
addressed the Cookery and Food Association in Wellington last July, I had a
suggestion to make to them. As I told them, 'A quick calculation on a scrap of paper
this afternoon suggested to me that, while we might sell a lamb chop overseas for 35c,
if we can sell that same lamb chop to an overseas visitor in a New Zealand hotel the
value is most likely to be about $1.50. These figures might not be accurate to the
nearest cent, but they make a point for all of us. In fact, if we can follow this through
to a logical conclusion, the most profitable way of selling all our export foods would be
to serve them to tourists in our own hotels', and I still think this is true."

Foreign Exchange Surcharge
196. Mr BIRCH (Franklin) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: Has he read of
the Labour Party proposal to impose a surcharge on the purchase of foreign
exchange, and, if so, has he asked his department to consider whether this proposal if
implemented would offend any trade pledges, international undertakings, or General
Agreement on Tariffs and Trade to which the New Zealand Government is a party?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade): Yes,
I have read of the proposal, and my department has looked into the sort of
implications mentioned in the question. I am informed that a tax on foreign exchange
would probably conflict with Article VIII of the International Monetary Fund
Articles of Agreement. In addition, there is a strong presumption that a tax on foreign
exchange would place New Zealand in breach of (1) the IMF Articles of Agreement;
(2) the specific Government undertakings in relation to borrowing from the IMF oil
facility; (3) the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade; and (4) the OECD trade
pledge, which the Labour Government adopted in 1974, and which the Deputy
Minister of Foreign Affairs has recently renewed. The Labour Party proposal to
impose a surcharge on the purchase of foreign exchange would invite immediate
retaliation from our principal trading partners. This could well take the form of
recourse to the IMF, GATT, and OECD provisions that I have mentioned.

State Rental Applications-Criteria
210. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) to the Minister of Housing: Is it
correctly stated in the New Zealand Law Society's newsletter Law Talk that his
department has decided, as a matter of principle, to reject applications for rental
accommodation from either party to a matrimonial separaton involving the sale of the
matrimonial home?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I have read the article in Law
Talk 74, and neither it nor the letter from the Housing Corporation on which the
article is based states that the corporation has decided, as a matter of principle, to
reject applications for rental accommodation from either party to a matrimonial
separation involving the sale of the matrimonial home. When a husband and wife
separate and there is a family home owned by the husband, or if a suitable home has
been sold with the agreement of the applicant, or because the applicant did not desire
to pursue legal avenues for obtaining possession for the benefit of, say, herself and her
children, housing allocation committees reasonably take the view that the housing
difficulties are self-created and that an allocation, when considered in relation to the
needs of other applicants, is not warranted. Nevertheless, while this represents the
general attitude of the corporation, it is not an inflexible policy, and each applicant's
circumstances and needs are taken into account.

Meat Shipments through Gisborne
213. Mr BELL (Gisborne) to the Minister of Transport: Can he advise the
quantity of frozen meat shipments through the port of Gisborne for the September
years 1973-74, 1974-75, 1975-76, 1976-77, and the destinations of the consignments?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Transport): The quantity and
destination of frozen meat exports through the port of Gisborne for the years 1973 to
1977 were as follows: 1973, 10 549 tonnes; 1974, 12 573 tonnes; 1975, 11 673 tonnes;
1976, 7891 tonnes, of which 77 tonnes were exported to Canada, 487 to Greece, 45 to
Hawaii, 558 to Iran, 667 to Iraq, 5415 to the United Kingdom, and 642 to the United
States; 1977, 6811 tonnes, of which 31 tonnes were exported to Bermuda and 6780 to
the United Kingdom. Figures relating to the destination of frozen meat exports out of
Gisborne for the years 1973 to 1975 are not available as they were not then
computerised. The meat trade between New Zealand and Europe is not 100 percent
containerised at this time. In fact, at the peak of the season some refrigerated
conventional ships will be used. Amongst the ports likely to receive calls is Gisborne.
With the growth of containerisation and its capacity to carry the entire meat trade
such calls will tend to diminish.

Air Freight Charges
230. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) to the Minister of Transport: Is he aware
that air freight per 1000 k minimum from New Zealand to Hong Kong is 84c per kilo
as against a freight rate from the United States to Hong Kong of 50c, and, in view of
the fact that this is Export Year, does the Government intend to take any action to
ensure competitiveness for air freight charges from New Zealand with those applying
elsewhere?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Acting Minister of Transport): I am aware of
that. The only rate in the vicinity of 50c per kilo for air freight from the United States
to Hong Kong is a stand-by non-priority rate for fresh fruit and vegetables. If an
exporter wants to take advantage of this special rate he must abide by certain
conditions. For example, no reservations for carriage may be made prior to 24 hours
before take-off. I am happy to report that New Zealand exporters benefit from the
availability of numerous special incentive rates known as 'specific commodity rates'.
If the member is aware of an exporter having particular difficulties in securing
competitive rates for the carriage of goods, I should be pleased to make an
investigation.

Police/Population Ratios
247. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) to the Minister of Police: What increases in
police staff strengths have been made in the last year, and how do they affect the ratio
of police to population, particularly in comparison with the ratio in 1975?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): In the 1977-78 financial year
the Government authorised an increase of 200 sworn police personnel and 80 public
servants. Staffing of the police is no longer based on a ratio of police to population,
but on actual determined annual needs. However, the authorised police strength is
now 4786, and would produce a ratio of 1:656, compared with 1:728 in 1975. The
1978 ratio is, of course, based on estimated population figures.

and he was not involved at all?

Beef Prices
258. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of
Agriculture: In the event of the minimum price for beef exceeding the "trigger
price", will the Meat Board receive 50 percent of this difference for its reserve funds?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): This is a hypothetical
question. It is quite obvious that the questioner does not understand the system of
setting prices for meat, and beef in particular, under the stabilisation scheme. The
question asks: "In the event of the minimum price for beef exceeding the 'trigger
price' will the Meat Board receive 50 percent of this difference for its reserve funds?”
The minimum price set for beef is 70c for cow beef, and 80c for prime beef. The Meat
Export Prices Committee has not met this year to fix next year's "trigger price". The
committee comprises an independent chairman, two representatives from the
Government, and two from the Meat Board. They will know what the minimum price
is, and would take into consideration that it would be somewhat stupid for them to set
the "trigger price" below the minimum price.
