satisfying grievances which cause a stoppage than it is to retaliate, as it were, with
suspensions...", and can he indicate what steps he has taken to encourage the
positive approach of investigating grievances and to discourage the negative
approach to retaliation by suspension of workers over the past 2 years?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister of Labour
replies: "In my position as Minister I always endeavour to investigate causes of the
industrial disputes that come to my attention, and to secure an amicable settlement
between the parties. The suspension of non-striking employees is simply based on the
principle that an employer should not be obliged to pay the wages of staff for whom he
has no work. It is my considered opinion that employers in this country exercise this
discretion with due responsibility. There is, of course, a right of appeal, and one
succeeded in the last 2 weeks".

Hubodometer Tests-DSIR Report
272. Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga) to the Minister of Transport: Has he
studied the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research report on hubodometer
tests, in which claims are made that variations due to tyre wear could be around 2 to 4
percent and that differences in tyre pressure, load and manufacturers' gearing ratios
on hubodometers could add up to as much as an 8 to 10 percent error; and is the
Government going to make allowances for these possible inaccuracies?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Lands): The Minister of Transport replies: "I
have studied the DSIR report and appreciate that variations in distance
measurements do occur because of the factors mentioned. Nevertheless,
hubodometers have been used and accepted by the road transport industry for many
years as accurate and reliable distance recorders and are considered to be the best
practical and available means of recording distances for the purposes of the Road
User Charges Act 1977. Distance measurement errors associated with hubodometers
that are correctly matched to the tyre size and fitted as required by law, should be no
more than 2 to 4 percent and should be largely self-cancelling over the life of the tyre
so that no allowances for them are necessary".

Income Tax Payments
280. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) to the Minister in Charge of the
Inland Revenue Department: What would be the tax paid from 1 October by: (a) a
single man who earns $250 a week and (b) a married man (single-income family) with
three teenage children, who also earns $250 a week?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister in Charge of the Inland Revenue
Department): On a weekly PAYE basis the single man would pay $79.95 from 1
October 1978, compared with $87.13 at present, and the married man would pay
$76.95 compared with $84.13 at present. The difference of $3 being the value of the
wife's rebate, is the same in each case, leaving the married man in 1978, as in 1975,
approximately 1.2 percent better off than the single man. In addition, it is reasonable
to include in any comparison the family benefit payable in respect of the three
children, amounting to $9 a week, or $468 untaxed a year. I think it is reasonable to
make this comparison between 1978 and 1975, and to include the family benefit, as I
did in answer to previous questions, because the honourable member for Manukau
has seen fit to accuse me in public of blatant dishonesty on these questions-an
accusation which, in the light of the answer pointing out the similarity of positions
percentagewise in 1978 and 1975, is patently absurd. This is the only reasonable way
in which the question can be kept in perspective, as the House would wish.

Housing Corporation Lending
284. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Housing: Can he confirm,
as is stated in the Housing Corporation's 1976 loans survey, that repayments that
would exceed 30 percent of a head of household's gross income are usually
unacceptable to any reputable lending institution, and can he indicate what
proportion of the Housing Corporation's clients were committed to mortgage
repayments exceeding 30 percent of the head of the household's gross income in 1976,
1977, and this year?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): No, the actual statement
made in the Housing Corporation's 1976 loans survey was "25 percent of the
household's total gross income is regarded as the maximum acceptable commitment
to mortgage repayments by many institutions". The proportion of Housing
Corporation mortgagors committed to mortgage payments exceeding 30 percent of
the head of the household's gross income in 1976 and 1977 was: 1976, 37.7 percent,
and 1977, 31.5 percent. No details are yet available for 1978. It is to be noted also that
the 1976 survey showed that almost 60 percent of those mortgagors paying more than
30 percent were two-income families. Consequently, repayments as a proportion of
total family earnings would be considerably less.

for converting from oil to natural gas?

gas, and, therefore, increased sales by Mr Wilson's company. The report referred to
does not appear to have taken these into account.

Indigenous Forests Management Policy
289. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North), on behalf of Dr SHEARER
(Hamilton East), to the Minister of Forests: What aspects of the 1975 indigenous
forests management policy have still to be implemented?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): The main areas of change in the new
indigenous forest policy involve giving greater emphasis to the setting aside of
scientific reservations, the introduction of selective logging systems to replace
clearfelling, and changes to the pricing of native timbers to ensure that their intrinsic
qualities are put to best use. A great deal of work has already been done in identifying
possible reserves on a national basis, and the proposals are being collated by a special
scientific committee. The change from clearfelling to selective logging systems has
also been progressing rapidly. Šince the policy was approved, the Government has
itself approved three price increases for the higher grades of indigenous timber
relative to the lower grades, aimed solely at encouraging higher grade uses for
domestic timber.

am surprised, however, that the member should consider that the additional
resources provided by this Government for the Customs operation-the most recent
approval being announced as recently as last December, with some equipment still
awaiting delivery-should have had some direct effect on the quantities of narcotics
seized in the last 3 years. Obviously the provision of extra staff and equipment will
not produce overnight miracles. The new staff must be trained, and the new

example in the Customs Department annual report, should know that drug seizure
statistics fluctuate markedly from year to year. I suspect that the member is well
aware that the seizure figures are not conclusive anyway, because they cannot be
related to the total amount of drugs in each category actually being imported into
New Zealand-figures no one knows or can know.

research orchard likely to be established at Earnscleugh?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Science and Technology): The Ministry of
Works and Development has recently purchased a farm at Earnscleugh, part of which
will be used for the re-location of the nearby DSIR research orchard. Some of the land
will also be available for trial plantings of several new crops thought likely to prove
commercially viable in Central Otago.
(28/6/78)
Electoral Roll, Christchurch Central
312. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of
Justice: How is it possible for nearly 30 000 people to be on the roll for the electorate
of Christchurch Central?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I have pointed out on several
occasions that the printouts at present being used in electorate offices are provisional
only, and comprise the names of those who re-enrolled at the time of the 1976 census
or subsequently, plus all those on the roll at the time of the last election who do not
appear to have re-enrolled. I repeat that these printouts are not the rolls. Corrections,
additions, and deletions are now being made, and when the roll is closed for the
printing of the main roll the number on the Christchurch Central roll is almost
certain to be much lower than in the printout.

1978-79-financial years?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): In 1977-78 the Government made
available a sum of $74,456 for the development of community psychiatric services by
the Auckland Hospital Board. This included provision for Henderson House, which
is run by the staff of Carrington Hospital. A further grant of $140,000 has been made
in the 1978-79 financial year for the continued operation and development of these
services.

Hastings Government Building Design
315. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata), on behalf of Mr FENTON (Hastings),
to the Minister of State Services: In the construction of the new Government
building in Hastings, what design factors have been incorporated to conserve the
energy used in lighting and heating, and over what floor area to be occupied by the
several departments are the design measures applicable?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of State Services): The main building design.
provides, by low-rise construction and reduced glazing, and insulation, the basic
design requirements for energy conservation. Internal lighting is to be on a task-
location arrangement, with photo-electric cells and time switches providing general
control. Solar water heating units will be used for the domestic water heating.
General office heating will be by circulating hot water from a gas-fired boiler.

Russian fishing vessels are working in the New Zealand 200-mile zone at present, and

Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): At present, six Russian trawlers
with two support vessels are working in our 200-mile zone. The Russian fin-fish quota
for the year ending 31 March 1979 is 60 000 tonnes. They are also permitted to take
4000 tonnes of squid by trawling by 31 August 1978.

Electricity Tariff
317. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What has he
done about the promise in the 1975 blue National Party manifesto, which stated that
"a more flexible tariff will be considered to discourage the wasteful use of electricity
and as a means of reducing any hardship that may result"?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): As a result of the Government's pricing
policy, electricity tariffs are now at a level at which most consumers are careful to
avoid wasteful use. Electricity supply authorities have also reviewed their tariff
policies and none now have declining block tariffs for domestic consumers; a few have
adopted the ascending block system. The Government is investigating the potential
advantages and disadvantages of the system.

Miss DEWE (Lyttelton): No member would deny that questions 155 and 167, dealing

Let us take the case of recent trade negotiations with Japan. The Leader of the
Opposition went around the country complaining bitterly that the National Government was
being far too tough in its attitude towards Japan, and that it should not have demanded a
quid pro quo. Now that negotiations have come to a successful conclusion—and I stress the

saying that the Government has been far too tough.

index was 1468 while the export volume index was 929. In the 1977 June year the import
volume index was 1195, while the export volume index was 1223.

ELECTORAL AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Electoral
Amendment Bill. I respectfully submit to the House that the composition of the electoral
commission should be extended at this stage to include nominees to represent the Social
Credit Political League and the Values Party. In the case of the New Zealand Social Credit
Political League, the basis of the request is that there is a substantial group of electors
throughout New Zealand who, except for one 3-year period from 1966 to 1969, has been
unrepresented in Parliament from 1954 until now. This group of electors is democratically
entitled to an opportunity to supervise the delineation of electoral boundaries equally with
the other parties. The current limitation of this privilege to the National and Labour parties
has the effect of reducing the status of votes cast by Social Credit supporters. To a lesser
extent, this argument also applies to the Values Party.
All candiates for election are deemed to be equal, but it can be argued that this equality
is materially watered down when it is possible for the two main parties to effect the
delineation of electoral boundaries. I am aware of the argument that political representation
on the commission has hitherto not been based on political parties as such, but on giving a
voice to both the Government and the Opposition.
Mr Couch: Who wrote that?
Mr BEETHAM: This argument might carry some weight if the party representatives
were members of the parliamentary National and Labour parties. However, the fact that
both the Government's and the Opposition's representatives in recent years have been party
stalwarts outside the parliamentary parties makes nonsense of the claim that it is the
Government and the Opposition as such, rather than political parties, which are
represented. That being the case, all political parties should be represented.
Mr Marshall: All of them?
Hon. L. W. Gandar: The Communist Party, the Mickey Mouse Party?
Mr BEETHAM: Well, if the Minister wants to describe his party that way, yes. If some
members feel that I have made an insinuation that political considerations play a part in
influencing the fixing of electoral boundaries, I respectfully suggest that they should ponder
the following question. For what purpose, other than to argue the case on partisan grounds,
is representation on the commission given to the National Party and the Labour Party? The
members of the commission representing those parties are unlikely to sit passively while
boundaries unfavourable to their particular causes are being fixed. I shall not go so far as to
suggest that a certain amount of horse trading might be involved, but if it were it could only
be to the advantage of the National Party and the Labour Party, and certainly not to that of
the Social Credit Political League or the Values Party under the present system of
representation.
Our present electoral system simply demands a demographic delineation of boundaries,
and these can most certainly be fixed on this basis without a contribution from
representatives of the National and Labour parties. If they are not represented on the
commission for the purpose of arguing the case on partisan grounds, it is a fair question to
ask what useful verbal contribution they make. If the answer is none, or nothing of any
consequence, then an alternative to this Bill would be another Bill to remove them from the
commission altogether. However, since I do not believe for one moment, largely for the
reason already suggested, that such a step would be seriously considered, I come back to the
question of extending representation on the commission through this Bill. If electoral
boundaries are fixed without partisan bias it would make no difference to the end result if 8
or 18 members sat on the commission, and in these circumstances a representative of the
Social Credit Political League and of the Values Party could be added without prejudice to
the ideal of impartiality.
If it is argued that this would open up the way for all political parties to demand, and
subsequently to obtain, representation on the commission, then I would draw the attention

Electoral Amendment Bill
of members to the 5 percent threshold level provided in the Bill—and that is the answer to

Colleen Dewe: Why?
Mr BEETHAM: Because, unlike other parties outside the House, it has fielded a full

Colleen Dewe: What has that to do with it?
Mr BEETHAM: It is a question of whether one is attached to the principles of
democracy, or whether one is not. Obviously the member is not, which is rather sad for the
country.
In a paper printed in the Political Science Journal back in September 1955, Professor
Ken Scott suggested the necessity for the addition of a clause to the Electoral Act to
introduce the factor of electoral fairness. He said: "The time has come to give legal
recognition to the importance of parties as the instruments through which the voters' choice
is made effective in a parliamentary democracy." He also said: "The members of a
government cannot afford to forget their responsibility to marginal electors." While such a
clause is probably impracticable in legal terms-and I am prepared to concede that-the
principle should be recognised. In this connection, it is worth noting that the former leader
of the British Liberal Party, Mr Jeremy Thorpe, at the Liberal Party's conference in 1971,
spoke out strongly on this vital question of fairness for minority voters. My desire to protect
Social Credit and Values voters is part of my total democractic concept of equality and
fairness for all voters, and I am of the opinion that the clauses in the Bill would go some
distance to meeting this principle.
With specific reference to the clauses of the Act in its present form, the term
"Opposition" in section 15(2)(b) is capable of varying interpretations. There is, I
understand, no legal definition of the term in its relation to the New Zealand Parliament.
This being the case, it can be argued that the representative of the Opposition on the
electoral commission should be selected by all the official and established political opponents
of the Government of the day. However, for the sake of fairness, I appeal to you to
introduce the changes I desire to the Electoral Act to create a just and equal voting status for
all electors in New Zealand.
I have been asked by the Values Party to represent its point of view, and I feel that it is
only right, just and proper that its view should be represented. I am happy to do this, I quote
from what the party sent me: "If partisan representation on the Electoral Representation
Commission is justified at all, then the logic of democratic rights requires representation
from all the significant parties involved. The Bill merely asks for the right to participate. The
rights of other parties to participate are in no way diminished. There is little change in the
overall balance of power on the commission. The combined partisan interests are still a
minority. Democracy as we see it involves the participation of those associated in the
decision making. This Bill extends the principle into an area of detail that does not place too
enormous a demand on the existing system. It is a minor step, but a step in the right
direction. The right direction is to ensure a much more faithful representation in Parliament
of voters' actual choices. Our present system fails to do this as effectively as we believe
democratic principles require. What is really needed is a major overhaul of the whole
system. The Values Party is keen to join or promote any multiple discussions towards the
goal of achieving a better democracy. Extending representation on the Electoral
Representation Commission is a valuable first step not simply in itself, but because it raises
these wider issues." So, on behalf of both the Social Credit Political League and the Values
Party-
An Hon. Member: Have you a warrant to speak?
Mr BEETHAM: Yes, I have authorisation to speak for the Values Party on this, and I
appeal to the House to introduce the changes I advocate to create a just and equal voting
status for all electors, not just for some.

must be preserved that senior officers of State, who are not subject to political pressure,

Political parties are not defined in the Bill; it refers to "organisations commonly known
as political parties". I thought the Social Credit Political League protested that it was not a
political party, but a movement-but that may have changed. The Bill provides that these
people could be any number: "Such number of persons as hereinafter provided shall be
appointed... each of those members being nominated to represent those organisations
commonly known as political parties whose candidates received, in the aggregate, not less
than 5 percent of the valid votes cast in the preceding general election." Therefore, the Bill
provides that senior officers of State, those statutory officers who are detached and
completely objective and whose position in that respect cannot be challenged, could be in
the minority on the Representation Commission. Would that be good for democracy? I do
not believe so.
The essence of the Representation Commission must be its impartiality, its application
without fear or favour to the criteria to which it is obliged to hold in determining boundaries
of electoral districts as they are set out in section 16(1)(f) of the Electoral Act. The last time
this was looked at was by the Electoral Act Committee of 1975, and I am delighted to read
on page 11 of its report: "There was little if any criticism of the Representation Commission
and most witnesses believed that the commission as constituted carried out its duties in a fair
and reasonable manner." The committee had only two proposals involving changes, neither
being the one set out in the Bill.
The bodies appearing before that committee are listed on page 26 of the report, and
include the New Zealand Social Credit Political League, the witnesses appearing being B. C.
Beetham and S. Lipa. Did the member for Rangitikei not make this suggestion to the select
committee in 1975? If he did not, what has happened since 1975 to make him change his

democratic representation is the essence of the Electoral Act, and our electorates as far as

the commission's work, but they should have no undue or dominant influence on the

Discussion of Motions
The alternative to the Bill is to scrap political representation on the electoral
commission altogether-that is the only reasonable argument. In fact, that is the logical
extension of the Minister's argument. Under our electoral system, it is not votes that count,
but seats. Therefore, the question of the delineation of electoral boundaries assumes an
importance in the democratic process that it would not have otherwise. That is one of the
main reasons for attaching importance to the principle that minor parties-third and fourth
parties should be represented.
Motion agreed to.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

Mr MALCOLM (Eden): I move, That this House notes that the consumer price index all-

Dr Willcox is not an expert in the law, but I do not take issue with him on this. It may be

it would not be quite as fearsome a prospect as he claims. We must remember that in this
situation we are faced not only with the ordinary law-enforcement agencies of the State;
there is in existence an organisation that I must acknowledge to be dedicated, but, at the
same time, and weighing my words, I must also describe as prejudiced and ruthless. It would
seize the slightest opportunity that came its way to try to make a victim of any doctor or any
other person it thought could be made responsible for what it regarded as a breach of the
law. Whether it succeeded or not, the situation to which a doctor would likely be exposed—a
Supreme Court trial with all the attendant expense, discomfort, embarrassment, and
anguish is one good reason for a doctor to think twice, and frequently more often, whether
he should participate in the operation of the law in its present uncertain state, as I think Dr
Willcox was right in saying.
Beyond that, there is always the possibility that Dr Willcox might have been convicted
and exposed to extreme penalties, not the least of which would have been his being struck off
the medical register and deprived of his livelihood. Who could possibly point a finger of
scorn or accusation at any doctor who paused and thought, "Even if I believe the aims of the
legislation as it now stands are deserving and well-intentioned, should I expose myself to the
consequences that might flow from my engaging in an activity of that kind," particularly

Parliament can try to make the law on some social issues, but in the end it is sometimes
made by juries, which represent the majority of the people. The law, as it prevailed before
any of this legislation came into the House, gave expression to the will of the people. This
was demonstrated in the Bourne case in England, in other cases in Australia the names of
which I do not have at my fingertips, and particularly in the Woolnough case in New
Zealand, in which files seized by the Crown from the Aotea Clinic as part of the Crown
exhibits were made available to the jury, which, after considering the facts revealed in those
files, came to the conclusion that none of the cases-and they were admittedly the strongest
cases the Crown could have produced from the large number of files available—was outside
the law. As a result, they entered an acquittal.
I believe that was the voice of the people speaking, as it is speaking to us here; but all
too few are listening. I believe it will continue to speak and that our ears will gradually
become more and more attuned to it. One day we will get a law on abortion that is not only
civilised and humane, but in accordance with the wishes of the majority of New Zealanders.
Dr WALL (Porirua): I listened with some amazement to the previous speaker, who was
advocating a return to case law. Together with other members, I have heard him, over the
years, decry the uncertainty that has existed about the law in New Zealand because if its
dependence on the law as stated in legal cases. He sympathised with the medical profession
in its fear of a law that it did not understand as well as lawyers, and also said that even
lawyers found the law uncertain because of the conflicting cases. It is with some amazement
that I hear him now saying that although a clarity he formerly sought—not perhaps the type
of clarity he wished-has been established, he now wishes to turn to the type of law he
formerly condemned. I find his argument and his logic hard to follow.
I am also amazed at his concern about the attitude of Dr Willcox. As far as I know,
every doctor who operates has to accept personally the responsibility for the result of his
operation. It does not matter whether he is told to by that person or any other, he is
personally responsible. Every doctor who operates, knowing that the result of his operation
will be the death of his patient, is, as the operating surgeon, most certainly answerable for his
actions. Every time a doctor carries out an abortion he is responsible for the death of one of
his patients; there are no exceptions. He kills one of his patients, so it is surprising that a
doctor should say he fears being personally responsible for the operation. The manner in
which the patient may have been referred to him-even if certain legal safeguards offer him
protection that would not be offered other surgeons who kill their patients-is, to me, beside
the point. He has the protection afforded him by the two certifying consultants who have
referred the case, who have said that the death of this patient is legally acceptable to them.
But, like every other doctor, he is still personally liable for what he does while performing a
surgical operation, and I do not see that he has any grounds for complaint. Why should he be
unique?
However, during the discussion that went on in the Committee of the Whole, it became
apparent that although the majority wanted to go along with the recommendations of the
supervisory committee to make it easier for the committee to supervise the decision-making
that would inevitably result in the killing of one of those two patients, it was also obvious that
not all members were satisfied that we should take it as lightheartedly as some in the
community are prepared to do. It was obvious that some members agreed with me that when
one of a doctor's patients is most certainly going to be killed, the doctor should look at all
possible reasonable alternative methods of treatment. It should not be unreasonable to ask
that of a doctor, and I do not think that members would think it unreasonable if the doctor
was dealing with two patients of equal status.

absence of status of the unborn child, that I drew the attention of the House to the close
resemblance between the position we are now faced with in dealing with the problem of the
unborn child, and the situation in England. Our predecessors in another House faced the
same type of argument concerning the protection and the status to be given to a then
unprotected section of the community, the slaves. I know of no statues anywhere in the
world to those who, for socio-economic reasons, opposed the legal protection of the slaves.

Immigration Amendment Bill (No. 2)
IMMIGRATION AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 4 July 1978
Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru): I refer to the matter raised last night by the member for
Mangere who, I believe, sat on the Statutes Revision Committee when the Bill was being
considered. Maybe he was not there, because I am told that he certainly did not bring the
point up at that stage. The point in the amending Bill that the member for Mangere was
questioning was about persons who were detained awaiting deportation, and he brought out
the difficulty arisin because people could be detained without any redress or right of appeal.
He even suggested the formation of a tribunal to consider cases when there was an objection
to this form of detention.
The Immigration Act provides for the department to issue a short-term permit, and the
question that the member for Mangere raised last night involved those people who arrive
with inaccurate or incorrect papers, or no papers at all. I am told by departmental officials
that there is a perfectly adequate provision for these individuals to be issued with very short-
term permits to allow them to remain pending their return to their place of origin. The
airlines give an undertaking to the immigration division that when they bring in people
whose papers are inaccurate or out of order they will provide transport back to where that
person came from. I suggest that the member for Mangere was flying a kite to try to score
some doubtful political points on an issue that is really quite clear, simple, and
straightforward, and has been and will continue to be implemented by reasonable people in a
reasonable way. The point raised by the member for Mangere can be discounted in the
second reading of the Bill.
The main purpose of the Bill, and I consider it very important, is to allow the detention
of people who have been brought to the notice of immigration division officials as dangerous
or who possibily or potentially may create major problems. It tidies up the procedure for an
immigration division official to go to the Police, and for the Police to obtain from a registrar
the right to detain an immigrant who is suspected of having some terrorist potential. He can
be detained and deported without further ado.
The other major consideration, and I believe this was well covered by the Minister in his
second reading speech, is the formation of a deportation review tribunal, which can take
various important things into account when deciding whether a deportation order should be
quashed. Those matters should be mentioned briefly. In deciding whether it is unjust to
deport the applicant the tribunal would consider his permanent or temporary residence in
New Zealand, his age, the period he has resided in New Zealand, his personal and domestic
circumstances, his employment record, the nature of the offence for which he has been
convicted, the nature of any other offence for which he has been convicted, the interests of
his family, and, lastly, any other matters that the tribunal considered relevant. This is a good
move in tidying up and streamlining procedures in a difficult area of deportation of people
with criminal records and also in preventing from entering, when they arrive, those people
who it is considered could be dangerous.
The amendment is part of a continuing, and, I believe, successful progression of
amendments to the Immigration Act by the Government. It is a continuing process that is a
result of changing circumstances in immigration laws and procedures. I compliment the
Government on its record, and support the second reading of the Bill.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I am sorry to have to tell the member for
Oamaru that out of his own mouth he convicts himself of misunderstanding entirely the point
made last night by the member for Mangere. His ostensible reply to the member for
Mangere's criticism was that the department could issue short-term permits that would
enable a person apprehended at an airport to be released. That was the very point that my
colleague criticised-that it would be left to some administrative indulgence that might or
might not be available, depending on the whim of some public servant. Any decision should
be open to appeal to a tribunal, and it should be open to the person who is held in custody to
have the fact of his being kept in custody examined by due process of law.

The member for Mangere spoke last night, only to be denigrated by Government

my subsequent consideration of the Bill as it now stands.
I return to the point made by the Council for Civil Liberties. It could be said that in the
hands of a benign Administration the Bill is an improvement. However, the fact remains that
in other hands it could be made an instrument of oppression. I do not think the Minister in
charge of the Bill would deny that. Governments change, and who is to say who this
Government's inheritors will be 50 years from now. We might have a Government that
would want to use the provisions of the Bill for purposes that are foreign to the mind of the
present Government. We have to think of legislation not just in terms of tomorrow, but of
how it might be interpreted in 20, 30, or 40 years' time.
The Bill is concerned with terrorists, among other things, and one of the difficulties is
defining a terrorist. It is a truism that the terrorist of today is the patriot of tomorrow, and if
one wants an illustration one needs look only at the leadership of the State of Israel. I shall
return to that aspect in a moment, but I return to the point I was dealing with earlier. On
rereading the Bill it seemed to me that there were three similar concepts, and indeed in my
judgment identical concepts, dealt with in differing languages. For instance, in the proposed
new section 22(2) we find that a Minister is entitled to certify in respect of somebody who
"constitutes a threat to national security," and that is the first phrase I single out. I hardly
need remind members of the malign purposes to which that phrase was put by the former
President Nixon who, in the name of national security, excused all sorts of personally
advantageous capers.
In subsection (3) of the same section we learn that action may be taken in respect of
a person whose continued presence in New Zealand constitutes a threat to "public safety". I
also refer the Minister to the proposed new section 22A by which, in subsection (3), the
Minister may in certain circumstances direct a course to be taken in the "public interest". I
believe that all of these three phrases-national security, public safety, and public interest-
encompass exactly the same ends, and if that is so surely the same language should be used to
describe each of them. It is again a truism that different words appearing in a statute tend to
lead to differing interpretations. A court finds one phrase, and it finds another phrase in the
same Act. Its immediate reaction is to say, "These two sets of words must necessarily mean
something different. If it were not so they would be expressed in the same words." If we are
really aiming at the same objective, should we not have the same words throughout instead
of three different phrases intending to attain the same objective? If the same objective is

I draw attention to one or two other matters, because we deal first with the part in which
the Minister has power to demand that a person leaves New Zealand. He may certify that a
person constitutes a threat to national security, and in that event he may order the person to
leave New Zealand. He may order a person who is not a New Zealand citizen to leave New
Zealand if he has reason to believe that a person is a member of or adheres to an
organisation or group of persons that is engaged in or has claimed responsibility for an act of
terrorism in New Zealand or, in a later clause, elsewhere.
Let us look at some of those words "He has reason to believe"-going on from that to
say that this decision on his part may be examined on appeal by the administrative division of
the Supreme Court. How can the court, unless it brings the Minister before it or requires an
affidavit to be made, really go into the Minister's mind to determine whether he has reason
to believe certain things? I am not sure what form of procedure is contemplated by this. An
appeal that enables a court to examine a Minister's belief is something of an illusion unless
the grounds for the Minister's belief are stated to the court; and there is nothing in the Bill to
state just how the grounds for the Minister's belief should be exhibited to the court.
However, we pass on from that, and look at the remainder of the clause: "He has reason
to believe that he is a member of or adheres to an organisation." What is meant by that? It
was the occasion for some discussion in the Statutes Revision Committee on just what was
meant by adhering to a group. I am not sure how one would define that, and I should
appreciate it if the Minister could tell me what his department considers constitutes
adherence to, rather than membership of, a group. Indeed, groups have claimed
responsibility for acts of terrorism. Unfortunately, one can seldom pick up a newspaper
these days without reading that an act of terrorism has occurred, with more than one
organisation claiming responsibility-and it is really a peculiar concept of "responsibility" to
use the words "claiming responsibility" for an act of terrorism. However, there it is. One
reads of two of three organisations claiming responsibility.
Is the fact that a person is a member of or adherent to one of these groups a ground for
saying that he is necessarily open to be ordered out of New Zealand? I have no brief for the
Ananda Marga movement. I believe it has been intimately involved in a number of acts of
terrorism throughout the world. I also believe that many people in the Ananda Marga
movement are sincere in their, acceptance of the tenets of that religion and would take no
part in any act of terrorism. Is the mere fact that they say, "Well, we have some sympathy
with a group of this kind”, of itself to be a ground for simply saying that a person has no
more grounds of appeal than the right to challenge a Minister's belief that he should then be
deported from New Zealand?
I do not want to go into this at any great length. Some aspects of the Bill, despite its
examination by the Statutes Revision Committee, still lend themselves to improper use. I do
not for a moment suggest that the present Administration would put them to improper use. I
remind the House that, when we legislate, we legislate for ever—at least until an Act is
specifically repealed. We give to ensuing Administrations a power to use or abuse what we
put on the statute book. I acknowledge that, when we move into the world of terrorism, we
move into something that is not only indefinable, but also frightening, and we may be forced
into taking steps that 10 years ago we would not have dreamt of taking. There is some
ground for doing that, so I am not criticising the Government for embarking in an
experimental way on a new field.
However, it is fact that circumstances change. We are giving the Administration of the
day, whatever it may be, enormous powers in this Bill, and putting it on trust and on its good
faith to see that they are used to proper ends, and not for improper purposes. One always
hesitates to give a Government a power that can be used for purposes other than that for
which it was intended. The Government invites us to arm it to deal with a hitherto
unprecedented situation or set of circumstances, and we respond to that, but I draw
attention to the fact that we are entering a field in which powers can be used well or badly,
and we are putting people on trust. It is appropriate that, in passing the Bill or assisting to
pass it, we should draw attention to the fact that it could be an instrument of repression.

The member for Henderson quoted at some length from comments made by the civil

two different categories of people.
The member for Mangere complained the other day about parts of clause 3, under
which those who enter New Zealand without temporary permits or without correct

departure. These people are not the non-citizen group referred to by the member for

the category of persons to whom the Government had refused a right of entry, and yet they
presented themselves at a customs or immigration desk at a New Zealand airport.
I am sure that, had the member for Henderson thought about it, he would not have
suggested that we take those non-citizen non-residents into our system and give them all the
rights of access to our courts and tribunals. They are not meant to be here, and are defying us
by being here. Clearly, we must have a right to deal with them. What we have normally.
done, and will continue to do, is to put such people on the first available flight or ship and
send them back whence they came. Sometimes difficulty arises when they cannot be put on a
flight immediately. Do you prepare some sort of security arrangement at the airport for 36
hours, with rosters of police bringing out food and arranging toilet facilities under difficult
circumstances, because airports are not made for security purposes, or do you arrange for
these people to go to a secure place for 24 hours before an outward flight? The Bill
recommends and I support the provision-that a person in that category, who clearly is not
entitled to be in New Zealand and is in some breach of our regulations, should stay in a
secure place until arrangements can be made for him to leave the country.
The member for Mangere, in a very emotive speech the other night, said that this would
not happen in "good old Blighty"—it would not happen in Britain. For his benefit I shall
quote from the United Kingdom Immigration Act 1971. Section 13 (5) states that "a person
shall not be entitled to appeal against a refusal of leave to enter, or against a refusal of an
entry clearance." A person shall not be entitled to appeal. Last night, the member for
Mangere was suggesting, in effect, that a person who had no right to enter New Zealand,
who was not here legally, but was de facto at an airport, should be taken under the wing of
British justice in New Zealand and given all the rights of appeal of a person who had a right
to be here. Clearly, that is absurd, because the whole purpose of administering an
immigration policy is to say to a person, "You are not entitled to be in New Zealand." If the
member for Mangere's advice were taken, those to whom we had said no could fly to New
Zealand, hop off the plane and go to the customs counter at an airport, with no visa or
documentation, and be able to take part in all the procedures and privileges of the New
Zealand system of justice. That simply is not on.

Mr T. J. YOUNG: Yes, 3 months, and I point out to the member for Eden that that is

Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): I am delighted that the Bill has been so well

had wanted to. It did not move at all. We have at least moved. It is said that we have been
slow, but we have been sure, and what we have done has been good. Within our second year
we introduced the Bill.
I do not want to refer too much to what the member for Hutt said. Obviously he has not
studied the Bill, and obviously he did not understand that the young man from Tonga that he
met at the Wellington Airport had not come from Tonga; he had come from Auckland. He
would have been received in Auckland and given a temporary permit by the immigration
division to allow him to travel to Wellington to visit the Japanese Embassy. The suggestion
that there was a young man from Tonga at the Wellington Airport in some sort of
immigration difficulties is absolute nonsense. It is just as nonsensical as suggesting that in
these days a man could wait 3 months for an aircraft to move him out of the country; it is just
as nonsensical as suggesting that we do not have adequate arrangements with the
Government of Fiji to allow us to transit through Fiji and under proper escort people who
have to be returned to their own country.
The member for Henderson expressed the view that threat to national security, threat to
public safety, and threat to public interest are all the same thing. That rather surprises me.
They are all in the general area of threats, but to my mind it is nonsense to say that national
security and public safety are identical, and that public safety and public interest are the
same thing. I understand that the member for Henderson was at the Statutes Revision
Committee when the Bill was discussed, and he must know that these words were used
deliberately, after a good deal of consultation and discussion, and that they mean exactly
what they say, and are meant to mean exactly what they say.
The member for Henderson said also that we must legislate for 30 or 40 years ahead. In
fact, he said later that we must legislate for forever. What sort of nonsense is that? In one
part of his speech he said that 10 years ago we did not know we would need this sort of
legislation, so not to have legislated for forever 10 years ago is all right, but it is not all right
not to legislate for forever today. He feels that in 30 or 40 years' time the Government of the
day might not be so benign as this Government is. Well, if the Government is vindictive, if it
intends to exploit possible weaknesses in the Act, in 40 years' time, it will introduce an
amendment or new legislation. The remarks of the member for Henderson inight explain
why the Minister of Justice in the Labour Government achieved so little in the way of
effective legislation in 3 years-he was trying to legislate for forever.
We are trying to legislate for today and the immediate future, with a flexibility in our
outlook that will enable us to make changes if we have to. So I shall not apologise for there
being no guarantee in the Bill that its various provisions will be effective for ever. I accept
that, at some time, some Government or the people of New Zealand might want to make
some changes.
I want to say something about the non-citizen resident. The member for Henderson
tended to deride the member for Oamaru for his criticism of what the member for Mangere
said last night. The member for Oamaru has a great respect for this legislation. He is the
chairman of the immigration committee, and he knew exactly what he was talking about.
When the member for Henderson congratulated the Government on the introduction of the
Bill, and read what the civil rights people had said, and when the next speaker congratulated
the Government and applauded it for introducing the Bill, they should have addressed their
remarks and applause to the member for Oamaru, who replied effectively to the debating
point.
I believe the member for Mangere knew better. Last night he was just making a
debating point when he said that, when a non-citizen arrives at an airport in the United

Environmental Impact Reporting Procedures
2. Hon. Mrs T. W. M. TIRIKATENE-SULLIVAN (Southern Maori), on behalf of Mr
PREBBLE (Auckland Central), to the Minister for the Environment: What changes have
been made in the environmental impact reporting procedures over the past 2 years?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister for the Environment): The changes that I announced on
16 June last are, first, that the departments will now carry out their own environmental
evaluations, and public input will be required. The Commissioner for the Environment has
the responsibility to examine and to report on the effectiveness of departmental processes.
The commissioner will report to the permanent head on his findings, and to me. Secondly,
environmental impact reports will be used for major policies or projects for which the
preparation of an impact report is the most suitable procedure. The existing criteria still
apply. Thirdly, the commissioner may vary the process of environmental assessment and
reporting to suit particular circumstances. Fourthly, outside the actual environmental
procedures there has been an important change in the role of the Commissioner for the
Environment, who will be empowered to make independent submissions to planning,
licensing authorities, and tribunals within the procedures for the submission of a Crown case.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: How do the changes made fit in with the Town
and Country Planning Act?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot answer that in detail, except to say that the delay in
reviewing and updating the procedures was the result of awaiting the Town and Country
Planning Act to ensure that the environmental impact reporting procedures fit in with that

6 July
Questions-Oral
legislation.
Hon. Mrs T. W. M. Tirikatene-Sullivan: As the Commission for the Environment put in

of town and country planning on environmental assessment?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I cannot imagine where the member would find the reasons for that

environmental practices are being followed in evaluating various developments.
Indigenous Timber Export Restrictions
3. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) to the Minister of Forests: What restrictions are there
on the export of native timbers overseas?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): On 3 July 1967, Cabinet uplifted the
prohibitions on the export of native timbers, with the exception of kauri. Exports are
approved, however, under a permit system provided that sawmills are accumulating stocks,
in excess of local demand, and are not cutting above their normal capacity, based on a 40-
hour working week, or in any other way increasing their output to supply any other export
orders. Major shipments are approved only after consultation between the Forest Service
and the Department of Trade and Industry.

Huntly Power Station
5. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) to the Minister of Energy: What is the reason for the
further delay in commissioning the first generator at the Huntly Power Station?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): There is likely to be a delay of several months in
the planned commissioning date of April 1979 for the first generating unit at the Huntly
Power Station. There is no one particular reason for this delay. It is the result of an
accumulation of many minor delays that have occurred during the 44 years since construction
began. Factors that have had an effect on progress have been delays in the receipt of design
and engineering information from equipment manufacturers and the late delivery of
fabricated structural steel work. These factors have contributed to delays in the civil
engineering aspects of the project, which have been reflected on the progress of plant
erection. Every effort is being made to keep the delay to the first unit to a minimum.
Mr Colman: What effect is this delay of several months likely to have on contractual
arrangements entered into by the power station to accept Maui gas from 1 April next year? Is

Venison and 1080 Poison
11. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Health: Has he seen the article in the
Marlborough Express of 24 June 1978 in which it is reported that a helicopter has been seen
lifting game from an area where 1080 had been laid; can he advise whether deer carcasses
from 1080-poisoned areas are identifiable; and, further, what guarantee can be given that
venison exported to Europe has not come from a 1080-poisoned area?


## p. 1581 (#691) ###########################################

6 July
1581
Questions-Oral
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The Minister of Health replies: "I
have seen the report referred to. The Minister of Health has no responsibility as to the
quality of verison exported to Europe, but the following comments may be of interest to the
honourable member. It is not usually possible to identify the carcasses of deer that have
eaten 1080 baits, but sometimes the contents of their stomachs might be dyed green from the
dye added to the 1080-treated carrots. No guarantee can be given that exported venison will
not contain 1080, but the law requires all persons who lay 1080 baits to advertise in the local
press well in advance of the time that poison will be laid specifying the areas in which they
propose to lay poison. As far as the Department of Health is aware, no work has been done
with deer in particular, but other animals, including sheep, have been fed 1080 and their
meat fed to dogs, which are particularly sensitive to 1080. The results have shown that there
is unlikely to be any hazard from eating meat from animals poisoned with 1080. No one is
known ever to have been poisoned by eating venison taken from an area treated with 1080."
Mr Rogers: Can the Minister confirm that the helicopter was seen lifting deer from the
area where 1080 had been laid?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I pleased to be able to say that following this report an
investigation was undertaken. The report was proved to be false, and it was repudiated 3
days later.
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Could the Minister confirm that 3 days after the article about
which the questioner has spoken appeared, the Marlborough Express published another
article in which it pointed out that the helicopter had been carrying chamois that had been
shot right outside the poisoned area?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Yes, I can confirm that.

Home Insulation-Inflammable Paper
14. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) to the Minister of Energy: Can he confirm that a Pakuranga
factory manufacturing macerated paper insulation that has been installed in the ceilings of
thousands of homes throughout New Zealand with the encouragement of the Government
was recently gutted by a fire in which the insulation material burned quite readily; and, if so,
can he justify the continued Government support for the use of chopped-up paper as an
insulant since its claims of being fire retardant are clearly suspect?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): There was a fire on 16 June 1978 at a Pakuranga
factory that manufactured macerated paper insulation. To produce this material, waste
paper is given a fire-retardant treatment. While the untreated paper at the factory burned
quite readily, the treated material did not burn even though the jute sacks in which it was
stored caught fire. The insulation material produced by the factory is regularly checked by
inspectors of the Standards Association of New Zealand. Prior to the fire, it was last checked
on 22 May and found to be completely satisfactory. I am satisfied that there is no basis for
the member's conclusion that the fire-retardant properties of this material are suspect, and
that there is no cause for alarm amongst the many thousands who have installed it.
Mr Malcolm: Is the Minister able to reassure the House absolutely that the fire-
retardant qualities of this material are (a) long lasting, (b) water resistant, and (c) not in any
way dependent on the skill of the person putting the stuff into the roof of a house?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I have no specific information that would help me to answer that
question, but I know that this is an important aspect of insulation, and the Standards
Association watches the production and development of the product very carefully. If the
honourable member wants further particulars, he will have to ask a special question.

Venison and 1080 Poison
17. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) to the Minister of Agriculture: Has he seen the article in
the Marlborough Express of 24 June 1978-and I now find the Minister has read it—in which
it is reported that a helicopter has been seen lifting game from an area where 1080 poison
had been laid; can he indicate how this practice might affect export of venison if European
countries were aware of it; and how does the Government propose to control indiscriminate
shooting by commercial operators?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): I am aware of the article in the
Marlborough Express of 24 June 1978 reporting the lifting of game from an area where 1080
poison had been laid. The New Zealand Forest Service investigated the matter and
established that, while it appeared that the helicopter concerned had flown out of the Black
Birch catchment where 1080 poison had been laid, it was actually on its way from the Jordan
Station in Awatere Valley delivering chamois carcasses to a truck in Taylor Pass Road. This
information was subsequently published in the Marlborough Express of 27 June 1978—and I
hope the questioner has read that newspaper also. Regarding the possibility of deer carcasses
being exported to European markets, stringent requirements related to controls of poisoning
operations and procurement of game are strictly enforced by the New Zealand Forest
Service and by my ministry to prevent the possibility of such occurrences.
Mr Latter: Would it be helpful to the member for Onehunga if he read every day's copy
of this excellent newspaper instead of just Saturday's edition?
Mr SPEAKER: That is seeking an opinion, and I do not think the Minister need answer
that question.

Agricultural Training Course, Waikato
19. Mr REWETI (Eastern Maori) to the Minister of Education: Can he indicate how
many Maori youths are attending the Waikato Technical Institute agricultural training
course?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education). Like most technical institutes, the
Waikato Technical Institute does not record separately the numbers of Maori or pakeha
youths who enrol as students. The exact number of Maori students attending agricultural
courses is therefore difficult to estimate. However, a survey in late 1977 of students
attending courses leading to the certificate of farming, which accounts for 350 or about one-
quarter of all agricultural students enrolled in agricultural courses, indicated that
approximately 2 percent were Maori. On this basis it is estimated that between 20 and 30
Maori students attend agricultural courses at Waikato Technical Institute.

Japan-New Zealand Trade Talks
21. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) to the Prime Minister: What specific advantages
did New Zealand get out of the Nakagawa talks that were not available at the time of the
Suzuki talks in Wellington earlier this year?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MÜLDOON (Prime Minister): Following the discussions I had with Mr
Suzuki in Melbourne, and the official-level talks consequent on these, Mr Nakagawa came to
New Zealand prepared to move the Japanese position forward to meet us on a number of
counts. For reasons that I have already explained to the House, the precise details of the
agreement between the two countries are, at Japan's request, not to be made public. I can,
however, assure the honourable member that the proposals Mr Nakagawa put forward
represented a significant advance on those made by Mr Suzuki in Wellington.
Hon. W. W. Freer: How long will the details of any agreement remain secret?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No time limit was set. The reason is fairly obvious. I think
it might have been made public, and there is no secret about it, but it would make it
somewhat difficult for the Japanese in negotiations with other partners if it were seen
publicly that preferential treatment had been given to New Zealand. It is as simple as that.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of the fact that it appears from press announcements that the
major advance has been Japan's acceptance of some of our dairy products for school meals
and for aid, and that these details were made public earlier this year, why the secrecy now?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The member is wrong in his surmise. Agreement on 12
specific points was reached, and included some matters that have not been made public at
any time.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: How can people in our trading community exploit the so-called
advances in the agreement if it remains a secret to everyone?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: It is not really very difficult. As I said on Friday, the New
Zealand Dairy Board was consulted on the details relating to dairy products, and authorised
the Government to say publicly that the board considered that what was proposed was a
considerable step forward. Some of the other matters will be made public at the end of the
GATT multilateral trade negotiations, and the effect of others will be to increase the
demand for our products, and that will become apparent when tenders are called. There is
no need for traders, to use the member's expression, to have specific information, because

Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) said that on 14 December 1977 the General Assembly of the
United Nations had passed a declaration that 1978 would be International Anti-Apartheid
Year. The 141 signatory nations, including New Zealand, had decided to do everything
possible within their own countries to publicise the evils of apartheid, to isolate South Africa
further, and to combat apartheid. What has the New Zealand Government done to uphold
that declaration? The General Assembly had also passed a resolution to make 1979 the
International Year of the Child, and committees involved in that activity had been set up
throughout New Zealand. That action was fully endorsed by the Labour Party, but, in
contrast, no action appeared to have been taken on the resolution to make 1978
International Anti-Apartheid Year.
Through the South African Information Office in Wellington the South African
Government was pouring thousands of dollars into propaganda and was distributing glossy
and expensive books to schools and libraries. A former Prime Minister of Great Britain, Sir
Harold Wilson, had warned about the activities of the South African Information Office
there, because it had been using all sorts of tactics, bordering on character assassination of
leading politicos in Britain. There had been some pretty strange happenings in New
Zealand. One wondered what money was being used by the South African Information
Office here to disseminate expensive propaganda, and whether the Minister had evidence of
activities similar to those in Britain referred to by Sir Harold Wilson. How could New
Zealand prevent that sort of thing happening here? What was being done to publicise that
New Zealand was opposed to the evils of apartheid? Was the Government pursuing policies
to isolate South Africa further and combat the evils of apartheid?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) said that the
Minister of Foreign Affairs had, on 22 March, issued a statement to mark the beginning of
International Anti-Apartheid Year. His statement had pointed out that the year had been
proclaimed unanimously in the United Nations General Assembly, and was aimed at making
world public opinion fully aware of the repressive and inhuman nature of the system; that
states had been asked to commemorate International Anti-Apartheid Year by assisting
victims of apartheid, and that New Zealand would contribute to three United Nations funds
which did that; that the United Nations would hold a world conference on racism and
discrimination in August, and New Zealand would attend it, as it had attended last year's
conference in Lagos; and that the New Zealand Government found apartheid particularly
abhorrent, supported International Anti-Apartheid Year, and was actively considering
further measures to commemorate the year.
As far as he was aware, the books circulated by the South African Consulate-General
were very similar to books circulated by other consulates and embassies in New Zealand and
around the world. Such offices also circulated calendars, which presumably members of the
Opposition took from time to time. That was a proper function of a Consulate-General. He
had been assured by the Consul-General that allegations that had been made recently about
the activities of the South African Consulate-General were incorrect, and that its funds were
used for proper purposes. He had been asked by representatives of the media and people
who supported the line taken by the member for Grey Lynn to instruct the department to
investigate the activities of the Consulate-General, but he had no reason not to accept the
word of the Consul-General that he was proceeding in the normal manner. The National
Government did not support apartheid, as it did not support some other political
philosophies held by other governments.

New Zealand and abroad. In dealing with one of the most dreadful scourges the world faced

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs) said that the
national consultative committee had been established by the National Government on the
initiative of the Minister of Foreign Affairs, who had worked closely with it. The
Government had been represented at the meeting in question by Ministry of Foreign Affairs
officers, who had reported to the Minister. The committee had met the Minister
occasionally, particularly after the report had been prepared. The Government had adopted
a positive attitude to disarmament, and had gone to the special session convinced of the need
to review New Zealand's disarmament policies.
The Government believed that it should continue to maintain a balanced and realistic
approach to the problem of disarmament and must ensure that it preserved and supported
the strategic relations so vital in avoiding nuclear war; that it was unrealistic to expect major
agreement in areas such as SALT II and the comprehensive test ban treaty until they could
be effectively monitored; that any proposals by the small powers must be practical and
reasonable before there could be agreement among the major powers.
The Government also believed that it should put forward reasonable political proposals
aimed at making progress and at achieving eventual success. At the special session New
Zealand had put forward the following practical proposals: that the so-called London Club-
a group of nuclear suppliers-should be placed on a formal footing to establish an institution
in which the major exporters and importers could maintain a continuing dialogue about
transfer conditions for sensitive nuclear items-in other words, to ensure that international
safeguard machinery should be established among suppliers and importers.
The New Zealand Government also recommended that the Geneva Consultative
Committee on Disarmament-the negotiating body-be improved by rotating its
membership, particularly the chairmanship, and not by the addition of other countries. The
New Zealand Government supported a French proposal for an international satellite
observation agency to assist in verifying arms control agreements, and it also supported a
proposal from the Dutch Government for an international disarmanent organisation to
undertake a variety of functions, including verification. None of these proposals had been
accepted at the special session. That had not been because of faults in the proposals, but
because it had been difficult to get agreement from the 149 sovereign members. The
Government had taken up many suggestions made by the consultative committee, and had
forwarded positive proposals to the special session. It had not been the fault of the Minister
of Foreign Affairs or of his officers that the proposals had not been accepted.
He thanked members for their kind words about the work of the ministry. A few years
ago New Zealand had had only a few overseas posts in relatively easy locations. In recent
years many new posts had been established, some in difficult locations. It was incorrect to
say that resources allocated to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs had been cut back. The
amount allocated to general administration had been increased by $100,000, and another
$200,000 had been made available. Because of the sinking-lid policy the ministry had lost
eight staff members, but six temporary staff members had been appointed. Approval had
been given to increase the number of staff by 35, which had taken the total number of staff
employed to 571. The ministry would become more effective, and the decision would prove
to be well justified.

The Opposition had displayed a distressing lack of vision. New Zealand was facing not
only economic difficulties, largely brought about by the Opposition, but also very difficult
times regarding the future redeployment of Civil Service staff. The so-called sinking-lid
policy instituted by the Government had been necessary, not only for economic reasons
because of the proliferation of civil servants, but also because of the difficult decisions that
had to be taken. People could not continue in their present capacities simply because they
had been employed in the service for many years. On taking office the National Government
had examined, not only expenditure, but also the way in which people were employed and
the jobs they did. The objectives of the sinking-lid policy had been twofold; first, to take
hold of mismanagement suffered in previous years, and, secondly, to put a clamp on any
increase in State servants, and to redeploy people within departments where they would best
serve the country.
All around the world there had been a revolution against too much Government
intervention. The National Government would, as far as possible, always remain outside the
socialistic influence to take more and more unto the State, leaving less and less with private
individuals. It was surprising that Opposition members, who often got on their hobby horse
of increasing bureaucracy in New Zealand, had not examined the many facets of the sinking-
lid system.
New Zealand had been served extremely well by its Civil Service, but the Opposition
had failed to consider what was happening in the country. Had consideration been given by
the Opposition to the long-term consequences of the 12 000 fall in live births between 1970
and 1978? Within the next 10 years civil servants would be given the task of examining the
consequences of the change in the demographic spectrum.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) said that the Minister should state categorically
whether he agreed with the criticism of State servants made by Mr Bayliss, a former
economic adviser to the Prime Minister. Was it correct that New Zealand had squandered a
large part of its resources and that the Government was the worst offender? If it was correct,
what did the Government intend to do about it? Was it correct also, as claimed by Mr Leay a
director of the National Party, that one-third of the total vote was being wasted on public
servants? Would the Minister give that an absolute denial, and also the statement by Mr
Bayliss? Public servants were entitled to know whether the Government thought the
remarks made were correct, and, if so, what the Government would do. Mr Leay had
criticised the Government's management, and had said that the country could not afford to
continue paying about $1,600 million in social welfare payments.
Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora) said that Mr Bayliss had compared the efficiency of the
public and private sectors. At page 6 of his speech he had said that the public sector had
equal pay with the private sector, was a closed shop, had inflation-proof pensions, and total
job security no matter how bad the performance. If inefficiency among private sector
management were to be penalised by loss of employment, equal penalties should apply to
senior public servants. The speech had dealt with the activities and development of New
Zealand under successive Governments, and had been critical of investment and
employment patterns. Only a small reference to the public sector had been made in the
speech. The State Services Commission reviewed the efficiency of Government
departments, and could not regard them as sacred cows above criticism. When one
considered the total economy, as Mr Bayliss had, and total development, as Mr Leay had,
one was entitled to make such comments.
Did the Opposition disregard the comments in the report by the Controller and
Auditor-General on financial management? The report had been highly critical of the
financial management of Government departments generally, and had suggested a number
of ways by which it could be improved. Surely all members were interested in improving the
efficiency of both public and private sectors. The Labour Government was interested only in
building up the public sector to try to add to its basic philosophy of socialism. In its last

POST OFFICE AMENDMENT BILL
Introduction
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General): I move, That the Post Office
Amendment Bill be introduced. This is a small and largely machinery Bill to amend the Post
Office Act 1959. Clauses 2 to 9 of the Bill provide for occupational classification to replace
divisional classification and to discontinue the previous system of 5-yearly service-wide
reviews of gradings in the Post Office. Provision is made for the establishment of
classification and grading committees such as are found in other branches of the State
services. Clause 10 provides for an expansion of the definition of the purposes of the Post
Office to make it clear that the use of land and buildings for Post Office purposes includes
the use thereof for ancillary matters such as workshops, training schools and hostels, etc.
Clause 11 excludes the Crown from liability from any error, default, delay, or omission in
respect of any services provided by the Post Office for off-shore oil drilling and production
platforms. Other amendments cover the completion of the Post Office metric amendment
programme.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

Export Statistics
9. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert), on behalf of Mr BRUCE BARCLAY
(Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Overseas Trade: Has he seen a statement in the
June Quarterly Predictions by the Institute of Economic Research that "a large decline in the
volume growth of exports is estimated to have occurred during the year to June 1978", and a
later statement that "the overall pattern is still one of low volume growth in exports”, and
why is this happening during Export Year, when New Zealand desperately needs a
substantial lift in the volume of exports?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Overseas Trade): Yes, I have
seen that statement made by the Institute of Economic Research. The institute qualified its
statements by attributing the decrease in the volume of exports to the decline in the volume
of agricultural production in New Zealand over the past year. World economic conditions
have meant a fall in demand for most of our exports, particularly those of the agricultural
sector. Export Year started only just over 3 months ago. Its effects will not become apparent
for some time.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Apart from the export of primary products, what steps has the
Minister taken to increase the volume of manufactured exports, which at the present level,
with an increase of 7.9 percent this year, is the lowest since 1972?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: One of the first steps taken was to introduce Export
Year--and there have been further incentives, particularly the high-priority activity
scheme-and to arrange, through the Export Year Committee, a committee of volunteers,
headed by Mr Hellaby, for a series of seminars. I have been very stimulated by the
attendance at these seminars and by the enthusiasm for exports. The 7.9 percent increase
mentioned by the honourable member is on a narrow range of manufactures, but if other
manufactures are added, including the products of the forests, there is a much higher
percentage, and that will increase. They are manufactured goods. I believe we will reach
$1,000 million for manufactured exports within the next 12 months.
Mr Falloon: Does the Minister know that the overall increase in the volume of exports
since the Government took office is nearly 33 percent, in spite of the decrease of 9 percent in
the Labour Government's term of office?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I am well aware of the increase that has taken place,
and of the enthusiasm of New Zealand manufacturers, who really get on with the export
drive.

South Pacific Aid from EEC Countries
13. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) to the Minister of Foreign Affairs: Can he state
whether New Zealand has had any discussions with EEC countries on the need to co-
ordinate aid programmes from them to South Pacific countries such as Fiji, and if so, why
were these discussions held without the knowledge of the recipient countries?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): New Zealand
aid officials attending the biannual Development Assistance Committee review of the New
Zealand aid programme in Paris last October also discussed aid questions with the EEC
commission secretariat in Brussels. Over the last 12 months there have been some
discussions in Wellington with aid administrators from Britain, France, Germany, and the
EEC commission, in addition to talks with similar visitors from Japan, the United States,
Canada, and Australia. We have found such exchanges of considerable value, because they
give us a clearer idea of other donor countries' aid policies and aid administrative
procedures. We have found that these European and other administrators wanted to draw
on New Zealand's substantial and detailed experience of the Pacific countries' needs. In a
number of cases we have arranged for the visitors to meet also representatives of Pacific
countries in Wellington to talk about their countries' specific needs.
Hon. M. Rata: Will the Minister accept that a leader of a South Pacific country has
expressed his dismay. that, because the recipient countries had not been a party to the
discussions with the donor countries, their future interests could be prejudiced?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: My answer is a positive no. I have no indication
whatsoever of that, but I do have an indication that some countries, including Fiji, have been
concerned at the South Pacific Economic Commission's suggestion, which we were going
along with, of a full-scale meeting of the donors and recipients. They were not happy about
that. We are taking the opportunity of speaking to these people and to representatives of the
Island countries in New Zealand.

Road User Tax-Ambulances and Fire Engines
15. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Transport: Why do ambulances and fire
brigade machines have to pay the new road user charge?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): Ambulances and fire appliances
are subject to road user charges because, like all other vehicles, they use and damage the
roadway. In all cases the actual tax payable is governed by the vehicle's weight and axle
configuration, to produce a fair rate.
Mr Isbey: In view of the social and humanitarian work performed by ambulances and
fire brigades, would the Minister remove their road user charge?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: The honourable member knows that the Ministry of
Works administers the Road User Charges Act. I am informed that very few ambulances
pass the 3 tonnes weight, the point at which the road user charge comes into effect.
