would it be true to say that they pay less under the new system than under the old heavy
traffic licensing system?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I can only say, as the Minister of Works and
Development said in answering an earlier question, that the principle behind the Road User
Charges Act is that the vehicle owner will pay his fair share of the damage the vehicle does to
the roads.

Economy-Fall in Production
21. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Finance: Has he read the article in the
Evening Post of 29 June quoting the New Zealand Institute of Economic Research comment
on the economy: "The most obvious effects are reduced production, a high rate of
unemployment, and surplus capacity in industry. Production is estimated to have fallen by 1
percent during the year to March 1978 and it is still falling", and, if so, what urgent action is
he taking to reverse the trend?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Minister of Finance): Yes, I have read the article.
Government economic policy since October 1977 has been directed towards stimulating
domestic activity and reducing the rate of unemployment, while continuing to limit inflation.
The measures recently announced in this year's Budget give considerable impetus to this
policy. In this regard I would refer the member to pages 5 to 12 of the Financial Statement,


## p. 1615 (#725) ###########################################

7 July
1615
Questions-Oral
which was read in the House on 1 June 1978. There is already evidence of an upturn in
expenditure and production, and, indeed, of productivity. The volume of retail trade
increased by about 2 percent in the March quarter of this year after taking account of
seasonal factors. The measures introduced over the last 12 months will lead to a sustained
improvement in production, and eventually in employment.
Mr Isbey: What is the prediction for a stop in the growth of unemployment and the
making of more jobs available?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: More jobs are becoming available, but there is a curious
phenomenon. The first is that absenteeism is down sharply, and labour turnover is down
sharply. As the member will know, there are reports that people are having difficulty in
filling jobs because people will not leave their present employment. The result of that is
increased productivity, and there is more output per man employed in the labour force. That
means that the absorption of those who are unemployed will require greater production than
was the case when they were previously employed. It is a curious phenomenon, but is
accepted as being correct, that those who are employed at present are producing more per
man than they were previously. That means that to take up the extra unemployed we will
have to have greater production than was the case previously, because we are getting greater
production per man. In regard to the time when the increase in unemployment will level out
and then diminish, it is impossible to say that it will be in this month or that month, because
it is highly seasonal. My belief is that it will be in the fourth quarter of this year, but I do not
make that as a confident prediction because these things are incapable of precise prediction.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Inside his economic policy is the Minister satisfied that sufficient
demand is being generated to create increased production over and above increased
productivity?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: A former colleague of mine who has now moved to higher
things used to say "I am never satisfied". I am never satisfied in that regard. I am never
satisfied that we have the ideal policies for economic management. We watch very closely
what is happening, virtually from week to week, and if we need to stimulate further then we
do it. That has been my policy as Minister of Finance for many years, and I commend it to
members on the other side.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: If the expectations in the Budget are not met by increased
demand, would any fine tuning by way of a mini-budget be to stimulate and not to depress?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: That is a reasonable assumption. It is not likely to happen
in the immediate future, except perhaps in the area of house construction, which the
Government deliberately did not do much about in the Budget. Some measures were in train
before the Budget was presented, and the effect of those measures is being assessed. If it is
found that they are not having an adequate effect then the Government will stimulate this
industry again. However, it is being kept under close consideration.

SALE OF LIQUOR AMENDMENT BILL
Mr ROGERS (Onehunga): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Sale of Liquor
Amendment Bill. A number of problems have arisen since the Sale of Liquor Amendment
Act was passed on 16 December 1976. One of the intentions of that amending legislation was
to legitimise the recreational and social drinking activities of many sporting clubs, which,
until then, had relied on the less than clear provisions of section 219 of the Sale of Liquor Act
1962. Many clubs have found that, rather than the change to the 1962 Act resulting in greater
clarity in the law and a legitimisation of the status quo, ancillary licences that have been
issued have proved to be more restrictive in the requirements they place on the use of club
facilities. Any legislation that engenders disrespect for the law-in this case the licensing
laws-is bad, and should be corrected as soon as possible. At present we have a totally
unsatisfactory situation, and the Auckland Rugby Union has already been committed to
$20,000 in legal expenses in an attempt to defend the status quo before the passage of the
1976 Act.
I do not believe that it should be a Government prerogative to extend the regulation of
the sporting and recreational activities of sporting bodies. Rather, I believe we should accept
that these clubs are responsible enough to discipline their own members, even to the extent
of expelling members if circumstances warrant. The Bill I have drafted will, I believe, lead to
a more sensible situation that we can expect to be respected by sporting bodies, because it
will allow them to continue, with legal sanction, the recreational activities to which they have
become accustomed in the past decade.
The substance of the amendments is to broaden the scope of the criteria under which the
Licensing Control Commission must consider the issue of ancillary licences. It is intended to
amend section 112N of the principal Act, which was inserted by section 26 of the 1976 Act.
This section sets out the matters the commission must take into account when deciding
whether it should grant an ancillary licence to a club. These matters are: (a) the support
given to the club by its members and the public, and the degree of participation in its
principal activity; (b) the suitability of its premises, or any effect the licence might have on
the neighbourhood; (c) the club's reputation; (d) the public interest; (e) other relevant
considerations.
My proposal is to add another criterion, which would specifically require the
commission to pay heed to the club's past record and performance. The nature and extent of
any prior use of the club's premises, associated with its principal activity, must be
considered. The other changes may seem at first glance to be trivial and technical, but that is
not so, and they should have profound consequences. The first is to delete the word
"holding" from paragraphs (c) and (d) in section 65E. That does not sound very impressive,
but it would enable the commission to take into account the fact that social gatherings take
place in club premises without it having to be shown that they are held and organised by
someone.
The second change is a simple substitution of the broad phrase for a very narrow one.
Section 65E (3) requires the consumption and supply of liquor to be incidental to the club's
main activity. My amendment would delete the words "incidental to" and substitute the
words "associated with". It is obvious that many more activities can be associated with, say,
football than are incidental to the game. The aim of the Bill is to restate Parliament's
intention in words that are unmistakable and restore the high hopes we had for the new
general ancillary licence. Its advantages in promoting healthy sporting pursuits are obvious.
No less socially valuable is the encouragement it is intended to give to having friends meet in
controlled and congenial companionship, rather than drink for drinking's sake. I thank the
people who helped me in drafting the Bill. It is a very simple one.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): This is a matter of conscience for all

members on this side of the House, and I am concerned that, on the face of it—and I speak,

public interest.
The Bill appears to have been rushed, and to make claims that are not justified by fact.
For example, the member for Onehunga said that one of the objects of the 1976 Sale of
Liquor Act, which provided for ancillary licences, was to legitimise drinking in sporting

at the time of the principal activity which, in the case of golf, would have been a jug of beer
after a round, or, in the case of bowls, a drink after the game. It was clearly understood by all

Royal Commission, from whose recommendations the ancillary licences were established,
said on page 159 of its report that the Liquor Industry Council and also the New Zealand
Licensing Trusts Association were quite rightly concerned at the prospects of increased
competition from the licensing of sports clubs and further chartered clubs, and that such
clubs were in direct competition with hotels.
It should be emphasised that hotels have a legal obligation to provide amenities for the
general public, and that cannot be done unless they are reasonably profitable. The
proliferation of licences would have serious effects on the services provided by hotels in food
and accommodation, up to the standard laid down by the Licensing Control Commission.
Taverns, of course, are released from the obligation to provide these amenities only on the
condition that they pay 3 percent on gross percentages of liquor to assist in the
accommodation for the travelling public. So the royal commission recommended, as it did
for new charter licences, that cognisance should be taken of the economic effect on
established outlets before licences for sports clubs were issued. It is clear that the member
for Onehunga wants us to ignore that entirely and give sporting clubs the right to function as
taverns, without paying a tavern tax.

us to have that as a subject ground for merit. It could well be argued that the more unlawful,
the more illegal, the greater the breach of the law by an applicant, the more merit there
should be in the eyes of the commission, which has to decide whether to grant an application.

## p. 1619 (#729) ###########################################

7 July
1619
Sale of Liquor Amendment Bill
There is a profound and widespread feeling of resentment among sportsmen. The Bill
proposes to give expression to that and put in precise and clear words what they believe the
intention of Parliament was in creating ancillary licences. The general idea was to make legal
what was being done with doubtful legality and sometimes illegally, as long as it was done
within public acceptance. It is well known that many clubs functioned under section 219 of
the Sale of Liquor Act, involving the supply of liquor with coupons. Some clubs managed to
come within the threshold of the law and others were on the wrong side of it. No doubt many
activities that were carried on, whether just within or without the line of the present law,
have met with public approval, or certainly no public disapproval, in the neighbourhood of
the club.
Many clubs believed in good faith that the purpose of the legislation was to state that
what they had been doing up to the present would continue to be done with the overt
blessing of the law. The Bill sets out to do this by conferring an additional consideration to
be taken into account by the commission when it considers an application from a club for an
ancillary licence. The operative words take into account, among the other considerations set
down in the existing law, "The nature and extent of any use or uses to which the premises
may have been put prior to the hearing of such application . . .". It is a truism that every
application must revolve around particular premises being submitted as the subject of the
licence to be issued. The commission is to take into account the prior use of the premises
"for or associated with the principal activity of the applicant".
In another section of the Act the principal activity is carefully defined, so it is not
necessary for me to go into that now. A specific direction is given to the commission to take
that into account, because the words "including the provision or consumption of liquor,
whether or not the same was made or done pursuant to a licence or other formal
authorisation" are used. I imagine that those words were chosen to encompass the grey area
under which activities under section 219 were carried on in the past. As I have said, these
were sometimes legal and at other times illegal, so the words "whether or not the same was
made or done pursuant to a licence or other formal authorisation" are used. I hope that will
be accepted by the commission as a guideline to take a broad view of the activities of the club
and that it will take that into consideration as well as the other factors, namely, the character
of the applicant and the members of the club, and the clear limitation in the section that
there is a careful demarcation for the supply of liquor to minors. That would remain
unaffected by the Bill. Those two matters have been dealt with by the member introducing
the Bill.
The word "holding" will be taken out of two such clauses in the general section setting
up ancillary licences, whereby the commission is directed to consider whether the premises
will be used for the holding of special social gatherings. That implies an organisation, but in
many cases activity takes place on club premises without the necessity of formal
organisation. After-game social fraternising is a typical example. It is not organised, but it is
clearly a social function. Nobody goes to the length of organising the function, and whether
it is formally organised should not be taken into account.
The other consideration is to add once more to that paragraph a consideration that the
commission must take into account the use of the premises for the social recreation of
members of the sporting club or association, who are participants in the sport, officials of the
club or association, supporters of the club or association, or associates or life members of the
club or association. The Minister of Justice said that by introducing the words "supporters of
a club" one would admit thousands to the gathering. Taken in association with the
requirement that the commission should have regard to previous practice, it would eliminate
the possibility of the gathering of thousands taking place under the grandstands of Eden
Park. That might happen after a test match, but it certainly would not happen after a club
match. If the commission were considering a licence for a club at Eden Park it would take
into account the ordinary club functions that occur there on a sporting day, whether after a
Saturday game, a practice, or whatever.
In short, the Bill would give the commission clearer guidelines than it has had in the
past, and indicates that it is the will of the Legislature, expressed, as the Minister said,
through a conscience vote and not on party lines, to approach the problem of ancillary
licences for sporting clubs on a rather broader base than it has been approached in the past. I
believe the commission will appreciate clearer guidelines for its duties.

remain on the old basis, hopefully inside the law but, frankly, not necessarily inside the law.
The licence poses a very real problem of age, because at after-match functions it is very
difficult to limit drinking to those are are legally of age. For that reason—and I do not want
to elaborate on this, or take the time of the House unduly-I believe that we should do as we
have done in other areas of the licensing law, and make haste slowly. I recall that in its dying

Hon. A. J. Faulkner: It was 10.

those days than there is today-we now have licensed restaurants established, I think on the
whole successfully, throughout the country. I do not mean commercially successful, but
successful in terms of the licensing legislation. It has taken a while, but the matter is
gradually being dealt with in a pragmatic way, and I think that, by and large, what many
people feared would happen with licensed restaurants has not come to pass. They have not
become drinking dens or anything of that kind. They have simply made drinking, in
association with food, more civilised in New Zealand. I believe we still have some distance to
go with the lower-priced licensed restaurants, but possibly that will be developed over the
years. As I said, I believe that it is early days yet, and that we have to move slowly and
quietly.
I do have one other question I want to put to whomever is leading the Labour Party on

Roskill extended. There could be a danger in allowing clubs in a dry area to stay open for too
long, because that would be contrary to our philosophy of drinking in as far as putting a club

is confusion about the existing law, and I look forward with considerable interest to the

Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): Over the years that I have

Sale of Liquor Amendment Bill
approved, the opportunity to have legal access to liquor. The last speaker, in his attempt to

member for Onehunga has seen a particular problem and is trying to remedy it. I commend
him for that and support him, even although the Bill does not go in full measure in the
direction I should like it to go.
The proposed new paragraph (ca) is at the nub of the problem. That is why the Bill has
not only to be introduced but carried. The whole idea of ancillary licences was that the
legitimate sporting, cultural, or recreational activities of a club would be fostered; but the
way in which licences have been awarded under the legislation passed by the House last year
works, in many instances, in the opposite direction. My own golf club has an ancillary
licence. The Remuera club is pretty busy. It gives the ladies a set time to start playing. It
allocates other times for men, juniors, mixed couples, and so on, but because of the
operation of the ancillary licence the lady members finish their game when the bar is
required to be closed by law. If the club had been allocated opening hours it would have
made sure that all members would have been catered for when they were normally playing
golf; but no, the licence with which the club was issued says that it has to close at certain
hours, and open at others.
I do not object to a limitation on the total hours that a club should be open, but I do
suggest that the hours of opening should be decided by the club within that total. That is
really what we are trying to get at in paragraph (ca), which states: "The nature and extent of
any use or uses to which the premises may have been put prior to the hearing of such
application". It is not what the pubs want or what they tell the Licensing Control
Commission is reasonable; it is what the clubs want adopted for their activities. Clubs should
be able to register the hours in which they will be open, and be required to observe them or
lose their licences for a limited period, or even permanently, if they fail to honour the terms
of their licences. The interests of clubs in serving the interests of their members would thus
be recognised. If the total number of hours in which they can remain open is confined to 30 a
week, or some other figure, those hours will then be fitted into the activities of the club.
There is provision for special permits, but the clubs would know the penalties, and that they
would be required to police the Act. The liability would be theirs if they failed to discharge
their responsibility.
This provision places a responsibility on the commission to look at what the club is
doing. If the club has a palatial bar, as some clubs do, that is quite reasonable, but if the club
has a large area of ground upon which rugby or hockey is played and a small shed in which
people gather for a drink, that too should be acceptable to the commission, provided there is
no danger to health. It should not be the concern of the commission to say that a club must
have a bar area of 1500 sq. ft. and six wash basins.
Clubs have applied for licences in the belief that they would be able to carry on legally
the activities their members want them to carry on. I admit that previously the law was not
actually being broken, but that subterfuge was resorted to. I have carried a wad of tickets in
my pocket for years. My wife has boiled them up with my shirts many times, and the club
secretary has not been sure whether he has an obligation to supply $1,000 or only $500 worth
of liquor, because the tickets have been lost. It was very difficult for a club to keep its books
properly under the old ticket system. A locker system was often used, and some of the most
reputable clubs in New Zealand still operate that system, which we all know is open to
abuse.
The simplest system is to give a club the right to sell liquor under an ancillary licence and
at such times and under such supervision as the club decides. General prescriptions such as
the age of the people who may be served, the latest hour the bar can be open, and the total
number of hours it can open would be written into the licence. The proposed amendment
would allow the commission to have regard to the previous activities carried on in the
premises.
I should like to know why it has to be an overall factor. Most club houses have separate
facilities for ladies and gentlemen, so why must there be one rule for the whole club? I can
understand that, in terms of the Sale of Liquor Act, a tavern or hotel is treated as one
location for the purpose of considering the licence. The hours during which the lady

those that the men follow. The lady members of most clubs would be there during the week,
and perhaps for a limited time on Saturday and Sunday mornings. On the other hand, the
men may have a limited midday or early afternoon facility during the week, but most of their

FAMILY BENEFITS (HOME OWNERSHIP) AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. As I explained when I introduced the Bill it legislates for the upgrading of the
family benefit capitalisation scheme announced in the Budget. The capitalisation scheme
allows future family benefit payments to be capitalised for housing purposes. Subject to an
income limitation it is available to buy a new house, a previously occupied house, or a State
house. It also provides for adding extra rooms to an existing house and, in some
circumstances, for repaying an existing encumbrance on a house. The scheme has been in
operation for almost 20 years. In that time it has been of prime importance in assisting many
thousands of young couples to buy a house.
If the scheme is to continue to play an important role in meeting the housing needs of
young couples it must be upgraded to compensate for increased building costs and other
costs. The Government has recognised this, and the Budget announced three separate
measures to upgrade the scheme. The first, which does not involve an amendment to the
Act, was a 32 percent increase in the income limit, which, for a one-child family, has been
raised from $95 a week to $125 a week. This limit is, as before, increased by $5 a week for
each additional child after the first. The latest increase in the income limit is the third this
Government has approved since taking office in 1975. This in itself is an indication of the
importance the Government places on the capitalisation scheme. During the 3-year term of


## p. 1632 (#742) ###########################################

1632
7 July
Family Benefits (Home Ownership) Amendment Bill
the last Labour Government the income limit was increased only once, despite an
undertaking in its 1972 election manifesto that it would adjust the income limit every 6
months in accordance with wage and salary movements.
The second measure announced in the Budget is legislated for in clause 2 of the Bill. It
increases the maximum amount that may be advanced against the capitalised value of the
family benefit from $2,000 to $3,000. Until now, the most a family could receive by way of
capitalisation was $2,000. In the past that represented a reasonable amount to bridge the gap
between the applicant's own resources and the first mortgage finance on the one hand, and
the cost of a reasonable housing proposition on the other. However, in recent times the
maximum capitalised advance of $2,000 has proved inadequate. The Government has
recognised this and increased the upper limit by 50 percent to $3,000. A similar increase was
promised in the former Government's 1972 election manifesto. It undertook to "raise the
present limit of $2,000 to a more realistic level", but at no stage during its 3 years in office
did the former Labour Government take any action to honour this undertaking.
The third measure announced in the Budget relates to the extent to which an individual
family benefit may be capitalised. Members are aware that the present rate of the family
benefit is $3 a week for each child. However, until now, only $1.50 a week of this could be
used for capitalisation purposes. This has, of course, restricted the capitalised advance that a
family could receive in respect of each child. In fact, unless families were permitted to
capitalise a portion of the family benefit greater than $1.50 a week, increasing the upper limit
of capitalisation from $2,000 to $3,000 would help only those families with three or more
children. In order to obtain the previous limit of $2,000 it was necessary to capitalise up to
$1.50 a week the value of the benefit for three children. For this reason the Government has
decided to combine the increase in the upper limit with a relaxation of the provision that
allows $1.50 a week of the benefit to be capitalised. Clause 3 does this by allowing the entire
benefit of $3 a week for each child to be capitalised. This will allow all but one-child families
to receive up to the new upper limit of $3,000, provided they are otherwise eligible for
capitalisation. The maximum advance for a one-child family will be about $1,900.
Incidentally, clause 3 legislates for yet another of the former Labour Government's 1972
election manifesto undertakings, which it failed to implement. In its manifesto it stated that
where circumstances warranted it capitalisation of the entire family benefit would be
permitted. As with its other capitalisation proposals the last Labour Government took no
action to implement that undertaking. Last year about 3000 families used the family benefit
capitalisation scheme to help them obtain a home of their own. It is expected that the
provisions in this Bill, combined with the substantial increase in the income limit, will help
many more families to take advantage of the scheme.

taken to speed up the availability of Hansard to members and the General Assembly

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The Minister in Charge of the
Government Printing Office replies: "To improve the availability of Hansard to members,
my department is co-operating with the Legislative Department, which is responsible for
preparing copy. The preparation of Hansard includes time for reference to members,
subediting, and proofing before printing. It is by shortening the time taken for this pre-press
work that the availability of Hansard will improve. The aim is to provide members with
advance copies within 3 weeks of the spoken word." I am advised today that the library has
been informed by the printer that copy of 20 June is now available.

## p. 1643 (#753) ###########################################

11 July
1643
Questions-Oral
of the Australian House of Representatives and Senate?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I am not too sure I should allow that question, because there is
nothing in the original question about the Australian Hansard. It is an interesting observa-
tion. The Minister may comment briefly if he wishes.
Mr Lange: Is the Minister aware that in other Legislatures-for instance, in Australia-
the time between the date of utterance and the date of printing is very much shorter than in
New Zealand?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I am aware of that, but the arrangements made here can be
improved only by making the pre-press procedures more efficient. Under the present
method of production, Hansard is typed by the Legislative Department; members are given
an opportunity to correct, and that takes time, particularly if members do not return the
corrected typescript promptly; then the subeditor corrects; it is retyped; it is sent to the
Government Printing Office for reading through the optical character reading device; after
processing through that, it is read, corrected, and paged; and it is then sent to the editor for
final reading and correcting before printing. No specific improvements can be made short of
cutting out some of the processes, and I believe that in other jurisdictions some are cut out.
It is observed that this would lower the quality, and detract from Hansard as a book of
reference. Recently, the Legislative Department employed an additional typist for copy
preparation, and this office is revising its processing methods to speed up the turnround of
Hansard. In comparison with previous years, there has been an improvement in the
availability, and this should continue until we reach our target of 3 weeks, which we are not
far away from now.
Indigenous Forest Logging
2. Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata) to the Minister of Forests: Is he satisfied that the
present logging programme will not do irreparable damage to the North Island rain forest,
and that present logging will create a road through the middle of the area, which would
restrict the kokako's habitat?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister of Forests): I am satisfied that the revised programme of
State indigenous forest logging, which means careful selective logging and emphasises
subsequent regeneration of the forest as well as wood production, will not do irreparable
damage to these rain forests. I acknowledge the positive manner in which Forest Service
personnel, both staff and logging gangs, have responded to the recent policy change that has
replaced traditional clear-felling practices with those of selective logging, calling for the
development of new skills and new techniques. The logging by the Forest Service in north
Pureora is being carried out with great care to ensure that a wide corridor of virgin forest is
retained for north-south bird movement, while the decisions regarding the future of these
west Taupo forests are being formulated.
Dr Shearer: Is the logging cutting through an area that would be ideally suited as an
ecological reserve?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: The area where the logging is taking place has not been
recommended by the scientific co-ordinating committee as an ecological reserve, although
ECO, which supports the wildlife point of view, has proposed that the whole area should be
set aside as a reserve.
Mr Prebble: When the Minister was formulating his reply, did he consult the Minister of
Internal Affairs, who said on 11 January this year that he favoured a cessation of logging in
that area, and whose wildlife division has advised a complete halt to logging?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: I do not know what the question was, but I am sure that in my
comprehensive answer I shall include the answer to the question, which I doubt if the
questioner understood. In the west Taupo forest-for which long-term management plans
are now being formulated, taking into account the submissions of the wildlife service-two-
thirds of the total area of 76 000 ha will be set aside to be untouched, either as a protection
reserve or as an ecological reserve. The remaining area of about 28 000 ha includes
18 000 ha of forest that has already been out over, and 13 000 ha of virgin forest.

Police-Educational Programmes
4. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel), on behalf of Miss DEWE (Lyttelton), to the Minister
of Police: In view of the comments made by the former Commissioner of Police, Mr K. B.
Burnside, in the report of the New Zealand Police for the year ended 31 March 1978, under

the police have taken to involve themselves in schools and other educational programmes
aimed at improving the respect in which the law is held?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): Incorporated within the youth aid
section is the law-related education programme that has been established for the purpose of
assisting the Department of Education to develop in children and young persons an
understanding of the law and order responsibility of society and the role of the police in our
society. Currently there are 21 members of the Police employed full time in law-related
education in schools, and of the other 116 youth aid members approximately 50 percent are
employed part time in this area. During 1977, Police youth aid officers spoke to 317 319
children in schools, and 36 141 children visited police stations to achieve the objects I have
set out.

Honey Marketing Authority-Interest Rates
12. Mr BRUCE BARCLAY (Christchurch Central) to the Minister of Finance: Why is it
proposed that the Government should charge up to 9 percent interest on advances to the
Honey Marketing Authority when 1 percent is charged on advances to the New Zealand
Dairy Board?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): By a long-standing
arrangement, interest has been charged on advances to the Honey Marketing Authority as
follows: 1 percent on advances up to $180,000, and 5.5 percent on advances in excess of that.
The upper limit on the overdraft was increased from $380,000 to $700,000 in 1977. Because
stocks of honey on hand are larger than usual, the level of overdraft accommodation has had
to be temporarily raised above the limit of $700,000. Interest at 9 percent is being charged
only on advances to the authority in excess of $700,000. It would therefore be inappropriate
to compare this rate with the rates charged to the Dairy Board.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Is the reason for charging up to 9 percent to the Honey Marketing
Authority for advances, in comparison with what is charged to the Dairy Board, the amount
of political clout the Dairy Board has as compared with the amount the Honey Marketing
Authority has?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I thought I made it clear that this was a temporary
advance to help the Honey Marketing Authority in a period of excess stockholding and to
encourage it to take action on those stocks.
Police Resignations
13. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel), on behalf of Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) to the Minister
of Police: In view of the comments in the report of the New Zealand Police for the year
ended 31 March 1978 about the decrease in the number of resignations, which are now at
their lowest level since 1974, can he give reasons for the substantial decline?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police): There are several reasons why the
number of resignations has gone down. One is that morale in the Police is at a very high
level, and that has been brought about by a considerably improved salary scale dating from
October 1976 and improvements generally in working conditions. Aside from salary
increases, two innovations that have been particularly beneficial are the introduction of a
special allowance payable to policemen in sole-charge positions as recompense for the
extensive intrusion into the lives of their families, and a vehicle programme approved by the
Government, which will provide a police car at rural police stations, thus enabling the family
car to be used for normal family purposes.

was increased by $1 for every $2 of income earned over $100. The increase today is less than
that.
Accident Compensation Act Anomalies
15. Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei) to the Minister of Labour: What effective steps is he
taking to implement the 1975 National Party manifesto proposal to eliminate anomalies
created by the Accident Compensation Act whereby those suffering from chronic
debilitating illness are placed at a major disadvantage in comparison with accident victims?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): As a first priority in removing the anomalies
referred to by the honourable member, the Government has, since taking office in 1975,
progressively introduced the provisions of the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act,
which provides for financial and other assistance to be made available to disabled persons.
Apart from one or two minor provisions, the Act is now fully operative. The implications of
taking additional steps to reduce the anomalies further are being examined now.
Mr Beetham: Is it expected that equality will apply before the end of the year?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I am not sure what the member means by equality. If he could
define the word a little more, I would be able to answer the question.
Mr Beetham: Before the end of the year, are disabled people likely to be on the same
financial footing as beneficiaries under accident compensation?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I do not think that is practical, because many accident victims still
receive lump sum payments. I have not heard of a proposal that would give lump sum
payments to persons suffering from a sickness.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: As the 1975 National Party manifesto proposal gave recognition
only to an existing inquiry being undertaken by the previous Labour Government, can we
take it from the Minister's answer that the National Party has thrown away the idea of
dealing with this matter under the Accident Compensation Act?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The latter part of the question is fair comment. The
Government's officials committee is preparing a paper for the Cabinet committee on social
affairs on the question of sickness, and maybe that is what the member for Rangitikei was
originally asking about. I have no knowledge of an earnings-related scheme or provision for
lump sum payments.

Housing Corporation Standards-House Foundations
20. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of Housing: Can he confirm as correct that
the Housing Corporation requires older homes to have continuing concrete foundations or
concrete piles to qualify for loans, while Housing Corporation homes on new subdivisions
are allowed wooden piles, and how long is this double standard to apply, thereby adding a
financial burden to home seekers seeking to buy older homes?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: It is not now correct that the Housing Corporation requires
older homes to have continuous concrete foundations or concrete piles to qualify for loans,
and I deny the suggestion that the corporation is operating a double standard. In some cases
the corporation may require renewal of wooden piles where decay has occurred. Because of
the difficulty of replacement under an existing house, repiling is often easier by using
concrete piles. There is no technical reason, however, why wooden piles treated to
commodity specification C2B as defined by the Timber Preservation Authority cannot be
used where this is practicable. In some areas, continuous concrete foundations for new
houses are required because the soil is of inadequate capacity to carry roof loads. However,
the corporation would not decline a loan on an existing house without continuous
foundations if the piles had performed satisfactorily.

Hon. D. MacINTYRE: The figure for the preceding year was $10.4 million.

Electoral Amendment Bill (No. 2)
ELECTORAL AMENDMENT BILL (No. 2)
Introduction
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY (Wigram): I move, That leave be given to introduce the
Electoral Amendment Bill (No.2). I introduce the Bill because of the irregularities, mistakes,
errors, and omissions in the rolls now being prepared for this year's general election. They
are causing confusion, which is a matter of grave concern to the people. The present system
of enrolment does not secure maximum enrolment. The purpose of the Bill is set out in the
preamble. It seeks to make better provision for those people legally entitled to vote to be
able to register a valid vote on election day, and bring the New Zealand law into line with the
practice in Australia, Canada, and the United Kingdom.
Clause 2 amends section 60 of the principal Act by placing the responsibility on the
Government, through the electorate officer, to enrol all qualified electors. It states: "The
electorate officer shall take such reasonable and necessary steps so as to ensure that all those
eligible to vote shall be enrolled." Clause 3 clarifies the entitlement to vote by adding two
new subsections to section 99 of the principal Act. These amendments will help any person
eligible to be enrolled in any of the 80 or so electorates changed last year by the boundaries
commission. They do that by defining more precisely two classes of persons whose rights are
not clearly enough defined under the Act.
The objective of the Bill is in accord with the democratic concept and tradition, and
seeks to further strengthen our form of parliamentary democracy. In a democracy, the
objective must be to ensure as far as practicable the maximum exercise of the franchise. The
prerequisite to that is that those eligible to vote should be on the appropriate roll.
Today, the responsibility for ensuring that people are on the roll rests with the people
themselves, but others do in fact accept some responsibility for ensuring that those eligible to
vote do enrol. For example, political parties canvass in order to place people on the roll; so
too does the licensed trade. From time to time other organisations interest themselves in
enrolment. Notwithstanding the additional enrolment activities carried out by political
parties, the licensed trade, and others, a significant number of people eligible to vote in
parliamentary elections are still not on the roll.
Some years ago when the Public Expenditure Committee examined enrolment it was
advised by the Chief Electoral Officer and the Government Statistician that the estimated
non-enrolment was about 1000 in each electorate, which is a significant number of people.
At that time, the Public Expenditure Committee expressed the view that, although the onus
for enrolment must finally rest on the individual, it should nevertheless be the Government's
responsibility to do everything possible within reason to ensure that people who are eligible
to vote are on the roll. That is the purpose of this Bill as well.
The Public Expenditure Committee took as an illustration the Australian system,
which, like the New Zealand system, provides for electors to enrol. The Australian system
also makes provision for the electoral officers to employ canvassers to check that all
residents are enrolled. The canvassers go from door to door, in much the same way as census
enumerators do in New Zealand, and record on a schedule the names and addresses of
residents eligible to enrol. The schedules are checked by the electoral office. Where
residents who are entitled to enrol have not enrolled, the electoral office sends an enrolment
card to the elector, who is given a prescribed time in which to reply, and a warning that a
penalty will be imposed for failure to do so. If the elector fails to enrol, a second notice
imposing a penalty is sent out. When the committee studied the system the penalty in
Australia was $10. If the penalty is not paid the action is automatically completed by the
courts.
My attention was drawn to a newspaper item in the Christchurch Star, in which the
electorate officer for Christchurch Central was reported as having said: "Some people in the
Yaldhurst area had been wrongly informed by card that they were in the Fendalton
electorate." I telegraphed the Yaldhurst electorate officer: "Are you able to give me an
assurance that the name of every elector who was formerly enrolled on a parliamentary roll
and who now on the boundary change is eligible to be enrolled in the Yaldhurst electorate is
in fact now on your Yaldhurst roll? Can you also give me an assurance that every person
eligible to be on the Yaldhurst roll apart from those who should have been transferred onto
the roll following the boundary change and who up to 2 weeks ago had completed an
enrolment card so as to be included on a parliamentary roll is in fact also included on your
Yaldhurst roll?" The Yaldhurst electorate officer telegraphed that he could not give me that
assurance and directed my attention to the Chief Electoral Officer. I then telegraphed the


## p. 1653 (#763) ###########################################

Electoral Amendment Bill (No. 2)
Chief Electoral Officer, who was not able to give me that assurance.
Twelve months after the boundary changes assurance cannot be given that people who
should be correctly enrolled are so enrolled. If members cannot receive that assurance after
12 months, what guarantee is there that, with limited time remaining to the Government,
such an assurance is possible. I believe this is not a matter of law, but of administration. The
Government's administration has failed-it has to take adequate steps to ensure that people
are enrolled. I have been told that when people have approached the electorate officer about
enrolment they have been told that the officer's only function is to accept enrolment cards,
process them, give them a mesh number, and send them to the Chief Electoral Officer in
Wellington. There is no reason why the rolls cannot be programmed to print out a street
index. People can be employed to check the indexes to ensure that the people are on the roll.
The Government has the time to carry that out. It should make my Bill a Government
measure and put the system into operation so that there will be no doubt that the names of
people who are entitled to vote will be on the roll. Any Government that wants to achieve
the democratic concept of maximum enrolment and turn out of those eligible to vote would,
in the prevailing circumstances, do so.

moment, the Department of Labour employs some experts, but they seem to be bogged
down, by the Government's direction, in updating and extending an analysis of conditions in
awards and agreements, and in compiling annual statistics about the number of disputes in
industry. That is not important to industrial relations. Clause (h) directs the Department of
Labour to play a far more creative and constructive role in industrial relations, to research
every avenue of communication and channel of conciliation, and to develop new techniques
of bringing together the employers and the unions, so as to get away from the atmosphere of
confrontation. The Minister of Labour and other Government speakers have completely
overlooked the importance of this, and the Government should be condemned for not
agreeing to that course being undertaken.
Clause (i) states, "To establish centres for employer-employee education and training."
The present Labour Department Act contains no section directing the Department of
Labour to do that, and Opposition members are endeavouring to include in the legislation a
direction to the Department of Labour to establish such centres. Will the next National
speaker say he opposes that? Training is important at all levels, in the unions and among the
employers, from the top director to the foreman on the floor of the factory. They should
understand how to deal with labour, awards, and the human aspect of industrial relations.
Government members, in their ignorance of the whole sphere, have pooh-poohed that
suggestion.
Clause (j) states, "To ensure that industrial conciliation and mediation services are
developed to their fullest extent." These services are not developed, despite what the
Minister of Labour said. He said that three more mediators had been appointed, but that
should be considered in the light of the 1 000 000 days of industrial unrest in New Zealand.
The clause implies that the Government should ensure that, through the Department of
Labour, we have mediators all over the country, particularly in the key industries such as the
freezing works. The mediators should be mobile, and able to discuss issues with the
employers and the unions even before a dispute starts. If they know that a dispute is
brewing, they can get the feeling of the employers and the unions, and attempt to prevent it
occurring.
It is nonsense for any Government member to pooh-pooh those four clauses, and
suggest that they are incorporated in the meaningless words "otherwise howsoever". I
commend the Bill to the House. I hoped that the Government would accept the rationale
contained in the Bill, which is an attempt by the Labour Opposition to assist the
Government to ease the present industrial scene, and to go forward in an atmosphere of
industrial peace.

SOCIAL SECURITY AMENDMENT BILL
Second Reading
Mr SPEAKER: The Bill provides for the payment of a disability allowance, and as such
would clearly involve the Crown in an expenditure that is more than merely incidental to the
Bill. In these circumstances it is my duty to rule the Bill out of order. However, as I indicated
earlier, the second reading debate may proceed with the leave of the House. Is it the
pleasure of the House that the second reading debate should proceed? There appears to be
no objection.
Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. Last
November, when I introduced the Bill to the House, some confusion arose in the Opposition
camp, particularly with the member for Wigram and the member for Mangere, about
whether the Bill related to the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act 1975. In fact, the
member for Mangere went so far as to say that had the Government moved faster on the
implementation of the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act this Bill would not be
necessary. He was wrong on two counts. First, if the provision I propose could have been
made possible in the disabled persons legislation, I would have amended that Act, not the
Social Security Act. Secondly, the Government has now implemented every section of the
disabled persons legislation, and the proposals in the Bill are still necessary.
Although I enter the debate knowing that the Bill will not go past its second reading, I
am nevertheless delighted with the outcome of my first attempt to contribute something
worthwhile to the statute book, in that the principle of the payment of a tax-free, non-means
tested disability allowance to parents of seriously disabled children has been adopted by the
Government in this year's Budget. The 1978 Budget has allocated $1.5 million for this
purpose. On the introduction of the Bill the Minister of Social Welfare said that the proposal
would cost about $1 million, made up of $600,000 for disabled children and $400,000 for
disabled adults. The Bill departs from the Budget statement in that it proposes financial
assistance to those caring for a disabled person of any age. If, for the present, the disability
allowance is to be limited to those caring for children, the Government has been more than
generous in allocating $1.5 million, compared with the earlier estimate of $600,000.
I want to make two major points. The first is that we still do not have an entirely
accurate indication of how many disabled people live in New Zealand. In a survey of five
regions in New Zealand in 1976 the best estimate of the prevalence of intellectually
handicapped people was 3.5 in every 1000, or about 10 800 people. The same survey showed
that about 40 percent of all intellectually handicapped people were children, so we are
dealing with an estimated population of more than 4300 intellectually handicapped children
throughout New Zealand. Added to that, about 8300 people are on the national register of
the New Zealand Crippled Children Society, of whom between 5000 and 6000 are children.
Many of those suffer from serious crippling conditions such as cerebral palsy, muscular
dystrophy, and spina bifida, but many others may well qualify for the proposed disability
allowance. It is estimated that, with the three conditions mentioned occurring at rates of
from 1 to 2 percent of all live births in a year, the percentage of seriously disabled children
born in a year is from 5 to 6 percent of the normal child population. It is also thought that a
further 10 percent have significant difficulties-perceptual difficulties is an example. This is
the major problem in implementing proposals in the Bill or in the Budget.
This brings me to the second major point. Someone must ultimately decide about those
who fall within the scope of the definition of a "disabled person" and those who do not. No
doubt many people have read of the concern expressed by the New Zealand Crippled
Children Society's National Services Adviser, Russell Kerse. His comments were not
criticism of the proposed legislation, but concern about how eligibility for the disability
aliowance would be decided. In the Bill I have suggested that the application be
accompanied by a certificate from a medical practitioner, but that some discretionary power
be vested in the Social Security Commission to guard against any possible abuse. This would
enable the commission to require an applicant to submit himself for examination by a
medical practitioner, and also, if necessary, to refuse to grant or to terminate a disability
allowance. If a claim for a disability allowance is declined on medical grounds, or a disability
allowance is cancelled on medical grounds, I have proposed that an appeal board comprising
three medical practitioners be appointed for that purpose by the commission. This would


## p. 1677 (#787) ###########################################

11 July
1677
Social Security Amendment Bill
mean that the usual appeal provision in section 123 of the Social Security Act to the Social
Security Appeal Authority would not be required.
I am fully aware of the dangers inherent in this proposed course of action. An
assessment of disability solely on medical grounds may well overlook a very definite
humanitarian need when a physical or intellectual disability is less pronounced but the
financial burden is appreciable. It may, therefore, be necessary, in the preparation of the
legislation foreshadowed by the 1978 Budget, to re-examine the proposal in the report of the
1972 Royal Commission on Social Security in New Zealand for assessment to be made by a
competent expert committee, and for appeals to be heard by the Social Security Appeal
Authority. This is just one small step along the right road.
I have received letters too numerous to mention from people throughout New Zealand

nullified the hopes of a benefit in almost all cases." That is the sort of letter I have received

These letters show that in a great many cases one of the largest additional costs incurred
by parents of a disabled child is for adequate educational opportunities. Until very recently,
education at and transport to privately run pre-schools for intellectually handicapped
children added tremendously to the financial burden parents had to face. The budgetary
provision of an $8 a week allowance will certainly help in this regard. However, considerable
progress has been made in the education of the disabled since the Government took office.
In three Budgets, the Government has added an extra $4.2 million to special education. As a
result, in my own electorate, I was able to announce last year that a crippled children's
classroom would be built at Fairfield Primary School at a cost of $155,000, and that
classroom is now in use.
In 1976, 42 new positions in special education were created and, in addition, 6 teachers
were appointed to work with severely handicapped children in conjunction with voluntary
organisations. In 1977, 17 more teachers for special education were approved, the pre-school
services for handicapped children were expanded by authorising the enrolment of isolated
and handicapped children with the Department of Education Correspondence School, and a
system of relocation allowances for the parents of handicapped children seeking appropriate
education facilities was approved on a pilot basis. In the 1978 Budget provision was made for
a further 30 teachers for special schools, special classes, and clinics, and itinerant positions as
teachers of reading and teachers of deaf children; 4 positions for advisers to provide
specialist guidance for parents of handicapped children; additional teaching positions for
special care services for severely handicapped children; and payment of transport assistance

Last year's Budget implemented the recommendations of the Advisory Council for the
Disabled, paying for disabled people to undertake treatment, examinations, and
assessments. It further extended the subsidy programme for approved organisations
providing residential care, and gave loan assistance to disabled people to buy motorcars. It
also provided loan assistance for breast prosthesis.
This year's Budget continued to extend provisions for the disabled, inasmuch as it
provided suspensory loans for alterations to houses to make them better suited for use by the
disabled. As I have already mentioned, it also provided for a non-taxable allowance of $8 for
each disabled child-which also earned the thanks and commendation of Mr Munro. The
Bill seeks to give broader assistance to disabled people. The member for Hamilton East

problem of his handicap, of the pain, and of learning to adjust, and it is socially unjust that
parents who look after their handicapped children should, in addition to those personal
problems, have to suffer financial hardship. The Bill means that disabled people will
automatically benefit from provisions made by the Government, the cost of which has been
quoted by the Minister of Health as $1 million. I believe that this money will be well spent.

garden and about the house. The handicapped cannot achieve these savings. According to
the New Zealand Crippled Children Society, the living costs of a disabled person are
approximately 25 percent higher than normal. This estimate includes housing, clothing,
food, heating, and all other expenses. The disabled must have a car adapted for them.
Disabled children have to be transported by motorcar or by taxi.

Mr Hunt: They do a good job.
MARILYN WARING: As the member for New Lynn said, they do a good job. These
families are, of necessity, one-income families because the mother--and it seems it is always
the mother-is constantly tied to the home caring for the disabled child. The previous
Government, and this Government, have adopted the policy of getting disabled children out
of the institutions as much as possible and of having them cared for in the community. It is
easy for those of us not directly involved to say that that is the best method of caring for the
children. The attitude of the parents is reflected in what the Minister of Health said when he
addressed the Psychopaedic Parents Association in 1977. He said that the position of parents
could only be theoretically appreciated by people not personally involved.
Parents of psychopaedic children have come to me, from time to time, worried about
increasing expenditure. Much of this was cited by the member for Western Hutt. Travel is
involved in going to Hamilton, the main centre where services are available. Frequently, a
large car is needed for a multi-handicapped child who cannot sit. Doctors' and specialists'
fees must be met. Furniture of a special type might be required, and, inevitably, there is the
continuous replacement of household crockery and furniture, because of breakages by
strong, excited youngsters. Higher insurance premiums have to be met, and special
equipment is needed for handicapped children. They need special footwear and clothes, and
often special diets are necessary. Frequently sections have to be fenced, and gates
padlocked.
In addition to all that, there are problems of short-stay placement costs, and relief for
the family to enable it to go into town or to attend family gatherings. Those problems are
immeasurable in terms of financial assistance. Problems are caused perhaps by resentment
by other children in the family, and the fact that these are overcompensated or
undercompensated for. Economic restraints are imposed on a one-income family, and there
is often the problem of finding a baby sitter for a psychopaedic child. There is no doubt that
the family with a handicapped child faces a changed life style that revolves around that child,
and this cannot be calculated in terms of dollars. But the proposed financial assistance will
alleviate many of the hardships that the life style imposes on many families.
It is interesting to note in the recently published Johnson report the reference to
children with special needs. It mentions that the parents of handicapped children suffer acute
stresses that affect their marriage, and that priority is needed for giving assistance and advice
to parents of psychopaedic children after the birth of their children. From my
communications with the Psychopaedic Parents Association, there is no doubt that the
economic restraints imposed by having a handicapped child can in many cases lead to marital
disharmony, and the $8 a week that is proposed in the Bill, and which has been superseded
by the Government, will be most welcome.
I noted earlier that it is probably very much welcomed by many mothers, and it is

MASSAGE PARLOURS BILL
Second Reading
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. In the course of introducing this measure I stated that the Bill is the
Government's response to the feeling, shared by the community and the police, that many of
the so-called massage parlours operating in our cities are merely fronts for those seeking to
make a living from prostitution and drugs. I also indicated that the way in which those
establishments are operated makes it difficult, if not impossible, for the police to obtain
sufficient evidence of prostitution offences.
The Bill has nothing to do with criminal prostitution, nor is it a measure designed to
enforce a particular view of sexual morality. It is wholly concerned with combating what is
perceived as the steady spread of organised criminal ventures into large-scale prostitution.
All the measures of control set out in the Bill have been included only in so far as they are
necessary to effect the purpose of the Bill. As members will recall, the Bill was referred to
the Statutes Revision Committee, where its provisions were exhaustively studied after the
committee heard a considerable number of submissions, some of which were given on oath.
Although other members of the committee will no doubt have something to say about
those proceedings, I am satisfied that nothing in the evidence presented to the committee
allays the concern to which this Bill is the response-namely, that there is widespread
prostitution in massage parlours, and that some massage parlour owners are taking
advantage of that situation in such a way as to avoid offending against the brothel-keeping
provisions of the Crimes Act 1961. In the main, this is accomplished by the proprietor hiring
a masseuse, whom he knows to be a prostitute, and in the full knowledge that a customer is
attracted to his premises by the likelihood that sex will be obtained, albeit at a further price.
Apart from the fee for a massage, the proprietor does not obtain any part of the price
charged by the masseuse, and he turns his back on what is taking place so that he cannot be
charged with brothel-keeping, and he committs no other offence. That is the situation the
Bill is designed to prevent.
There are two main ways in which the situation I have outlined could be prevented.
First, by changing the criminal law to ensure that a charge of brothel-keeping can more easily
be proved, perhaps by imposing vicarious responsibility on the owner of a massage parlour;
and, secondly, to licence those who seek to operate such establishments. The former course
was contemplated, but rejected as being unduly repressive. In considering the submissions
made to it the Statutes Revision Committee made several substantive changes to the Bill as
introduced, and I shall deal with those in context. I should add that the police are concerned
not so much because drug offending is taking place on those premises, but because the
proceeds from operating massage parlours are used to finance criminal offences, including
drug dealing, and that drug contacts are made at or from massage parlours.
Part I of the Bill makes provision for licensing those who seek to operate a massage
parlour. A licence will be issued to such a person only after a magistrate is satisfied that the
applicant has not been convicted of an offence involving prostitution or drugs within the
previous 10 years and that he or she is otherwise a proper person to operate such a business.
In determining whether the latter criterion has been satisfied, the magistrate may be assisted
by evidence from the Police, to whom copies of all applications for licences must be sent.
Part I also makes provision for the renewal of licences, a procedure that again requires
the intervention of the police. Hearing the evidence, the Statutes Revision Committee
became aware that several occupational groups whose activities are manifestly not within the
contemplation of the Legislature, could come within the definition of operating a massage
parlour. Clause 3 makes provision for such persons and excludes those who are licensed to
undertake massage under some other Act, or who massage sportsmen or sportswomen,
having been engaged to do so by any sporting body. The rule also applies to cultural events.
Beauticians are excluded from the provisions of the Bill. Health studios were not excluded
from the provisions and proprietors who gave evidence welcomed the provisions of the Bill
as they apply to health studios.


## p. 1686 (#796) ###########################################

1686
11 July
Massage Parlours Bill
Part II prescribes the manner in which a licensee must supervise his business. In the Bill
as introduced there was provision for certificates of approval to be issued to managers and
masseuses. Although there is good reason for a manager to be certified by a magistrate to be
a fit and proper person to manage a massage parlour, the Statutes Revision Committee
considers that the requirment for massage parlour employees to be approved should be
struck out. The certificate of approval provisions in question were thought to be not only
unwieldy, but also out of keeping with the intention of the Bill-namely, to place a heavy
onus on licensees to ensure that improper or criminal conduct does not occur on their
premises.
Those who are employed as masseurs or masseuses in massage parlours are not,
however, entirely beyond the reach of the Bill. Under new provisions inserted by the
Statutes Revision Committee an employee may be objected to by the police after he or she
has commenced employment. A register of those who are employed by a licensee must be
available for police inspection. When an act of prostitution has been committed the police
will be able to complain to a magistrate that that employee is not a proper person to be
employed as a masseur or masseuse. No persons may be employed as a masseur or a
masseuse if they are under the age of 18 years, if they have been convicted of a drug offence
or a prostitution offence within the previous 10 years.
Day-to-day control of massage parlours is provided for under Part III of the Bill. It also
provides that the police, or other persons with the leave of the court, may make a complaint
against a licensee. A complaint may be made where a licensee has committed an offence
relating to drugs or prostitution or to an offence against the Massage Parlours Act within the
previous 3 years. Most importantly it is a ground for complaint, when a drug or prostitution
offence has occurred in a massage parlour, that the offence is attributable to the licensee's
negligent supervision of his business. The provision allowing a magistrate to suspend a
licence without notice, after a complaint has been made, has been struck out by the Statutes
Revision Committee and replaced by a provision allowing the licence to be suspended after
notice. This part of the Bill contains the provision under which the police may complain
against a masseur or masseuse on the grounds I have already indicated. In tandem with the
provisions of this Part of the Bill are the provisions in clause 32 that allow police to enter and
inspect licensed premises and when they have a warrant, to use force. A decision that affects
an applicant for a licence under the Act, or affects a person who is a licensee or who is the
holder of a certificate of approval, may be appealed against in the Supreme Court.
One other matter arising from the control of massage parlours requires specific
mention. Recent decisions in the Supreme Court have made it clear that in only a few cases
will a masseuse who commits an act of prostitution be guilty of the offence of brothel
keeping a charge that is usually brought in those circumstances. To counter that situation
the Bill provides that in any case where a masseur or a masseuse commits an act of
prostitution, that person may be the subject of a complaint. If the complaint is proved a
magistrate may order that the person be no longer employed in a massage parlour. Any
person against whom such an order is made commits an offence if he or she seeks or gains
employment in a massage parlour, and any person employing such a masseur or masseuse
also commits an offence if he knows that an order has been made against a person whom he
employs.
Summarising, the Bill is designed to prevent organised criminal incursions into
prostitution, which there is good reason to believe is now occuring in some massage parlours.
It is for this reason, and this reason alone, that the Bill has been introduced. The situation is
to be controlled by a licensing system that allows the police to have considerable influence in
determining who should be licensed to operate a massage parlour and who should be
approved to manage such an institution.
There is also a measure of control over the sort of person who can be employed as a
masseur or masseuse. These controls, and the complaint procedure, are designed to do no
more than provide a mechanism whereby the primary purposes of the Bill can be effected. It
is perhaps regrettable that Parliament must create another area where a commercial
undertaking must be licensed, but it is clear that no other course is open if the Government is
to remedy the present situation in massage parlours. I commend this Bill to the House.

Hon. G. F. Gair: A point of order, Mr Speaker. The member speaking made a claim

Hon. G. F. Gair: The member for Porirua completely missed the point I was making.

Mr SPEAKER: Perhaps I could rule on this before the House adjourns. It would be out

Speaker's Ruling
WEDNESDAY, 12 JULY 1978
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
SPEAKER'S RULING
Mr SPEAKER: Yesterday a notice of motion was lodged on behalf of the member for
Dunedin North dealing with a quotation from the National Business Review about Matai
Industries. I was not aware at the time, but it was drawn to my attention in the House
yesterday afternoon, that that motion could infringe the sub judice rule in Standing Order
183. I have been informed that the case has been set down for hearing by the Supreme
Court. Therefore, it comes under Standing Order 183-matters awaiting judicial decisions.
It might be pertinent to point out that, although matters are before the court, this does not
preclude the House from discussing them or from legislating on any matter that it wishes, in
spite of the fact that there may be an infringement of the rule of sub judice. Parliament's
right to legislate is paramount. The acceptance of a motion of this sort is at my discretion,
and the discretion I exercise is on the basis of whether there is real or substantial danger of
prejudice to the trial of the case-in other words, prejudice to justice being done in the
court. In my opinion, there is no justification for departing from the sub judice rule on this
occasion. Therefore, I have to rule that the motion is out of order.
NOTICE OF MOTION-ADMISSIBILITY
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I give notice that next sitting day I shall move, That
this House notes with no surprise the resignation of Mr G. A. Turney, Chairman of the
Ngaio branch of the National Party in Wellington Central, and this House recalls the

Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): A point of order, Mr Speaker. I ask that you check
the text of that notice of motion, because there is a glaring inaccuracy in it, which I think will
be corrected in the Evening Post today. Mr Turney's resignation has not been accepted.
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I am prepared to table a copy of this morning's
Dominion, on the front page of which the member will find that statement in rather large
headlines. It may be that the reporter should have checked his information.
Mr SPEAKER: I shall certainly have a look at the notice of motion. Again, all I have to
do is to make sure that if a notice of motion includes a reference to a newspaper report the
statement made is accurately based on the report. I shall certainly not shoulder any
responsibility for the accuracy or otherwise of reports in the news media.
ORAL QUESTIONS
Defamation Actions, Ministers
1. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) to the Attorney-General: In view of the fact that
Ministers' costs and damages in defamation actions have been paid by the State, can he state
whether damages awarded to any Minister in future would be retained by the Minister or
paid into the Public Account?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Attorney-General): The reasons that justify the State
supporting a Minister who is sued in a defamation action do not apply to a Minister suing to
recover damages for defamation. There is no precedent for the State paying the costs of a
Minister who is plaintiff in such a case. If a Minister sues personally he will presumably, like
any other member, retain any damages he recovers.

Citizenship Applications
2. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East),
to the Minister of Internal Affairs: Can he indicate the average length of time taken to
process a request for New Zealand citizenship in 1975, 1976, 1977, and 1978?

Meadowbank St. John's-Proposed School
3. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) to the Minister of Education:
Have any plans been made or has site development been undertaken for the school proposed
to be built in the area of land currently being developed for sale by the St. John's College
Trust in the Meadowbank St. John's district?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The Auckland Education Board hopes
to undertake site development work this year for the proposed Waiatarua School, depending
on completion of negotiations with the St. John's College Trust Board by the Ministry of
Works and Development for the purchase of the site.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Can the Minister indicate when it is intended to build on the
developed site?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The negotiations for the purchase of the land have been
proceeding since 1974. It will not be possible to give an answer to that question until the land
is purchased and satisfactory arrangements have been made between the trust board and the

obtaining fresh valuations to enable the negotiations to continue, and I hope an agreement
will be reached before the end of the year. It is proposed that the school will be opened in
1981.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: How many children of primary school age are expected to go to the
school from the development area?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: That will depend upon the rate of growth and the development
of the area itself. I presume that the picture will become clearer as the development
proceeds, but until such time as the development begins and the houses are constructed we
will not have an accurate picture.
Pinus Radiata for Finishing Timber
4. Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North), on behalf of Mr. LATTER (Marlborough), to
the Minister of Forests: To what extent can good-quality kiln-dried Pinus radiata replace
native timbers in finishing uses?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The Minister of Forests replies: "On
the basis that 'finishing' uses embrace mouldings, panelling, door and door frames,
staircases, balustrades, cabinet work, and window joinery, good quality kiln-dried Pinus
radiata is used in place of native timbers for many of these uses to some extent. However,
when Pinus radiata is used for these purposes it is generally either painted or stained. There
are many specifiers, manufacturers, and users-in the sense of ultimate owners-who do not.
regard good-quality kiln-dried Pinus radiata as a suitable alternative to native timbers for
these uses on the grounds that its physical and/or decorative properties are unsuitable. For
these reasons many specifiers and joiners demand native timbers or alternatively selected
imported timbers for finishing uses."
Economic Comment-Mr Barrie Leay
5. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) to the Minister of National Development: Does he intend to
counter or correct the reported statement of Mr Barrie Leay, the National Party's General
Director, that "New Zealand squandered a large part of its resources and the Government
was the worst offender"?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of National Development): This question draws our
attention to the importance of not quoting out of context. I presume the honourable member
is referring to Mr Leay's address, "It's time to think", given to the second Colenso seminar


## p. 1696 (#806) ###########################################

1696
12 July

held in Auckland in November last year. Mr Leay, in the context of a wide-ranging speech
concerned more with the future than the past, was seeking to stress that, as a community, we
tended to squander too large a proportion of our resources. It was in reference to this point
that he felt Governments were usually the worst offenders. It is not possible, of course, to
see "Government" as a single industry. The activities of central government cover a
multitude of areas. If one looks at Government trading departments it is true that, on
average, their profitability is less than average profitability in the private sector. There are
many reasons for this, not all related to efficiency. The Government is at present looking at
the financial objectives of trading departments with a view to improving efficiency, and in

standing that sometimes one or two sentences taken out of context can be misused against
him. That, in fact, was the basis of this question.
