Natural Gas Distribution
8. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) to the Minister of Energy: What plans does the
Government have for the extension to the pipelines distribution system of the Natural Gas
Corporation of N.Z. Ltd., and what is the estimated timetable for the extensions?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy): The Government has approved the plans of the
Natural Gas Corporation of New Zealand Ltd. for the construction of pipeline extensions to
link the Maui on-shore production station at Oaonui with the company's treatment plant at
Kapuni. It is expected that this pipeline will be completed towards the end of next year and
will enable Maui gas to be treated at the Natural Gas Corporation's Kapuni plant to a
specification compatible with Kapuni gas. Another pipeline extension will transport Maui
gas from the Maui pipeline near Te Awamutu to the Kinleith plant of New Zealand Forest
Products Ltd. It is envisaged that the pipeline should come into operation during 1980, but
the precise timing depends largely on when the Kinleith plant can accept Maui gas.
State House Rentals
9. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) to the Minister of Housing: What is the present formula used
to assess State house rentals?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The present formula used to assess
State house rentals is one-sixth of family income up to $100 per week; thereafter it increases
to 30c in the dollar for a weekly income between $101 and $140 and it increases to 40c in the
dollar for income exceeding $140 a week. The rent is reviewed annually and may not be
increased by $10 a week in any one year and may not exceed the fair or market rent for the
particular property.
Mr Christie: In assessing family income is a working wife's income assessed with the
husband's?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: There are additions to the basic formula that I have given. In
the case of a working wife two-thirds of her income is taken into account.
Mr Christie: Would the Minister take steps to publicise the formula so that people are in
no doubt about how State rentals are assessed?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I do not think there is any particular need for that, but I have
no objection. Judging by the number of letters I receive, very few people are in any doubt


## p. 1698 (#808) ###########################################

Questions-Oral
about how their State house rentals are assessed.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: Since inflation has been at the rate of 50 percent in the last 3 years
does the Minister not think it is time to review the $100 a week figure?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: Since the Labour Government did nothing when inflation
was a great deal higher than 50 percent I feel no special urge to do anything. As I stated in

mainland Turkish occupation of nearly half of the territory of our Commonwealth brother
country of Cyprus, and will the Government consider sanctions against Turkey?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Acting Minister of Foreign Affairs): At the
Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in London in June 1977, and at the thirty-
second session of the United Nations General Assembly last year, the New Zealand
Government supported resolutions calling for the withdrawal of all foreign troops from
Cyprus. The Government deplores the armed division of Cyprus. It supports the
Government of Cyprus under President Kyprianou, but does not recognise the Turkish
Federated State of Cyprus. The possibility of sanctions being imposed on Turkey by the
international community to wrest concessions from Turkey on Cyprus has not been formally
proposed. If and when it is, the Government will have to consider the matter in the light of
the position at the time, and in view of the likely prospects of any such actions achieving the
goals they seek..

EMPLOYMENT PROMOTION BILL
Introduction
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Employment
Promotion Bill. It has never been more urgent to take action to combat the scourge of
unemployment. No amount of Government sweet talk can stand up against the cold harsh
reality of the unemployment figures, which are escalating from week to week.
Rising unemployment has run away from any of the feeble attempts of the Government
to contain it. The Government has lost control. The fear of unemployment haunts every
home. New Zealand faces the bleak prospect of up to 70 000 people officially without work
by August or September. The unofficial figures most probably would be about 120 000. The
Government seems helpless and clueless in the face of such impending doom. The Bill is a
sincere attempt to give the Government a positive plan of action that would provide useful,
productive, and meaningful employment to counter the tragic waste of high unemployment.
Thousands and thousands of people are being paid millions of dollars of taxpayers' money to
do nothing.
In south Auckland alone, almost 3000 people are paid the unemployment benefit to the
tune of $3,000 an hour to stay idle. How much would this be for 1 year? It would be much
more beneficial to everyone if the money were used for productive employment in an
enterprise or enterprises in south Auckland. It would reap not only economic benefits, but
untold social benefits as well. This is the motivation behind the Employment Promotion Bill.
The scheme we propose is simple. It involves the establishment of an employment
promotion commission which, after identifying critical problems in unemployment, would
establish special work projects. Unemployed persons would be offered full-time
constructive and, in the case of the young, educative-work on projects selected for their
redeeming value in the region concerned.
A similar approach in the United States of America resulted in the establishment of a
national park system that is the envy of the world today. That is one example of what could
be done here. Others that spring to mind are irrigation projects and harbour development. A
key principle would be that selected projects would be socially valuable and offer genuine
job training and job enrichment. One thing that Labour will not stand for is the demeaning
weed-chipping kind of work that is common under the present scheme. We want to develop
something that New Zealand can look back on with pride, something that a man can show
his kids. How many people now on special work would boast about weed chipping?
The Opposition's scheme will not cost much or add much to the ranks of bureaucracy.
The Bill would empower existing Government departments to work together to implement
the decisions of a 10-man commission drawn largely from employers, unions, and regiona!
government. It has often been said that it is not the job of an Opposition to do the governing,


## p. 1707 (#817) ###########################################

12 July
1707
Employment Promotion Bill
but the position has now deteriorated to such an extent that the Government must swallow
its pride and take heed of sound advice. The Bill would encourage full and meaningful
employment without disrupting existing trade structures. Clause 13 would make it possible
to absorb the massive amount of real unemployment. The criteria in clause 13 for special
work projects would ensure the provision of meaningful and educative work.
Membership of the employment commission, as established under clause 3, would
ensure proper manpower planning-of which the Government has done little. A high-level
inter-departmental committee on manpower planning was set up under the Labour
Government, but abandoned by this Government. Such manpower planning is vital;
otherwise existing trades could be disadvantaged by the sudden injection of fresh skills into
the labour market. At the moment there is a run-down in apprentice intake on the one hand,
and a shortage of skilled trades people on the other. With no trades people to train
apprentices, fewer apprentices can be taken on. This has nothing to do with manpower needs
in the area.
The key to the philosophy behind the Bill is in clause 13. It gives the commission the
power to establish special work projects, which must be designed according to the criteria
laid down in subclause (2). If special work is to be used to fight unemployment, it is
important that such criteria should exist. Otherwise, unemployment becomes simply a
blessing in disguise for factory and farm owners. The subsidised special work that is provided
now is degrading for the workers and represents another invisible public drop for the so-
called private sector.
Considerable opposition has been expressed to the subsidised farm workers scheme. It
has been suggested that many farmers take unfair advantage of it by having working for them
people who are largely paid by the Government. The Minister of Labour knows full well that
that is happening. It should be stopped. The farm workers scheme is at the expense of the
farm cadet scheme. Many farmers are getting workers on the cheap-workers they need not
bother to train, or send away to courses.
In the critical position faced by New Zealand, with the numbers of unemployed rising
every day, with a factory closing here and another closing there, the Labour Party seeks to
assist and encourage the Government to take steps to curb unemployment. The Minister of
Labour should persuade his colleagues that this type of legislation is urgently needed. The
Bill is a call for concerted action on a wide scale in order to curb unemployment and to
involve people with Government departments and regional development by providing for
useful activities in productive employment, and in developing educational skills to improve
efficiency.
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I certainly cannot criticise the genuineness
of the member in trying to assist in a serious and somewhat unique situation—the most
serious unemployment problem we have faced for some time. The member referred to
clause 13, which deals with the mechanics of his proposed scheme, but before I speak of that
I should like to mention some of the quite outrageous claims he made. He had plucked from
somewhere a file that he described as official, which contained a prediction of 70 000
unemployed by August. I should like the next Labour speaker to tell me where that figure
came from. It reminded me of the Leader of the Opposition, who, at the Nelson by-election,
said there would be 200 000 unemployed. Last year the figure suggested was 100 000.
Perhaps the member for Roskill will produce the official record from which the suggested
figure of 70 000 was taken.
The member for Grey Lynn referred to the usefulness and productivity of jobs, and said
that he would not have workers chipping weeds. I am reminded of the time when
unemployment started to grow under the last Labour Government, and we saw a television
programme of people washing windows. That was under the Labour scheme, but at the
moment there are not too many washing windows. The member for Grey Lynn omitted to
mention some basic elements. He suggested that it is merely a matter of the Army providing
the logistics, the Department of Education providing the education, and a commission of 10

COMMUNITY SERVICE BILL
Introduction
Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Community
Service Bill. The first Community Service Bill I drafted was more ambitious than the one I
am now introducing. It provided for compulsory community service for up to 12 weeks on
the basis of part in-service training and part community-based programmes. The aim of that
scheme was threefold: first, to encourage greater respect for the opinions and property of
other people, which would have been achieved by requiring people of similar ages to live and
work together for a reasonably long period; secondly, to provide a work force that would
have been available for community-based projects; and, thirdly, to encourage more and
more young people to continue their association with work of that nature, once they had
completed their compulsory obligation, because of the experience of taking part in
community service programmes and the enjoyment of being involved in that way. Obviously
that scheme would have been expensive to administer and would have required more
facilities for the numbers who would have taken part than we have now.
The Bill I am now introducing is of more modest proportions. It does not provide for
compulsory service, and does not provide for community service workers to be paid.
However, it still preserves the basic objective of encouraging young people to become more
involved in community-based activities. The aim of the scheme is outlined in clause 2(2),
which reads: "This Act shall be read and implemented so as to ensure that the Scheme is
adapted and reviewed from time to time to enable community service workers to acquire and
use skills which are relevant and useful to themselves and their communities, and for this
purpose and to the extent that the law of New Zealand permits, the administration of the
Scheme shall be kept simple and community-orientated."
Clause 3 establishes the community service scheme. The relevant part of the clause
reads as follows: "The Scheme shall consist of classes, lectures, demonstrations, work, and
other programmes designed to provide a community service worker with knowledge,
practical skills, and expertise of use and benefit to himself and his community." The clause
then becomes more specific, and shows that the scheme is in two parts. These are, first,
attendance at classes and lectures to learn such things as civil defence and first aid, and,
secondly, work programmes in hospitals, health centres, charitable institutions for the old,
the infirm, the handicapped, or the disabled, and work for the Crown or for any local
authority or local service agencies, or on land owned by those organisations. There is a
specific prohibition on training in the use of firearms or for any military purpose.
Participation in the scheme is confined to persons aged from 15 to 24, with preference given
to those who apply either while still attending secondary school or within a reasonable time
of completing their secondary education, Clause 8 covers that provision.
The period of community service would be between 100 and 200 hours, with an
obligation on the administering committee to attempt to allow the community service
workers to choose the times when they take part in the scheme. This would allow school
children to be involved during school holidays. Community service workers would not be
paid for the work they do, although on completion of their training they would be entitled to
a tax rebate of from $200 to $400, depending on their length of service. That rebate is
worked out at the rate of $2 for every completed hour, and this provision is contained in
clause 11. As the scheme is to be community-orientated, the Bill provides for community
involvement.
Clause 4 sets up community service committees, which would work under a director of
community service. The committees would consist of three persons-one recommended by
the local authority or authorities in the region, and another representing the local voluntary
service agencies that have indicated their support for the scheme. Committees are to be
bodies corporate, and are to be responsible for implementing, developing, and administering
the scheme in their district. They have the responsibility for appointing community service
workers, giving preference, as I said earlier, to those who have enrolled while still attending
secondary school, or shortly after leaving secondary school. Community service committees


## p. 1715 (#825) ###########################################

12 July
1715
Community Service Bill
also have the power to employ paid supervisors, organisers, and lecturers.
Clause 6 provides for apportionment of costs. Initially the costs of administration would
be paid by the local authority or authorities in the district, and a refund of these costs would
be obtained from central government at the end of the financial year. The costs of a
particular project--for instance expenses incurred for materials, equipment, transport, and,
of course, the wages of any supervisors-would be borne by the person or body for whom
the actual work was done. This provision is contained in clause 6(3). This means that if
community service workers assist with the erection of such projects as the Cust Community
Centre in North Canterbury or the landscaping of the old people's home to be built in
Rangiora, or the painting of a community health centre, the labour content of that work
would be free to the organisation concerned, but it would have to pay for material used and
for the wages of any supervisor. In this way it is hoped that voluntary organisations and
charities will be able to proceed with projects that they cannot afford now because of the cost
of labour.
As I said initially, the scheme is designed to encourage young people to become much
more active and interested in some of the organisations within their local community. It is
designed, not to take young people away from such organisations as Girl Guides, Boy
Scouts, St. John Ambulance, and the like, but to complement the work those bodies are
doing. I also hope that it will encourage young people to become more involved in their
community.

Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa): The Bill is most attractive and compels the attention

awareness, especially in rapid-growth and metropolitan areas, of the need for the community
to come to its own aid-a realisation that community problems are not solved by throwing
money at them. As our metropolitan areas develop in size, complexity, and anonymity, and

their environment. Coincidentally there has been a growth of leisure time and a widening of

neighbourhood, and community have converged, and for that reason the Bill is particularly
apposite and timely. The climate is right.

work can be facilitated and streamlined without in any way intruding on the integrity,
autonomy, and independence of any community voluntary groups or organisations, of which
there are a great many. Opposition members have voiced doubt about whether the Bill gives
sufficient incentive. It gives incentive and encouragement to young people to participate in a
scheme with a tax rebate. It builds on the provisions of this year's Budget. The Bill does not
provide for payment for community social workers, and it should not, because voluntary
contribution is one of the hallmarks of New Zealand society. The member has been very
careful to ensure that that has not been impinged upon. By granting a tax rebate the Bill

apply to all young people. Military service did not encompass all young people, because
about one-third of an annual intake was excluded for medical reasons. The member's
scheme is comprehensive and includes everybody. Our young people, properly motivated,
encouraged, and recognised, have the capacity to make a worth-while contribution to the
community. The Bill introduced by the member for Rangiora motivates, encourages, and
recognises. It deserves bipartisan support, which I am confident it will get. I have much

Mr QUIGLEY (Rangiora): I thank the members who have spoken, particularly the

community service. I envisage that what they would do would be complementary to the work

young age group, would be able to make a contribution. That is all I have time to answer
now. I trust that, on the second reading of the Bill, I shall get a further opportunity to deal
with some of the other matters raised.

## p. 1721 (#831) ###########################################

Electoral Amendment Bill

Mr BEETHAM (Rangitikei): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. First, I
draw to the attention of the House a paraphrase of a quotation from Thomas Mann:
"Politicians are most opposed to some idea when they are not quite certain of their position
with the public and are inwardly tempted from a sense of justice to take the other side." The
Bill I am promoting is concerned with an aspect of electoral reform, and the way in which the
House receives it will be a test of the extent to which democracy applies, or will be applied.
The Bill itself is fairly simple. What I seek is elementary electoral justice—that when
boundaries are extended for different electorates the unofficial component of the
commission that establishes them should not consist exclusively of Labour and National
Party members, but should include members from each political party that received 5
percent or more of the vote at the previous election.
Our electoral system stacks the odds in a wide variety of ways against third and fourth
parties. It also stacks the odds to some extent against the Labour Party, but the Labour Party
has not yet had the mathematical wit to work that out. The National Party and the Labour
Party have said that the Bill is trivial. Well, they can say that, of course, because they are
represented. It is understandable that they would say it. Social Credit and Values are not
represented, and therefore, far from seeing the Bill as trivial, they see it as being very
important. It has been suggested that the Bill came out of the blue. It did nothing of the
kind. Social Credit has been concerned about the matter for a long time, and I believe that I
owe it to the large number of people who have voted for Social Credit over the years, and
more recently for Values, to promote the matter at the earliest opportunity.
I have found it somewhat amusing that on one aspect of electoral matters, namely the
state of the rolls, members on both sides of the House are to a man utterly opposed to each
other, but on another aspect, namely my Bill, both sides of the House are utterly united in
opposition, in preservation of their vested interest in the entrenched status quo. The public
has already seen one display of that union, and will undoubtedly see more displays. I have
been interested to see, on the part of the Labour Party, a display of what could be called
selective democracy. The Labour Party thinks it important to be democratic when the rolls
are under consideration, but not when the drawing of the boundaries is under consideration.
On the introduction of the Bill, allegations were made that gerrymandering would be
encouraged if it were put into effect. All I can say to that is-National and Labour can talk! I
refer members to Hansard of the years 1955 and 1956. There have been several changes in
the membership of the boundaries commission. At present Labour and National have an
unofficial membership, and this was decided by the House on 26 October 1956, the last day
of the 1956 session. The present balanced membership of the Labour and National unofficial
representation arose primarily because of accusations of gerrymandering.
Members of the Labour Opposition might say there is a risk of gerrymandering in the
Bill-in fact, the member for Henderson has already said it—but before pursuing that line
they would be well advised to look at their own past attitudes. The Labour Party accused the
National Party of gerrymandering and manipulating the boundaries to give advantage to
National in the 1954 general election, and the Hansard of that period makes interesting
reading. I refer to Hansard, Volume 305, at page 517, where the Hon. Mr Hanan is reported
as saying: "I refer to the shockingly bad taste of the member for Avon in repeating his
absurd and cruel allegations against the Commission which fixed the boundaries for the last
election." Later he said: "In actual fact, we all know that, on the whole, the changes made in
the boundaries helped the Opposition. For instance, we lost the electorate of Mount Victoria
solely through the boundary changes, and we were undoubtedly prejudiced in many other
electorates.'

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): As I indicated when the Bill was
introduced by the member for Rangitikei, there is little point in it—either in its timing,
because it could not have effect before 1982, 4 years away, or in its merits, which I propose
to discuss. The thrust of the Bill is to provide the minor political parties with membership of
the Representation Commission. Section 15 of the Electoral Act 1956 provides for a
Representation Commission, whose function is to adjust the boundaries of the country's
general electoral districts after each census-that is, every 5 years. This is to ensure
uniformity of numbers in each general electoral district, thus ensuring as far as possible that
each elector's vote carries the same weight, irrespective of the electorate he resides in.
Sir George Grey made the first attempt to establish a representation commission of
sorts when he introduced a Bill into Parliament in 1879. However, his ministry was defeated
12 days later, and his Bill was not proceeded with. Until 1887, Parliament itself dealt with the
thorny problem of the redistribution of electoral boundaries. The obvious difficulties that
such a process entailed for parliamentarians of the day, coupled with demands to ensure
equal representation, led Parliament to establish a representation commission in 1887. As I
understand it, that commission was the first of its type in the world, and was used as a model
by other countries, such as Australia and Britain. Unlike the commissions in other countries,
however, our commission has, since 1887, been charged with adjusting boundaries in
accordance with criteria laid down in the statutes. Other countries have preferred to
constitute their commissions as recommendatory bodies only, leaving it to their Legislatures
to make the final decision.
The first commission comprised five members, two of whom were, in effect, public
servants, with the remaining three appointed as unofficial members on the nomination of the
House of Representatives. Those unofficial members were, as they are today, political
appointees, and were clearly then in the majority. In 1896, the single national commission
was replaced by the North Island Representation Commission and the Middle Island
Representation Commission. As with their forerunner, each commission had five members,
although three were public servants and official members, and two were unofficial members.
Thus, political appointees became minority members of those commissions from 1896
onwards.
This decentralisation into the North Island and the Middle Island was reversed in 1945,
when the two representation commissions were replaced by a single seven-member
commission. Three members were public servants, and four were political appointees. I
suspect that this increase in political appointees was to accommodate the four appointees
then serving on the commissions in the North Island and the Middle Island, or South Island,
as it is now known, rather than any overt move to ensure political domination of the
commission.
In 1956, under the present Act, however, while a seven-member commission was
retained, the emphasis was clearly placed on an impartial commission, comprising four


## p. 1723 (#833) ###########################################

12 July
1723
Electoral Amendment Bill
senior officers of State-public servants-two political appointees, and a chairman
appointed on the recommendation of the commission, usually a magistrate, as he is today.
The Act provides for the political appointees to represent the Government of the day and
the non-Government members of the House-the Opposition. Membership of the
commission was increased to eight in 1975 by the addition of the chairman of the Local
Government Commission as an official, but non-voting, member of the Representation
Commission. This followed the recommendations of the 1975 select committee, which felt
that the chairman of the Local Government Commission should not be a voting member, as
he was a Government appointee. Neither party wished to be seen as obtaining an advantage
in any way in electoral matters by such an appointment.
The present membership of the commission is, therefore, the Surveyor-General, the
Government Statistician, the Chief Electoral Officer, and the Director-General of the Post
Office as official voting members, the chairman of the Local Government Commission as an
official non-voting member, a representative of the Government, a representative of the
Opposition, and one person nominated by members of the commission as chairman. The
balance is, therefore, five voting members as opposed to two political appointees.
I have taken time to trace the development of the commission to show the move away
from any suggestion of political domination of the commission. Quite clearly, the trend since
1896, with the exception of the period from 1945 to 1956, has been for political nominees to
be outnumbered by other members of the commission, and those other members to be
completely objective, detached, and not subject to political pressures.
The proposal by the member for Rangitikei would have the effect of reversing that
trend, and I suggest it is only for political ends. Under his proposal, unofficial members of
the commission would be appointed to represent each political party that receives in total
over the whole country not less than 5 percent of the valid votes cast in the preceding general
election. It is easy to see why the figure of 5 percent was selected as the threshold. At the last
general election, Values received 5.2 percent and Social Credit 7.42 percent of the total valid
votes cast, and accordingly, under this proposal, would have been entitled to a
representative on the commission. The member for Rangitikei made no point of the fact
that, under 5 percent validation for one member, the Labour Party would be entitled to
about seven or eight members, and the National Party to about eight or nine members.
There is no suggestion of fairness from the member for Rangitikei there.
There will be many who may well be initially attracted to this type of proposal on the
basis that what is good enough for the major parties is good enough for the minor political
parties. Leaving aside for a moment the moot point of just what is meant by a
"representative of the Opposition", the danger with the member's proposal is that it is open-
ended. A 5 percent threshold, coupled with any growth in the number of minor political
parties, could lead to the dominance of the commission by political appointees.
Implementation of the proposal for the purposes of the last boundary adjustments would
have resulted in a commission of 10 persons, comprising 4 voting official members-being
senior public servants and therefore objective-4 political appointees, 1 official non-voting
member, and the chairman. Five votes to four does not indicate the impartiality that could
be expected from the present commission of five votes to two.
The Bill introduced by the member representing the Social Credit Political League in
the House raises the twin questions of whether there is a place at all for political
appointments on the commission, and, if so, on what basis they should be made. For 22
years that is, through seven elections-two political appointees only, one from the
Government side and one from the non-Government side of the House of Representatives,
have been considered enough. Most appointees are completely objective and non-political.
In my view, democracy as a result is in the hands of an impartial majority, and the country is
well served by it, as was indicated by the last select committee reporting on the Electoral
Act.

the staff of the New Zealand Railways and the Railways Officers Institute, the two groups
concerned, about replacing the Railways' quinquennial regrading system-which is the
continuous review-and bringing it into line with the system in other departments. The
institute agreed with the proposal, as did Railways management. To do otherwise would
have been to forego the usual quinquennial regrading due in 1976. That was the first reason
the Railways Officers Institute supported the legislation. It could also see the longer-term
advantages. The Post Office and Railways have been out of step with other Government
departments, and the Bill rectifies that for the Railways.
Because of recruitment in the 1940s, Railways management can call on the experience
of many senior people who are due to retire at the same time. The system that has been in
operation to date, and which will be in operation until the Bill is passed, will aggravate the
problems that can be expected in 1981, when retirements will be particularly heavy. The
quinquennial regrading will be held in that year. Those factors would have meant a major
dislocation that will be eased by the progressive regrading after the measure becomes law.
The institute saw the quinquennial review as a chance for the reorganisation of the
Railways. The new system will allow for all positions to be reviewed in isolation, instead of
allowing an overview of the Railways as a trading organisation. The institute believes that
the Bill is the best arrangement that can be made at this time. The same can be said for the
New Zealand Railways, which has been a party to the discussions. It believes the measure to
be a considerable improvement. Since the Bill was initiated by the Labour Government the
Opposition has no scope for argument. The Opposition is pleased that the Bill is before the
House, and the sooner it is implemented the better.

1731
New Zealand Ports Authority Amendment Bill
a second time. The purpose of the Bill is to introduce the amendments arising from the
Government's manifesto undertaking to review the New Zealand Ports Authority Act with a
view to increasing its effectiveness as overseer of harbour planning and port development.
Although the Bill as introduced was drafted following consultation with the Ports Authority,
the Harbours Association, and other interested parties, members will be aware that it has
also been before the Local Bills Committee for recess study. Interested groups have had
every opportunity to make their views known on matters in the Bill, and a number of them
did so. As a result, several amendments to the Bill were recommended at the Local Bills
Committee, and these have been incorporated into the Bill now before the House. I know
most members will share my pleasure in learning that the further revisions made by the
committee after considering submissions had the committee's unanimous support.
The Bill represents the first substantial amendment to the Ports Authority Act since
1968, when the authority was established. Since then the container revolution has brought
dramatic changes to shipping services, and consequently to New Zealand's port facilities.
These changes have re-emphasised the need we face as a community for rationally controlled
port development. The precise degree of control exercised by the Ports Authority over
expenditure on harbour equipment and facilities has been carefully examined by the Local
Bills Committee. Clearly it is crucially important from an overall national viewpoint. The
Bill as amended clarifies this concept, extends the authority's powers in certain areas,
improves the expression of its functions in relation to national ports planning, and also
clarifies aspects of the procedures followed by the authority. It is my view, in short, that the
proposed changes will enable the authority to do a better job.
Much debate has taken place since the inception of the authority over the meaning of
the national ports plan. Indeed, it is true to say that the general concept of planning as an on-
going process of port development in the national interest has come to be better understood
by all those involved, and the Bill represents an endeavour to recognise that change in the
legislation.
Clause 1 is the short title. Clause 2 amends or introduces certain definitions. The main
effect is to establish the meaning of "plan" as a proposal or series of proposals rather than a
single document, in which form, it appears, the national ports plan has previously been
understood. The clause also repeals the present Act's definition of "harbour works" in
section 2, as the definition will now be contained in section 13 as amended by clause 6 of the
Bill. Clause 3 amends section 8 of the principal Act to empower the chairman, a member, or
the chief executive officer of the Ports Authority duly authorised by the chairman, to issue
summonses and undertake any other steps preliminary or incidental to proceedings by the
authority.
Clause 4 basically rewrites section 11. Along with clause 5, this represents the major
area of concern and subsequent revision recommended by the Local Bills Committee.
Clause 4 revises the obligation of the authority to prepare-and I emphasise this—a national
ports plan. Again, the objective is to make it clearer that the plan is to be evolutionary in
nature for the progressive development of ports and harbours. The process of national ports
planning is to be approached by continually developing and keeping such a plan under
review.
Many of the parties making submissions to the committee addressed themselves to the
issue of what is meant by national ports planning. We are bound to listen to the experienced
views of those involved. The clause, as amended, considerably clarifies present thinking and
clearly conveys the idea of a progressive process involving the acceptance of port
development proposals deemed to be in a wider national interest.
Clause 5 entirely replaces section 12 of the principal Act and inserts a new section 12A
dealing with the consultation process to be used by the authority in reaching any decision on
a particular proposal relating to the ports plan. The changes here include a widening of the
authority's powers to enable it to undertake any investigations and consultations it considers
desirable, and to exercise any of its powers under section 15 of the principal Act. A provision
also requires the authority to give public notice of its decision in daily newspapers circulating
in Auckland, Wellington, Christchurch, and Dunedin, and in a daily newspaper circulating
in the area in which the port, in respect of which any decision has been made, is sited. This
provision is an addition to that requiring written copies of decisions on proposals to be sent
to every harbour board and party consulted under subclause (1).
A further change is the requirement that intention to appeal against any decision on a
proposal on the grounds that it is not in the national interest be notifed within 14 days. It is


## p. 1732 (#842) ###########################################

1732
12 July
New Zealand Ports Authority Amendment Bill
important for members to realise that this is not a restriction on rights or on the time allowed
in which to prepare an appeal, but simply a requirement that notification be given of
intention to appeal. Any person who, in the opinion of the Minister, is directly concerned or
who otherwise has a material interest may appeal and have that appeal heard. The Minister
of Transport is then required to give public notice of the time and place for appeals to be
heard so that the last date of publication is not less than 14 days before the date of the
hearing. Following appeals and the adoption of any proposals as part of the national ports
plan by the authority, it shall then submit the proposal to the Minister for approval. Once
approved, the relevant part of the national ports plan shall be published in the Gazette or in
any other manner deemed fit.
The new section 12A provides for variations in the national ports plan to be dealt with in
exactly the same manner. Clause 5 also adds a similar power to section 12 of the principal
Act as already exists in section 13, namely, for the Minister to send any matter appealed
against back to the Ports Authority for reconsideration before an appeal is decided.
Clause 6 also largely replaces section 13, which deals with the control of capital
expenditure. I know that most parties involved will welcome the amendment to the limits on
expenditure made by the Local Bills Committee. The prescribed amount for the Auckland,
Wellington, Lyttelton, and Otago harbour boards has been increased to $500,000. The
thinking here is that the container ports are required to expend considerable sums of money
to provide facilities for container transport. The limits for the Northland, Bay of Plenty,
Gisborne, Hawke's Bay, Marlborough, Nelson, Timaru, and Southland harbour boards and
the Taranaki Harbours Board have likewise been doubled to $300,000. The limits for any
other harbour board have been increased from $50,000 to $100,000, and the amounts that
will apply for parties other than harbour boards are those already increased and prescribed
for the particular port in which a project is undertaken.
The Local Bills Committee recognised that harbour works, whether or not carried out
by a harbour board, still affect the national ports plan and the facilities provided in other
ports. Accordingly, in addition to applying controls to any body or persons incurring
expenditure within harbours, this clause as amended also provides for an extension of Ports
Authority control to expenditure on works carried out in inland container terminals and to
harbour works outside all existing harbour limits. Control is now to be applied to all
expenditure above the newly prescribed limits, and no longer merely to expenditure of
borrowed money.
A further provision in this clause will enable the Ports Authority to control the use of
designated items of equipment within harbour or wharf limits, or inland container terminals.
The authority may designate such items by notice in the Gazette when it is satisfied that the
item is intended primarily for such use, that the nature of the item exceeds the amount
prescribed for that port, and that its use would have significant consequences for the national
ports plan. The items of equipment envisaged for designation include wharfside cranes,
transtainer cranes, straddle carriers, bulk cargo handling plant, and linkspans. It is certainly
not intended that the provision should cover items that cost less. Indeed, the wording of
clause 6 makes it quite clear that, unless all the criteria are met, the item cannot be
designated by the Ports Authority. To reiterate, the criteria are: first, that the equipment is
intended primarily for use within wharf or inland container terminal limits; secondly, that
the value is more than the prescribed amount; and, thirdly, that the use of the item will have
significant consequences for the national ports plan.
A further amendment aligns the time limit for filing notice of intention to appeal with
that in section 12 of the principal Act. Members should note that during the Committee stage
I intend to introduce by way of a Supplementary Order Paper a consequential amendment
that will ensure that the Ports Authority's controls under section 13(7) and section 20B are
able to be exercised over harbour works, container works, and designated items of
equipment.
During the Committee stage members will observe that clause 7 has been rewritten.
There was never any doubt about the intentions of clause 7-and I refer to the remarks I
made when introducing the Bill. At that time I said that the provision was designed to
provide a check on leases for berths or back-up areas to ensure that sole-user rights do not
preclude a potential user from taking advantage of underutilised facilities. Those people
making submissions on the clause had no quarrel with the principle as enunciated in those
comments. However, they pointed out that the clause went much further than this principle.
Consequently, it has been redrafted, and now reflects the original intention. In examining


## p. 1733 (#843) ###########################################

New Zealand Ports Authority Amendment Bill
lease agreements the authority's sole regard shall be the desirability of ensuring that
underutilised areas are available to persons seeking to use them.
Finally, subclause 7(a) has been introduced into the Bill to enable the Minister to extend
the time limit for bringing an appeal should he consider it just to do so. This will enable any
particular circumstance, such as a Ports Authority decision immediately prior to the
Christmas break, to be provided for.
The amendments I have outlined will provide for a greater flexibility in port planning
and development. They also underline the way. in which the Government considers that
national ports planning should be seen to work. The Bill considerably improves the manner
in which the authority will be able to approach its important task of co-ordinating and
rationalising port and harbour development. I thank the members who served on the
committee, who gave so much time to it, and went through the Bill so thoroughly. I am sure
that the previous Minister would agree with me that the only disappointment I have is that,
after all the criticism, no one, during deliberations, could come up with an appeal authority
that was acceptable and workable. It still remains in the hands of the Minister of Transport,
whoever he may be; and I know that my predecessor will agree that that is a very difficult
task. Nevertheless, the Bill does not alter it, and it still has to be considered.

Dr WALL (Porirua): I was present at all the committee meetings when the Bill was
considered. This is one of those difficult problems in political and administrative life, when
machinery that has been set up after much discussion is unable to function effectively
because of rapidly changing technology. No members will dispute that. However, because
we are dealing with a situation that runs across the whole political spectrum and confuses any
political approach to it, does not mean there has not been a difference of emphasis and
approach by both sides of the House. Both sides of the House agree that, for the economic
development of New Zealand, there must be an overall comprehensive development of our
ports.
We have lived through the stage when New Zealand seemed about to be held to ransom
by overseas shipping interests. Many members will recall the time when container shipping
was just something in the future. New Zealand was being sold the idea that the only way for
it to go was to establish a single container port as close as possible to overseas markets, and
Whangarei was widely canvassed as that port. Much money was spent, many glossy
brochures were brought out, and a lot of propaganda was carried out to support that idea.
Fortunately for New Zealand, parochial, petty, local interests overcame that, because it was
not widely canvassed then that what was being promoted would be entirely to the advantage
of the major shipping interests. It was very much to their advantage to be able to load the
containers on their ships in any order they chose, to carry them to one port, and to dump
them off in any order they chose. That was the end of their responsibility. Their ships could
leave quickly and carry out the more efficient and profitable part of their enterprise.
Parochial interests broke that down, and it was insisted that there should be two or three
container ports.
Since then, the overall dominance of the Conference Lines has been challenged, in
some ways successfully, and by other shippers who are prepared to serve our ports. With the
appearance of these other shippers, there is now a wide diversity of technology. The
significance of that on the legislation, promoted by both sides of the House, has been
profound. Arguments have gone on in this city, and are still going on further south, about
whether a particular type of crane for lifting containers off ships should be allowed to be
purchased at a considerable capital outlay by a harbour board. That is still a hot political
issue, but it has become outdated.

NEW ZEALAND NATIONAL AIRWAYS CORPORATION DISSOLUTION BILL
Second Reading
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. As I explained during the introduction, the basic aim of the Bill is to give
effect to the Government's decision to amalgamate the National Airways Corporation and
Air New Zealand. The Bill has two purposes: first, to remove all doubt as to the validity of
some of the steps taken to date to effect an amalgamation of the two airlines; and, secondly,
to dissolve the corporation and transfer its assets and liabilities to Air New Zealand when the
time is appropriate.
On the introduction of the Bill I gave members a short outline of the scope of the
legislation. Today I shall explain each clause in more detail, but before I do I should like to
take the time to comment on why we have the Bill before the House. In March this year I
released a detailed statement on the airline amalgamation. In that statement I explained the
background to the Government's decision, and I summarised the basis upon which the
decision had been taken. I can do no better, in explaining why we have the Bill before the
House tonight, than to go over some of the ground covered in that statement.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: When are you going to release the report?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: There is no need for me to read it to the Opposition,
because the member for Timaru says he has already read it. I shall not waste time reading it
again, although he always needs to have things read about 10 times before he understands
them. We have a New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill because the
Government has decided that there will be substantial benefits to the nation and to the
public in combining the country's two main airline operations. The decision was taken and
the conclusion was reached after the Government had considered the detailed reports put
before it by the specialist and expert committees set up to investigate first the feasibility of an
amalgamation between the airlines, and secondly to establish whether an amalgamation


## p. 1742 (#852) ###########################################

1742
New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill
12 July
would substantially improve the service to the public and efficiency in the use of resources.
It is worth going back to the beginning of that exercise so that members are aware of the
background to the merger. The Government was elected in 1975 on a transport platform that
promised to co-ordinate all transport services and equipment to obtain full use so that the
best result for the consumer could be obtained.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: It stacked up secret reports'
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: This principle has guided our thinking on transport policy
throughout our term in office, and it is this thinking that gave rise to the initiative that in turn
resulted in the merger of the airlines. My reading of all the current information available on
the question of an airline amalgamation indicated clearly that it was well worth opening the
issues again in the light of changing circumstances. There had always been evidence to show
that there was a sufficiently high degree of commonality between the airlines to warrant the
closest co-operation at the very least. The Government recognised, however, that the time
could be right to move a step beyond simply encouraging such co-operation.
On 13 September 1977 I announced that the Secretary for Transport would be directed
to bring down a report on the feasibility of joining the two airlines. The report was to isolate
the advantages that were likely if an amalgamation were to proceed, and at the same time to
identify what disadvantages might be involved-essentially to subject the matter to a cost-
benefit study. When we announced that the study would go ahead we undertook to ensure
that those most intimately affected by an amalgamation would be consulted—and they were.
This was achieved by forming a steering committee, chaired by the Secretary for Transport,
and comprising senior management personnel from both airlines, as well as senior ministry
personnel.
Specialist subcommittees were also set up to examine particular areas of each airline's
administration and organisation. The investigations were carried out in a confidential
atmosphere. The member for Timaru burbles on about secret reports. He was a Minister of
the Crown, and he knows that, in a merger such as this, a Minister has a duty to obtain
information, and if the information is confidential it must remain confidential. But
permanent heads-and others who might be involved if we have the unfortunate disaster of
another Labour Government-will now know that it will be the policy of Labour Ministers
to table the reports they receive.
As I have explained on many occasions, this was absolutely essential if we were to have
a frank and penetrating investigation. Early in December last year the steering committee
produced a bulky and very detailed report. The Secretary for Transport also reported
separately to the Government, as he was required to do under his directive. On the basis of
the evidence presented by the steering committee and of the conclusions and
recommendations drawn by the Secretary for Transport, the Government announced on 19
December that a merger would proceed. The Government announced that the investigations
had pointed to a quantifiable net financial benefit through a full amalgamation of the order
of $10 million annually in the longer term. The figure in the reports is actually $10,365,000,
and it is said to be “conservative and reasonable”. This financial benefit would be achieved
not only through actual savings in capital expenditure on facilities that, without a merger,
would have duplicated plant and equipment, but also would flow from the stronger
commercial basis on which a combined operation would work.
Those who have read their newspapers in the last week or two will realise that that is a
fact with the competition that is about to eventuate, especially in international travel.
Through attrition, a rationalisation of staff numbers in the longer term would be possible.
Less directly quantifiable benefits were identified in terms of the service of a new and larger
airline could offer to the travelling public, and in terms of the enhanced opportunities
available for staff. As I said in March, in cost-benefit terms there was no doubt in the
Government's mind that the time was ripe for an amalgamation of the airlines; on balance,
the vast benefits far outweighed any inevitable minor short-term costs. So much for the steps
leading up to the Government's decision.
I shall now briefly cover the reasons for the amalgamation. Many people have wanted to
know where the financial benefits of the merger are to come from. Time prevents me from
describing all these areas in detail, but I refer those who are interested to a copy of a
statement released in March that clearly and specifically sets out the areas of financial
benefit. On this occasion I want to talk in general terms about the reasons for the
amalgamation. Since 1964, when Barr, Burgess and Stewart investigated the case for an
amalgamation between the airlines, efforts have been made to encourage them to work more


## p. 1743 (#853) ###########################################

12 July
1743
New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill
closely together in areas where mutual benefits would result.
It was pointed out in the reports put before the Government in December last year that,
by and large, most of those attempts had failed to produce the full benefits possible, and that
experience had shown that, without a common direction, such attempts are unlikely to
succeed fully. It would seem that, as a matter of principle, two separate commercialy based
organisations will always continue to order their commercial priorities to their own
individual advantage-which is to be expected. Separate commercial direction was the
largest single impediment to fully effective collaboration between National Airways and Air
New Zealand. A nation of New Zealand's size and population cannot afford the luxury of
such separate development between the two major sectors of its airline industry.
Furthermore, it is in the interests of the public and the country as a whole that New
Zealand's public investment in the airline industry, whether domestic or international, is
sound, and that the Government's airline or airlines are strong financial units. That is in
everybody's interests-the Government, and the public, the travellers, and the staff of both
airlines.
It is no secret that Air New Zealand finds itself facing aggressive competition, including
that from new international operators. Air New Zealand, in the national interest, must meet
the situation by, amongst other things, consolidating its marketing strength. It is the
Government's view that a single airline comprising both domestic and international arms will
constitute a stronger financial unit, with the capability to withstand fluctuations in both the
domestic and the international markets. Against this background, and with evidence that
showed, first, that the advantages of an amalgamation far outweighed the inevitable minor
short-term costs and, secondly, that a conservative and reasonable estimate of actual
financial benefit exceeded $10 million a year in the longer term, made it sound logical sense
to amalgamate the airlines. So much for the reasons for the amalgamation.
I want now to comment on the timing of this legislation and on its retrospective clauses.
At the first reading stage I said, "The Ministry of Transport and both airlines were
unanimous in strongly advising against any delays in giving effect to a decision to
amalgamate the airlines because of the effects of delay on the morale of the airlines' 8600
staff. For that reason an early date had to be chosen."
Mr Rogers: Release the report.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Sometimes I wish the member for Onehunga would
release himself and stop yapping. I also said that some people have expressed an opinion on
the validity of some of the steps taken to effect the merger. It is not uncommon that legal
opinion can differ over an interpretation of the law. On the one hand, some legal opinion has
debated the validity of some of the steps so far taken, but, on the other hand, some legal
opinion has claimed that there is no doubt that the steps are valid. I am satisfied that a sound
and sustainable legal case can be mounted to prove the validity of those steps, but to allow
even a shadow of doubt to remain in the mind of one person would be irresponsible.
Debate on the validity of the steps taken to give effect to the merger is, in my view,
damaging to staff morale in the new airline. It is important that the legislation necessary to
give full effect to the merger-and there was never any doubt that some legislation would be
necessary-should place beyond doubt the validity of the steps taken to prepare for the
merger on 1 April.
It has taken me some time to come to a discussion of the actual content of the Bill. I felt
that it was important, however, to preface my discussion of the clauses of the Bill with a
more general comment, especially on the second reading. It is a short Bill, but an extremely
important one. It is short because it is largely procedural, but it is important because it gives
effect to one of the most dramatic and far-reaching moves in New Zealand's aviation history.
The Bill contains only 5 clauses. Clause 1 deals with the short title and the dates of
commencement. Members will note that clauses 2, 3, and 5 are deemed to commence on 1
March 1978, and that clause 4, which deals with the actual dissolution of NAC, is deemed to
commence at a date to be fixed by Order in Council. As I have explained earlier, the reason
for the commencement date being set at 1 March 1978 for clauses 2, 3, and 5 is to place
beyond doubt the validity of the preparatory steps towards the amalgamation, taken after
the Government's decision was announced.
The reason for the commencement date for clause 4 is simply that the corporation must
continue as a legal entity, at least until consent it obtained to the assignment to Air New
Zealand of certain contracts that are governed by foreign law, and which cannot be effected
by an Act of the New Zealand Parliament. As I explained in the first reading, it is only a


## p. 1744 (#854) ###########################################

1744
12 July
New Zealand National Airways Corporation Dissolution Bill
matter of time before the formalities are completed. Although only a few consents remain
outstanding, it is not possible to predict exactly when all the formalities will be completed.
Clause 2 simply defines "Air New Zealand Ltd." and the "Corporation", and requires
no further elaboration. Clause 3 deals with the transfer of air service licences, held by NAC,
to Air New Zealand. The clause provides that Air New Zealand may maintain and operate
domestic air services previously run by NAC, and placed beyond doubt the validity of the
transfer of the licences, which took effect on 1 April 1978.
Clause 4, as I mentioned earlier, deals with the dissolution of the National Airways
Corporation. Under this clause, the corporation is dissolved. Its assets and liabilities,
including its tax losses, are transferred to Air New Zealand, and its employees are deemed to
become employees of Air New Zealand on the same terms and conditions of employment.
The clause also provides for the repeal of the New Zealand National Airways Act 1945, its
amendments and associated regulations, and its bylaws approval order. Clause 5 makes it
clear that Part III of the Commerce Act 1975 does not apply to the airline merger.
Mr Rogers: That's right.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: My word, the member for Onehunga has woken up
again. I did not hear whether he said "Haw haw", or "Hee haw" Part III of the Commerce
Act deals with monopolies, mergers, and takeovers, and requires the Examiner of Trade
Practices to be notified by a party to a business merger or takeover. NAC consulted with the
Department of Trade and Industry to find out whether the airline merger was of the type
required to be notified. While the department and the Examiner of Trade Practices
confirmed that, in their view, Part III of the Act does not apply, this clause placed the matter
beyond doubt. I do not intend to delay the House any longer.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): The New Zealand National Airways Corporation
Dissolution Bill could better be termed the "NAC Destruction Bill". It deals with a merger
between Air New Zealand and NAC, but from the commencement of discussions it was
obvious that the fate of NAC-proudly known to all New Zealanders as the "wings of the
nation" had been sold out. Senior executives of Air New Zealand, led by its general
manager, had convinced the Prime Minister and the Minister of Transport that the airlines
should become one.
I do not believe that suggestions put forward by NAC to the committee established
under the chairmanship of the Secretary for Transport were given proper and adequate
consideration. NAC fought a rearguard action for survival. I remind the Minister that I have
read a report that he should have released. I accept the Minister's word that only the Prime
Minister and he know what it contains, and that no other Government member has read it. I
have read it.
An Hon. Member: Who gave it to you?
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: I have no intention of saying who gave the report to me,
but
it should have been made public. I have seen nothing in that report to substantiate the
amount of $10 million again quoted by the Minister tonight as being the saving in one year
through the merger, as he calls it. I maintain it is a takeover. Although the amount of $10
million is not in the report, much valuable evidence was given to the committee by
representatives of NAC. As I said earlier, they fought a rearguard action for survival, but
they knew the cards were stacked against them. Executives of NAC, led by the former
general manager, Mr Doug Patterson, presented some very worthwhile suggestions. I know
that he is now a member of the board of Air New Zealand, and so he should be. He has
certainly earned that position by serving aviation in this country and elsewhere. Let no one
cast aspersions upon him for the service he has given to this country; the people of New
Zealand know better than that. It has been argued that a closer relationship was desirable
between international and domestic air services and that something short of a complete
takeover or merger was desirable. That came out in the report that I have read. It was
mentioned in the committee, and it is revealed in the secret report that the Prime Minister,
the Minister, and others have claimed fully justifies the merger. It is like a whitewash with
invisible ink.
People are told that the conclusions indicated overwhelmingly that there should be one
airline, but they cannot see the report. They are told that the decision was unanimous and
clearcut but must take the Minister's word for it. NAC knew that Barr, Burgess, and Stewart
had published a report in the mid-1960s. That report did not indicate any preconceived
objectives or decided course of action, but it recommended that there should be independent
international and domestic air services in New Zealand. What has changed in the intervening

period? Nothing emerged from the report that I read.
Hon. C. C. A. McLachlan: How many pages?
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR" It had 40 foolscap pages.
Hon. C. C. A. McLachlan: It was not the report.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: The report the Minister is speaking about had 110 pages, as

for all the opposition and the problems that face the Government and the Minister is their

The Government has not recognised the public's right to be told about a decision
affecting two publicly owned airlines. Not one shred of evidence has been made public. In its
report, NAC said that it believed the domestic air services were best served by an
organisation dedicated to that purpose. However, NAC did recognise that a common service
had some advantages. I shall detail areas in which there could be advantages, and then the
Minister can tell me whether I have read the report. It was recognised that there could be
advantages in common data processing, reservations, and printing facilities, as well as
personnel. However, NAC suggested that each airline should retain its identity, but come
under the control of a New Zealand Airlines Commission. The corporation said it was
prepared to look constructively at the merger proposal if it could be shown to be in New
